- A quotient with order divisible by Δ must not be excluded merely by the prime-to-Δ group supplier.

- Only the chosen sqrt(t) completion is in the imaginary function-field family, not every nonsplit completion.

- A split-infinity real field has no canonical outside inertia involution; its rigid data include a twist y.


### 0.20 Exact quadratic function-field slices


<a id="imaginary-exact-slice-parametrization"></a>


**Imaginary exact slice parametrization.** Let q be odd and n ≥ 1. The quadratic extensions K of F_q(t) whose completion at ∞ is F_q((t^{−1}))(√(t)) (Wood's imaginary infinity type) and whose discriminant has norm q^{2n} (Wood's slice IQ_{=q^{2n}}) are exactly the fields F_q(t)(√f) for f monic squarefree of degree 2n − 1, each obtained from exactly one f. Consequently #IQ_{=q^{2n}} = q^{2n−1} − q^{2n−2} for n ≥ 2 and = q for n = 1.

Throughout this assertion, q odd n ≥ 1 Wood's imaginary infinity type fixes the square class of the leading coefficient (the completion at ∞ is the one generated by √t)


To prove the assertion, A quadratic extension of F_q(t) is F_q(t)(√f) with f ∈ F_q[t] squarefree, unique up to (F_q^×)² ([odd degree quadratic function field family](#odd-degree-quadratic-function-field-family)). The place ∞ ramifies iff deg f is odd; for odd deg f the completion at ∞ is F_q((t^{−1}))(√(a t)) with a the leading coefficient, and it equals the prescribed one iff a is a square; choosing the square-class representative with a = 1 gives a unique monic f. The discriminant divisor is the zero divisor of f plus the ramified place ∞, of degree deg f + 1, so norm q^{2n} ⇔ deg f = 2n − 1. The count is [count of squarefree monic polynomials over a finite field](#count-of-squarefree-monic-polynomials-over-a-finite-field) in degree 2n − 1.

*Needs:* [odd degree quadratic function field family](#odd-degree-quadratic-function-field-family), [count of squarefree monic polynomials over a finite field](#count-of-squarefree-monic-polynomials-over-a-finite-field), [wood infinity and type adapter](#wood-infinity-and-type-adapter).

([[50]](#ref-50), Proof of Theorem 4.8, p.24 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.408).)


**Checks.**


- n = 1: IQ_{=q²} consists of the q fields F_q(t)(√(t − c)), c ∈ F_q.

- The other ramified square class at ∞ (leading coefficient a nonsquare) is excluded from IQ; it belongs to neither IQ nor RQ (Wood §2 p.5).


<a id="real-exact-slice-parametrization"></a>


**Real exact slice parametrization.** Let q be odd and n ≥ 1. The quadratic extensions K of F_q(t) split completely at ∞ and with discriminant of norm q^{2n} (Wood's slice RQ_{=q^{2n}}) are exactly the fields F_q(t)(√f) for f monic squarefree of degree 2n, each from exactly one f. Hence #RQ_{=q^{2n}} = q^{2n} − q^{2n−1}. The place ∞ contributes nothing to the discriminant.

Throughout this assertion, q odd n ≥ 1


To prove the assertion, ∞ splits in F_q(t)(√f) iff deg f is even and the leading coefficient is a square in F_q; normalise it to 1. ∞ is then unramified, so the discriminant divisor is the zero divisor of f, of degree deg f; norm q^{2n} ⇔ deg f = 2n. Count by [count of squarefree monic polynomials over a finite field](#count-of-squarefree-monic-polynomials-over-a-finite-field) in degree 2n ≥ 2.

*Needs:* [odd degree quadratic function field family](#odd-degree-quadratic-function-field-family), [count of squarefree monic polynomials over a finite field](#count-of-squarefree-monic-polynomials-over-a-finite-field), [wood infinity and type adapter](#wood-infinity-and-type-adapter).

([[50]](#ref-50), Proof of Theorem 4.8, real case, p.25 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.410).)


**Checks.**


- n = 1: q² − q fields.

- The discriminant exponent is Σ n_i = 2n, not Σ n_i + 1.


### 0.21 Embedded types and infinity markings


<a id="wood-average-normalizations"></a>


**Wood average normalizations.** Use the discriminant family, restricting its base to the prescribed imaginary or real infinity type. The imaginary rigid numerator sums type-H continuous surjections; the real numerator sums type-H pairs (ρ,y). Divide both by the number of quadratic base fields in the same carrier. Over Q use |Disc(K)|≤X for a height average; over F_q(t) use exact |Disc(K)|=q^(2n) slices when applying Layer 5’s parametrizations. A genuinely empty slice is assigned zero at the finite level; a claimed limiting statement must specify a sequence of inhabited slices. For fixed unmarked extensions the imaginary multiplicity is |Aut_H(G)|; in the good real case it is |c(H)|·|Aut_H(G)|.


To prove the assertion, Restrict the base carrier, then use the weighted count with the exact rigid fiber count as weight. Kernel fibers give the imaginary torsor factor. For real good H, Wood Lemma 2.1 conjugates twists inside the top kernel and counts c(H) choices, each with the same type-preserving automorphism fiber. Do not identify exact and cumulative slices. The function-field imaginary monic family is one leading-coefficient squareclass, not all odd-degree squarefree equations.

<a id="wood-root-unity-and-tame-comparison"></a>


**Wood root unity and tame comparison.** Wood’s correction is the |μ_K|-torsion subgroup of the reduced multiplier H₂(H,c), where μ_K is the roots-of-unity group of the base global field K. Over Q use 2; over F_q(t) use q−1. Use InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.3 for the reduced multiplier and IG.4 for the global lifting invariant. Restricting the quadratic base to the tame subfamily changes the denominator too. Moment counts refined by invariant value partition the rigid numerator; summing them does not by itself prove the arithmetic distribution law.

Throughout this assertion, Tame ramification and the lifting invariant’s hypotheses remain those of its owner.

### 0.22 Symmetric pencils and Jacobian torsors


<a id="refinement-symmetric-pencil"></a>


**Symmetric pencil.** Let Wₙ(R) be pairs (A,B) of symmetric n×n matrices over a commutative ring. Define f_A,B(x,y)=(−1)^{n(n−1)/2}det(xA−yB), represented by coefficients f_i of x^{n−i}y^i. SLₙ acts by simultaneous congruence. For even n the scalar μ₂ acts trivially, giving a group-scheme action of SLₙ/μ₂. Its R-points generally exceed SLₙ(R)/μ₂(R). Over C the invariant ring of SLₙ is the polynomial ring in the n+1 determinant coefficients.

Throughout this assertion, No halving of off-diagonal entries: these are bilinear Gram matrices. Arithmetic solubility later requires a field of characteristic not2 and nonzero discriminant.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencilInvariant`: For any two n×n matrices, return the n+1 coefficients of the signed determinant; restrict to symmetric matrices for Wₙ.

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencilInvariant_congr`: Replacing A,B by gAgᵀ,gBgᵀ multiplies every coefficient by det(g)².

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.pencilInvariant_scalar`: For A=aIₙ and B=bIₙ the invariant is (−1)^{n(n−1)/2}(ax−by)ⁿ.


To prove the assertion, Expand the determinant universally, checking homogeneity. Congruence multiplies the invariant by det(g)². The two scalar factors cancel for the μ₂ action. The invariant-ring theorem is used over C as in the source; an integral invariant-ring theorem is not inferred from it.

*Needs:* `Matrix.IsSymm` (Mathlib), `Matrix.det` (Mathlib).

<a id="refinement-binary-discriminant"></a>


**Binary discriminant.** Use the fixed-degree universal binary discriminant Δ_n of [binary discriminant](#binary-discriminant). For n≥2, identify it with the signed universal resultant quotient Res(F,F′)/a₀, where the universal divisibility is established before specializing a₀. At degree 3 it agrees with the binary-cubic discriminant, at degree 4 with Layer 0’s quartic invariant discriminant. The later refinement-binary-form-order target supplies the trace-discriminant equality for its associated rank-n order, using this normalization. Leading-zero specializations use Δ_n, not the lower-degree affine discriminant. ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.binaryDiscriminant is the evaluation interface for the same Layer 0 polynomial, not a second construction.

Throughout this assertion, The homogeneous degree n is fixed even when the dehomogenized polynomial drops degree.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:

The D-lattice R_f=⟨1,ζ₁,…,ζ_{n−1}⟩ is a ring. For 0≤k≤n−1, I_f(k)=⟨1,θ,…,θᵏ,ζ_{k+1},…,ζ_{n−1}⟩ is an R_f-stable full lattice. Disc R_f=Δ(f), and f′(θ)^{-1}I_f(n−2) is its trace dual. ### 0.23 Coefficient boxes and local discriminants


<a id="stickelberger-binary"></a>


**Stickelberger binary.** For every integral binary n-ic form with n≥2, Δ_n is congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 4. In particular 2|Δ_n implies 4|Δ_n, so weak square divisibility at 2 is empty. The theorem includes leading-zero forms.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST0.binary_no_weak_two`: The binary weak 2²-locus is empty.


To prove the assertion, Use the Layer 1 discriminant-preserving rank-n ring of a binary form. The integral trace Gram matrix of a based ring has determinant congruent to a square modulo 4 (Stickelberger); alternatively establish the universal binary polynomial congruence before specialization. Deduce invariance for all coefficient vectors congruent modulo 2.

([[59]](#ref-59), §1 p.2 and Appendix A p.54.)

<a id="monic-density-formulas"></a>


**Monic density formulas.** For prime p, ν₀(0,p)=ν₀(1,p)=1 and ν₀(n,p)=1−1/p for n≥2. At p=2, ν₁(n,2)=0. For odd p, ν₁(0,p)=ν₁(1,p)=0, ν₁(2,p)=p^−1(1−p^−1), and for n≥3, ν₁(n,p)=(1−p^−1)²(1−(−p)^(2−n))/(p+1). Thus λ_n(p)=ν₀+ν₁ equals 1 for n≤1, 1/2 at p=2,n≥2, 1−1/p² for n=2, odd p, and 1−[3p^(n−1)−p^(n−2)+(−1)^n(p−1)²]/[p^n(p+1)] for n≥3, odd p. The exponent 2−n is essential.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST0.nuOneFormula`: The corrected valuation-one closed formula.

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST0.monic_nu_one`: The finite count equals the corrected formula.


To prove the assertion, Squarefree residue polynomials give generating series (1−t²/p)/(1−t). A single repeated linear factor, a squarefree complementary factor avoiding it, and a nonvanishing first-order lift give H(t)=(p−1)t²/p² · (1−t²/p)/((1−t)(1+t/p)). Extract coefficients; this yields exponent 2−n, also at n=3. Combine the two strata algebraically.

### 0.24 Monic local Euler factors


<a id="monic-euler-products"></a>


**Monic euler products.** For n≥2 set λ_n=product over all primes of λ_n(p), with λ_n(p)=ν₀(n,p)+ν₁(n,p). The product converges to a strictly positive real number because its factors are positive and 1−λ_n(p)=O_n(p^−2). As n→∞ it tends to (1/2) times the product over odd primes of [1−(3p−1)/(p²(p+1))]. For degree two λ₂=4/π². These are local Euler constants; identifying them with global family densities still requires the infinite-prime tail theorem in Layer 2.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST0.monicEulerProduct`: The product over prime local factors.

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST0.monicEulerProduct_pos`: The degree-n product is strictly positive.

- `ArithmeticStatistics.ST0.monicEulerProduct_limit`: The products tend to the limiting odd-prime product.


To prove the assertion, Separate the factor at 2. Bound the defect at odd p by a summable constant times p^−2 uniformly for n≥2. Establish nonzero convergence from positivity and the defect bound. Pointwise convergence plus the uniform product tail permits exchanging the degree limit and the product.

*Needs:* [monic density formulas](#monic-density-formulas).

([[58]](#ref-58), §1 pp.1–2, constants λ_n and limiting λ.)

- The corrected monic quartic factor at 3 is 62/81.

- The quadratic global local-product constant is 4/π².


### Supporting constructions

<a id="support-squareclasses"></a>

For the number-field squareclass height, prove the finite-fibre description over a squarefree support ideal using `Cl(F)[2]`, units modulo squares and the prescribed archimedean signs. In each nonempty finite local rectangle prove `#Σ(H<X)=c_Σ X+o(X)` with `c_Σ>0`, counting each squareclass once. Representatives are chosen by finitely many ideal classes and a unit fundamental domain; the nonarchimedean local measure is the pullback of additive Haar on integral representatives. An arbitrary union of coupled residue conditions is decomposed into disjoint rectangles before averaging. The zero-mass and empty cases remain separate. The required reference is BKLOS, Theorems 2.1 and 7.2, §§7–8; the ideal-counting and unit-domain steps use the native class-field and number-field contracts. Prove the Möbius/CRT squarefree density first for a finite modulus, with an error uniform enough for this passage; over Q the six squarefree residues modulo eight have equal relative mass `1/6`.

<a id="support-abelian-counts"></a>

For finite-field abelian counts, establish the following specialization on the imported isogeny and polarization carriers. Honda–Tate identifies simple isogeny classes with Weil q-numbers and specifies their endomorphism division algebras, local invariants and dimension. The isogeny category decomposes up to isogeny into its simple factors, while the integral isomorphism classes inside an isogeny class require order/lattice data and finite class sets. Lang's theorem gives `H¹(F_q,A)=0` for a connected abelian variety. For fixed dimension and q, prove finiteness of unpolarized classes and of principal-polarization orbits; retain `#pol(A)` when changing the probability denominator. These are the counting inputs of Lipnowski–Tsimerman, §§3–5, pp. 8–27, especially Proposition 4.11 and Lemma 5.11. The Rosati orbit identification itself is supplied by A6. The estimates for the number and sizes of these fibres belong to the concentration argument in Layer 5.

<a id="support-function-fields"></a>

For an odd-characteristic function field `F_q(C)`, relate rational divisor classes, ideal classes after removing infinity, and `J(F_q)` by the degree exact sequence, retaining the degrees of the removed places. A rational relative Picard point descends to a line bundle over a finite field because the Brauer obstruction vanishes. Use the norm/pushforward on divisors and the Frobenius action on the unramified fundamental group to obtain the split-infinity class-field quotient. For a quadratic hyperelliptic model distinguish ramified infinity, split infinity and nonsplit infinity. The real exact slice counts the split case and its marked points, not all even-degree equations. Sources are EVW, §8, pp. 776–782, and Wood, §§2–4, pp. 4–25 in arXiv:1702.04644v2. The Picard/Brauer machinery comes from SF.3; the field and infinity specialization is proved here.

The hypersurface adapter identifies degree-d homogeneous forms with the native monomial-indexed coefficient space of rank `binomial(n+d,d)` using the Veronese monomials, not an arbitrary enumeration with a hidden degree shift. For the local statistic `σ(a;Q)=Q^(-n)# {primitive x mod Q:f_a(x)=0}`, prove residue dependence, CRT multiplicativity for coprime positive moduli and the normalization at Q=1. It is an intensity, not necessarily a probability. These are the interfaces used by the later incidence and variance calculations (Le Boudec, §2, and Poonen–Voloch, §§2–3).

### Examples

For integers of height absolute value, the inclusive count at three is seven and the strict count is five. The height on a rational coefficient line is not Northcott without a denominator restriction: infinitely many rationals lie in `[0,1]`.

The coefficient reversal sends `x⁴-y⁴` to `y⁴-x⁴`, preserves I and Δ, and changes the sign of J only as dictated by degree six; here J is zero. In contrast a scalar substitution multiplies the ordinary invariants by powers eight and twelve. A scalar matrix acts trivially for the determinant-to-the-minus-two action. The pair `(I,J)=(-12,0)` has `27Δ=-6912=4(-12)³`, fixing the discriminant convention.

At degree zero the monic polynomial is one, with discriminant one; a strict weighted box at a positive bound has one empty vector. Over F_q the squarefree monic counts begin `1,q,q²-q`, so the formula `q^n-q^(n-1)` is restricted to `n≥2`. The odd quadratic exact slice at its smallest degree has q monic polynomials, not `q-1`.

### Dependencies

Mathlib's finite counts, polynomial invariants, p-adic measures and number-field finiteness; Tau Ceti's Northcott/summatory interface; EllipticCurves Layers 5 and 8; GlobalNumberFields and ClassFieldTheory; PolynomialGaloisGroups; SF.0–SF.3; GN.0; A2, A3 and A6; and the embedded arithmetic marking contracts IG.3–IG.5. All local coefficient and exact-slice definitions needed later are constructed in this layer.


## Layer 1: Integral orbit dictionaries

The arithmetic dictionaries retain integral bases, orientations, resolvent data and group-scheme stabilizers until the relevant quotient is taken. Discriminant identities are polynomial identities, including degenerate tensors. Étale comparisons and Selmer interpretations impose their nonzero-discriminant hypotheses separately. This order is essential for the later p-adic masses.


### 1.1 Binary cubics and cubic algebras


<a id="quotient-by-scalars-is-free"></a>


**Quotient by scalars is free.** Let R be a principal ideal domain or a local ring and A an R-algebra that is free of rank n >= 1 as an R-module. Then R -> A, r |-> r.1, is injective, the quotient A/R.1 is free of rank n - 1, and 1 extends to an R-basis <1, a_2, ..., a_n> of A. For n = 3 there is a basis b of A indexed by Fin 3 with b 0 = 1.

Throughout this assertion, R is a PID or a local ring (over an arbitrary base the quotient is only projective, and the parametrization must be phrased with rank-2 projective modules; that generality is not used by any consumer and is not planned here).


To prove the assertion, Injectivity: if r.1 = 0 then r annihilates the nonzero free module A, so r = 0. Local case: 1 is nonzero modulo mA (else A = mA and Nakayama gives A = 0); extend its image to a basis of A/mA and lift; by Nakayama the lift is a basis. PID case: A/R.1 is finitely generated and torsion-free (if r a = s.1 with r != 0 then a is integral over R and equals s/r in A tensor Frac(R); a PID is integrally closed, so s/r is in R), hence free by the structure theorem (Mathlib Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'); a basis of the quotient lifts, together with 1, to a basis of A.

*Needs:* `Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'` (Mathlib), `Module.Free` (Mathlib).

([[7]](#ref-7), Lemma 1.1 and its proof, printed pp. 1-2.)


**Checks.**


- For A = Z[x]/(x^3 - 2): the basis <1, x, x^2> has first vector 1.

- For R = Z/4 (local) and A = R^3 the vector (1,1,1) extends to a basis.


<a id="index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring"></a>


**Index form of a based cubic ring.** Let A be an R-algebra with an R-basis b = <1, b_1, b_2>. For u, v in A let D_b(u, v) be the determinant of the coordinate vectors of 1, u, v in b. The index form of b is the binary cubic form I_b(x, y) = D_b(xi, xi^2) for xi = x b_1 + y b_2, i.e. 1 ^ xi ^ xi^2 = I_b(x,y) (1 ^ b_1 ^ b_2) in the top exterior power; its coefficients are (D(b_1, b_1^2), D(b_2, b_1^2) + 2 D(b_1, b_1 b_2), 2 D(b_2, b_1 b_2) + D(b_1, b_2^2), D(b_2, b_2^2)). It depends only on the images of b_1, b_2 in A/R.1; a change of basis of A/R.1 by gamma in GL2(R) replaces I_b by gamma . I_b (twisted action); the normal basis <1, omega, theta> of R(f) has index form f; and over Z, |I_b(m, n)| is the index of Z[m b_1 + n b_2] in A when it is nonzero.

Throughout this assertion, The determinant is taken in the coordinates of the same basis b, which is what produces the twist (det gamma)^{-1}. Orientation convention: with Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman's table the normal basis has index form +f; with Gross-Lucianovic's basis <1, i, j> = <1, -omega, -theta> the index form is -f.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `CubicRing.det3`: det3 b u v = det(coords 1, coords u, coords v) in the basis b.

- `CubicRing.indexForm`: The index form of a basis indexed by Fin 3.

- `CubicRing.eval_indexForm`: (indexForm b)(x,y) = det3 b xi xi^2 for xi = x b_1 + y b_2.

- `CubicRing.indexForm_translate`: Translating b_1, b_2 by scalars does not change the index form.

- `CubicRing.indexForm_eq_smul`: Two bases with first vector 1 have index forms in one twisted GL2(R)-orbit.

- `CubicRing.indexForm_cubicRing_basis`: The normal basis of R(f) has index form f.

- `CubicRing.index_adjoin_eq_natAbs_indexForm`: Over Z: [A : Z[m b_1 + n b_2]] = |I_b(m, n)| when nonzero.


To prove the assertion, Polarization of the trilinear expression D(xi, xi^2) gives the four coefficients. Translation invariance: adding scalars to b_1, b_2 changes xi by a scalar and xi^2 by a scalar plus a multiple of xi, which do not change the determinant with first row the coordinates of 1. Change of basis: take the column of new basis vectors to be gamma times the column (b_1,b_2), modulo scalars. Then the row of coordinates (x,y) is replaced by (x,y) gamma and D_{b'} = (det gamma)^{-1} D_b; hence I_{b'} = gamma . I_b. With a row of basis vectors transformed on the right, the acting matrix would instead be gamma transposed. For the normal basis of R(f) the coefficients are computed from the multiplication table: I(x,y) = det(1; xi; xi^2) = f(x, y) (the footnote of Gross-Lucianovic). Index formula (Gan-Gross-Savin, Lemma 5.3): <1, xi, xi^2> spans Z[xi], and its coordinate matrix in b has determinant I_b(m, n).

*Needs:* [binary cubic forms and the twisted action](#binary-cubic-forms-and-the-twisted-action), [cubic ring](#cubic-ring), [cubic ring of a binary cubic form](#cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form), `Matrix.det` (Mathlib), `Module.Basis` (Mathlib).

([[6]](#ref-6), Proof of Theorem 9, printed p. 5; [[8]](#ref-8), Lemma 5.3, printed pp. 117-118.)

- For the basis <1, e_0, e_1> of Z^3 the index form is (0, -1, 1, 0) = x y^2 - x^2 y.

- The normal basis of R(x^3 + 2y^3) has index form x^3 + 2y^3.

- Over Q, fixing 1 and replacing b_1,b_2 by 2b_1,2b_2 multiplies the index form by 2, whereas untwisted substitution multiplies it by 8. Thus the determinant twist is necessary.

- For the basis <1, e_0, e_1> of Z^3 (e_i idempotents) the index form is x y^2 - x^2 y.

- Negating b_1 and b_2 negates the index form (the twisted action of -1).


<a id="normal-bases-of-a-cubic-ring"></a>


**Normal bases of a cubic ring.** Let A be an R-algebra with basis <1, b_1, b_2>. There are unique r, s in R such that b'_1 = b_1 + r, b'_2 = b_2 + s satisfy b'_1 b'_2 in R (a normal, or good, basis). For a normal basis <1, omega, theta> with index form f = (a, b, c, d) the multiplication table is omega theta = -ad, omega^2 = -ac - b omega + a theta, theta^2 = -bd - d omega + c theta; in particular A is isomorphic to R(f) by omega |-> omega, theta |-> theta.

Throughout this assertion, A is associative and commutative; the basis contains 1.


To prove the assertion, Write b_1 b_2 = n + s b_1 + t b_2 with n, s, t in R; then (b_1 - t)(b_2 - s) = n + st is in R, so b'_1 = b_1 - t, b'_2 = b_2 - s is normal (Gross-Lucianovic, proof of Proposition 2.1: i = omega_2 - t, j = omega_3 - s). Uniqueness: if (b'_1 + u)(b'_2 + v) is also in R then v b'_1 + u b'_2 is in R, so u = v = 0 because <1, b'_1, b'_2> is a basis. In a normal basis write omega^2 = m + beta omega + alpha theta and theta^2 = l + delta omega + gamma theta; the coefficients of the index form are then read off (the determinant computation of the index form), identifying (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) with (a, -b, c, -d). Associativity forces the constants n, m, l = -ad, -ac, -bd (as in the construction of R(f)).

*Needs:* [index form of a based cubic ring](#index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring), [cubic ring of a binary cubic form](#cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form).

<a id="delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings"></a>


**Delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings.** Let R be a principal ideal domain or a local ring (e.g. Z, Z_p, Q, Q_p, R, F_p). The map f |-> R(f) induces a bijection between the GL2(R)-orbits (twisted action) on binary cubic forms over R and the isomorphism classes of cubic R-algebras. The inverse sends A to the index form of any basis <1, b_1, b_2> (which exists by quotient-by-scalars-is-free); disc(R(f)) = disc(f), so the discriminant (in R/(R^x)^2; in Z for R = Z) is preserved. Concretely: every cubic R-algebra A is isomorphic to R(f) for some f; and R(f) is isomorphic to R(g) if and only if g = gamma . f for some gamma in GL2(R).

Throughout this assertion, R a PID or a local ring (Gross-Lucianovic's hypothesis); over Z this is Delone-Faddeev (for nonzero discriminant) and Gan-Gross-Savin (in general). The action is the twisted action; with the untwisted action the statement is false (the scalar u would act by u^3).


To prove the assertion, Existence: choose a basis <1, b_1, b_2> (quotient-by-scalars-is-free), normalize it (normal-bases-of-a-cubic-ring), and send omega |-> b_1, theta |-> b_2; the multiplication tables agree, giving A = R(I_b). Well-definedness of the inverse on isomorphism classes: an isomorphism A -> A' carries bases to bases, and two bases of A/R.1 differ by gamma in GL2(R), changing the index form to gamma . I (index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring). R(gamma . f) = R(f) (cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form); combining: R(f) = R(g) iff g is in the orbit of f. Discriminant: discriminant-of-the-cubic-ring-of-a-form.

*Needs:* [binary cubic forms and the twisted action](#binary-cubic-forms-and-the-twisted-action), [cubic ring](#cubic-ring), [quotient by scalars is free](#quotient-by-scalars-is-free), [cubic ring of a binary cubic form](#cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form), [discriminant of the cubic ring of a form](#discriminant-of-the-cubic-ring-of-a-form), [index form of a based cubic ring](#index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring), [normal bases of a cubic ring](#normal-bases-of-a-cubic-ring).

([[6]](#ref-6), Theorem 9, printed p. 4; [[7]](#ref-7), Proposition 2.1, printed p. 4; [[6]](#ref-6), End of Section 2, printed p. 6.)

- disc is preserved: the orbit of x^2 y - x y^2 (disc 1) corresponds to Z^3.

- The zero form corresponds to Z + Z omega + Z theta with all products 0 (content infinity); x^3 corresponds to Z[x]/(x^3).

- Over F_p the five GL2(F_p)-orbit types of nonzero forms with distinct factorization patterns (111), (12), (3), (1^2 1), (1^3) give F_p^3, F_p x F_{p^2}, F_{p^3}, F_p[t]/(t^2) x F_p, F_p[t]/(t^3) (Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman, Section 4).


<a id="automorphisms-of-cubic-rings-are-stabilizers"></a>


**Automorphisms of cubic rings are stabilizers.** For a binary cubic form f over a PID or local ring R, the group of R-algebra automorphisms of R(f) is isomorphic to the stabilizer of f in GL2(R) under the twisted row-variable action. If T_sigma is the usual column-coordinate matrix of sigma on R(f)/R in the basis <omega, theta>, the group homomorphism sends sigma to (T_sigma inverse) transposed. Conversely each stabilizer element determines a unique automorphism.

Throughout this assertion, Twisted action; R a PID or local ring.


To prove the assertion, The image basis has column of vectors T_sigma transposed times the original column, and hence index form (T_sigma transposed) . f. Automorphisms preserve the index form, so this equals f. The inverse matrix also stabilizes f. Since T_(sigma tau) = T_sigma T_tau, inverse-transpose, unlike transpose alone, respects multiplication for the chosen left action. A stabilizer element determines the quotient matrix by inverse-transpose. Lift its two basis vectors and normalize them; normality uniquely determines the scalar translates. The multiplication table then gives the unique algebra automorphism, inverse to the preceding construction.

*Needs:* [delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings](#delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings), `MulAction.stabilizer` (Mathlib).

- For irreducible f defining a non-Galois cubic field the stabilizer is trivial.


<a id="reducible-forms-and-zero-divisors"></a>


**Reducible forms and zero divisors.** (a) For a nonzero integral binary cubic form f, R(f) is an integral domain if and only if f(x, y) != 0 for all (x, y) in Z^2 \ {0}, i.e. f has no linear factor over Q (f is irreducible over Q). (b) Over a field K, R(f) is a field if and only if f != 0 and f has no zero in P^1(K). In particular the irreducible integral forms correspond to the orders R(f) whose fraction algebra R(f) tensor Q is a cubic field.

Throughout this assertion, f != 0 in (a); for f = 0 the ring has nilpotents.


To prove the assertion, Over a field K, a projective zero can be moved to (1:0) by GL2(K). Then a = 0 and omega theta = 0, with both omega and theta nonzero basis vectors. If f has no projective zero, a = f(1,0) is nonzero. Scaling f by the unit a inverse preserves R(f) up to isomorphism. For a = 1 the multiplication table gives theta = omega² + b omega + c and omega³ + b omega² + c omega + d = 0. Thus R(f) is K[t]/(t³ + bt² + ct + d), which is a field because a cubic without a K-root is irreducible. For integral f, R(f) is torsion-free and embeds in R(f) tensor Q. A nontrivial zero-divisor relation in the latter can have its denominators cleared to give one in R(f); hence R(f) is a domain exactly when its rational algebra is. Apply the field argument, and clear denominators in projective roots to obtain the stated integral criterion. This avoids treating a primitive element of R as a primitive class in R/Z.

*Needs:* [delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings](#delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings), [normal bases of a cubic ring](#normal-bases-of-a-cubic-ring).

<a id="nondegenerate-forms-and-etale-cubic-algebras"></a>


**Nondegenerate forms and etale cubic algebras.** For a binary cubic form f over a field K, R(f) is an etale K-algebra if and only if disc(f) != 0. Over Z, disc(f) != 0 if and only if R(f) tensor Q is a product of number fields (an order in an etale cubic Q-algebra); forms of discriminant 0 are the degenerate locus.

Throughout this assertion, K any field.


To prove the assertion, disc(f) = Disc R(f) is the determinant of the trace form (discriminant-of-the-cubic-ring-of-a-form). A finite-dimensional commutative K-algebra is etale iff it is a finite product of finite separable field extensions iff its trace form is nondegenerate: separable extensions have nondegenerate trace form (Mathlib traceForm_nondegenerate), and a nonzero nilpotent or an inseparable residue extension lies in the kernel of the trace form.

### 1.2 Cubic maximality and index-p switching


<a id="davenport-heilbronn-sets"></a>


**Davenport heilbronn sets.** For a prime p, U_p is the set of integral binary cubic forms f such that (i) f is not congruent to 0 modulo p, and (ii) no GL2(Z)-translate gamma . f has p^2 | a and p | b. U_p is GL2(Z)-invariant, is defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2 (membership depends only on f mod p^2), and contains every form with p^2 not dividing disc(f). The same definition over Z_p (with GL2(Z_p)) gives an open compact subset of V_3(Z_p) whose intersection with V_3(Z) is U_p.

Throughout this assertion, p prime; the twisted and untwisted actions give the same divisibility conditions over Z since det = +-1.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `BinaryCubicForm.U`: The set U_p.

- `BinaryCubicForm.mem_U_iff`: Membership unfolded into (i) and (ii).

- `BinaryCubicForm.smul_mem_U`: U_p is GL2(Z)-invariant.

- `BinaryCubicForm.mem_U_of_modEq`: Membership depends only on the coefficients modulo p^2.

- `BinaryCubicForm.mem_U_of_not_dvd_disc`: If p^2 does not divide disc f then f is in U_p.


To prove the assertion, Invariance: immediate from the definition (orbits are closed under GL2(Z)). Dependence modulo p^2: conditions (i) and (ii) only involve the coefficients modulo p^2 after substitution by integral matrices. p^2 not dividing disc: condition (ii) forces p^2 | disc (disc(g) with p^2 | a, p | b is divisible by p^2 term by term), and (i) likewise; so p^2 not dividing disc(f) implies f in U_p. For equality with the Z_p definition, reduce a bad GL2(Z_p) matrix modulo p². Multiplying on the left by a suitable diagonal unit matrix normalizes its determinant to 1 while preserving the conditions p² | a and p | b. Every matrix in SL2(Z/p²Z) lifts to SL2(Z): over this local ring elementary row operations reduce it to a diagonal unit matrix, itself a product of elementary matrices, and each elementary entry lifts to Z. The lift acts identically modulo p². The reverse implication is immediate by extension of scalars.

*Needs:* [binary cubic forms and the twisted action](#binary-cubic-forms-and-the-twisted-action).

([[6]](#ref-6), After Lemma 13, printed p. 7.)

- x^3 + y^3 is not in U_3 although it is not divisible by 3: condition (ii) fails after y -> y - x.

- The zero form is not in U_p.

- x^3 + 2y^3 is in U_3; x^3 + y^3 is not (the substitution y -> y - x gives 3x^2 y - 3 x y^2 + y^3).

- The zero form is in no U_p.


<a id="nonmaximal-cubic-rings-have-small-overrings"></a>


**Nonmaximal cubic rings have small overrings.** If a cubic ring R = R(f) is not maximal at p, there is a basis <1, omega, theta> of R such that Z + Z(omega/p) + Z theta or Z + Z(omega/p) + Z(theta/p) is a ring. Equivalently, in terms of the form: either all coefficients of f are divisible by p, or some GL2(Z)-translate of f has p^2 | a and p | b.

Throughout this assertion, p prime; R free of rank 3 over Z.


To prove the assertion, Choose a finite overring R′ with nontrivial p-primary quotient over R by intersecting an overring with R[1/p]. Let m ≥ 1 be the least integer with p^m R′ contained in R. Then S = R + p^(m−1)R′ is a ring, strictly contains R, and pS is contained in R. The ring property follows by expanding products; every cross term lies in p^(m−1)R′. The unit 1 is primitive in S because a finite Z-algebra has no nonintegral rational scalars. Smith normal form on R/Z inside S/Z, followed by normalization of the chosen basis, gives the shapes (omega/p,theta) and (omega/p,theta/p). The multiplication table gives p² | a and p | b in the first shape, and p | a,b,c,d in the second. Their indices are p and p² respectively. This argument avoids the exponent-reduction iteration and any negative congruence exponents. When normalizing a Smith basis after the overring has been chosen, closure of the divided basis implies that each scalar translation of alpha_i used to impose the normal-basis convention is divisible by p^{e_i}. Thus the translation preserves the scaled overring lattice; arbitrary integral translations would not suffice.

*Needs:* [cubic ring](#cubic-ring), [normal bases of a cubic ring](#normal-bases-of-a-cubic-ring), [delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings](#delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings).

<a id="davenport-heilbronn-maximality-criterion"></a>


**Davenport heilbronn maximality criterion.** For an integral binary cubic form f and a prime p, the cubic ring R(f) is maximal at p if and only if f is in U_p. Hence R(f) is maximal if and only if f is in U_p for every prime p. (The identification of the maximal cubic domains with the rings of integers of cubic fields is [maximal irreducible cubic rings are rings of integers of cubic fields](#maximal-irreducible-cubic-rings-are-rings-of-integers-of-cubic-fields).)

Throughout this assertion, p prime; f integral.


To prove the assertion, If f is not in U_p: in case (i) f = p g and R(f) = Z + p R(g) is contained in R(g) with index p^2 (content relation of cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form); in case (ii) the basis with p^2 | a, p | b makes Z + Z(omega/p) + Z theta a ring (congruences (14) with (i,j) = (1,0)). So R(f) is not maximal at p. If R(f) is not maximal at p then f is not in U_p (nonmaximal-cubic-rings-have-small-overrings). Maximality at all primes: the definition of IsMaximal.

*Needs:* [davenport heilbronn sets](#davenport-heilbronn-sets), [nonmaximal cubic rings have small overrings](#nonmaximal-cubic-rings-have-small-overrings), [cubic ring of a binary cubic form](#cubic-ring-of-a-binary-cubic-form), [cubic ring](#cubic-ring).

### 1.3 Quartic rings and cubic resolvents


<a id="pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms"></a>


**Pairs of ternary quadratic forms.** For a commutative ring R, an (integer-valued) ternary quadratic form is Q(x) = sum_{i<=j} a_ij x_i x_j with a_ij in R (Gram matrix with a_ii on the diagonal and a_ij/2 off it), and W(R) = (Sym^2 R^3 tensor R^2)* is the module of pairs (A, B). The group GL3(R) x GL2(R) acts by (g_3, g_2) . (A, B) = (r A' + s B', t A' + u B') with A' = g_3 A g_3^T, B' = g_3 B g_3^T and g_2 = (r s; t u). Attached invariants: 4 Det(Q) = 4 a_11 a_22 a_33 + a_12 a_13 a_23 - a_11 a_23^2 - a_22 a_13^2 - a_33 a_12^2; the cubic resolvent form f_{(A,B)}(x, y) = 4 Det(A x - B y), a binary cubic form over R; the discriminant Disc(A, B) = disc(f_{(A,B)}); the fifteen SL2-invariants lambda^{ij}_{kl} = a_ij b_kl - a_kl b_ij; and, over Z, the content ct(A, B) = gcd of the lambda^{ij}_{kl}. One has f_{(g . (A,B))} = (det g_3)^2 (f_{(A,B)} composed with the substitution by (r -s; -t u)), hence Disc(g . (A,B)) = (det g_3)^8 (det g_2)^6 Disc(A, B).

Throughout this assertion, Integer-valued convention (Bhargava HCL III (11), (19)): diagonal coefficients integral, off-diagonal Gram entries half-integral; 4 Det has integer coefficients. Sign convention pinned: the resolvent form is 4 Det(Ax - By) (Bhargava-Shankar); HCL III writes 4 Det(Ax + By), which differs by (x, y) |-> (x, -y) and is inconsistent with its own multiplication table. Over Z, GL3(Z) = {+-1} x SL3(Z) and -1 acts trivially on pairs, so GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits are the GL2(Z) x SL3(Z)-orbits of Bhargava-Shankar.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `TernaryQuadraticForm`: Integer-valued ternary quadratic forms, six coefficients.

- `TernaryQuadraticForm.eval`: Q(t) = sum_{i<=j} a_ij t_i t_j.

- `TernaryQuadraticForm.det4`: 4 Det Q.

- `TernaryQuadraticForm.comp`: The form t |-> Q(M^T t), Gram matrix M G M^T.

- `TernaryQuadraticForm.lincomb`: x A + y B.

- `TernaryQuadraticForm.toQuadraticForm`: The Mathlib QuadraticForm R (Fin 3 -> R) with the same values.

- `TernaryQuadraticForm.toQuadraticForm_apply`: toQuadraticForm Q t = Q.eval t.

- `TernaryQuadraticForm.det4_comp`: 4 Det (Q o M^T) = (det M)^2 4 Det Q.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair`: Pairs (A, B).

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.instMulAction`: The GL3 x GL2 action of HCL III (11).

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.resolventForm`: The binary cubic form 4 Det(Ax - By).

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.disc`: Disc(A, B) = disc of the resolvent form.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.coeffA`: The symmetric coefficient a_ij.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.coeffB`: The symmetric coefficient b_ij.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.lam`: lambda^{ij}_{kl} = a_ij b_kl - a_kl b_ij.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.content`: Over Z: the gcd of the lambda^{ij}_{kl}.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.resolventForm_A_eq`: The x^3-coefficient of the resolvent form is 4 Det A.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.disc_smul`: Disc(g . (A,B)) = (det g_3)^8 (det g_2)^6 Disc(A,B).

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.lam_smul_SL2`: The lambda^{ij}_{kl} are invariant under SL2.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.lam_eq_zero_iff`: All lambda vanish iff A, B span a space of dimension <= 1 (over Q).


To prove the assertion, Define the six-coefficient ternary forms with evaluation, linear combination and composition t |-> Q(M^T t) (coefficients by polarization at e_i and e_i + e_j); the pair action is then explicit; its axioms are polynomial identities. Transformation of 4 Det: Det(g A g^T) = det(g)^2 Det(A); for the GL2 part, 4 Det((r A + s B) x - (t A + u B) y) = f(r x - t y, -s x + u y) (expand). Disc: disc of a binary cubic form scales by c^4 under multiplication by c and by det(M)^6 under substitution by M.

<a id="quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent"></a>


**Quartic ring and cubic resolvent.** A quartic ring is a commutative ring free of rank 4 over Z. Following HCL III Definitions 19-20, a cubic resolvent of a quartic ring Q is a cubic ring C together with an isomorphism xi : wedge^3(Q/Z) -> wedge^2(C/Z) and a quadratic map phi : Q/Z -> C/Z such that (29) xi(x ^ y ^ xy) = phi(x) ^ phi(y) for all x, y in Q, and (34) the binary cubic form that C corresponds to under Delone-Faddeev is Disc(phi) (this implies xi(x ^ x^2 ^ x^3) = phi(x) ^ phi(x)^2, identity (25); the converse requires that the image of phi span rank two and fails for degenerate rank-smaller images). In bases <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3> of Q and <1, omega_1, omega_2> of C, with phi(sum t_i alpha_i) = B(t) omega_1 + A(t) omega_2 modulo Z, the data is a pair (A, B) in W(Z) and the conditions read: det(1, x, y, xy) = B(x) A(y) - A(x) B(y) for all x, y in Q (coordinates of x on alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3), and the index form of <1, omega_1, omega_2> is -4 Det(Ax - By) (in the orientation of index-form-of-a-based-cubic-ring). The content ct(Q) is the supremum in N union {infinity} of positive integers n for which Q = Z + n Q′ inside Q tensor Q, where Q′ is an overring free of rank four over Z. The trivial square-zero quartic ring has infinite content.

Throughout this assertion, Base Z (the coordinate-free definition works over Z_p and F_p verbatim; HCL III, Appendix). The orientation xi is part of the data; with the pinned orientation the sign in (29) is +. Degenerate quartic rings (discriminant 0) are included: the definition does not use S_4-closures. Retain the full discriminant/index-form condition (34). Identity (25) alone does not specify the cubic ring when the image of phi has rank at most one (HCL III, p. 1351).

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `QuarticRing.coords`: Coordinates of x on alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3.

- `QuarticRing.IsResolventPair`: The based conditions (12) and the index-form identity for (bQ, bC, (A,B)).

- `QuarticRing.HasCubicResolvent`: C is a cubic resolvent of Q: some bases and pair satisfy IsResolventPair.

- `QuarticRing.ringContent`: The supremum in ENat of positive n such that the image of Q in its rational algebra equals Z + n Q′ for a rank-four overring Q′. Overrings are essential: using a subring of Q would give 1 for every quartic ring.

- `QuarticRing.isResolventPair_smul`: Changing bases realizes every (g_3, g_2)-translate of the pair.

- `QuarticRing.discr_eq_of_isResolventPair`: Disc(bQ) = Disc(bC) = Disc(A,B).


To prove the assertion, State the based conditions (determinant identity (12) and the index-form identity) and the coordinate-free Definition 20; show that changing bases of Q/Z and C/Z by (g_3, g_2) replaces (A, B) by (g_3, g_2) . (A, B), so the based notion descends to the coordinate-free one. Discriminants: Disc Q = Disc C = Disc(A, B) follow from the explicit multiplication table (quartic-ring-of-a-pair) and Delone-Faddeev. Content: define as the supremum; it is finite for nondegenerate rings and infinity only for the trivial ring Z + Z x_1 + Z x_2 + Z x_3 with all x_i x_j = 0.

<a id="quartic-ring-of-a-pair"></a>


**Quartic ring of a pair.** For a pair (A, B) of ternary quadratic forms over a commutative ring R, Q(A, B) is the R-algebra with basis <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3> and alpha_i alpha_j = c^0_ij + sum_k c^k_ij alpha_k, where for every permutation (i, j, k) of (1, 2, 3) with sign epsilon: c^i_ii = epsilon lambda^{ik}_{ij} + C_i, c^j_ii = epsilon lambda^{ii}_{ik}, c^i_ij = epsilon (1/2) lambda^{ik}_{jj} + (1/2) C_j, c^k_ij = epsilon lambda^{jj}_{ii}, with C_1 = lambda^{23}_{11}, C_2 = -lambda^{13}_{22}, C_3 = lambda^{12}_{33}, and c^0_ij = sum_r (c^r_jk c^k_ri - c^r_ij c^k_rk) for any k != i. All c^k_ij are integral polynomials in the coefficients (the halves cancel: c^1_12 = c^2_12 = c^1_13 = 0, c^3_13 = lambda^{23}_{11}, c^2_23 = lambda^{12}_{33}, c^3_23 = -lambda^{13}_{22}); the basis is normal (c^1_12 = c^2_12 = c^1_13 = 0). The cubic resolvent ring is R(A, B) = R(-4 Det(Ax - By)) (Delone-Faddeev); with phi(sum t_i alpha_i) = B(t) omega_1 + A(t) omega_2 the triple is a based cubic resolvent, and Disc Q(A,B) = Disc R(A,B) = Disc(A,B).

Throughout this assertion, The index condition in the formula for c^0_ij is k != i; HCL III prints k != j, for which the expression depends on k and the table is not associative. The sign of the resolvent form: with the table above and HCL III's normal basis of the resolvent, identity (25) holds for 4 Det(Ax - By), not 4 Det(Ax + By) as printed in (26).

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `TernaryQuadraticPair.structConst`: The structure constants c^k_ij (k = 0 the constant term).

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.quarticRingIdeal`: The ideal of relations in R[X_1, X_2, X_3].

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.quarticRing`: Q(A, B) as a quotient ring.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.quarticBasis`: The normal basis <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3>.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.quarticBasis_zero`: quarticBasis 0 = 1.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.mul_quarticBasis`: alpha_i alpha_j = c^0_ij + sum_k c^k_ij alpha_k.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.structConst_normal`: c^1_12 = c^2_12 = c^1_13 = 0: the basis is normal.

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.discr_quarticBasis`: Disc Q(A, B) = Disc(A, B).

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.cubicResolventRing`: R(A, B) = R(-4 Det(Ax - By)).

- `TernaryQuadraticPair.isResolventPair_quarticRing`: (Q(A,B), R(A,B), (A,B)) is a based cubic resolvent.


To prove the assertion, The structure constants are forced by Lemma 9 (identity (12)) with phi = (B, A): equating the coefficients of the degree-4 polynomials p = q in r_1, ..., s_3 (HCL III (17)-(18)) gives the linear system with the unique solution (21)-(22); associativity then forces (23). Associativity of the resulting table, the independence of c^0_ij from k != i and integrality were checked by expansion for generic and random integral pairs; they are polynomial identities in Z[a_ij, b_ij]. Disc Q(A,B) = Disc(A,B): explicit polynomial identity (HCL III Proposition 10), also checked by expansion. For the generic nondegenerate pair, identity (25) gives the cubic index form −4 Det(Ax − By) in the pinned orientation. Verify that equality as an integral polynomial identity, so it also holds after specialization to degenerate pairs and arbitrary base rings. Together with identity (29), this supplies the full discriminant/index-form condition (34). Identity (25) alone does not determine a resolvent for a degenerate pair. Construct Q(A,B) as R[X_1, X_2, X_3] modulo the six relations X_i X_j - c^0_ij - sum_k c^k_ij X_k; freeness of rank 4 is the Groebner-basis argument as for cubic rings.

<a id="bhargava-parametrization-of-quartic-rings"></a>


**Bhargava parametrization of quartic rings.** There is a canonical bijection between GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits on W(Z) = (Sym^2 Z^3 tensor Z^2)* and isomorphism classes of pairs (Q, R) with Q a quartic ring and R a cubic resolvent ring of Q; it sends (A, B) to (Q(A,B), R(A,B)) and a pair (Q, R) to the pair of ternary quadratic forms representing the resolvent map phi : Q/Z -> R/Z in bases. It preserves discriminants: Disc(A, B) = Disc(Q) = Disc(R). In based form: every pair (A, B) is the resolvent pair of a based quartic ring and cubic resolvent, unique up to isomorphisms preserving the chosen quotient bases modulo scalar translates, and changing the bases realizes exactly the GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbit.

Throughout this assertion, Base Z (the same proof works over Z_p and F_p with the appendix's definition). Cubic resolvents in the sense of quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent; degenerate pairs included. A cubic resolvent includes its quadratic map and orientation. Keeping only the isomorphism classes of the two underlying rings can identify different resolvent data. Based uniqueness refers to bases of Q/Z and C/Z; arbitrary lifts can differ by scalars, and exact equality of lifted bases requires normality.


To prove the assertion, (A,B) |-> (Q(A,B), R(A,B)) is a based cubic resolvent (quartic-ring-of-a-pair). Conversely, for a based cubic resolvent the identity (12) determines the structure constants of the normal basis as in (21)-(23), so Q is Q(A,B) (HCL III Proposition 10), and (34) determines R as R(A,B) by Delone-Faddeev (Proposition 11; in the degenerate case by the appendix's definition). The two constructions are mutually inverse on based objects; changing bases of Q/Z and R/Z by (g_3, g_2) acts on (A,B) by the action of pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms, so isomorphism classes correspond to orbits. Discriminants: quartic-ring-of-a-pair.

*Needs:* [quartic ring of a pair](#quartic-ring-of-a-pair), [quartic ring and cubic resolvent](#quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent), [pairs of ternary quadratic forms](#pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms), [delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings](#delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings).

<a id="existence-and-number-of-cubic-resolvents"></a>


**Existence and number of cubic resolvents.** (a) Every quartic ring Q has at least one cubic resolvent ring. (b) The number of cubic resolvent rings of Q (with Q fixed: isomorphisms of resolvent data must induce the identity on Q) depends only on the content n = ct(Q) and equals sigma(n) = sum_{d | n} d, the number of index-n sublattices of Z^2. (c) In particular a primitive quartic ring (content 1), hence every maximal quartic ring and every ring of integers of a quartic field, has a unique cubic resolvent ring up to isomorphism, namely the cubic invariant ring R_inv(Q). (d) Two pairs give the same quartic ring iff they are related by GL3(Z) x GL2^{+-1}(Q).

Throughout this assertion, Q nontrivial for (b)-(d) (the trivial ring has infinite content). Maximal quartic rings of nonzero discriminant are Gorenstein and have content 1. The count sigma(n) retains the fixed quartic ring Q. Quotienting also by Aut(Q), as in the unbased GL3 x GL2 orbit classification, can identify these resolvent structures and changes the count.


To prove the assertion, The structure constants of a normal basis of Q determine the fifteen lambda^{ij}_{kl} by (21), and associativity gives the Pluecker syzygies (27) (HCL III Section 3.8). Lemma 16: fifteen constants satisfying (27), not all zero, are the lambda-invariants of a unique SL2(C)-orbit, which contains an integral point when the constants are integers (elementary divisors). With a fixed normal basis of Q, the fifteen lambda-invariants are fixed. Their nonzero gcd n specifies an orientation of the pencil. The relevant SL2(Z)-orbits, not full GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-orbits, correspond to index-n sublattices in the maximal integral pencil lattice, with the induced orientation. Hermite normal form counts these as Σ_(d|n) d. Arbitrarily oriented bases would produce both lambda and −lambda, so the orientation is retained throughout. Apply the based parametrization and then forget the chosen basis of the fixed ring Q, transporting it by the identity of Q. This counts resolvent structures over Q without quotienting by its automorphisms. The gcd of lambda is ct(Q) by (21)–(23). Maximal rings: a ring Z + nQ' with n > 1 is not maximal (contained in Q'), so maximal rings are primitive.

<a id="maximality-of-quartic-rings-at-p"></a>


**Maximality of quartic rings at p.** If a quartic ring Q is not maximal at p, there is a Z-basis <1, alpha_1, alpha_2, alpha_3> of Q such that Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z alpha_2 + Z alpha_3, or Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z(alpha_2/p) + Z alpha_3, or Z + Z(alpha_1/p) + Z(alpha_2/p) + Z(alpha_3/p) is a ring. For Q = Q(A, B) these read, after a GL3(Z) x GL2(Z)-change of the pair: (i) lambda^{11}_{22}, lambda^{11}_{23}, lambda^{11}_{33}, lambda^{12}_{13} = 0 mod p and lambda^{11}_{12}, lambda^{11}_{13} = 0 mod p^2; (ii) lambda^{11}_{13}, lambda^{11}_{23}, lambda^{12}_{13}, lambda^{12}_{23}, lambda^{13}_{22}, lambda^{22}_{23} = 0 mod p and lambda^{11}_{12}, lambda^{11}_{22}, lambda^{12}_{22} = 0 mod p^2; (iii) all lambda = 0 mod p. Q(A, B) is maximal at p iff (A, B) is in the set U_p of pairs for which none of (i)-(iii) can be achieved; the U_p are defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2.

Throughout this assertion, p prime; quartic rings of nonzero discriminant for the geometric reading of (i), (ii) (double intersection points, double lines) in HCL III Section 4.2.


To prove the assertion, Choose a finite p-primary overring Q′ and let m ≥ 1 be minimal with p^m Q′ contained in Q. Then S = Q + p^(m−1)Q′ is a proper overring and pS is contained in Q (expand products to see that S is a ring). Since 1 is primitive in these finite Z-algebras, Smith normal form on Q/Z inside S/Z gives a basis containing 1 and the three displayed possibilities. This direct construction replaces the incomplete exponent-reduction iteration in the printed proof of HCL III Lemma 22. Translate the three shapes into congruences on the lambda through the explicit c^k_ij (quartic-ring-of-a-pair). Conversely each of (i)-(iii) exhibits the overring, so Q(A,B) is not maximal. When normalizing a Smith basis after the overring has been chosen, closure of the divided basis implies that each scalar translation of alpha_i used to impose the normal-basis convention is divisible by p^{e_i}. Thus the translation preserves the scaled overring lattice; arbitrary integral translations would not suffice.

<a id="splitting-types-of-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms"></a>


**Splitting types of pairs of ternary quadratic forms.** For a pair (A, B) over Z (or Z_p, F_p) whose conics A = 0, B = 0 meet in four points of P^2 over F_p-bar counted with multiplicity, let ((A,B), p) = (f_1^{e_1} f_2^{e_2} ...) record the residue degrees and multiplicities of the intersection points. Then (A,B) is in T_p(sigma) iff Q(A,B)/(p) = F_{p^{f_1}}[t_1]/(t_1^{e_1}) + ..., except for sigma = (1^4), where Q(A,B)/p may also be F_2[x,y]/(x^2, xy + y^2), F_p[x,y]/(x^2, y^2) or F_p[x,y]/(xy, x^2 + n y^2). In particular Disc(A,B) is nonzero mod p iff the conics meet in four distinct points iff Q(A,B)/p is etale over F_p; for maximal Q(A,B), ((A,B), p) is the splitting type of p.

Throughout this assertion, p prime; the two conics have no common component, so their intersection is zero-dimensional of length four. This allows discriminant-zero and nonreduced intersections; it does not require four distinct geometric points.


To prove the assertion, The ring Q(A,B)/p depends only on the GL3(F_p) x GL2(F_p)-orbit of (A,B) mod p (base change of quartic-ring-of-a-pair). Write the multiplication table at one representative of each of the eleven orbit types (HCL III Section 4.1, 'direct calculation'). Nonzero discriminant mod p: four distinct intersection points, and Disc(Q/p) = Disc(A,B) mod p is nonzero, so Q/p is etale.

*Needs:* [quartic ring of a pair](#quartic-ring-of-a-pair), [nondegenerate forms and etale cubic algebras](#nondegenerate-forms-and-etale-cubic-algebras), `Algebra.Etale` (Mathlib).

### 1.4 Quintic rings and alternating tensors


<a id="quadruples-of-quinary-alternating-forms"></a>


**Quadruples of quinary alternating forms.** For a commutative ring R, V(R) = R^4 tensor wedge^2 R^5 is the module of quadruples A = (A_1, ..., A_4) of alternating 5 x 5 matrices over R (recorded by their entries above the diagonal). The group GL4(R) x SL5(R) acts by (g_4, g_5) . A = (sum_s (g_4)_{rs} g_5 A_s g_5^T)_r. The 4 x 4 sub-Pfaffian map Q(X) = (Q_1(X), ..., Q_5(X)), Q_i(X) = (-1)^{i-1} Pf(X with row and column i deleted), is a quadratic covariant: X Q(X) = 0 for every alternating X, and Q(cX) = c^2 Q(X). The SL5-invariants {ijklm} = Q(A_i, A_j)^T A_k Q(A_l, A_m) (Q(.,.) the symmetric bilinear form with Q(X,X) = 2Q(X)) determine the multiplication table of the quintic ring R(A); the fundamental relative invariant is the degree-40 discriminant Disc(A), with Disc((g_4,g_5) . A) = det(g_4)^10 Disc(A). Thus it is invariant under GL4(Z) x SL5(Z), but is generally only a relative invariant over other base rings. The same matrix formula extends to GL4(R) x GL5(R), with relative discriminant weight det(g_4)^10 det(g_5)^16. Over Z this has the same orbits as GL4(Z) x SL5(Z), since replacing a determinant-minus-one g_5 by −g_5 leaves its congruence action unchanged. Over a field the full rational orbit for minimality uses this extended group.

Throughout this assertion, The discriminant is not written out as a polynomial (degree 40); it is characterized in HCL IV Section 3 and equals Disc R(A). The displayed GL4 x SL5 action can have a nontrivial kernel away from Z: (zeta^(-2) I_4, zeta I_5) acts trivially whenever zeta^5 = 1. Do not identify its stabilizers or rational orbits with those of the effective quotient without accounting for this kernel and descent.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple`: Quadruples of alternating 5 x 5 matrices by upper-triangular entries.

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.toMatrix`: The r-th alternating matrix.

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.ofMatrices`: The quadruple with given matrices (upper triangle).

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.instMulAction`: The GL4 x SL5 action.

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.subPfaffian`: The signed 4 x 4 sub-Pfaffians.

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.toMatrix_transpose`: Each matrix is alternating: A_r^T = -A_r.

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.subPfaffian_smul_scalar`: Q(cX) = c^2 Q(X).

- `QuinaryAlternatingQuadruple.mulVec_subPfaffian`: X Q(X) = 0.

X Q(X) = 0: the Pfaffian expansion of the 6 x 6 alternating matrix with a repeated row (checked by expansion; verified symbolically for the sign convention (-1)^{i-1}). The invariants P^+ and P^- of HCL IV (11)-(14) and the brackets {ijklm} (18) are polynomial SL5-invariants of degree 5.

<a id="bhargava-parametrization-of-quintic-rings"></a>


**Bhargava parametrization of quintic rings.** (a) There is a canonical bijection between GL4(Z) x SL5(Z)-orbits on V(Z) = Z^4 tensor wedge^2 Z^5 and isomorphism classes of pairs (R, S) with R a quintic ring and S a sextic resolvent ring of R (HCL IV Theorems 1 and 8; for nondegenerate pairs Disc(A) = Disc(R) = (1/16) Disc(S)^{1/3}); the sextic resolvent is defined by HCL IV Definitions 10-11 (a sextic ring S with a Z-linear map phi : R/Z -> wedge^2(S/Z) such that R(phi) = R and S(phi) = S). (b) Every quintic ring is R(A) for some A, so every quintic ring has a sextic resolvent (Theorem 17, Corollary 18). (c) If R is maximal, A is unique up to GL4(Z) x SL5(Z), so a maximal quintic ring has a unique sextic resolvent (Theorem 17, Corollary 19). (d) The classical resolvent map of Cayley is 4 times the sub-Pfaffian covariant (Theorem 9).

Throughout this assertion, The multiplication tables of R(A) (HCL IV Section 4, (16)-(25)) and S(A) (Section 6) are part of the statement; they are specified by the source and not re-derived here.


To prove the assertion, From A, Lemma 4 expresses the determinants built from conjugates through the invariants P^+, P^- and the brackets {ijklm}, which determines the normalized structure constants of R(A) (Section 4) and of S(A) (Section 6). The fundamental map g : wedge^2 S~ -> R~ realizes the inverse (Sections 5 and 7), giving Theorem 8 for nondegenerate elements; the appendix-style Definitions 10-11 extend it to all elements (Section 9). Existence and uniqueness for maximal rings: the invariant theory of Section 10 (Theorem 12 and Lemmas 13-16) constructs an integral A with prescribed structure constants and shows uniqueness when R is maximal (minimal integral model), giving Theorem 17 and Corollaries 18-19.

<a id="maximality-of-quintic-rings-at-p"></a>


**Maximality of quintic rings at p.** For A in V(Z), R(A) is maximal iff A is in U_p for every prime p, where U_p is the union of the seventeen sets U_p(sigma) of elements of splitting type sigma whose ring is maximal at p (defined by congruence conditions modulo p^2); R(A) is maximal exactly when A is a minimal integral model (smallest nonzero absolute discriminant in its GL4(Q) x GL5(Q)-orbit meeting V(Z)).

Throughout this assertion, p prime; nondegenerate A. Minimality is in the full GL4(Q) x GL5(Q) orbit and orders by absolute discriminant. Restricting to GL4(Q) x SL5(Q) only allows discriminants to scale by tenth powers and can miss an overring of index p.


To prove the assertion, For a proper finite p-primary overring R′, choose m ≥ 1 minimal with p^m R′ contained in R. Then S = R + p^(m−1)R′ is a proper overring with pS contained in R. Smith normal form on R/Z inside S/Z gives four shapes, of indices p,p²,p³,p⁴, dividing a nonempty subset of the four nonconstant basis vectors by p. Ring closure is detected by structure-constant congruences modulo p². Use the polynomial multiplication table and normalize determinant units before lifting elementary basis changes from Z/p²Z to Z. Section 12 supplies the splitting-type decomposition; it does not state the erroneous three-shape index-p assertion. Theorem 12 and Lemma 16 (minimal integral models) give maximality iff minimality.

### 1.5 Quartic covariants and rational orbits


<a id="pgl2-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-quartic-forms"></a>


**Pgl2 orbits and stabilizers of binary quartic forms.** Let R be a commutative ring and V(R) the binary quartic forms over R (Layer 0), with the twisted action gamma * f = (det gamma)^{-2} f((x,y) gamma) of GL2(R) (Layer 0), on which the centre acts trivially. It therefore induces an action of PGL2(R) = GL2(R)/centre (Mathlib's Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup). The invariants I and J are PGL2(R)-invariant, so the orbit space PGL2(R)\V(R) maps to R x R; its fibre over (I, J) is the set of orbits of forms with invariants I, J. The stabilizer of f is Stab_{PGL2(R)}(f). Over Z (and any ring whose units have square 1) the PGL2-orbits are the orbits of GL2 under plain substitution.

Throughout this assertion, The twist exponent is -2, so that I and J are invariant (Layer 0 records the untwisted weights (det gamma)^4, (det gamma)^6). PGL2 is the quotient by the full centre (scalar matrices), not PSL2.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `BinaryQuartic.instPGLAction`: The PGL2(R)-action induced by the twisted action.

- `BinaryQuartic.pgl_smul_mk`: mk gamma . f = twistedSMul gamma f.

- `BinaryQuartic.invI_pgl_smul`: I is PGL2-invariant.

- `BinaryQuartic.invJ_pgl_smul`: J is PGL2-invariant.

- `BinaryQuartic.PGLOrbit`: The orbit space PGL2(R)\V(R).

- `BinaryQuartic.PGLOrbit.invariants`: The invariants (I, J) of an orbit.

- `BinaryQuartic.pgl_orbits_eq_gl_orbits_int`: Over Z, PGL2-orbits are GL2(Z)-orbits under plain substitution.


To prove the assertion, Define the action through a set-theoretic section of GL2(R) -> PGL2(R); well-definedness is Layer 0's twistedSMul_scalar (scalars act trivially); the action axioms follow from twistedSMul_mul. Invariance of I and J: the twisted action multiplies I by (det gamma)^4 (det gamma)^{-4} (Layer 0 relative invariance). Over Z: det gamma = +-1 so the twist is trivial and the orbits agree with those of the plain action.

<a id="soluble-binary-quartic-forms"></a>


**Soluble binary quartic forms.** A binary quartic form f over a field K is K-soluble if z^2 = f(x, y) has a solution with x, y, z in K and (x, y) != (0, 0). Over a number field K, f is (everywhere) locally soluble if f is K_v-soluble for every completion K_v: at every finite place (Mathlib's adicCompletion at each height-one prime of O_K) and at every infinite place (Mathlib's InfinitePlace.Completion). Over Q this means R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for every prime p; an integral form is locally soluble if its rational form is. The rational-linear-factor locus consists of forms with a zero in P^1(Q); this is only part of the polynomial-reducible locus, which also includes products of two quadratic factors. Ordinary irreducible forms have a != 0 and f(X, 1) irreducible over Q. Solubility is invariant under PGL2(K), stable under field extension, and holds whenever f has a zero in P^1(K) or its leading coefficient is a square.

Throughout this assertion, (x, y) != (0, 0) is required; z may be 0. When char K ≠ 2, for forms of nonzero discriminant, K-solubility is equivalent to the genus-one curve z^2 = f(x, y) having a K-point, but the definition does not refer to curves.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `BinaryQuartic.IsSoluble`: K-solubility.

- `BinaryQuartic.IsEverywhereLocallySoluble`: Solubility over every completion of a number field.

- `BinaryQuartic.IsLocallySolubleQ`: A rational form: R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for all p.

- `BinaryQuartic.IsLocallySoluble`: An integral form is locally soluble: its rational form is IsLocallySolubleQ.

- `BinaryQuartic.HasRationalLinearFactor`: An integral form has a zero in P¹(Q), the rational-linear-factor locus corresponding to the identity Selmer class. It is not the whole polynomial-reducible locus.

- `BinaryQuartic.IsIrreducibleOverQ`: An integral form is irreducible over Q (a != 0 and f(X,1) irreducible).

- `BinaryQuartic.isLocallySoluble_iff`: An integral form is locally soluble iff it is R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for every prime p.

- `BinaryQuartic.isSoluble_pgl_smul`: Solubility is PGL2(K)-invariant.

- `BinaryQuartic.IsSoluble.map`: Solubility is preserved by field homomorphisms.

- `BinaryQuartic.isSoluble_of_eval_eq_zero`: A zero in P^1(K) gives solubility.

- `BinaryQuartic.isSoluble_of_isSquare_a`: A square leading coefficient gives solubility.

- `BinaryQuartic.isLocallySolubleQ_iff`: Unfolding of local solubility over Q.


To prove the assertion, PGL2-invariance: if f(x,y) = z², then its twisted transform has the solution ((x,y) gamma inverse, z/(det gamma)). The inverse transformation proves the converse. Base change: a solution over K maps to one over L. Zeros of f give solutions with z = 0; f(1, 0) = a a square gives (1, 0, sqrt a).

**Cubic invariant of a binary quartic.** Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 and I, J in K with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0. (b) Every such g is PGL2(K)-equivalent to the normal form q_0 = (1/27) Y (27 X^3 - 9 I X Y^2 - J Y^3) = X^3 Y - (I/3) X Y^3 - (J/27) Y^4; hence the forms with a linear factor and invariants I, J form one orbit.

Throughout this assertion, char K not 2,3, and #K ≠ 5 for the chosen admissible-evaluation construction of z.


To prove the assertion, (a, linear factor implies z = 1) At a zero (x, y) of g, g_4(x, y) != 0 and g_6(x,y) != 0 (resultants Delta^2/3^2, Delta^3/3^9), and the syzygy gives G(x, y) = g_4(x,y)/3 = (3 g_6/g_4)^2, a square (Cremona-Fisher Lemma 3). (a, z = 1 implies linear factor) If a = 0 the factor Y already gives the conclusion; otherwise, with r = g_6(1, 0) != 0 after a proper change, z = G(1,0) has characteristic polynomial Z^3 - pZ^2 + qZ - r^2; if z = z_1^2 then h(Z^2) = -h_1(Z) h_1(-Z) and -(u + b)/(4a) is a root of g (Cremona-Fisher Proposition 8). (b) Move the linear factor to Y, translate X to kill c, and rescale with (M, lambda) of determinant 1 (Cremona-Fisher Proposition 7).

<a id="linear-factor-of-the-comparison-quartic-gives-equivalence"></a>


**Linear factor of the comparison quartic gives equivalence.** Let g_1, g_2 have the same invariants with r_1 = g_{1,6}(1, 0) != 0. If p_1 g_2 - a_1 h_2 has a zero in P^1(K), then g_1 and g_2 are PGL2(K)-equivalent.

Also a_2 ≠ 0, since a_2 = p_2 = 0 would force b_2 = 0 and make g_2 singular. Put t = a_2/a_1, so p_2 = t p_1, without dividing by p_1 (which may be zero). The seminvariant syzygy gives r_2² = t³ r_1². Since t and r_1 are nonzero, r_2 is nonzero and t = (r_2/(t r_1))². A proper diagonal change makes a_2 = a_1, p_2 = p_1 and r_2 = r_1; a shift makes b_2 = b_1. Then p,r,I recover c,d,e successively because a_1,2,3 are invertible, so g_2 = g_1.

<a id="image-of-the-cubic-invariant"></a>


**Image of the cubic invariant.** Let K be a field of characteristic not 2 or 3 with #K != 5, I, J with 4I^3 - J^2 != 0, and m in A_{I,J}^x with square norm. ### 1.7 Integral two-covering representatives


<a id="primitive-vectors-extend-to-special-linear-matrices"></a>


**Primitive vectors extend to special linear matrices.** Let O be a principal ideal domain and v in O^3 with coordinates generating the unit ideal (a primitive vector). Then for every j there is M in SL3(O) whose j-th column is v; in particular SL3(O) acts transitively on P^2(Frac O) (on primitive vectors up to units).

Throughout this assertion, O a PID (Z, Z_p, Z_(p)).


To prove the assertion, O^3/Ov is finitely generated and torsion-free (v primitive), hence free of rank 2 over the PID (Mathlib Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'); so v extends to a basis of O^3. First permute the extended basis so that v is its j-th column. Its determinant is a unit u; multiply a different column by u^{-1}. This preserves the chosen column and makes the determinant 1, including the sign of the permutation.

*Needs:* `Module.free_of_finite_type_torsion_free'` (Mathlib), `IsCoprime.exists_SL2_col` (Mathlib), `Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup` (Mathlib).

<a id="ternary-cubic-forms-and-their-invariants"></a>


**Ternary cubic forms and their invariants.** A ternary cubic over a commutative ring R is U = a x^3 + b y^3 + c z^3 + a_2 x^2 y + a_3 x^2 z + b_1 x y^2 + b_3 y^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c_2 y z^2 + m x y z. Its invariants c_4(U) (25 terms, degree 4) and c_6(U) (103 terms, degree 6) are the integer polynomials in the coefficients determined by Fisher's normalization H(lambda U + mu H) = 3(c_4 lambda^2 mu + 2 c_6 lambda mu^2 + c_4^2 mu^3) U + (lambda^3 - 3 c_4 lambda mu^2 - 2 c_6 mu^3) H, where H(U) = -(1/2) det(Hessian of U); c_4 = -216 abcm + 144 abc_1c_2 + ... + m^4 and c_6 = 5832 a^2b^2c^2 - 3888 a^2 b b_3 c c_2 + ... - m^6. For the Weierstrass cubic y^2 z - x^3 - A x z^2 - B z^3 they are c_4 = -48A and c_6 = -864B, the usual invariants of y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B; and c_4^3 - c_6^2 = 1728 Delta. Substitution: (U o M)(x, y, z) = U(M^T (x, y, z)).

Throughout this assertion, The polynomials are written out explicitly (derived from the Hessian identity and checked on the Weierstrass family); their leading terms agree with Fisher's printed partial expansions.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `TernaryCubicForm`: Ternary cubics by ten coefficients (Fisher's coordinates).

- `TernaryCubicForm.eval`: Evaluation.

- `TernaryCubicForm.c4`: The invariant c_4.

- `TernaryCubicForm.c6`: The invariant c_6.

- `TernaryCubicForm.comp`: The cubic U(M^T (x,y,z)).

- `TernaryCubicForm.eval_comp`: Evaluation of the substituted cubic.

- `TernaryCubicForm.weierstrass`: The Weierstrass cubic y^2 z - x^3 - A x z^2 - B z^3.

- `TernaryCubicForm.c4_weierstrass`: c_4 = -48 A.

- `TernaryCubicForm.c6_weierstrass`: c_6 = -864 B.

- `TernaryCubicForm.c4_cube_sub_c6_sq`: c_4^3 - c_6^2 is divisible by 1728 (defines Delta).


To prove the assertion, Compute H(U), the first and second directional derivatives of H at U in the direction H(U), and read off c_4, c_6 from the lambda^2 mu and lambda mu^2 coefficients (exact polynomial division by the coefficient a; checked symbolically). Evaluate on the Weierstrass cubic.

*Needs:* `Matrix.det` (Mathlib).

<a id="invariance-of-ternary-cubic-invariants"></a>


**Invariance of ternary cubic invariants.** For a ternary cubic U and a 3 x 3 matrix M over a commutative ring, c_4(U o M) = det(M)^4 c_4(U) and c_6(U o M) = det(M)^6 c_6(U).

Throughout this assertion, Polynomial identities in the coefficients of U and the entries of M.


To prove the assertion, Both sides are polynomials; the identities are multiplicative in M, so it suffices to check them for elementary transvections and diagonal matrices over Q (these generate GL3(Q), which is Zariski dense), and they then hold over every commutative ring (Cremona-Fisher-Stoll Theorem 2.8(i); Fisher, Section 4).

<a id="projection-of-a-plane-cubic-from-a-rational-point"></a>


**Projection of a plane cubic from a rational point.** Let U be a ternary cubic with b = 0, i.e. with (0:1:0) on U = 0, written U = f_1(x,z) y^2 - f_2(x,z) y - f_3(x,z) with f_1 = b_1 x + b_3 z, f_2 = -(a_2 x^2 + m x z + c_2 z^2), f_3 = -(a x^3 + a_3 x^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c z^3). Its projection quartic is the binary quartic F_U = f_2^2 + 4 f_1 f_3 in (x, z) (the discriminant in y of U along the line through (0:1:0) with slope (x : z)). If U is integral then F_U is integral, and I(F_U) = c_4(U), J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U). For the Weierstrass cubic of y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B, F = 4(x^3 z + A x z^3 + B z^4), with invariants (-48A, -1728B) = (2^4 I, 2^6 J) for I = -3A, J = -27B.

Throughout this assertion, U(0,1,0) = b = 0. The generalized quartic y^2 + f_2 y = f_1 f_3 of Cremona-Fisher-Stoll (3.4) becomes F_U after completing the square (times 4), which is how integrality at 2 is kept.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:

- `TernaryCubicForm.invJ_projectionQuartic`: J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U) when b = 0.

- `TernaryCubicForm.projectionQuartic_eval`: F_U(x, z) = (a_2 x^2 + m x z + c_2 z^2)^2 - 4 (b_1 x + b_3 z)(a x^3 + a_3 x^2 z + c_1 x z^2 + c z^3).


To prove the assertion, Lines through (0:1:0) are parametrized by (x:z). Their residual homogeneous quadratic has discriminant F_U. In characteristic different from 2, when f_1(x,z) ≠ 0 its two residual intersection points are rational (with multiplicity) iff F_U(x,z) is a square. The direction f_1(x,z)=0 requires the separate linear/tangent case; the polynomial construction and invariant identities impose neither restriction. I(F_U) = c_4(U) and J(F_U) = 2 c_6(U) for b = 0: polynomial identities (checked symbolically; Cremona-Fisher-Stoll: 'a generic computation shows that the genus one models (3.4) and (3.5) have the same discriminant', here with c_4, c_6 themselves).

Consequently its cubic invariant is mu(P′), with the corrected representative at 2-torsion. For P=O the same construction has a rational linear factor and cubic invariant 1. The orbit statement itself also holds over F_5; only the evaluation construction of z excludes that field.

Throughout this assertion, char K ≠ 2,3 and 4A³+27B² ≠ 0; #K ≠ 5 when expressing the conclusion using z. The middle row represents the projective point: a nonzero scalar multiple is allowed, as required for primitive integral coordinates.


To prove the assertion, Invariants follow from det(M)=1, the ternary-cubic transformation laws, and I(projection U)=c_4(U), J(projection U)=2c_6(U). Its projection is z⁴−6xi·x²z²−8eta·x³z−(3xi²+4A)x⁴, exactly q(P′)(z,x). The variable swap has determinant −1 and trivial determinant-square twist. For any permitted M, L=M M_0^{-1} has middle row (0,lambda,0). Write its other rows as (a,b,c),(d,e,f). The induced change in (x,z) is Gamma=((a,c),(d,f)), and det(Gamma)=lambda^{-1}. Translation of y by bx+ez leaves the quadratic discriminant unchanged; scaling y by lambda multiplies it by lambda². Thus projection(U∘M)=Gamma twistedSMul projection(U∘M_0). This also proves independence of the primitive projective representative. Apply z(q(P′))=mu(P′) and invariance of z under PGL2. This identity handles 2-torsion without evaluating a nonunit representative. For O, the original Weierstrass projection 4(x³z+Axz³+Bz⁴) has the factor z; the same block-matrix calculation proves the assertion for every M representing O.

<a id="integrality-from-local-integrality"></a>


**Integrality from local integrality.** Let f be a binary quartic over Q such that for every prime p there is gamma_p in PGL2(Q_p) with gamma_p * f integral over Z_p. Then there is gamma in PGL2(Q) with gamma * f integral over Z.

Throughout this assertion, Twisted action; scalars act trivially, so lattices up to scaling suffice.


To prove the assertion, For almost all p, f is already Z_p-integral (finitely many denominators); take gamma_p = 1 there. Lift each gamma_p to GL2(Q_p), using the identity at almost all p, and set Lambda_p=Z_p² gamma_p. Choose a positive integer D supported on the finite exceptional set such that D Z_p² ⊂ Lambda_p ⊂ D^{-1}Z_p² for all p. Set Lambda={v in D^{-1}Z² : v belongs to every Lambda_p}. It lies between D Z² and D^{-1}Z². The Chinese remainder theorem on these finite quotient lattices shows Lambda tensor Z_p = Lambda_p for each p; density at a single prime alone would not establish simultaneous compatibility. Lambda is free (Z a PID): Lambda = Z^2 gamma for gamma in GL2(Q); then gamma_p = k_p gamma with k_p in GL2(Z_p). gamma * f = k_p^{-1} * (gamma_p * f) is Z_p-integral for every p (GL2(Z_p) preserves V(Z_p)), hence integral.

### 1.8 Ternary-pair embedding and its fibres


<a id="embedding-into-pairs-of-ternary-quadratic-forms"></a>


**Embedding into pairs of ternary quadratic forms.** Let A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2 (Gram matrix antidiag(1/2, -1, 1/2)) and, for f = (a, b, c, d, e) in V_Z, B_f = a x_1^2 + b x_1 x_2 + c x_2^2 + d x_2 x_3 + e x_3^2 (Gram matrix (a, b/2, 0; b/2, c, d/2; 0, d/2, e)). Then phi(f) = (A_1, B_f) in W_{Z,1} = {(A_1, B)} (Bhargava-Shankar (30)). phi is injective, its image is the set of (A_1, B) with B_13 = 0, and every F_{Z,1}-class of W_{Z,1} (F_{Z,1} the lower unitriangular matrices of GL2(Z), acting by (A_1, B) |-> (A_1, B + r A_1)) has a unique representative in the image. phi preserves discriminants, and 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y) = x^3 + c x^2 y + (bd - 4ae) x y^2 + (a d^2 + b^2 e - 4ace) y^3 is the monic cubic resolvent of f (same I, J). With rho(gamma) = (det gamma)^{-1} (a^2, ab, b^2; 2ac, ad + bc, 2bd; c^2, cd, d^2) for gamma = (a b; c d), rho : GL2(Z) -> SO(A_1, Z) is a homomorphism and phi(gamma . f) = rho(gamma) . phi(f) modulo F_{Z,1}. The induced map psi : PGL2(Z)\V_Z -> (GL2(Z) x SL3(Z))\W_Z is the composite of the orbit bijection with forgetting the slice.

Throughout this assertion, rho is written in the coordinate order that makes phi equivariant for the action g . B = g B g^T; the matrix printed as (31) in Bhargava-Shankar has the coordinates in the reverse order. The resolvent form is 4 Det(A x - B y); the 'Det(Ax - By)' printed on p. 16 has leading coefficient 1/4.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `BinaryQuartic.veroneseForm`: A_1 = x_1 x_3 - x_2^2.

- `BinaryQuartic.embed`: phi(f) = (A_1, B_f).

- `BinaryQuartic.rho`: rho : GL2(Z) -> SL3(Z), in the coordinate order compatible with (30).

- `BinaryQuartic.slice`: W_{Z,1} = {(A, B) : A = A_1}.

- `BinaryQuartic.embed_injective`: phi is injective.

- `BinaryQuartic.mem_range_embed_iff`: The image of phi is {(A_1, B) : B_13 = 0}.

- `BinaryQuartic.exists_unique_normalized`: Each F_{Z,1}-class of the slice meets the image of phi exactly once.

- `BinaryQuartic.disc_embed`: Disc phi(f) = Disc f.

- `BinaryQuartic.resolventForm_embed`: 4 Det(A_1 x - B_f y) = x^3 + c x^2 y + (bd - 4ae) x y^2 + (ad^2 + b^2 e - 4ace) y^3.

- `BinaryQuartic.rho_det`: det rho(gamma) = 1.

- `BinaryQuartic.veroneseForm_comp_rho`: rho(gamma) preserves A_1.

- `BinaryQuartic.embed_smul`: phi(gamma . f) = rho(gamma) . phi(f) modulo F_{Z,1}.
