### 1.13 Weak-discriminant lifts and marked hyperdeterminants


<a id="refinement-weak-discriminant-divisibility"></a>


**Weak discriminant divisibility.** Specialize [strong weak discriminant](#strong-weak-discriminant) to the fixed-degree binary discriminant Δ_n and the Layer 1 coefficient order. For a prime p and integral fixed-degree coefficient vector f, p² strongly divides Δ(f) if p² divides Δ(f+p h) for every integral coefficient vector h. It weakly divides if p² divides Δ(f) and some h makes Δ(f+p h) indivisible by p². For a positive squarefree m, W_m^(2) imposes weak divisibility at every prime factor of m. For binary forms the p=2 weak locus is empty. These are the same strong and weak loci as Layer 0; this interface transports them to pencils and projective-root criteria.

Throughout this assertion, Binary homogeneous discriminant with fixed degree n≥2. Monic specialization permits only monic-family perturbations where the source specifies that family.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.StrongSquareDivides`: Every p-multiple coefficient perturbation still has discriminant divisible by p².

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.WeakSquareDivides`: The original discriminant is divisible by p² and there is a perturbation violating divisibility.

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.weak_strong_exclusive`: Weak and strong square divisibility cannot both hold.


To prove the assertion, Define perturbations in the actual coefficient lattice. Reduce the discriminant polynomial modulo p²; for odd p, the source characterizes the weak locus by a unique simple double root over F_p. Use Δ≡0 or1 modulo4 for the binary p=2 convention.

*Needs:* [strong weak discriminant](#strong-weak-discriminant), [binary discriminant](#refinement-binary-discriminant).

- For f=x³, every coefficient perturbation by a prime p has discriminant divisible by p².

<a id="refinement-q-hyperdeterminant"></a>


**Q hyperdeterminant.** For g≥1 and two g×(g+1) matrices U,V, remove column i from xU−yV and form the signed maximal minor (−1)^i det((xU−yV)_without_i), indexed from zero. Put their coefficients of x^{g−j}y^j into a (g+1)×(g+1) matrix and define Q(U,V) as its determinant. For a symmetric pair with upper-left g×g blocks zero, Q means this polynomial on the top-right blocks. It has degree g(g+1), is SL₂×SL_g×SL_{g+1}-invariant, and transforms under row and column changes with weights det(h)^{g+1}det(k)^g.

Throughout this assertion, Coefficient and minor order are fixed, so the sign is testable.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.qHyperdeterminant`: Return the signed-minor coefficient determinant.

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.qHyperdeterminant_transform`: Q(hUkᵀ,hVkᵀ)=det(h)^{g+1}det(k)^gQ(U,V).

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.qHyperdeterminant_scale`: Q(tU,tV)=t^{g(g+1)}Q(U,V).

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.qHyperdeterminant_sl2`: If ad−bc=1, Q(aU+bV,cU+dV)=Q(U,V). This is the invariance needed to undo the binary-variable change in the odd weak lift.


To prove the assertion, Compute signed maximal minors in the universal polynomial ring, extract their coefficient matrix, and take its determinant. Row and column transformations give the determinant weights. Binary-variable changes have determinant weight g(g+1)/2 and hence disappear for SL₂.

*Needs:* [symmetric pencil](#refinement-symmetric-pencil), `Matrix.det` (Mathlib).

([[75]](#ref-75), §3.2, (4)–(5), pp.9–10; BSWI (6), p.7.)

- For U=[[1,0,0],[0,1,0]],V=[[0,1,0],[0,0,1]], Q=−1.

- If g≥1 and U=V=0, Q=0.


<a id="refinement-q-discriminant-divisibility"></a>


**Q discriminant divisibility.** On the universal integral coordinate ring of pairs of symmetric (2g+1)×(2g+1) matrices with zero upper-left g×g blocks, Q² divides Δ(f_A,B). Consequently every integral evaluation satisfies Q(A,B)² | Δ(f_A,B). This polynomial divisibility is stronger than a statement at one prime.

Throughout this assertion, g≥1; universal integral coordinates before evaluation.


To prove the assertion, The Q polynomial is irreducible and primitive. A generic point of Q=0 can be put into the special minor normal form, which forces a double root of f. Perturbing a suitable entry gives a first-order Q zero but a second-order discriminant zero. This proves divisibility by Q twice over the fraction field; primitivity and Gauss’s lemma descend it to Z.

*Needs:* [q hyperdeterminant](#refinement-q-hyperdeterminant), [binary discriminant](#refinement-binary-discriminant).

<a id="refinement-marked-q"></a>


**Marked q.** For an integral symmetric pair (A,B) in odd dimension2g+1 with nonzero discriminant, mark a common rational g-plane U and its saturated lattice Λ=U∩Z^{2g+1}. Complete a Z-basis of Λ to a unimodular ambient basis and evaluate |Q| on the transformed top-right blocks. This is independent of the integral completion and is invariant on marked SL_{2g+1}(Z)-orbits. Forget Λ only when uniqueness of the common isotropic plane has been proved, e.g. for irreducible odd-degree f.

Throughout this assertion, The marking is a saturated lattice; arbitrary rational bases are not permitted.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.markedQ`: Evaluate absolute Q after an explicitly adapted unimodular matrix; retain the marking as data.

- `ArithmeticOrbitRefinement.markedQ_independent`: Two unimodular completions of the same primitive isotropic lattice give equal absolute Q.

To prove the assertion, Primitivity permits unimodular completion. Any two completions differ by an integral parabolic matrix whose determinant on the first block is ±1; the Q character therefore preserves the absolute value. The odd irreducible invariant has trivial rational Jacobian two-torsion, giving uniqueness of the marked plane.

<a id="refinement-weak-lift-odd"></a>


**Weak lift odd.** Let n=2g+1≥3 and m be an odd positive squarefree integer. There is a map σ_m:W_m^(2)→W₀(Z) with f_{σ_m(f)}=f and |Q|(σ_m(f))=m. **Even weak lift.** For n=2g+2≥4, odd positive squarefree m and f in the weak locus with gcd(m,f(0,1))=1, lift xf by the odd-degree σ_m into pairs of size n+1. ### 1.14 Genus-one stabilizer group schemes


<a id="refinement-genus-one-stabilizer-schemes"></a>


**Genus one stabilizer schemes.** Over a field of characteristic different from2,3,5, the nondegenerate binary quartic, ternary cubic, pair of quaternary quadrics and quintuple of quinary alternating matrices give the degree d=2,3,4,5 line-bundle presentations of smooth genus-one curves. Their full linear-group stabilizers are extensions of Aut(Jac(C)) (automorphisms fixing its elliptic origin) by the theta group Θ_{Jac(C),d}, which extends Jac(C)[d] by G_m. For rational-divisor formulations quotient the ineffective central scalars; the stabilizer becomes the corresponding extension by Jac(C)[d]. For fixed invariants and the differential-preserving degree2 PGL₂ action, recover the E[2] stabilizer with Galois action. These are different acting groups and must not be conflated. The acting groups are GL₂ twisted by det⁻² times the weight-two scalar G_m for degree2; GL₃ twisted by det⁻¹ times G_m for degree3; GL₂×GL₄ for degree4; and GL₅×GL₅ for degree5. The last two act naturally on 2⊗Sym²(4) and 5⊗∧²(5); their ineffective scalar kernel is (a,b) with ab²=1.

Throughout this assertion, The conservative common characteristic restriction is stronger than each degree2–4 source theorem and avoids the degree5 exceptional characteristic. Degree d line bundles and rational divisor classes are distinguished where the Brauer obstruction matters.

### 1.15 Quartic invariant index and étale resolvents


<a id="refinement-quartic-invariant-index"></a>


**Quartic invariant index.** For an integral quartic order Q of nonzero discriminant with cubic resolvent R, the subring generated by the scalar element and the quadratic resolvent map image is the cubic invariant order R_inv(Q), independent of the choice of R inside the rational resolvent algebra. Its index in R equals the content of Q. Thus R_inv(Q)=R exactly when Q has content one. For Q=Z+nQ′ with primitive Q′, the invariant order is Z+n²R_inv(Q′).

Throughout this assertion, Use the based quadratic resolvent map and scalar-compatible orientation. Content is the maximal positive integer n with Q=Z+nQ′. Nonzero discriminant ensures finite positive content and a full-rank invariant order; the infinite-content boundary is a separate obligation.


To prove the assertion, The gcd of coefficient minors equals content. In the primitive case the six coefficient columns generate the entire rank-two quotient of R, so the map image generates R. In general the quadratic map scales by n². The invariant-order index in the primitive resolvent is n⁴ and the given resolvent index is n³; divide to obtain n.

*Needs:* [quartic ring and cubic resolvent](#quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent), [existence and number of cubic resolvents](#existence-and-number-of-cubic-resolvents), [integral minor fibres](#refinement-integral-minor-fibres).

<a id="refinement-quartic-etale-resolvent"></a>


**Quartic etale resolvent.** Let Q be a quartic étale algebra over a characteristic-zero field K. The three partitions of its four geometric embeddings into two unordered pairs form a Galois set of size three. The associated cubic étale algebra is the rationalization of any cubic resolvent order of Q when such an order is given. A quartic field does not force its cubic resolvent algebra to be a field: a cyclic quartic extension has a fixed partition and yields K times a quadratic algebra. The discriminants of an integral quartic order and its cubic resolvent order agree; this is an equality of order discriminants, not a claim that both orders are maximal.

Throughout this assertion, Characteristic zero; four distinct geometric embeddings. An integral order/resolvent is specified for the discriminant comparison.


To prove the assertion, The S4 action on pair partitions factors through S3 with kernel the Klein four group. The quadratic resolvent expression xx′+x″x‴ takes one value for each partition. Descent identifies the resulting rank-three algebra with the invariant subalgebra in the rational S4-closure. Use the discriminant-preserving map to compare integral orders.

*Needs:* [quartic ring and cubic resolvent](#quartic-ring-and-cubic-resolvent), [nondegenerate forms and etale cubic algebras](#nondegenerate-forms-and-etale-cubic-algebras).

### 1.16 Good-prime integral pencils


<a id="refinement-good-prime-integral-pencils"></a>


**Good prime integral pencils.** Let p be odd, f an integral binary form of even degree n≥4 over Z_p with f₀≠0 and p² not dividing Δ(f). If the curve z²=f has an actual degree-one rational divisor over Q_p, extension of scalars gives a bijection from all SL_n/μ₂(Z_p)-orbits with invariant f to the soluble SL_n/μ₂(Q_p)-orbits with invariant f. For each integral representative, its integral and rational stabilizer point groups are equal. This is a local uniqueness theorem under the discriminant restriction, unlike the unrestricted existence theorem.

Throughout this assertion, p odd, p²∤Δ(f), f₀≠0. Div¹(C)(Q_p) is nonempty, rather than only a degree-one Picard class.


To prove the assertion, The discriminant restriction makes R_f maximal and the projective model regular. Proposition34 supplies integral representatives because powers of2 are units. Integral ideal-pair classes are the norm-one quotient of order units. Compare this group with J(Q_p)/2J(Q_p) through the connected Néron model. Norm-one two-torsion units are integral. In the n divisible by4 case, an additional quadratic splitting field is unramified, so the central quotient adds no nonintegral stabilizer.

### Supporting descent and integral realization

For degree three, four and five genus-one models prove the locally soluble rational-orbit dictionary with the actual `E[n]`-coverings, the identity covering, isogeny-compatible localization and the quotient group scheme. Over Q, an everywhere locally soluble class at the indicated integral invariants has an integral representative; local representatives patch with exactly the stated lattice, scalar and discriminant scaling. For degree three use the determinant-twisted PGL3 action, for degree four the determinant-constrained GL2×GL4 central quotient, and for degree five the determinant-constrained GL5×GL5 central quotient on `5⊗Λ²5`. The 40-dimensional quintic-ring representation is unrelated to the last carrier. Retain the rational versus integral stabilizer quotient in each fibre. Sources: Bhargava–Shankar, cubic Theorems 9–14, §§2–3; quaternary Theorems 7–10, §2; quinary Theorems 7–10, §2, with the numbered local orbit and integrality results cited in those sections. These assertions supply the exact descent-to-count bridge for the Layer 4 averages.

The BSS marked genus-one statistic requires an *even-degree monicization* adapter: from a locally soluble irreducible binary quartic and a two-covering of its Jacobian, construct the associated monic invariant and the integral self-adjoint/symmetric data with their leading-coefficient scaling. Prove injectivity at the required orbit level, describe every integral multiplicity and stabilizer, and identify the increasingly sparse congruence support as the leading coefficient grows. This is BSS, §§3–4 and the monicization steps in §§6–7, pp. 13–47. The odd-degree symmetric-pencil dictionary does not supply this even-degree map. Its local support is the input to the sparse quaternary count in Layer 2.

For a degree-three isogeny `φ:A→A′` over a number field, construct the mirror étale quadratic algebra and normalized binary-cubic discriminant, identify rational SL2 orbits with the appropriate `H¹(F,A[φ])` classes and identify soluble orbits with the local Kummer image. The ordinary binary-cubic discriminant is minus 27 times the normalized invariant. Prove the integral orbit multiplicity and local mass identities for that algebra, including the primes above two and three. This is the isogeny-specific dictionary of BKLOS §§3–7 and Theorem 7.2; cubic-field discriminant parametrization is not its substitute. The extension from elliptic to general abelian degree-three kernels uses the same finite kernel and its Galois action, with the actual isogeny Kummer maps.

Quintic integral realization also includes rational *nonétale* algebras. Prove the polynomial multiplication construction is associative and unital over every coefficient ring, not merely after checking the generic S5 closure. Compare the nonzero-discriminant locus with the trace-dual resolvent construction and then extend the universal identities by polynomial density. The based sextic discriminant is `(16 disc R)³`. Sources are HCL IV, §§2–4, including its multiplication and resolvent formulas. When checking the quartic structure formula, the summed index condition is `k≠i`; swapping it to `k≠j` fails the ring identities.

### Examples

For `xy(x-y)` the integral twisted cubic stabilizer has six elements, so the order-three-or-trivial assertion must assume rational irreducibility. A zero cubic remains a cubic-ring tensor with degenerate discriminant; it is not an étale algebra. The cubic `x³-x` has nonzero discriminant four, and its reduction modulo two is not squarefree, illustrating why maximality and squarefree polynomial discriminant are distinct predicates.

The point-quartic construction sends the point at infinity to the specified linear-factor orbit. For a finite point the denominators 6, 27 and 432 require the characteristic exclusions in the formula. For pencils, a vector-space isotropic g-plane is a projective `(g-1)`-plane. At p=2 a polar-isotropic plane need not make the quadratic form vanish. The quotient `(SL_n/μ₂)(Q)` must be evaluated as rational points of a group scheme; it can exceed `SL_n(Q)/{±1}`.

## Layer 2: Uniform orbit counts and sieves

Start with compact semialgebraic counts and then average arithmetic fundamental domains, preserving multiplicities and stabilizers. A finite-congruence asymptotic and a uniform large-prime tail are separate assertions. Only after both are proved may finite truncations converge to an infinite Euler product. Summed square-divisor tails count a divisor multiplicity and require more than an estimate for the union of bad loci.


### 2.1 Geometric sieves and prime tails


<a id="chebyshev-bounds-for-prime-sums"></a>


**Chebyshev bounds for prime sums.** (a) There is an absolute constant C such that π(x) ≤ C·x/log x for every real x ≥ 2, where π(x) is the number of primes p ≤ x. (b) For every real s > 1 there is a constant C_s such that Σ_{p prime, p > N} p^{−s} ≤ C_s·N^{1−s}/log N for every real N ≥ 2. (c) Consequently, for every integer k ≥ 2 there is C_k with Σ_{p prime, M < p ≤ r} r^n/p^k ≤ C_k·r^n/(M^{k−1} log M) for all reals 2 ≤ M ≤ r and every n ≥ 0.

Throughout this assertion, x, N, M ≥ 2 so that the logarithms are positive; the sums run over rational primes The constants are absolute (C) or depend only on s (C_s) or k (C_k); in particular they are independent of N, M, r and n


To prove the assertion, (a) Split the primes p ≤ x at √x. Every prime in (√x, x] has log p > (1/2) log x, so π(x) − π(√x) ≤ 2θ(x)/log x ≤ 2 log 4 · x/log x by Chebyshev's bound θ(x) ≤ (log 4)x (Chebyshev.theta_le_log4_mul_x, with θ written as a sum over primes by Chebyshev.theta_eq_sum_primesLE); and π(√x) ≤ √x ≤ 2x/log x for x ≥ 2. (b) Decompose (N, ∞) into dyadic blocks (2^j N, 2^{j+1} N], j ≥ 0. By (a) the block contains at most C·2^{j+1}N/log(2^{j+1}N) ≤ 2C·2^j N/log N primes, each contributing at most (2^j N)^{−s}. Summing the geometric series Σ_j 2^{j(1−s)} = (1 − 2^{1−s})^{−1} gives C_s = 2C/(1 − 2^{1−s}). (c) is (b) with s = k, multiplied by r^n, after dropping the upper limit r.

*Needs:* `Chebyshev.theta_le_log4_mul_x` (Mathlib), `Chebyshev.theta_eq_sum_primesLE` (Mathlib), `Nat.Prime` (Mathlib).

<a id="lattice-points-on-a-subvariety-in-a-dilated-region"></a>


**Lattice points on a subvariety in a dilated region.** Let B ⊂ ℝ^n be a compact set and let Y ⊆ 𝔸^n_ℚ be a Zariski-closed subset of codimension ≥ k ≥ 1, i.e. Y = V(𝔞) for an ideal 𝔞 ⊆ ℚ[x_1, …, x_n] with Krull dimension of ℚ[x_1, …, x_n]/𝔞 at most n − k. Then there is a constant C = C(B, Y) such that #{a ∈ rB ∩ ℤ^n : a ∈ Y(ℚ)} ≤ C·r^{n−k} for every real r ≥ 1.

Throughout this assertion, B compact (the source says 'compact region having finite measure'; only boundedness is used) r ≥ 1: for 0 < r < 1 the left side can be 1 (the origin) while r^{n−k} → 0 The constant depends on B and Y only, not on r


To prove the assertion, Work with reduced closed subsets and sum over finitely many irreducible components. For an integral Y of dimension d ≤ n−k, prove the O(r^d) bound by lexicographic induction on (d,n); the empty variety contributes zero and a zero-dimensional variety has finitely many rational points. Let pi forget the last coordinate and Z be the Zariski closure of pi(Y). Since its coordinate ring is generated over that of Z by one element, dim Z is d or d−1. If dim Z=d−1, the closed inclusion Y ⊂ Z×A¹ of integral varieties of equal dimension is equality. Apply induction to Z and multiply by the O(r) choices of the last coordinate. If dim Z=d, the last coordinate is algebraic over Frac(Q[Z]). Clearing denominators gives f in I(Y), viewed as a polynomial in x_n, whose leading coefficient h is nonzero on Z. For b with h(b)≠0, there are at most deg_{x_n} f rational roots above b. Induction on the smaller ambient dimension bounds the number of b in pi(rB)∩Z(Q)∩Z^{n−1} by O(r^d). The exceptional closed subset Y∩V(h) has dimension at most d−1. Apply the induction hypothesis in the same ambient space but smaller dimension to obtain O(r^{d−1}) points, hence O(r^d) for r≥1. The projection/dimension and finite-decomposition interfaces are requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.0; no unsupported resultant replacement is used.

*Needs:* SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.0, `Polynomial.card_roots'` (Mathlib), `MvPolynomial` (Mathlib).

**Quantitative ekedahl geometric sieve.** Let B ⊂ ℝ^n be a compact set and let Y ⊆ 𝔸^n_ℤ be a closed subscheme of codimension k ≥ 1 (Krull dimension of its coordinate ring ≤ n + 1 − k). Then there is a constant C = C(B, Y) such that for all reals r ≥ 1 and M ≥ 2, #{a ∈ rB ∩ ℤ^n : a mod p ∈ Y(𝔽_p) for some prime p > M} ≤ C·(r^n/(M^{k−1} log M) + r^{n−k+1}).

Throughout this assertion, r ≥ 1 and M ≥ 2 The content is for k ≥ 2; for k = 1 the right side is of order r^n and the statement is trivial The region is a fixed compact set dilated by r; Bhargava's Theorem 3.5 (diagonal SL_n-transforms of rB) is a variant not needed by the consumers here


To prove the assertion, For k=1 use the trivial O(r^n) bound. For k≥2, apply the following three bounds directly to Y; the two sieve lemmas already handle its components and finitely many exceptional primes. Points of Y(ℤ) in rB: O(r^{n−k}) by [lattice points on a subvariety in a dilated region](#lattice-points-on-a-subvariety-in-a-dilated-region). Points a ∉ Y(ℤ) reducing into Y(𝔽_p) for some p with M < p ≤ r: O(r^n/(M^{k−1} log M)) by [geometric sieve small primes](#geometric-sieve-small-primes). Points a ∉ Y(ℤ) reducing into Y(𝔽_p) for some p > max(M, r): O(r^{n−k+1}) by [geometric sieve large primes](#geometric-sieve-large-primes) (a point is counted at most once per prime, and the count of pairs bounds the count of points). Sum the three bounds.

*Needs:* [lattice points on a subvariety in a dilated region](#lattice-points-on-a-subvariety-in-a-dilated-region), [geometric sieve small primes](#geometric-sieve-small-primes), [geometric sieve large primes](#geometric-sieve-large-primes).

- Bhargava-Shankar apply it with n = 5, k = 2, r = X^{1/6} to Y = V(Δ, ∂Δ/∂e) on binary quartic forms and obtain O(X^{5/6}/(M log M) + X^{2/3}) (their Theorem 2.18); the cubic analogue has n = 4, k = 2, r = X^{1/4}, giving O(X/(M log M) + X^{3/4}).

- Ekedahl's qualitative statement is the limit form: lim_{M→∞} lim sup_{r→∞} r^{−n}·#{…} = 0 for k ≥ 2.

- For k = 2 and Y = V(x_1, x_2), the left side counts points with a prime p > M dividing gcd(a_1, a_2); its density is 1 − ∏_{p > M}(1 − p^{−2}) ≍ 1/(M log M), so the first term is sharp.


<a id="strongly-and-weakly-divisible-values"></a>


**Strongly and weakly divisible values.** Let f ∈ ℤ[x_1, …, x_n], a ∈ ℤ^n, p a prime and j ≥ 1. The value of f is strongly a multiple of p^j at a if f(a′) ≡ 0 (mod p^j) for every a′ ∈ ℤ^n with a′ ≡ a (mod p); it is weakly a multiple of p^j at a if p^j | f(a) but f is not strongly a multiple of p^j at a. For binary quartic forms V_ℤ ≅ ℤ^5 (coefficients (a, b, c, d, e) of ax^4 + bx^3y + cx^2y^2 + dxy^3 + ey^4) with the discriminant Δ = (4I^3 − J^2)/27 of [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs), put W_p(V) := {f ∈ V_ℤ : p^2 | Δ(f)}, W_p^(1)(V) := {f : Δ is strongly a multiple of p^2 at f} (equivalently p^2 | Δ(f + pg) for every g ∈ V_ℤ) and W_p^(2)(V) := W_p(V) \ W_p^(1)(V). For binary cubic forms U_ℤ ≅ ℤ^4 (coefficients (a, b, c, d) of ax^3 + bx^2y + cxy^2 + dy^3) with Disc = b^2c^2 − 4ac^3 − 4b^3d − 27a^2d^2 + 18abcd, put W_p(U), W_p^(1)(U), W_p^(2)(U) in the same way.

Throughout this assertion, p is a rational prime; the definitions make sense for every p, but the splitting-type descriptions below hold only for p ≥ 3 Strong divisibility depends only on a mod p; weak divisibility of p^2 depends on a mod p^2 For j = 1 there are no weak multiples: f(a′) ≡ f(a) (mod p) for a′ ≡ a (mod p)

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `StronglyDvdAt`: The predicate 'f is strongly a multiple of p^j at a': ∀ a′ ≡ a (mod p), p^j | f(a′).

- `WeaklyDvdAt`: The predicate 'p^j | f(a) and not StronglyDvdAt'.

- `stronglyDvdAt_two_iff`: StronglyDvdAt f p 2 a ↔ p^2 | f(a) ∧ ∀ i, p | ∂f/∂x_i(a).

- `stronglyDvdAt_congr`: a ≡ a′ (mod p) → (StronglyDvdAt f p j a ↔ StronglyDvdAt f p j a′).

- `weaklyDvdAt_of_not_dvd_pderiv`: p^2 | f(a) and p ∤ ∂f/∂x_i(a) for some i imply WeaklyDvdAt f p 2 a.

- `stronglyDvdAt_one_iff`: StronglyDvdAt f p 1 a ↔ p | f(a) (no weak multiples of p).

- `quarticW_smul`: γ ∈ GL_2(ℤ): γ·f ∈ W_p(V) ↔ f ∈ W_p(V), and likewise for W_p^(1)(V), W_p^(2)(V), W_p(U), W_p^(1)(U), W_p^(2)(U).

- `quarticW1_iff_splittingType`: For p ≥ 3: f ∈ W_p^(1)(V) iff f ∈ pV_ℤ or f mod p has splitting type (1^3 1), (1^2 1^2), (2^2) or (1^4).

- `cubicW1_iff_tripleRoot`: For p ≥ 3: f ∈ W_p^(1)(U) iff f ∈ pU_ℤ or f mod p has a triple root in ℙ^1(𝔽_p).


To prove the assertion, The predicates are decidable conditions on residue classes: strong divisibility quantifies over the finitely many a′ mod p^j with a′ ≡ a (mod p). For j = 2, Taylor expansion f(a + pb) ≡ f(a) + p Σ_i b_i ∂f/∂x_i(a) (mod p^2) (MvPolynomial.pderiv) shows: f is strongly a multiple of p^2 at a iff p^2 | f(a) and p | ∂f/∂x_i(a) for every i. GL_2(ℤ)-invariance of W_p, W_p^(1), W_p^(2) on V_ℤ and U_ℤ: Δ(γ·f) = Δ(f) (resp. Disc(γ·f) = Disc(f)) for γ ∈ GL_2(ℤ) because det γ = ±1 and the weights are even, and γ·(f + pg) = γ·f + p(γ·g) with γ·g integral.

*Needs:* [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs), `MvPolynomial` (Mathlib), `MvPolynomial.pderiv` (Mathlib), `Nat.Prime` (Mathlib).

- Every f ∈ pV_ℤ lies in W_p^(1)(V), since Δ is homogeneous of degree 6 and Δ(pg) = p^6 Δ(g).

<a id="strong-divisibility-lies-on-a-codimension-two-locus"></a>


**Strong divisibility lies on a codimension two locus.** Let f ∈ ℤ[x_1, …, x_n] and let Y_f ⊆ 𝔸^n_ℤ be the closed subscheme V(f, ∂f/∂x_n). (a) For every prime p and every a ∈ ℤ^n at which f is strongly a multiple of p^2, a mod p ∈ Y_f(𝔽_p). (b) If f is primitive (the gcd of its coefficients is 1) and f and ∂f/∂x_n have no common factor of positive degree in ℚ[x_1, …, x_n], then Y_f has codimension at least 2 (possibly empty) in 𝔸^n_ℤ.

Throughout this assertion, In (b) the hypothesis is coprimality of f and ∂f/∂x_n over ℚ; the source assumes f irreducible and nonconstant in x_n, which implies it Primitivity excludes vertical components: if every coefficient of f were divisible by p_0, the whole fibre over p_0 would lie in Y_f


To prove the assertion, (a) Taylor: f(a + p t e_n) ≡ f(a) + p t ∂f/∂x_n(a) (mod p^2) for t ∈ ℤ. Strong divisibility gives p^2 | f(a + p t e_n) for all t, hence p | f(a) and p | ∂f/∂x_n(a). (b) Horizontal part: coprimality in ℚ[x] makes V(f, ∂f/∂x_n) ⊆ 𝔸^n_ℚ of dimension ≤ n − 2, so the closure in 𝔸^n_ℤ has dimension ≤ n − 1. Vertical part: over a prime p_0, f mod p_0 is a nonzero polynomial by primitivity, so the fibre of Y_f over p_0 lies in the hypersurface V(f mod p_0) of dimension n − 1. Hence dim Y_f ≤ n − 1 = (n + 1) − 2.

*Needs:* [strongly and weakly divisible values](#strongly-and-weakly-divisible-values), `MvPolynomial.pderiv` (Mathlib), `MvPolynomial` (Mathlib).

- The converse of (a) fails: the weakly divisible form 25x^4 + x^2y^2 + y^4 at p = 5 reduces into Y_Δ(𝔽_5). Consumers therefore bound the larger set {a : a mod p ∈ Y_f(𝔽_p)}, which is what the geometric sieve counts.

- Without primitivity (b) fails: f = 3x_1 x_2 has Y_f ⊇ V(3), a component of codimension 1 in 𝔸^2_ℤ.

- The conclusion is codimension at least two: f=x_n has derivative 1 and Y_f is empty. Exact codimension two would be false without an additional nonemptiness hypothesis.


<a id="discriminant-loci-of-codimension-two"></a>


**Discriminant loci of codimension two.** (a) The binary quartic discriminant Δ(a, b, c, d, e) = (4I^3 − J^2)/27 ∈ ℤ[a, b, c, d, e] is primitive, has degree 3 in e with leading coefficient 256a^3, and Δ and ∂Δ/∂e have no common factor of positive degree in ℚ[a, b, c, d, e]. (b) The binary cubic discriminant Disc(a, b, c, d) = b^2c^2 − 4ac^3 − 4b^3d − 27a^2d^2 + 18abcd ∈ ℤ[a, b, c, d] is primitive, has degree 2 in d with leading coefficient −27a^2, and Disc and ∂Disc/∂d have no common factor of positive degree in ℚ[a, b, c, d]. (c) Consequently Y_4 := V(Δ, ∂Δ/∂e) ⊆ 𝔸^5_ℤ and Y_3 := V(Disc, ∂Disc/∂d) ⊆ 𝔸^4_ℤ have codimension 2.

Throughout this assertion, The polynomials are those of [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) (Δ) and of the Delone-Faddeev normalisation (Disc)


To prove the assertion, Primitivity: Δ contains 256a^3e^3 and −27a^2d^4, and gcd(256, 27) = 1; Disc contains b^2c^2 with coefficient 1. No common factor free of e: the e-coefficients of Δ have gcd 1 in ℚ[a, b, c, d], since the leading one is 256a^3 and the constant term is Δ(a, b, c, d, 0) = d^2·Disc(a, b, c, d), which is not divisible by a (it contains b^2c^2d^2). Likewise the d-coefficients of Disc, −27a^2 and b^2c^2 − 4ac^3, are coprime. No common factor involving e: the resultant Res_e(Δ, ∂Δ/∂e) ∈ ℚ[a, b, c, d] is nonzero because its specialisation at (a, b, c, d) = (1, 0, 0, 1) is Res_e(256e^3 − 27, 768e^2) ≠ 0 (e = 0 is not a root of 256e^3 − 27); by Polynomial.resultant_eq_zero_iff over the field ℚ(a, b, c, d) and Gauss's lemma, Δ and ∂Δ/∂e are coprime. For Disc specialise (a, b, c) = (1, 0, 1): Res_d(−4 − 27d^2, −54d) ≠ 0. (c) follows from (a), (b) and part (b) of [strong divisibility lies on a codimension two locus](#strong-divisibility-lies-on-a-codimension-two-locus).

*Needs:* [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs), [strong divisibility lies on a codimension two locus](#strong-divisibility-lies-on-a-codimension-two-locus), `Polynomial.resultant` (Mathlib), `Polynomial.resultant_eq_zero_iff` (Mathlib).

- deg_e Δ = 3, so ∂Δ/∂e has degree 2 in e.


<a id="local-density-of-values-divisible-by-p-squared"></a>


**Local density of values divisible by p squared.** Let f ∈ ℤ[x_1, …, x_n] be primitive and coprime to ∂f/∂x_n in ℚ[x_1, …, x_n]. There is C = C(f) such that for every prime p, #{v ∈ (ℤ/p^2ℤ)^n : f(v) ≡ 0 (mod p^2)} ≤ C·p^{2n−2}; equivalently, the Haar measure (total mass 1) of {v ∈ ℤ_p^n : p^2 | f(v)} is at most C·p^{−2}.

Throughout this assertion, Applies to f = Δ on V (n = 5) and f = Disc on U (n = 4) by [discriminant loci of codimension two](#discriminant-loci-of-codimension-two) The bound is uniform in p; the constant depends only on f


To prove the assertion, Group the classes v mod p^2 by a = v mod p with p | f(a). Classes with a ∈ Y_f(𝔽_p) (p | ∂f/∂x_n(a) as well): there are at most C p^{n−2} such a for p > M_0 ([uniform bound for points of a subscheme modulo p](#uniform-bound-for-points-of-a-subscheme-modulo-p), Y_f of codimension 2 by [strong divisibility lies on a codimension two locus](#strong-divisibility-lies-on-a-codimension-two-locus)), each with p^n lifts, giving at most C p^{2n−2}; the primes p ≤ M_0 are absorbed into C. Classes with p ∤ ∂f/∂x_n(a): there are at most deg(f)·p^{n−1} such a, since f mod p is a nonzero polynomial by primitivity (MvPolynomial.schwartz_zippel_totalDegree). For each, f(a + pb) ≡ f(a) + p Σ_i b_i ∂f/∂x_i(a) (mod p^2) is an affine condition on b mod p whose b_n-coefficient is a unit, so exactly p^{n−1} of the p^n lifts satisfy p^2 | f; this gives at most deg(f)·p^{2n−2}. Divide by p^{2n} for the measure statement (the set is a union of classes mod p^2 in ℤ_p^n).

*Needs:* [strongly and weakly divisible values](#strongly-and-weakly-divisible-values), [strong divisibility lies on a codimension two locus](#strong-divisibility-lies-on-a-codimension-two-locus), [uniform bound for points of a subscheme modulo p](#uniform-bound-for-points-of-a-subscheme-modulo-p), `MvPolynomial.schwartz_zippel_totalDegree` (Mathlib), `PadicInt` (Mathlib).

- For f = Δ this is the bound (43) of Bhargava-Shankar, 1 − ∫φ_p ≤ ∫_{p^2 | Δ} df ≪ p^{−2}, which the source takes from Poonen's paper; the proof here needs only the codimension-two locus and Schwartz-Zippel.

### 2.2 Real quartic orbits and fundamental sets


<a id="real-root-types-of-binary-quartic-forms"></a>


**Real root types of binary quartic forms.** Let V_ℝ be the space of real binary quartic forms f = ax^4 + bx^3y + cx^2y^2 + dxy^3 + ey^4 with the discriminant Δ of [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs). For f with Δ(f) ≠ 0 the roots of f in ℙ^1(ℂ) are four distinct points permuted by complex conjugation; let r(f) ∈ {0, 2, 4} be the number of real ones (a root at [1 : 0] when a = 0 included). For i = 0, 1, 2 put V_ℝ^(i) := {f : Δ(f) ≠ 0, r(f) = 4 − 2i}; V_ℝ^(2+) (resp. V_ℝ^(2−)) is the set of positive (resp. negative) definite forms, f(x, y) > 0 (resp. < 0) for all (x, y) ≠ (0, 0), so V_ℝ^(2) = V_ℝ^(2+) ⊔ V_ℝ^(2−). The index set is T := {0, 1, 2+, 2−}. For i ∈ T put V_ℤ^(i) := V_ℝ^(i) ∩ V_ℤ.

Throughout this assertion, Only forms with Δ ≠ 0 lie in any locus The loci are defined for the standard action f ↦ f((x, y)γ) of GL_2(ℝ), which preserves them

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `QuarticRealType`: The four-element index type T = {0, 1, 2+, 2−}.

- `quarticLocus`: quarticLocus i ⊆ V_ℝ, the locus V_ℝ^(i).

- `mem_quarticLocus_iff_realRoots`: For i ∈ {0, 1}: f ∈ V_ℝ^(i) ↔ Δ(f) ≠ 0 ∧ r(f) = 4 − 2i; f ∈ V_ℝ^(2±) ↔ Δ(f) ≠ 0 ∧ ±f > 0 on ℝ^2 \ {0}.

- `disc_pos_of_mem_quarticLocus`: Δ > 0 on V_ℝ^(0), V_ℝ^(2+), V_ℝ^(2−) and Δ < 0 on V_ℝ^(1).

- `iUnion_quarticLocus`: The loci are pairwise disjoint with union {f : Δ(f) ≠ 0}.

- `isOpen_quarticLocus`: Each V_ℝ^(i) is open in V_ℝ ≅ ℝ^5.

- `smul_mem_quarticLocus_iff`: For γ ∈ GL_2(ℝ): γ·f ∈ V_ℝ^(i) ↔ f ∈ V_ℝ^(i) (standard action).

- `neg_mem_quarticLocus_twoPos_iff`: −f ∈ V_ℝ^(2−) ↔ f ∈ V_ℝ^(2+).

- `intQuarticLocus`: V_ℤ^(i) := {f ∈ V_ℤ : (f : V_ℝ) ∈ V_ℝ^(i)}.


To prove the assertion, The real roots are counted on ℙ^1(ℝ): the number of real roots of f(x, 1) (Polynomial.roots over ℝ) plus 1 when a = 0. Definiteness: a real binary quartic with Δ ≠ 0 and no real root takes one sign on ℝ^2 \ {0} (connectedness), so V_ℝ^(2) splits into the two definite loci.

*Needs:* [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs), `MvPolynomial.IsHomogeneous` (Mathlib).

([[1]](#ref-1), Section 2.1, printed p. 8.)


**Checks.**


- x^3y − xy^3 ∈ V_ℝ^(0) and Δ(x^3y − xy^3) = 4.

- x^3y + xy^3 ∈ V_ℝ^(1) and Δ(x^3y + xy^3) = −4.

- x^4 + y^4 ∈ V_ℝ^(2+), −x^4 − y^4 ∈ V_ℝ^(2−), and Δ(x^4 + y^4) = 256.

- x^3y − xy^3 and x^4 + y^4 both have Δ > 0 but lie in different loci, so the loci are not determined by the sign of Δ.

- x^2y^2 (Δ = 0) lies in no V_ℝ^(i).

- x^3y − xy^3 = xy(x − y)(x + y) ∈ V_ℝ^(0) with Δ = 4; x^3y + xy^3 = xy(x^2 + y^2) ∈ V_ℝ^(1) with Δ = −4; x^4 + y^4 ∈ V_ℝ^(2+) with Δ = 256.

- The sign of Δ does not separate V_ℝ^(0) from V_ℝ^(2): both have Δ > 0.


<a id="real-orbits-of-binary-quartic-forms-with-fixed-invariants"></a>


**Real orbits of binary quartic forms with fixed invariants.** Let (I_0, J_0) ∈ ℝ^2 with 4I_0^3 − J_0^2 ≠ 0. (a) If 4I_0^3 − J_0^2 < 0, the forms f ∈ V_ℝ with (I(f), J(f)) = (I_0, J_0) form exactly one SL_2^±(ℝ)-orbit, and it lies in V_ℝ^(1). (b) If 4I_0^3 − J_0^2 > 0, they form exactly three SL_2^±(ℝ)-orbits, one contained in each of V_ℝ^(0), V_ℝ^(2+) and V_ℝ^(2−). (c) Consequently, for i ∈ T, two forms f_1, f_2 ∈ V_ℝ^(i) are GL_2(ℝ)-equivalent iff there is λ > 0 with I(f_1) = λ^2 I(f_2) and J(f_1) = λ^3 J(f_2).

Throughout this assertion, SL_2^±(ℝ) = {γ : det γ = ±1} acts by the standard action f ↦ f((x, y)γ), which preserves I and J (weights (det γ)^4 and (det γ)^6) 4I^3 − J^2 = 27Δ, so the two cases are Δ < 0 and Δ > 0


To prove the assertion, SL_2^±(ℝ)/{±1} = PGL_2(ℝ) acts on ℙ^1(ℝ) simply 3-transitively and on the upper half-plane transitively with stabiliser SO_2(ℝ)/{±1} at i; −1 acts trivially on quartic forms. Four real roots: move three roots to ∞, 0, 1, so f = c·xy(x − y)(x − μy) with c ≠ 0, μ ∈ ℝ \ {0, 1}; then I = c^2(μ^2 − μ + 1), J = c^3(μ + 1)(2μ − 1)(μ − 2) and 4I^3 − J^2 = 27c^6μ^2(μ − 1)^2 > 0. The ratio J^2/I^3 is a degree-6 function of μ invariant under the anharmonic group generated by μ ↦ 1/μ and μ ↦ 1 − μ (the relabellings of the roots), takes every value in [0, 4) on ℝ \ {0, 1}, and each fibre is one orbit; so (I_0, J_0) determines μ up to relabelling and then c (c^2 = I_0/(μ^2 − μ + 1), the sign from J_0; for J_0 = 0 the forms ±xy(x − y)(x + y) are exchanged by (x, y) ↦ (y, x)). Two real roots: move them to 0 and ∞ and the conjugate pair onto the unit circle (the diagonal torus fixes 0, ∞ and rescales), so f = c·xy(x^2 + pxy + y^2) with |p| < 2; I = c^2(p^2 − 3), J = c^3 p(9 − 2p^2), 4I^3 − J^2 = 27c^6(p^2 − 4) < 0; the symmetry (x, y) ↦ (−x, y) identifies (c, p) with (−c, −p), and for c > 0 the map p ↦ (I, J) up to the weighted scaling is a bijection from (−2, 2) onto the ratios with 4I^3 < J^2. No real roots: move one conjugate pair to ±i and rotate by the stabiliser of i so that the other is ±iρ with 0 < ρ < 1, so f = c(x^2 + y^2)(x^2 + ρ^2y^2); I = c^2(ρ^4 + 14ρ^2 + 1), J = −2c^3(1 + ρ^2)(ρ^2 − 6ρ + 1)(ρ^2 + 6ρ + 1), 4I^3 − J^2 = 432c^6ρ^2(1 − ρ^2)^4 > 0; the sign of c is the definiteness, and for fixed sign ρ ↦ (I, J) up to scaling is a bijection from (0, 1) onto the ratios with 4I^3 > J^2. Assemble: in each root type the normal form is determined by (I, J), which gives (a) and (b) and shows that the invariants map each type onto the stated sign of Δ. (c): I(γf) = (det γ)^4 I(f), J(γf) = (det γ)^6 J(f), so GL_2(ℝ)-equivalent forms have (I, J) related by λ = (det γ)^2 > 0; conversely scale by λ^{1/4}·1 ∈ Λ to equalise the invariants and apply (a)/(b) within the fixed locus.

<a id="stabilizers-of-real-binary-quartic-forms"></a>


**Stabilizers of real binary quartic forms.** Let f ∈ V_ℝ^(i) (so Δ(f) ≠ 0). Then the stabiliser of f in GL_2(ℝ) for the standard action has order 8 if i ∈ {0, 2+, 2−} and order 4 if i = 1; it contains ±1 and consists of elements of determinant ±1. Define n_i := #Stab_{GL_2(ℝ)}(f)/2, so n_0 = n_{2+} = n_{2−} = 4 and n_1 = 2.

Throughout this assertion, Standard (untwisted) action f ↦ f((x, y)γ) Δ(f) ≠ 0 is essential: x^2y^2 has an infinite stabiliser


To prove the assertion, If γ·f = f then I(f) = (det γ)^4 I(f) and J(f) = (det γ)^6 J(f); as (I, J) ≠ (0, 0) (Δ ≠ 0), det γ = ±1. On matrices of determinant ±1 the standard action agrees with the twisted action γ·f = (det γ)^{−2} f((x, y)γ), which factors through PGL_2(ℝ); every class in PGL_2(ℝ) has a representative of determinant ±1, unique up to ±1. Hence #Stab_{GL_2(ℝ)}(f) = 2·#Stab_{PGL_2(ℝ)}(f). By [stabilizer of a binary quartic is two torsion](#stabilizer-of-a-binary-quartic-is-two-torsion) (second paragraph of Bhargava-Shankar Theorem 3.2, with K = ℝ), Stab_{PGL_2(ℝ)}(f) ≅ E(ℝ)[2] for E : y^2 = x^3 − (I/3)x − J/27. #E(ℝ)[2] = 1 + (number of real roots of x^3 − (I/3)x − J/27). The discriminant of this cubic is 4(I/3)^3 − 27(J/27)^2 = Δ(f); by Cubic.discr_eq_prod_three_roots it is a positive multiple of ((x − y)(x − z)(y − z))^2, which is positive for three real roots and negative for one real root and a conjugate pair. So #E(ℝ)[2] = 4 if Δ > 0 and 2 if Δ < 0. Combine with the sign of Δ on the loci ([real root types of binary quartic forms](#real-root-types-of-binary-quartic-forms)): orders 8, 4, 8, 8.

<a id="fundamental-sets-for-real-binary-quartic-orbits"></a>


**Fundamental sets for real binary quartic orbits.** Define bounded sets of real binary quartic forms: L^(0) := {x^3y − (1/3)xy^3 − (J/27)y^4 : −2 < J < 2}; L^(1) := {x^3y − (I/3)xy^3 ± (2/27)y^4 : −1 ≤ I < 1} ∪ {x^3y + (1/3)xy^3 − (J/27)y^4 : −2 < J < 2}; L^(2+) := {(1/16)x^4 − (√(2 − J)/(3√3))x^3y + (1/2)x^2y^2 + y^4 : −2 < J < 2}; L^(2−) := {−f : f ∈ L^(2+)}. Then for each i ∈ T: (a) L^(i) ⊆ V_ℝ^(i) and every f ∈ L^(i) has H(f) = max(|I(f)|^3, J(f)^2/4) = 1; (b) f ↦ (I(f), J(f)) is a bijection from L^(i) onto {(I, J) : H(I, J) = 1, 4I^3 − J^2 > 0} (i ∈ {0, 2±}) or onto {(I, J) : H(I, J) = 1, 4I^3 − J^2 < 0} (i = 1); (c) every GL_2(ℝ)-orbit in V_ℝ^(i) meets L^(i) in exactly one point, and the same holds for h·L^(i) for every h ∈ GL_2(ℝ); (d) all coefficients of all forms in L^(i) have absolute value at most 1. Put R^(i) := Λ·L^(i) = {λ·f : λ > 0, f ∈ L^(i)} (λ·f = f((x, y)λ) = λ^4 f); then f ↦ (I(f), J(f)) is a bijection from R^(i) onto {(I, J) : 4I^3 − J^2 > 0} (resp. < 0), with inverse (I, J) ↦ p^(i)_{I,J}.

Throughout this assertion, The ± in the first family of L^(1) gives J = ∓2 Scaling by λ ∈ Λ multiplies (I, J) by (λ^8, λ^12), i.e. by (μ^2, μ^3) with μ = λ^4

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `quarticFundSet`: quarticFundSet i = L^(i) ⊆ V_ℝ, given by the explicit parametrisations of Table 1.

- `quarticFundSet_subset_locus`: L^(i) ⊆ V_ℝ^(i).

- `height_eq_one_of_mem_quarticFundSet`: f ∈ L^(i) → H(f) = 1.

- `invariants_bijOn_quarticFundSet`: (I, J) is a bijection from L^(i) onto the height-one pairs with the sign condition of i.

- `existsUnique_smul_mem_quarticFundSet`: For f ∈ V_ℝ^(i) and h ∈ GL_2(ℝ) there is a unique f′ ∈ h·L^(i) that is GL_2(ℝ)-equivalent to f.

- `abs_coeff_le_one_of_mem_quarticFundSet`: Every coefficient of every f ∈ L^(i) has absolute value ≤ 1 (boundedness).

- `quarticSection`: The section p^(i) : {(I, J) : sign condition} → R^(i) = Λ·L^(i) with invariants (I, J).

- `invariants_quarticSection`: (I, J)(p^(i)_{I,J}) = (I, J).


To prove the assertion, Compute invariants: for x^3y − (1/3)xy^3 − (J/27)y^4, I = −3·1·(−1/3) = 1 and J(f) = −27·(−J/27) = J; for x^3y − (I/3)xy^3 ± (2/27)y^4, (I(f), J(f)) = (I, ∓2); for x^3y + (1/3)xy^3 − (J/27)y^4, (I(f), J(f)) = (−1, J); for the L^(2+) forms, I = 12/16 + 1/4 = 1 and J = 9/4 − 27·(2 − J)/27 − 1/4 = J. Hence H = 1 and the sign of 4I^3 − J^2 is as stated, and the pieces of the curve H = 1 are covered bijectively: for Δ < 0 the curve H(I, J) = 1 is {I = −1, |J| ≤ 2} ∪ {|J| = 2, −1 ≤ I < 1}, matching the two families with the overlap (−1, ±2) assigned to the first. The root types: x^3 − x/3 − J/27 has discriminant (4 − J^2)/27 > 0 for |J| < 2, so the L^(0) forms (with the root [1 : 0]) have four real roots; the L^(1) forms have 4I^3 − J^2 < 0 and hence two real roots by [real orbits of binary quartic forms with fixed invariants](#real-orbits-of-binary-quartic-forms-with-fixed-invariants); the L^(2+) forms are positive definite (positive at J near 2 and Δ ≠ 0 on the connected parameter interval). (c) from (b), H(λ^2 I, λ^3 J) = λ^6 H(I, J) (a unique λ > 0 normalises the height to 1) and part (c) of [real orbits of binary quartic forms with fixed invariants](#real-orbits-of-binary-quartic-forms-with-fixed-invariants); h·L^(i) inherits the property since h permutes the GL_2(ℝ)-orbits trivially. (d): |J| < 2 and −1 ≤ I < 1 bound the listed coefficients by 1 (the largest is |√(2 − J)/(3√3)| < 2/(3√3) < 1).

<a id="gauss-fundamental-domain-in-iwasawa-coordinates"></a>


**Gauss fundamental domain in iwasawa coordinates.** Every g ∈ GL_2(ℝ) with det g > 0 has a unique Iwasawa decomposition g = n(u)a(t)k(θ)λ with n(u) = [[1, 0], [u, 1]] (u ∈ ℝ), a(t) = diag(t^{−1}, t) (t > 0), k(θ) = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]] (θ ∈ ℝ/2πℤ) and λ = λ·1 (λ > 0). The measure dg = t^{−2} du d^×t dk d^×λ (d^×t = dt/t, d^×λ = dλ/λ, dk = dθ/2π of total mass 1 on SO_2(ℝ)) is a Haar measure on GL_2^+(ℝ). Let ν(t) := {u ∈ [−1/2, 1/2] : u^2 + t^4 ≥ 1}, N′(t) := {n(u) : u ∈ ν(t)}, A′ := {a(t) : t ≥ 3^{1/4}/√2}, K_+ := {k(θ) : 0 ≤ θ < π} and Λ := {λ·1 : λ > 0}. Then F := N′(t)A′K_+Λ is a fundamental domain for the left action of GL_2(ℤ) on GL_2(ℝ) (GL_2(ℝ) = ⋃_{γ ∈ GL_2(ℤ)} γF up to a null set, the translates pairwise almost disjoint), and its image F_PGL2 in PGL_2(ℝ) is a fundamental domain for PGL_2(ℤ). Moreover g ↦ z(g) := −u + it^2 identifies N′(t)A′ with the standard domain fd of the upper half-plane, and t^{−2} du d^×t = (1/2)·dx dy/y^2 under z = x + iy.

Throughout this assertion, K_+ is a set of representatives of SO_2(ℝ)/{±1}; with the full SO_2(ℝ), as printed in the source, F would contain both g and −g ∈ GL_2(ℤ)g and would be a union of two fundamental domains GL_2(ℤ) acts on the left; F ⊆ GL_2^+(ℝ), which suffices because GL_2(ℤ) contains matrices of determinant −1 ν(t) is a union of one or two intervals depending only on t, and ν(t) = [−1/2, 1/2] for t ≥ 1 The circular and vertical edges of the upper-half-plane region are included, so K_+ only removes the central ±1 ambiguity: this remains a measure-theoretic fundamental domain, not an exact transversal on its boundary. Exact pointwise orbit-multiplicity claims require a boundary selector, or the almost-everywhere-in-h formulation used below.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `iwasawaN`: n(u) = [[1, 0], [u, 1]].

- `iwasawaA`: a(t) = diag(t^{−1}, t) for t > 0.

- `iwasawaK`: k(θ) = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]].

- `iwasawa_existsUnique`: det g > 0 → ∃! (u, t, θ mod 2π, λ) with t, λ > 0 and g = n(u)a(t)k(θ)λ.

- `gaussDomain`: F = {n(u)a(t)k(θ)λ : u ∈ ν(t), t ≥ 3^{1/4}/√2, 0 ≤ θ < π, λ > 0}.

- `mem_gaussDomain_iff`: For t,lambda>0 and the canonical representative 0≤theta<2pi, n(u)a(t)k(theta)lambda lies in F iff −u+it² lies in fd and theta<pi. The angular restriction is essential because k is periodic.

- `isFundamentalDomain_gaussDomain`: F is a measure-theoretic fundamental domain for GL_2(ℤ) acting on GL_2(ℝ) by left multiplication, for the Haar measure dg.

- `gaussDomain_haar`: The Haar measure dg = t^{−2} du d^×t dk d^×λ in Iwasawa coordinates, as a measure on GL_2^+(ℝ).

- `neg_mem_gaussDomain_iff`: g ∈ F → −g ∉ F (the half circle K_+ removes the ±1 ambiguity).


To prove the assertion, Iwasawa: Gram-Schmidt on the rows of g gives g = (lower unitriangular)(positive diagonal)(orthogonal); det g > 0 forces the orthogonal factor into SO_2(ℝ), and the diagonal factor is a(t)λ. Uniqueness from N ∩ AΛ ∩ SO_2 = {1}. Haar density: the left-invariant form g^{−1}dg in these coordinates has density proportional to t^{−3}λ^{−1} (a direct computation), i.e. t^{−2} du d^×t dθ d^×λ. Upper half-plane: the positive definite binary quadratic form (x, y)gg^T(x, y)^T equals λ^2 t^{−2}((x + uy)^2 + t^4y^2), whose root in the upper half-plane is z(g) = −u + it^2; left multiplication by γ ∈ SL_2(ℤ) acts on z(g) by the Möbius action of γ (up to the transpose-inverse convention), and k(θ), λ do not change z(g). The conditions u ∈ ν(t), t ≥ 3^{1/4}/√2 say exactly |Re z| ≤ 1/2 and |z| ≥ 1, i.e. z(g) ∈ fd (ModularGroup.fd). Covering and disjointness: a GL_2(ℤ)-coset meets GL_2^+(ℝ) in one SL_2(ℤ)-coset. By ModularGroup.exists_smul_mem_fd every z is moved into fd, and by ModularGroup.eq_smul_self_of_mem_fdo_mem_fdo (or the measure form ModularGroup.isFundamentalDomain_fdo of Tau Ceti, a MeasureTheory.IsFundamentalDomain for PSL_2(ℤ)) two points of the open domain in one orbit coincide; the kernel {±1} of SL_2(ℤ) → PSL_2(ℤ) acts on the K-coordinate by θ ↦ θ + π, which K_+ resolves. Measure: with y = t^2, dy = 2t dt, so dx dy/y^2 = 2t^{−3} du dt = 2t^{−2} du d^×t.

<a id="hyperbolic-area-of-the-modular-fundamental-domain"></a>


**Hyperbolic area of the modular fundamental domain.** For the invariant measure on the upper half-plane (Mathlib's volume on ℍ, density 1/(Im z)^2 with respect to Lebesgue measure), volume(ModularGroup.fd) = π/3.

Throughout this assertion, The measure is Mathlib's MeasureSpace instance on ℍ


To prove the assertion, By UpperHalfPlane.volume_eq_lintegral, volume(fd) = ∫∫ y^{−2} dy dx over {|x| ≤ 1/2, y ≥ √(1 − x^2)}. The inner integral is ∫_{√(1−x^2)}^∞ y^{−2} dy = (1 − x^2)^{−1/2}. ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} (1 − x^2)^{−1/2} dx = arcsin(1/2) − arcsin(−1/2) = π/3 by the fundamental theorem of calculus (intervalIntegral.integral_deriv_eq_sub with Real.hasDerivAt_arcsin; the integrand is continuous on [−1/2, 1/2]).

<a id="covolume-of-pgl2-z"></a>


**Covolume of pgl2 z.** (a) Let ω be the left-invariant top form on PGL_2(ℝ) whose value at the identity is the dual of the ℤ-basis E_11, E_12, E_21 of pgl_2(ℤ) = gl_2(ℤ)/ℤ·1 (well defined up to sign; |ω| is the associated Haar measure). In the coordinates [n(u)a(t)k(θ)] of PGL_2^+(ℝ), |ω| = 2t^{−3} du dt dθ, and Vol_ω(F_PGL2) = Vol_ω(PGL_2(ℤ)\PGL_2(ℝ)) = 2ζ(2) = π^2/3. (b) For the Haar measure dg = t^{−2} du d^×t dk d^×λ of [gauss fundamental domain in iwasawa coordinates](#gauss-fundamental-domain-in-iwasawa-coordinates), the domain N′(t)A′K_+ (λ omitted) has measure π/12 = ζ(2)/(2π); equivalently Vol(GL_2(ℤ)\GL_2^{±1}(ℝ)) = ζ(2)/(2π). (c) On PGL_2^+(ℝ), |ω| = 4π·t^{−2} du d^×t dk.

(b) ∫ t^{−2} du d^×t over N′(t)A′ equals (1/2)·volume(fd) = π/6, and K_+ has dk-mass 1/2; the product is π/12 = ζ(2)/(2π). (c) Compare the densities: 2t^{−3} du dt dθ = 4π·t^{−2} du d^×t (dθ/2π).

<a id="orbit-multiplicities-in-fundamental-multisets"></a>


**Orbit multiplicities in fundamental multisets.** Let i∈T and let F be the Gauss region with K_+, retaining the boundary of the modular domain. For each fixed x∈V_R^(i), for Haar-almost every h∈GL2^+(R), the sum of multiplicities in Fh·L^(i) over the GL2(Z)-orbit of x equals m(x)=#Stab_GL2(R)(x)/#Stab_GL2(Z)(x), an integer between 1 and n_i. This ratio equals n_i whenever the integral stabilizer is {±1}, and for almost every real x. For the countable set of integral x, choose one common conull set of h. On that set the irreducible count of height<X, with multiplicity, is the sum over classes of n_i·2/#Stab_GL2(Z)(x). Consequently the averaged count has these class weights. The assertion for every h would require an exact boundary selector, which F as defined does not supply.

Throughout this assertion, F must be the strict domain (K_+); with the full SO_2(ℝ) every multiplicity doubles N(S; X) is the number of GL_2(ℤ)-classes of irreducible elements of S of height < X


To prove the assertion, For fixed x choose the unique point x_L of L^(i) in its real orbit. The set of g taking x_L to x is a finite coset of its real stabilizer. For each gamma∈GL2(Z), the condition that one of the corresponding points of gamma g Stab(x_L) h^{-1} lies on the boundary of F defines a Haar-null set of h, by translation and inversion invariance of Haar measure. The countable union over gamma and the finite stabilizer remains null. Outside this null set each relevant GL2(Z)-coset meets F exactly once. The double-coset calculation then gives #Stab_GL2(R)(x)/#Stab_GL2(Z)(x). Both stabilizers contain ±1, giving the bounds and the claimed class weight. For each gamma outside {±1}, its fixed locus on binary quartics is a proper linear subspace. Countability of GL2(Z) makes their union null, so the generic ratio is n_i. For integral x use the countable union of the exceptional h-sets to obtain the common conull set needed to sum the counts. Integrate over a compact averaging set of positive Haar measure. Boundary changes have no effect on this integral; a null set in the real coefficient space alone would not justify discarding integral points.

### 2.3 Averaging quartic orbits and cutting the cusp


<a id="averaged-count-of-binary-quartic-orbits"></a>


**Averaged count of binary quartic orbits.** Fix a compact semialgebraic set G_0 ⊂ GL_2(ℝ) that is left SO_2(ℝ)-invariant, is the closure of a nonempty open set, and has det h ≥ 1 for h ∈ G_0; let dh be the Haar measure of [gauss fundamental domain in iwasawa coordinates](#gauss-fundamental-domain-in-iwasawa-coordinates) and F the strict Gauss domain. For i ∈ T, S ⊆ V_ℤ^(i) (not necessarily GL_2(ℤ)-invariant) and X > 0 define N(S; X) := (1/C_{G_0}^(i)) ∫_{h ∈ G_0} #{x ∈ F h·L^(i) ∩ S^irr : H(x) < X} dh, where C_{G_0}^(i) := n_i ∫_{G_0} dh, S^irr is the set of elements of S irreducible over ℚ, and the count is taken with the multiplicities of the multiset F h·L^(i). For a weight φ : V_ℤ → ℝ, N_φ(S; X) is defined in the same way with each x counted with weight φ(x). For n = n(u), t > 0, λ > 0 put B(n, t, λ, X) := n a(t) λ G_0·L^(i) ∩ {x ∈ V_ℝ^(i) : H(x) < X}, a bounded semialgebraic multiset.

Throughout this assertion, G_0, i and the fundamental set L^(i) are fixed; for GL_2(ℤ)-invariant S the value does not depend on G_0 Only irreducible elements are counted; H is the height max(|I|^3, J^2/4) of [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs) G_0 is a set of matrices with Haar measure. An arbitrary subset of Iwasawa coordinate space can cover the same matrix different numbers of times; invariance of its image alone does not give the invariant averaging measure. The prototype now integrates on the matrix carrier. The general semialgebraic predicate and multiset Davenport interface remain GN.4 supplier work.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `quarticAveragedCount`: N(S; X) for S ⊆ V_ℤ, with G_0 and i as parameters, by the formula (11).

- `quarticAveragedCount_weighted`: N_φ(S; X), the same average with weights φ(x).

- `quarticRegionB`: B(n, t, λ, X) = n a(t) λ G_0·L^(i) ∩ {H < X} as a multiset in V_ℝ.

- `quarticAveragedCount_eq_sum_classes`: For GL_2(ℤ)-invariant S: N(S; X) = Σ over irreducible classes [x] ⊆ S with H(x) < X of 2/#Stab_{GL_2(ℤ)}(x).

- `quarticAveragedCount_union`: N(S_1 ∪ S_2; X) = N(S_1; X) + N(S_2; X) for disjoint S_1, S_2.

- `quarticAveragedCount_mono`: S_1 ⊆ S_2 → N(S_1; X) ≤ N(S_2; X), and X ↦ N(S; X) is monotone.

- `quarticAveragedCount_indep`: For GL_2(ℤ)-invariant S, N(S; X) does not depend on G_0 or on the choice of the fundamental set L^(i).

- `quarticAveragedCount_reducible`: N(S; X) = 0 when every element of S is reducible over ℚ (for example when every element has a = 0).


To prove the assertion, On a compact averaging set the height bound and a≠0 for irreducible forms bound lambda and then the cusp parameter t by the leading-coefficient estimate. Thus the union of contributing integral irreducible points is bounded and finite. Their finite multiplicity functions are measurable (using the semialgebraic descriptions), so the count and each fixed weighted count are integrable. For GL_2(ℤ)-invariant S, [orbit multiplicities in fundamental multisets](#orbit-multiplicities-in-fundamental-multisets) gives, for Haar-almost every h (one common conull set for the countable integral lattice), #{x ∈ F h·L^(i) ∩ S^irr : H(x) < X} = Σ over irreducible GL_2(ℤ)-classes [x] ⊆ S of height < X of n_i·2/#Stab_{GL_2(ℤ)}(x); averaging over h gives N(S; X) = Σ_{[x]} 2/#Stab_{GL_2(ℤ)}(x), which is the number of classes counted with weight 1 except for the classes with a stabiliser larger than {±1}.

Write g = n(u)a(t)kλ with k ∈ K_+: since kG_0 = G_0 (left SO_2(ℝ)-invariance) the integrand does not depend on k, and ∫_{K_+} dk = 1/2, which gives the formula with B(n, t, λ, X) ([averaged count of binary quartic orbits](#averaged-count-of-binary-quartic-orbits)). The Gauss region is only a transversal away from its boundary; use the almost-everywhere-in-h multiplicity statement. If Cλ ≥ t then all five ranges are bounded below by a positive constant and the range of a is the smallest up to a constant; every projection of B onto a coordinate subspace has volume at most a constant times the product of the four largest ranges, O(λ^4/t^2·λ^4·λ^4t^2·λ^4t^4) = O(t^4λ^16), and scaling by 1/m (to pass to the lattice L′) only decreases the projection volumes. B(n, t, λ, X) is a bounded semialgebraic multiset whose number of defining inequalities, their degrees and its maximum multiplicity are bounded in terms of G_0 and L^(i) (it is a linear image of G_0·L^(i) cut by H < X); apply Davenport's lemma (requested from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4) to the image of B under v ↦ (v − v_0)/m, whose volume is m^{−5}Vol(B). Davenport first counts all lattice points with the multiset multiplicity. Subtract those on a=0: their number is bounded by the product of one plus the four remaining coefficient ranges, hence O(t^4 lambda^16) when t≤C lambda and t has its fixed positive lower bound. ### 2.4 Quartic invariant volumes and main terms

**Jacobian change of measure for binary quartic forms.** Let PGL_2(ℝ) act on V_ℝ by the twisted action γ·f := (det γ)^{−2} f((x, y)γ), let ω be the ℤ-normalised invariant form of [covolume of pgl2 z](#covolume-of-pgl2-z), dv = da db dc dd de, and for i ∈ T let p^(i) : (I, J) ↦ p^(i)_{I,J} ∈ R^(i) be the section of [fundamental sets for real binary quartic orbits](#fundamental-sets-for-real-binary-quartic-orbits). Then for every measurable U ⊆ PGL_2(ℝ) and every measurable φ : V_ℝ → [0, ∞], ∫_{U·R^(i)} φ(v) dv = (1/27) ∫_{(I,J)} ∫_{g ∈ U} φ(g·p^(i)_{I,J}) ω(g) dI dJ, the left side over the multiset U·R^(i) (multiplicity #{(g, r) ∈ U × R^(i) : g·r = v}) and the outer integral over {4I^3 − J^2 > 0} (i ∈ {0, 2±}) or {4I^3 − J^2 < 0} (i = 1). In particular this holds for U = F_PGL2.

Throughout this assertion, The constant 1/27 is for the ℤ-basis E_11, E_12, E_21 of pgl_2(ℤ); a different normalisation of ω changes it Only the real case is planned here; the p-adic analogue (Proposition 3.7, with |1/27|_p) belongs to Layer 4


To prove the assertion, Jacobian at the identity: for the polynomial section s_{I,J} = x^3y − (I/3)xy^3 − (J/27)y^4 (which has invariants (I, J), [invariants height and eligible pairs](#invariants-height-and-eligible-pairs)), the 5 × 5 determinant of the vectors E_11·s, E_12·s, E_21·s, ∂s/∂I, ∂s/∂J (infinitesimal twisted action; E_11 acts by f ↦ x∂_x f − 2f) is −1/27 identically in (I, J) (a direct computation, rechecked by computer algebra). Independence of the section and of the point: for f with Δ(f) ≠ 0, the orbit tangent vectors E·f span the kernel of (dI, dJ) at f, so det[E_11·f, E_12·f, E_21·f, w_1, w_2] with (dI, dJ)(w_j) = e_j depends only on f; it is invariant under PGL_2(ℂ) (the twisted action has determinant of absolute value 1 on V, and Λ^3 of the adjoint action is trivial). Forms with equal invariants and Δ ≠ 0 are PGL_2(ℂ)-equivalent ([binary quartic parametrization of e mod 2e](#binary-quartic-parametrization-of-e-mod-2e) over ℂ, where every form is soluble and E(ℂ)/2E(ℂ) = 0 (multiplication by 2 on a complex elliptic curve is surjective)), and s_{I,J} meets every such level set, so the determinant is −1/27 at every f with Δ(f) ≠ 0 and for every smooth section. Left translation by g ∈ PGL_2(ℝ) preserves ω and changes dv by |det(g acting on V)| = 1, so the Jacobian of ψ(g, I, J) = g·p^(i)_{I,J} has absolute value 1/27 everywhere. The explicit sections are smooth on finitely many pieces of the invariant region; along their joins a piecewise change of coordinates is required. On each smooth piece, the invertible Jacobian gives a local diffeomorphism. Cover by countably many open sets on which the map is injective, make them disjoint measurably, and apply MeasureTheory.integral_image_eq_integral_abs_det_fderiv_smul, then pass to nonnegative measurable functions by monotone approximation. The joins are lower-dimensional, hence null, and the finite fibres supply the stated multiplicity.

**Binary quartic counts with finitely many congruence conditions.** (a) Let m ≥ 1 and let L_j = v_j + mV_ℤ be a translate of mV_ℤ. (c) If the allowed residues of S form the CRT product of local allowed sets at finitely many distinct prime powers, then N(S ∩ V_ℤ^(i); X) = N(V_ℤ^(i); X)·∏_p μ_p(S) + O_{S,ε}(X^{3/4+ε}), where μ_p(S) is the p-adic density of [acceptable weight function](#acceptable-weight-function).

(b) Sum over the k translates. (c) By the Chinese remainder theorem k·m^{−5} = ∏_p μ_p(S) because the allowed residue set is a Cartesian product under CRT, with m the product of the distinct prime powers involved; combine with [count of binary quartic forms of bounded height](#count-of-binary-quartic-forms-of-bounded-height).

**Real orbits and stabilizers of binary cubic forms.** Let U_ℝ be the space of real binary cubic forms f = ax^3 + bx^2y + cxy^2 + dy^3 with the twisted action γ·f := (det γ)^{−1} f((x, y)γ) of GL_2(ℝ) (the action (9) of [delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings](#delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings)), and Disc(f) = b^2c^2 − 4ac^3 − 4b^3d − 27a^2d^2 + 18abcd. (a) Disc(γ·f) = (det γ)^2 Disc(f), and the scalar matrix λ·1 acts by f ↦ λf. (b) U_ℝ^(0) := {Disc > 0}, the forms with three distinct real roots in ℙ^1(ℝ), and U_ℝ^(1) := {Disc < 0}, the forms with one real root and a pair of complex conjugate roots, are each a single GL_2(ℝ)-orbit. (c) The stabiliser in GL_2(ℝ) of f ∈ U_ℝ^(0) has order n_0 := 6 and acts on the three roots as the full symmetric group; the stabiliser of f ∈ U_ℝ^(1) has order n_1 := 2. Put U_ℤ^(i) := U_ℝ^(i) ∩ U_ℤ.

Throughout this assertion, The twisted action (det gamma)^{-1} is the Delone–Faddeev action; the untwisted scalar action would be lambda³ instead of lambda, although over R the stabilizer orders are still 6 and 2 because every nonzero real scalar has a unique real cube root. Only forms with Disc ≠ 0 are in U_ℝ^(0) ∪ U_ℝ^(1)


To prove the assertion, (a) Disc is homogeneous of degree 4 and relatively invariant of weight 6 under substitution, Disc(f((x, y)γ)) = (det γ)^6 Disc(f); the factor (det γ)^{−1} multiplies Disc by (det γ)^{−4}. For λ·1: f((x, y)λ)/λ^2 = λf. (b) Roots: by Cubic.discr_eq_prod_three_roots (after moving a root away from [1 : 0] if a = 0), Disc > 0 iff the three roots are real and distinct, and Disc < 0 iff one is real and two are complex conjugate. PGL_2(ℝ) is simply 3-transitive on ℙ^1(ℝ), and transitive on pairs (real point, conjugate pair) (move the pair to ±i, then rotate by the stabiliser SO_2(ℝ) of i, which is transitive on ℙ^1(ℝ)). A form is determined by its roots up to a nonzero scalar, and the scalars λ·1 realise every scalar factor by (a). (c) An element of the stabiliser permutes the roots; the map to permutations is injective (an element fixing three points of ℙ^1 is a scalar λ·1, which fixes f only for λ = 1). Every permutation of three real roots is induced by a unique class in PGL_2(ℝ), and exactly one scalar multiple of a representative fixes f; for one real root and a conjugate pair, only the identity and the swap of the pair preserve the real structure, and the swap is realised by a reflection.

<a id="index-p-switching-for-binary-cubic-forms"></a>


**Index p switching for binary cubic forms.** Let p be a prime and use the twisted action on U_ℚ. (a) If f = (a, b, c, d) ∈ U_ℤ has p^2 | a and p | b, then f′ := diag(p^{−1}, 1)·f = (a/p^2, b/p, c, pd) ∈ U_ℤ, Disc(f′) = p^{−2}Disc(f), f′(0, 1) ≡ 0 (mod p), and f = diag(p, 1)·f′. (b) Conversely, if g ∈ U_ℤ and α ∈ ℙ^1(𝔽_p) is a root of g mod p, choose γ_α ∈ GL_2(ℤ) whose bottom row reduces to a representative of α; then f_{g,α} := diag(p, 1)·(γ_α·g) ∈ U_ℤ has p^2 | a and p | b, and its GL_2(ℤ)-class depends only on the GL_2(ℤ)-class of g and on α modulo the action of Stab_{GL_2(ℤ)}(g). (c) Consequently every GL_2(ℤ)-class of forms f with Disc(f) ≠ 0 having a translate with p^2 | a and p | b is the class of some f_{g,α} with |Disc(g)| = |Disc(f)|/p^2, and the number of such classes attached to one class [g] is at most the number of roots of g mod p in ℙ^1(𝔽_p): at most 3 if g ≢ 0 (mod p), at most p + 1 otherwise.

Throughout this assertion, This is the form-theoretic content of BST Lemma 13 and Propositions 15-16 (index-p overrings and subrings of cubic rings); no ring theory is used The twisted action is the one of [delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings](#delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings)


To prove the assertion, (a) diag(p^{−1}, 1)·f = f(x/p, y)/det(diag(p^{−1}, 1)) = p·f(x/p, y) = (a/p^2)x^3 + (b/p)x^2y + cxy^2 + pdy^3, and Disc(γ·f) = (det γ)^2 Disc(f) with det γ = 1/p ([real orbits and stabilizers of binary cubic forms](#real-orbits-and-stabilizers-of-binary-cubic-forms) (a)). (b) γ_α·g vanishes at [0 : 1] mod p, i.e. its y^3-coefficient d′ is divisible by p; then diag(p, 1)·(γ_α·g) = (p^2a′, pb′, c′, d′/p) is integral. Two choices γ_α, γ′_α differ by δ ∈ GL_2(ℤ) with p | δ_21, and diag(p, 1)δ diag(p, 1)^{−1} = [[δ_11, pδ_12], [δ_21/p, δ_22]] ∈ GL_2(ℤ); replacing g by ε·g (ε ∈ GL_2(ℤ)) moves α accordingly. (c) Given f, move it so that p^2 | a and p | b, and take g = f′ from (a), α = [0 : 1]; then f = f_{g,α}. A nonzero binary cubic form over 𝔽_p has at most 3 roots in ℙ^1(𝔽_p) (Polynomial.card_roots' for its dehomogenisation, plus possibly [1 : 0]); the zero form has p + 1.

### 2.12 Summed square-divisor tails


<a id="refinement-square-divisor-tail"></a>


**Square divisor tail.** Given an integer-valued invariant Delta and real height H on a type A, T(Delta,H;M,X) consists of a with H(a)<X, Delta(a) nonzero, and an integer m>M, m>=1, squarefree, with m^2 dividing Delta(a). The multiplicity w_M(a) counts these m by filtering the natural divisors of |Delta(a)|. At Delta=0 define w_M=0. This finite multiplicity is the one used in summed tails; a union-tail bound alone does not bound it.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticCountingRefinement.squareDivisorTail`: Membership is exactly H(a)<X, Delta(a) nonzero, and existence of the indicated squarefree positive square divisor.

- `ArithmeticCountingRefinement.squareDivisorMultiplicity`: Return the finite filtered positive-divisor cardinal, with the deliberate value 0 at Delta=0.

- `ArithmeticCountingRefinement.tail_iff_multiplicity_pos`: For H(a)<X and Delta(a) nonzero, membership is equivalent to 0<w_M(a), whose natural cardinal equals the finite filtered-divisor count.

- `ArithmeticCountingRefinement.tail_antitone`: If M<=Mprime, T(Mprime,X) is contained in T(M,X) and w_Mprime(a)<=w_M(a).


To prove the assertion, Use the finite positive divisor set of the nonzero invariant. Restrict its squarefree members by m>M and m^2 divisibility. The zero convention agrees with removal of the singular locus, not with the infinitely many actual square divisors of 0.

<a id="refinement-kappa-acceptable"></a>


**Kappa acceptable.** For coordinate rank r, Delta:Z^r→Z and local factors phi_p:Z^r→[0,1], kappa-acceptability consists of residue dependence modulo p^kappa at every prime p and a threshold P such that phi_p(a)=1 whenever p>P and p^2 does not divide Delta(a). Infinite-product convergence and real signatures remain the congruence-function interface. Residue dependence is a quantitative addition, not a replacement of that interface.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticCountingRefinement.IsKappaAcceptable`: The predicate is the conjunction of residue dependence, range [0,1], and eventual good-discriminant factor 1.

- `ArithmeticCountingRefinement.kappa_good_prime`: An acceptable family has a threshold P with phi_p(a)=1 for every prime p>P with p^2 not dividing Delta(a).

- `ArithmeticCountingRefinement.kappa_finite_product_residue`: For a finite set of distinct primes, the product factors through the coefficient residue modulo their product to the kappa power. This is compatible with the finite congruence function.


To prove the assertion, Compare coordinates modulo p^kappa. Keep a single threshold valid for every coefficient vector. The modulus dependence is what controls the total small-modulus error.

### 2.14 Invariant geometric-sieve criterion


<a id="refinement-invariant-geometric-sieve-criterion"></a>


**Invariant geometric sieve criterion.** Let G act integrally on V of positive rank r and let f be a primitive geometrically squarefree relative invariant of positive degree d. Put G^1=ker(det(rho)), for the representation rho:G→GL(V). Require a G(Z)-invariant density-one generic coefficient locus with uniformly bounded finite geometric stabilizers, a continuous homogeneous degree-d G^1-invariant height, finite-volume fundamental domains F_X=X^(1/d)F_1, and finite-congruence main terms at scale X^(r/d), with actual CRT residue densities. For every weakly p^2-divisible generic v require a rational group element g such that g v is again integral and generic, H(g v)=H(v)/p^a, and g v modulo p lies in a closed G-invariant subscheme Y_k of codimension at least k. Here Y_k depends only on k, k is uniformly bounded, a>=0, (r/d)a+k−1>=eta>0, and for fixed k each resulting G(Z)-orbit has uniformly boundedly many original G(Z)-orbits. Then coefficient boxes have squarefree density product_p(1−c_p/p^(2r)), where c_p counts the f-zero residues modulo p^2. The compact-domain approximation and boundary regularity used to pass from fundamental regions to boxes are included in the supporting estimates below; all six representation-specific conditions are required.


To prove the assertion, Strong divisibility is handled by the codimension-two sieve; split the weak cases by k and apply the height-lowering map. The positive eta makes the large-prime tail negligible after compact truncation. Take the height limit before prime truncation; do not assert this for arbitrary multivariate polynomials. Verify all six hypotheses for every representation to which the criterion is applied. For the coefficient-box conclusion approximate the box by finitely many translated height domains, then take the prime threshold, compact truncation and cover-size limits in that order. Use c_p/p^(2r), correcting (40)–(44).

*Needs:* [quantitative ekedahl geometric sieve](#quantitative-ekedahl-geometric-sieve), [strongly and weakly divisible values](#strongly-and-weakly-divisible-values), GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4/davenport-semialgebraic-count.

### Supporting uniform estimates

<a id="support-sieves"></a>

The geometric sieve needs a projection/spreading adapter, not just a codimension slogan. For a fixed closed subscheme of affine r-space of codimension k, choose integral coordinate projections and a finite exceptional-prime set so that finite fibres have a uniform degree bound after reduction. For a bounded semialgebraic region B and dilation t≥1, prove the required finite-field point bound, the small-prime lattice estimate and the large-prime elimination estimate. The result is `O_B(t^r/(M^(k-1) log M)+t^(r-k+1))` for primes greater than M≥2, with the stated dimension restrictions and the customary harmless weakening at the boundary. Codimension one does not give a vanishing tail. Source: Bhargava, geometric sieve, Theorem 3.3 and its proof in §3. The strongly divisible discriminant locus is checked representation by representation; it is not assumed smooth at p=2.

For weakly square-divisible quartics the required transport estimate is on *all* relevant ternary-pair orbits, not merely S4-field orbits. Separate nonmaximal, overramified and reducible-resolvent contributions, with the uniform fixed-resolvent bound `O_ε(|d|^(1/4+ε))`. Quartic suborder and quadratic-extension multiplicities must be summed with the source stabilizer weights; Proposition 23 of the quartic counting paper alone is restricted to the S4 locus. For quintic rings supply the corresponding uniform suborder bound before invoking its nonmaximal tail. The references are Bhargava's quartic paper, Lemma 12 and Proposition 23, pp. 1044–1046 and 1056–1058, and the quintic paper, Proposition 19, pp. 1586–1588. Retain ε in the fixed-resolvent estimate.

For the monic sieve prove an average divisor-sum estimate for the rational-root and reducible loci; a pointwise assertion that every nonzero integer has boundedly many divisors is false. Degree four's extra quadratic-factor locus has the weaker exponent `22/3+ε`. A commensurable S-arithmetic lattice requires a finite-index denominator comparison of both generic orbit counts and bad-prime tails; it does not inherit a standard-lattice estimate without that comparison. The source is BSW I, Lemma 4.2, Proposition 4.3 and Theorems 4.1, 4.4, pp. 20–23, and Global Fields I, Theorems 4.7, 5.1–5.3, pp. 18–21.

For the even-degree binary sieve isolate the following implication. Assume a paired-fibre lattice count on actual full-rank `(A,B)` rows and the restricted Gram lower bound on `L_good(M)`, after deleting small discriminants and small constant terms. Then combine main, shallow and deep estimates and the non-Sn exclusion to obtain positive `δ,η` and `ξ≥0` with `τ=max(η,(η+ξ)/δ)<1` and `(2n+1)τ<n+1`. These assumptions give the summed tail and fixed-modulus sieve with those parameters. No numerical even-degree endpoint is inferred without those assumptions. The supporting tasks are to prove the paired-fibre count, the Cauchy–Binet/determinantal-ideal lower bound and the quantitative excluded-locus bound with logarithmic slack. A row-space condition is not a proof that a small coordinate block vanishes; use the deep-box inequalities themselves. Degree two has its own quadratic discriminant sieve. Source: BSW II, §§5–6, especially the restricted replacement for Lemma 6.25. The numerical exponent `1/(88n⁶)` is a proposed endpoint of this implication, rather than an unconditional consequence of the odd-degree argument.

The three-isogeny coregular count is the following conditional interface. Fix the normalized mirror representation, an integral representative lattice, a finite-volume archimedean squareclass window and compatible additive local Haar measures. Assume: rational orbit classification with its identity orbit separated; integral representatives with bounded and computed multiplicity; finite-congruence equidistribution at the specified height; a uniformly negligible nongeneric locus; a uniform tail for the acceptable local exclusions; and a local orbit-Jacobian/mass formula with one global differential normalization. Then the average of the nonidentity soluble orbits is the product of the local Selmer ratios. Prove each of these six assertions for the chosen representation before removing the conditional hypothesis. In particular a raw archimedean sign cone has infinite volume and cannot be inserted as the representative window. Source: BKLOS Theorems 2.1 and 7.2, §§7–8; these conditions state the exact counting input used there.

For the marked-genus-one second moment, sum the sparse quaternary estimates over leading-coefficient/monicization ranges with their actual a-dependent support. Preserve the relation between X,Y,θ,δ and the absolute positive saving λ: choose `10θ+62δ<λ` before absorbing logarithms. The fixed-slice smoothed count is an input to this sum, not the whole second-moment argument. Source: BSS Theorem 5.1 and the counting and monicization assembly in §§5–7, pp. 24–47.

### Examples

For the invariant `Δ(a)=a`, one residue out of p² is divisible by p². For `Δ(a)=a²`, the bad locus has codimension one and one residue out of p is bad; its prime tail cannot be treated by a codimension-two estimate. If `Δ=0`, infinitely many squarefree moduli divide it, which is why the finite divisor-multiplicity statistic assigns that case zero and the singular locus is counted separately.

For quartic invariant height, the positive and negative real regions have respective areas `8/5` and `32/5` at height one. Combining them as equal sign masses loses a factor four. The ordered PGL2 tangent basis `(E11,E12,E21)` gives the orbit-Jacobian determinant `-1/27`; the measure uses its absolute value. At p=3 that factor is 27, whereas it is one at every other prime. A coupled CRT condition such as equal residues modulo two and three must use its actual proportion modulo six, rather than multiplying its full marginal projections.
