Layers 0–1; the Mathlib Chebyshev estimate and partial summation; GN.0–GN.4 and GlobalNumberFields lattice/coset bounds; real and p-adic integration; AdelicAlgebraicGroups reduction and Haar contracts; the companion AN.2–AN.5 secondary-density analysis; and IG.2 for quantitative Galois exclusion. The moving-lattice, all-orbit transport, paired even-degree and specialized coregular assertions above are local supporting targets.


## Layer 3: Fields, class groups and moment tools

Integral orbit counts become field and class-group statistics only after maximality, resolvent multiplicity, real-place conditions and base-field characters are matched. Secondary terms need a second local density and a stronger sieve, not an application of the first-order density theorem. The finite-group moment tools are built before their use in quadratic four-rank laws; their probability conclusions are distinct from the arithmetic moment hypotheses.


### 3.1 Field counts and class-group statistics


<a id="number-field-counting-function"></a>


**Number field counting function.** Fix an algebraic closure Q̄ of Q (Mathlib's AlgebraicClosure ℚ). For an integer n ≥ 1, a predicate P on number fields that is invariant under Q-algebra isomorphism, and real numbers ξ < η, let S_n(P; ξ, η) be the set of intermediate fields K of Q̄/Q with [K : Q] = n, ξ < Disc(K) < η and P(K), where Disc(K) = NumberField.discr K ∈ Z is the signed absolute discriminant (its sign is (−1)^{r₂(K)}). S_n(P; ξ, η) is finite by Hermite's theorem. Define N_n(P; ξ, η) as the number of classes of S_n(P; ξ, η) under the relation K ~ K' iff K ≃ₐ[Q] K'; since every number field of degree n embeds into Q̄, N_n(P; ξ, η) is the number of Q-isomorphism classes of degree-n number fields K with ξ < Disc(K) < η and P(K). Abbreviations: N_n^+(P; X) := N_n(P; 0, X), N_n^-(P; X) := N_n(P; −X, 0), and N_n(P; X) := N_n^+(P; X) + N_n^-(P; X) (all fields with 0 < |Disc(K)| < X). The weighted count N_n^{Aut}(P; ξ, η) := Σ_{classes [K]} 1/#Aut(K/Q). The three standard restrictions are pinned as follows. Signature: P(K) is nrComplexPlaces K = r₂. Galois group: for a transitive subgroup Γ ≤ S_n, P(K) says that the image of Gal(Q̄/Q), acting by composition on the n embeddings K → Q̄ (MulAction.toPermHom), is conjugate to Γ under some bijection between the embeddings and {1, …, n}; this is the permutation Galois group of PolynomialGaloisGroups, Layer 0 (the degree-n action of (minpoly ℚ α).Gal for K = Q(α)) with its label predicate of Layer 6. Local specifications: for a collection Σ = (Σ_v) of sets of isomorphism classes of étale algebras of degree n over Q_v (v a prime or ∞), P(K) says K ⊗ Q_v ∈ Σ_v for every v.

Throughout this assertion, n ≥ 1; for the Galois-group restriction Γ is a transitive subgroup of S_n, identified up to conjugacy P must be invariant under Q-algebra isomorphism; otherwise the count depends on the chosen subfield in the class The discriminant is Mathlib's signed NumberField.discr; the interval (ξ, η) is open at both ends, matching BST's N₃(ξ, η) Fields are counted up to isomorphism, not as subfields of Q̄ (a non-Galois cubic field has three conjugate subfields and is counted once)

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `numberFieldCount`: N_n(P; ξ, η) ∈ ℕ, the number of Q-isomorphism classes of degree-n number fields K with ξ < Disc(K) < η and P(K), for an isomorphism-invariant predicate P.

- `finite_numberFieldsInInterval`: The set S_n(P; ξ, η) of intermediate fields of Q̄/Q of degree n with ξ < discr < η and P is finite (from NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd).

- `numberFieldCount_eq_sum_card_aut`: N_n(P; ξ, η) = Σ_{K ∈ S_n(P; ξ, η)} #Aut(K/Q)/n (each isomorphism class has n/#Aut(K/Q) conjugate subfields).

- `numberFieldCount_mono`: N_n(P; ξ, η) ≤ N_n(P'; ξ', η') whenever P ⇒ P' and (ξ, η) ⊆ (ξ', η').

- `numberFieldCount_add_of_disjoint`: For disjoint isomorphism-invariant predicates P, P': N_n(P ∨ P'; ξ, η) = N_n(P; ξ, η) + N_n(P'; ξ, η); in particular N_n(P; ξ, η) = Σ_{r₂=0}^{⌊n/2⌋} N_n(P ∧ (r₂(K) = r₂); ξ, η).

- `numberFieldCount_neg_eq_odd_nrComplexPlaces`: For X≥0, N_n(P; −X, 0) = N_n(P ∧ (r₂(K) odd); −X, X) = N_n(P ∧ (r₂(K) odd); X), where the last notation is the absolute-discriminant count. A positive signed interval (0,X) would give zero for the odd-r₂ predicate.

- `numberFieldCount_eq_ncard_of_two`: For n = 2 every quadratic field is Galois with exactly one subfield of Q̄ in its class, so N₂(P; ξ, η) = #S₂(P; ξ, η).

- `numberFieldCount_congr`: If P and P' agree on all number fields of degree n then N_n(P; ξ, η) = N_n(P'; ξ, η).


To prove the assertion, The set S_n(P; ξ, η) is contained in the set of intermediate fields K of Q̄/Q with |discr K| ≤ ⌈max(|ξ|, |η|)⌉, which is finite by NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd; take Nat.card of the quotient by the isomorphism relation. Invariance of P and of finrank and discr under Q-isomorphism makes the quotient well defined; the embedding of every number field of degree n into Q̄ (its minimal polynomial splits in Q̄) shows that every isomorphism class is represented. The subfield formula: the members of S_n(P; ξ, η) isomorphic to a fixed K are the images of the n embeddings K → Q̄, two embeddings having the same image iff they differ by an automorphism of K, so the class of K has n/#Aut(K/Q) members and N_n(P; ξ, η) = Σ_{K ∈ S_n(P; ξ, η)} #Aut(K/Q)/n. The family of degree-n number fields up to isomorphism, ordered by |Disc|, with weight 1 (or 1/#Aut(K/Q) for the weighted count), is an instance of the arithmetic family of [arithmetic family](#arithmetic-family); its counting function is N_n(P; X), and its bounded-height finiteness is Hermite's theorem.

*Needs:* [arithmetic family](#arithmetic-family), `NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd` (Mathlib), `NumberField.discr` (Mathlib), `NumberField.sign_discr` (Mathlib), `NumberField.InfinitePlace.nrComplexPlaces` (Mathlib), `AlgebraicClosure` (Mathlib), `IntermediateField` (Mathlib), `MulAction.toPermHom` (Mathlib).

<a id="torsion-count-of-class-groups"></a>


**Torsion count of class groups.** For a number field K and an integer m ≥ 1, h_m(K) := #{c ∈ Cl(K) : c^m = 1} = Nat.card {c : ClassGroup (𝓞 K) // c ^ m = 1}, the order of the m-torsion subgroup Cl(K)[m] of the ideal class group. For a quadratic field K₂ of discriminant D this is BST's h*_3(K₂) = #Cl₃(D) when m = 3. For a prime p, h_p(K) = p^{rk_p Cl(K)} where rk_p A = dim_{F_p} A/pA.

Throughout this assertion, m ≥ 1; the class group is Mathlib's ClassGroup (𝓞 K) of the ring of integers (the wide class group); narrow class groups, where used, are named explicitly Cl(K) is finite (NumberField.classNumber), so h_m(K) is a positive integer dividing the class number

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `classGroupTorsionCard`: h_m(K) = Nat.card {c : ClassGroup (𝓞 K) // c ^ m = 1}.

- `classGroupTorsionCard_pos`: 1 ≤ h_m(K) (the trivial class is m-torsion).

- `classGroupTorsionCard_dvd_classNumber`: h_m(K) divides NumberField.classNumber K.

- `classGroupTorsionCard_mul_of_coprime`: For coprime m, m': h_{mm'}(K) = h_m(K) h_{m'}(K).

- `classGroupTorsionCard_prime_eq_pow_rank`: For p prime, h_p(K) = #(Cl(K)/Cl(K)^p) = p^{rk_p Cl(K)} with rk_p A = dim_{F_p} A/pA.

- `classGroupTorsionCard_two_eq_card_elementaryTwoQuotient`: h₂(K) = Nat.card (TauCeti.ClassGroup.ElementaryTwoQuotient (𝓞 K)) (Tau Ceti's TauCeti.ClassGroup.card_elementaryTwoQuotient_eq_card_twoTorsion).

- `classGroupTorsionCard_congr`: A Q-algebra isomorphism K ≃ K' gives h_m(K) = h_m(K').


To prove the assertion, Define h_m(K) as Nat.card of the subtype {c : ClassGroup (𝓞 K) // c ^ m = 1}; it is the kernel of the m-th power endomorphism of the finite abelian group Cl(K). For a finite abelian group A, #A[m] = #(A/mA) = #Hom(A, Z/mZ) (duality of finite abelian groups), and for m = p prime #A[p] = p^{rk_p A}. For coprime m, m': A[mm'] ≅ A[m] × A[m'], so h_{mm'} = h_m h_{m'}; and h_m(K) divides h(K) = NumberField.classNumber K by Lagrange.

*Needs:* `ClassGroup` (Mathlib), `NumberField.RingOfIntegers` (Mathlib), `NumberField.classNumber` (Mathlib), `TauCeti.ClassGroup.card_elementaryTwoQuotient_eq_card_twoTorsion` (Tau Ceti).

### 3.2 Cubic splitting densities and field counts


<a id="splitting-symbol-and-local-sets-of-binary-cubic-forms"></a>


**Splitting symbol and local sets of binary cubic forms.** Let V_Z be the space of integral binary cubic forms f(x, y) = a x³ + b x² y + c x y² + d y³ (coefficients (a, b, c, d) ∈ Z⁴, the carrier of [delone faddeev parametrization of cubic rings](#delone-faddeev-parametrization-of-cubic-rings)) and p a prime. If f ≢ 0 (mod p), f mod p has exactly three zeros in P¹(F̄_p) counted with multiplicity; the splitting symbol (f, p) = (f₁^{e₁} f₂^{e₂} …) lists the degrees f_i over F_p of the fields of definition of the distinct zeros and their multiplicities e_i, and takes one of the five values (111), (12), (3), (1²1), (1³). For each symbol σ, T_p(σ) := {f ∈ V_Z : f ≢ 0 (mod p), (f, p) = σ}. With U_p ⊆ V_Z the set of forms f such that the cubic ring R(f) is maximal at p (the Davenport-Heilbronn set of Layer 1: f ∉ U_p iff f ≡ 0 (mod p), or some GL₂(Z)-translate of f has a ≡ 0 (mod p²) and b ≡ 0 (mod p)), put U_p(σ) := U_p ∩ T_p(σ), V_p := U_p \ T_p(1³) (maximal at p and not totally ramified at p), Y_p := U_p ∩ T_p(1³) (maximal and totally ramified at p), W_p := V_Z \ U_p and Z_p := V_Z \ V_p = W_p ⊔ Y_p. Over Z_p use the corresponding coefficient conditions in Z_p⁴. Only the splitting-symbol sets T_p descend to F_p⁴; U_p and the maximality-dependent sets require coefficients modulo p² and cannot be defined from a residue in F_p⁴ alone.

Throughout this assertion, p is prime; the symbol is undefined for f ≡ 0 (mod p), and such f lie in W_p All the sets depend only on f mod p² (T_p(σ) only on f mod p), so they are finite unions of translates of p²V_Z and have well-defined p-adic densities The symbol is invariant under the twisted GL₂(Z)-action (γf)(x, y) = det(γ)^{-1} f((x, y)γ) of Layer 1, since GL₂ permutes the zeros in P¹ preserving degrees and multiplicities Z_p is BST's set of forms 'whose discriminants are not fundamental'; W_p and Y_p are its two parts

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `cubicSplittingSymbol`: (f, p) as a multiset of pairs (degree, multiplicity), defined for f ≢ 0 (mod p).

- `splittingTypeSet`: T_p(σ) = {f ∈ V_Z : f ≢ 0 mod p, (f, p) = σ}.

- `maximalNotTotallyRamifiedSet`: V_p = U_p \ T_p(1³).

- `maximalTotallyRamifiedSet`: Y_p = U_p ∩ T_p(1³).

- `notFundamentalSet`: Z_p = V_Z \ V_p.

- `cubicSplittingSymbol_mem_five`: For f ≢ 0 (mod p), (f, p) ∈ {(111), (12), (3), (1²1), (1³)}.

- `cubicSplittingSymbol_smul`: (γf, p) = (f, p) for γ ∈ GL₂(Z) (twisted action of Layer 1).

- `splittingTypeSet_mod`: Membership in T_p(σ) depends only on f mod p; membership in U_p, V_p, Y_p, Z_p only on f mod p².

- `notFundamentalSet_eq_union`: Z_p = W_p ⊔ Y_p, a disjoint union.


To prove the assertion, Factor f mod p over F_p into irreducible binary forms (homogeneous factorisation in F_p[x, y]); the pairs (degree, multiplicity) of the distinct irreducible factors, as a multiset, is the symbol; the five values are the multisets with Σ f_i e_i = 3. GL₂(F_p) acts on binary forms over F_p by linear substitution and scaling by det^{-1}, which maps irreducible factors to irreducible factors of the same degree with the same multiplicities; reduction mod p commutes with the action, so T_p(σ), U_p and hence V_p, Y_p, W_p, Z_p are GL₂(Z)-invariant. U_p is imported from Layer 1 (Davenport-Heilbronn's maximality criterion, BST Theorem 14); the remaining sets are Boolean combinations.

By Delone-Faddeev (Layer 1), GL₂(Z)-orbits of forms correspond to isomorphism classes of cubic rings with Disc(f) = Disc(R(f)); restricting to orbits with R(f) ≅ O_K for a cubic field K gives a bijection with isomorphism classes of cubic fields (K ≅ K' iff O_K ≅ O_{K'}), and Disc(O_K) = NumberField.discr K. ### 3.3 Quadratic resolvents and mean three-torsion


<a id="nowhere-totally-ramified-cubic-fields-and-unramified-cubic-extensions-of-the-resolvent"></a>


**Nowhere totally ramified cubic fields and unramified cubic extensions of the resolvent.** Let K₃ be a cubic field. (a) If K₃ is nowhere totally ramified (no prime p has p O_{K₃} = 𝔭³), then K₃ is not Galois (an S₃-cubic field). (b) For an S₃-cubic field K₃ with Galois closure K₆ and quadratic resolvent K₂ ⊆ K₆ (the fixed field of A₃ = Gal(K₆/K₂); K₂ = Q(√Disc(K₃))), the extension K₆/K₂ is unramified at all finite primes iff K₃ is nowhere totally ramified, and in that case Disc(K₃) = Disc(K₂). (c) Conversely, if K₂ is a quadratic field and L/K₂ is an unramified cyclic cubic extension that is Galois over Q with Gal(L/Q) ≅ S₃, then each of the three conjugate cubic subfields of L is nowhere totally ramified and has discriminant Disc(K₂). (The archimedean places impose no condition: a Galois extension of odd degree is unramified at infinity.)

Throughout this assertion, 'Unramified' is at finite primes; K₆/K₂ is Galois of odd degree, so its real-place inertia groups, of order at most two, are trivial. Odd degree alone would not suffice for an arbitrary non-Galois extension. K₂ is Q(√Disc(K₃)): √Disc(K₃) generates the fixed field of A₃ in K₆ Disc(K₃) ∈ Disc(K₂)·(Q^×)² always; equality needs the nowhere-totally-ramified hypothesis


To prove the assertion, (a) A cyclic cubic field has Disc = f² with f its conductor and every ramified prime totally ramified (inertia groups are subgroups of Z/3Z); a field with no ramified prime would be an unramified extension of Q, which does not exist (Minkowski, |Disc| > 1: NumberField.abs_discr_gt_two); so a nowhere totally ramified cubic field is S₃. (b) For a prime 𝔓 of K₆ over p with inertia group I ≤ S₃ acting on the three embeddings of K₃: the ramification indices of the primes of K₃ above p are the orbit lengths of I on {1, 2, 3} (Galois correspondence for inertia groups; NumberFieldArithmetic Layer 6 and LocalFieldsRamification Layer 3). p is totally ramified in K₃ iff I acts transitively iff 3 divides #I iff I ∩ A₃ ≠ 1 iff 𝔓 ∩ K₂ ramifies in K₆/K₂ (the inertia group of K₆/K₂ at 𝔓 is I ∩ A₃). Discriminant equality: at a prime p not totally ramified in K₃, K₃ ⊗ Q_p is either unramified (both discriminants prime to p; in the case (12) p is inert in K₂ but unramified) or Q_p × F with F/Q_p a ramified quadratic extension, and then K₂ ⊗ Q_p ≅ F (the discriminant algebra of Q_p × F is F), so v_p(Disc K₃) = v_p(disc F) = v_p(Disc K₂); the signs agree because Disc(K₃)/Disc(K₂) is a square. Hence Disc(K₃) = Disc(K₂). (c) The three cubic subfields of L are the fixed fields of the three transpositions; they are conjugate, and by (b) applied to L = K₆ they are nowhere totally ramified with discriminant Disc(K₂).

<a id="three-torsion-of-quadratic-class-groups-counts-cubic-fields"></a>


**Three torsion of quadratic class groups counts cubic fields.** For every quadratic field K₂, the number of isomorphism classes of cubic fields K₃ that are nowhere totally ramified and whose quadratic resolvent is K₂ (equivalently, by [nowhere totally ramified cubic fields and unramified cubic extensions of the resolvent](#nowhere-totally-ramified-cubic-fields-and-unramified-cubic-extensions-of-the-resolvent), with Disc(K₃) = Disc(K₂)) equals (h₃(K₂) − 1)/2, where h₃(K₂) = #Cl(K₂)[3]. Each such L is Galois over Q (its norm subgroup is stable under Gal(K₂/Q), whose generator σ acts on Cl(K₂) by c ↦ c^{−1}, because c·σ(c) is the class of the ideal norm to Q, which is principal), and Gal(L/Q) ≅ Z/3Z ⋊ Z/2Z with σ acting by inversion, i.e. S₃. By the resolvent lemma, the three cubic subfields of such an L form one isomorphism class of nowhere totally ramified cubic fields with resolvent K₂, and conversely the Galois closure of such a K₃ is such an L; distinct L give non-isomorphic cubic fields (L is the Galois closure). ### 3.4 Cubic local mass specifications


<a id="acceptable-local-specifications-for-cubic-orders"></a>


**Acceptable local specifications for cubic orders.** A local specification for cubic orders is a collection Σ = (Σ_p)_p ∪ Σ_∞ where, for each prime p, Σ_p is a set of isomorphism classes of nondegenerate cubic rings over Z_p (orders in étale cubic Q_p-algebras; by Delone-Faddeev over Z_p, equivalently a GL₂(Z_p)-invariant set of binary cubic forms over Z_p of nonzero discriminant), and Σ_∞ ⊆ {R³, R ⊕ C}. An order R in a cubic field is a Σ-order if R ⊗ Z_p ∈ Σ_p for all p and R ⊗ R ∈ Σ_∞. Σ is acceptable if for all sufficiently large p, Σ_p contains every maximal cubic Z_p-order that is not totally ramified; it is strongly acceptable if for all sufficiently large p, Σ_p is one of: all nondegenerate cubic Z_p-orders, all maximal ones, or all maximal ones not totally ramified. The local mass of Σ_p is m_p(Σ_p) := Σ_{R ∈ Σ_p} 1/(Disc_p(R) · #Aut(R)), where Disc_p(R) = p^{v_p(Disc R)}; the archimedean mass is m_∞(Σ_∞) := Σ_{R ∈ Σ_∞} 1/#Aut(R) with #Aut(R³) = 6 and #Aut(R ⊕ C) = 2.

Throughout this assertion, Isomorphism classes over Z_p, not over Q_p: several orders can lie in the same étale algebra Nondegenerate means nonzero discriminant; degenerate rings never occur as R ⊗ Z_p for an order R in a cubic field The infinite sum m_p over all nondegenerate orders converges (BST (57))

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `CubicLocalSpecification`: A family Σ_p (p prime) of GL₂(Z_p)-invariant sets of binary cubic forms over Z_p of nonzero discriminant, and a subset Σ_∞ of {R³, R ⊕ C}.

- `CubicLocalSpecification.IsAcceptable`: For all sufficiently large p, the forms of V_p ⊗ Z_p (maximal, not totally ramified) lie in Σ_p.

- `CubicLocalSpecification.IsStronglyAcceptable`: For all sufficiently large p, Σ_p is all nondegenerate forms, the maximal ones, or the maximal not totally ramified ones.

- `CubicLocalSpecification.IsStronglyAcceptable.isAcceptable`: Strongly acceptable implies acceptable.

- `CubicLocalSpecification.maximal`: The specification of maximal orders (all real types at ∞).

- `CubicLocalSpecification.nowhereTotallyRamified`: The specification of maximal orders not totally ramified at any p.

- `CubicLocalSpecification.localMass`: m_p(Σ_p) = Σ_{R ∈ Σ_p} 1/(Disc_p(R) #Aut(R)), as an element of [0, ∞].

- `CubicLocalSpecification.archimedeanMass`: m_∞(Σ_∞) = Σ_{R ∈ Σ_∞} 1/#Aut(R) ∈ {0, 1/6, 1/2, 2/3}.


To prove the assertion, Represent Σ_p as a GL₂(Z_p)-invariant subset of V_{Z_p} of forms of nonzero discriminant (Delone-Faddeev over Z_p, Layer 1) and Σ_∞ as a subset of the two real orbits; the predicates are statements about all but finitely many p. The three standard specifications: 'all orders' (Σ_p = everything, Σ_∞ = both), 'maximal' (Σ_p = the p-adic closure of U_p, equivalently its residue preimage modulo p²) and 'maximal and not totally ramified' (Σ_p = the p-adic closure of V_p, equivalently its residue preimage modulo p²); each is strongly acceptable, and strongly acceptable implies acceptable. The prototype must use the full residue preimage modulo p². Requiring one integral g congruent to a p-adic f modulo p^k for every k would restrict f to the countable integral image and would not even be GL₂(Z_p)-invariant. Equivalently one may use ∀k∃g, not ∃g∀k.

### 3.6 Classical quadratic and cubic orbit counts


<a id="mertens-count-of-positive-definite-binary-quadratic-forms"></a>


**Mertens count of positive definite binary quadratic forms.** For D < 0 let h⁺(D) be the number of SL₂(Z)-equivalence classes of positive definite integral binary quadratic forms a x² + b x y + c y² (a > 0) of discriminant b² − 4ac = D, all forms counted (primitive or not). Then Σ_{−X<D<0} h⁺(D) = (π/18) X^{3/2} + O(X log X).

Throughout this assertion, Positive definite forms only: counting the negative definite classes as well doubles the sum Non-primitive forms are included (they are irreducible over Q); the primitive count has constant (π/18)/ζ(3) Classes, not weighted classes: the forms x² + y² and x² + xy + y² and their multiples are counted with weight 1 (Hurwitz's weights 1/2, 1/3 change only lower-order terms)


To prove the assertion, Reduction: every positive definite form is SL₂(Z)-equivalent to exactly one reduced form (|b| ≤ a ≤ c, with b ≥ 0 if |b| = a or a = c). Write f = a(x − τy)(x − τ̄y) with τ in the upper half plane; SL₂(Z) acts on τ by Möbius transformations, and f is reduced iff τ lies in the closed fundamental domain ModularGroup.fd with the boundary identified (ModularGroup.exists_smul_mem_fd, ModularGroup.eq_smul_self_of_mem_fdo_mem_fdo). The canonical representatives are those pinned in ModularForms Layer 11. Counting: h⁺ summed over −X < D < 0 is the number of integer triples (a, b, c) with |b| ≤ a ≤ c, 4ac − b² < X and the boundary convention. Slice by a: a ≤ √(X/3), and for each (a, b) the number of c is max(0, (X + b²)/(4a) − a) + O(1); summing over |b| ≤ a and a ≤ √(X/3) gives the integral V(X) over the actual nonempty slices plus O(X log X) (the O(1) terms contribute O(X), the Riemann-sum error in b and a contributes O(X log X)). Volume: in coordinates (a, τ = x + iy), b = −2ax, c = a|τ|², the Jacobian is 4a²y and the discriminant condition is 4a²y² < X, so V(X) = ∫_{fd} ∫_0^{√X/(2y)} 4a²y da dx dy = (X^{3/2}/6) ∫_{fd} dx dy / y² = (X^{3/2}/6)(π/3) = (π/18) X^{3/2}, using the hyperbolic area ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} ∫_{√(1−x²)}^∞ dy dx / y² = 2 arcsin(1/2) = π/3.

**Siegel count of indefinite binary quadratic forms.** For positive nonsquare discriminants D≡0 or 1 (mod4), let h_D^prim be the number of SL₂(Z)-classes of primitive integral binary quadratic forms of discriminant D, and ε_D=(t+u√D)/2 for the least positive solution of t²−Du²=4. Equivalently, counting all forms with each class weighted by the regulator of its primitive part gives Σ_{g≥1,D>0,g²D<X} h_D^prim log ε_D ~ (π²/18)X^{3/2}. The class number is the strict class number of the quadratic order of discriminant D. The positive norm-one unit convention is fixed. The primitive/order version is Siegel’s mean theorem as stated in Andrade–Jung, Theorem1.2(2), with constant π²/(18ζ(3)) and error O(X log X). For fundamental D, the class-number formula identifies h_D^prim log ε_D with √D times the Dedekind zeta residue; extending the average to all orders requires the corresponding imprimitive Dirichlet characters. This analytic mean is still a quoted input, not a proved consequence of the library class-number formula. For the all-form stabilizer-weighted corollary, write each form uniquely as g times a primitive form. Its discriminant is g²D and its stabilizer is unchanged. Sum the primitive asymptotic at X/g²; the leading constants multiply by Σg^{-3}=ζ(3). Dominate by O(X^{3/2}/g³) to justify the limit and the tail. This does not weight an imprimitive form by the Pell regulator of its larger discriminant.

### 3.8 Quadratic four-rank moments


<a id="fouvry-kluners-moments-of-four-ranks"></a>


**Fouvry kluners moments of four ranks.** Let C_D be the narrow class group of the quadratic field of fundamental discriminant D and rk₄(C_D) = rk₂(C_D²) its 4-rank. For every integer k ≥ 0 and ε > 0, with N(k, 2) the number of F₂-subspaces of F₂^k and R(X, ε, k) = X(log X)^{−2^{−k}+ε}: Σ_{0<−D<X} 2^{k·rk₄(C_D)} = N(k, 2) Σ_{0<−D<X} 1 + O_{ε,k}(R(X, ε, k)) and Σ_{0<D<X} 2^{k·rk₄(C_D)} = 2^{−k}(N(k + 1, 2) − N(k, 2)) Σ_{0<D<X} 1 + O_{ε,k}(R(X, ε, k)) (and the same within each of the classes D ≡ 1 (mod 4), 0 (mod 8), 4 (mod 8)). Equivalently (FK Theorem 1) the moment prediction Conj^±(2, α) holds for every α ≥ 0, and (FK Theorem 3) for every r ≥ 0 the density of negative fundamental discriminants with rk₄(C_D) = r is 2^{−r²} η_∞(2) η_r(2)^{−2} and of positive ones 2^{−r(r+1)} η_∞(2) η_r(2)^{−1} η_{r+1}(2)^{−1}, where η_k(t) = ∏_{j=1}^{k} (1 − t^{−j}).

Throughout this assertion, The narrow class group is used; for D < 0 it equals the class group, and FK's Corollary 1 transfers the statements to the ordinary class group Cl_D The error term saves only a power of log X; the theorem is an unconditional limit, not a heuristic Use the Rédei-matrix, linked character-sum and good-subspace targets of this layer.


To prove the assertion, Rédei: rk₄(C_D) is the corank of an explicit F₂-matrix (the Rédei matrix) built from Legendre symbols between the prime factors of D. Expand 2^{k·rk₄} as a sum of products of Jacobi symbols over factorizations of D, and show that only the 'diagonal' terms contribute to the main term (Siegel-Walfisz and large-sieve estimates for the others); FK Theorems 6-11 treat the six families (3). Proposition 1 turns the moments into Conj^±(2, α); FK Theorem 2 (from [5]) turns all moments into the distribution (Theorem 3).

<a id="cohen-lenstra-moment-prediction"></a>


**Cohen lenstra moment prediction.** For a prime p and an integer α ≥ 0, the propositions Conj^−(p, α) and Conj^+(p, α) are: M^−(∏_{0≤i<α} (p^{rk_p(C_D²)} − p^i)) = 1 and M^+(∏_{0≤i<α} (p^{rk_p(C_D²)} − p^i)) = p^{−α}, where C_D is the narrow class group of the quadratic field of discriminant D, C_D² its subgroup of squares, and M^±(f) := lim_{X→∞} (Σ_{0<±D<X} f(D))/(Σ_{0<±D<X} 1) over fundamental discriminants D (the limit is asserted to exist). For odd p, rk_p(C_D²) = rk_p(Cl_D) and p^{rk_p} = h_p ([torsion count of class groups](#torsion-count-of-class-groups)), so the moment is the average of ∏_{i<α}(h_p(K) − p^i), i.e. of the number of injections (Z/pZ)^α → Cl(K)[p]. These are conjectural propositions: every theorem of this construction that uses one takes it as an explicit hypothesis, and none is assumed.

Throughout this assertion, For odd p this is Cohen-Lenstra's conjecture (C6), (C10); for p = 2 Gerth's modification replaces C_D by C_D² (genus theory fixes rk₂(C_D) = ω(D) − 1) The mean over fundamental discriminants of one sign ordered by |D| A proposition with content (a limit statement), never a hypothesis-free axiom

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `cohenLenstraMomentPrediction`: Conj^±(p, α) as a proposition about the limit of the mean of ∏_{i<α}(h_p(K) − p^i) over quadratic fields of one sign (odd p; p = 2 uses C_D²).

- `cohenLenstraMomentPrediction_zero`: Conj^±(p, 0) holds (the mean of 1 is 1).

- `cohenLenstraMomentPrediction_three_one`: The Davenport-Heilbronn theorem is equivalent to Conj^−(3, 1) ∧ Conj^+(3, 1).

To prove the assertion, Define M^± as the limit of ratios of finite sums over the finite sets of fundamental discriminants with 0 < ±D < X ([count of quadratic fields](#count-of-quadratic-fields) gives the denominators ~ 3X/π²). Define the proposition as the statement that this limit equals 1, resp. p^{−α}.

### 3.9 Malle predictions and their cyclotomic obstruction


<a id="malle-invariants-of-a-permutation-group"></a>


**Malle invariants of a permutation group.** Let 1 ≠ G ≤ S_n be transitive on Ω = {1, …, n}. For g ∈ G, ind(g) := n − (number of orbits of ⟨g⟩ on Ω) = Σ over the cycles of g of (length − 1). ind(G) := min{ind(g) : 1 ≠ g ∈ G} and a(G) := ind(G)^{−1}. For a number field k, the absolute Galois group of k acts on the set of conjugacy classes of G through the cyclotomic character: σ sends the class C of g to the class of g^{χ(σ)}, χ(σ) ∈ (Z/eZ)^× the action on e-th roots of unity, e the exponent of G; the orbits are the k-conjugacy classes, and b(k, G) := the number of k-conjugacy classes C with ind(C) = ind(G). Equivalently, with H_k ≤ (Z/eZ)^× the image of Gal(k(ζ_e)/k), b(k, G) is the number of orbits of H_k acting by powering on the conjugacy classes of minimal index.

Throughout this assertion, G ≠ 1 and transitive ind is a class function, so ind(C) is well defined b depends on k only through H_k; H_Q = (Z/eZ)^× and H_k = 1 when ζ_e ∈ k

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `malleIndex`: ind(g) = #support(g) − #cycles(g) for g ∈ S_n.

- `malleIndexGroup`: ind(G) = min over g ∈ G, g ≠ 1, of ind(g).

- `malleA`: a(G) = 1/ind(G) ∈ Q.

- `malleB`: b(H, G): the number of orbits of H ≤ (Z/eZ)^× acting by powering on the conjugacy classes of G of minimal index (b(k, G) with H = H_k).

- `malleIndex_conj`: ind(h g h^{−1}) = ind(g).

- `malleIndex_pow_of_isUnit`: ind(g^u) = ind(g) for u prime to the order of g.

- `malleB_pos`: 1 ≤ b(H, G) for G ≠ 1.

- `malleB_anti`: H ≤ H' implies b(H', G) ≤ b(H, G): enlarging k (shrinking H_k) can only increase b.


To prove the assertion, ind(g) = #support(g) − #cycles(g) (cycle type of the permutation). The powering action of (Z/eZ)^× on conjugacy classes is well defined because g^e = 1, preserves ind (⟨g^u⟩ = ⟨g⟩ for u a unit), and b counts orbits of H_k on the minimal-index classes.

*Needs:* `Equiv.Perm` (Mathlib), `Fintype.card` (Mathlib).

([[23]](#ref-23), Definitions 1.1 and 1.2, p. 1; [[23]](#ref-23), Definition 1.2, p. 1.)

- For a prime ℓ and G = C_ℓ in its regular representation, ind(G) = ℓ − 1, so a(G) = 1/(ℓ − 1), and b(Q, G) = 1.

- For G = C₃ ≤ S₃ and H = 1 (k ∋ ζ₃), b = 2.

- For G = S₂ = C₂: ind(G) = 1, a(G) = 1, b(Q, G) = 1.

- Counting ordinary conjugacy classes of minimal index (H = 1) for G = C₃ ≤ S₃ over Q gives 2, not b(Q, C₃) = 1: the cyclotomic action must be included.

- S_n (n ≥ 2): transpositions have index 1, so a(S_n) = 1 and b(Q, S_n) = 1.

- C₃ ≀ C₂ ≤ S₆: a = 1/2, b(Q, G) = 1 and b(Q(ζ₃), G) = 2 (Kluners).

- S₃ ≤ S₆ (regular): a = 1/3, b(Q) = 1.


<a id="malle-conjecture"></a>


**Malle conjecture.** For a number field k and a transitive 1 ≠ G ≤ S_n, let Z(k, G; x) be the number of extensions K/k inside a fixed algebraic closure k̄ of degree n whose Galois group (the normal closure's group acting on the n embeddings over k) is permutation-isomorphic to G, with N_{k/Q}(d_{K/k}) ≤ x. The strong Malle conjecture MalleStrong(k, G) is the proposition: there is c(k, G) > 0 with Z(k, G; x) ~ c(k, G) x^{a(G)} (log x)^{b(k,G)−1} as x → ∞. The weak Malle conjecture MalleWeak(k, G) is: there is c₁ > 0 with Z(k, G; x) ≥ c₁ x^{a(G)} for x large, and for every ε > 0 there is c₂(ε) with Z(k, G; x) ≤ c₂(ε) x^{a(G)+ε}. For k = Q, counting isomorphism classes instead of subfields of Q̄ changes Z by the constant factor n/#Aut(K/Q) (which depends only on G), so the statements are unchanged when Z(Q, G; x) is replaced by N_n(Gal = G; −x, x) of [number field counting function](#number-field-counting-function). These are conjectural propositions: MalleStrong is false in general (Kluners), and theorems using either form take it as an explicit hypothesis.

Throughout this assertion, The invariants a(G) and b(k, G) are those of [malle invariants of a permutation group](#malle-invariants-of-a-permutation-group) Z counts subfields of k̄, not isomorphism classes; the conversion factor is constant for fixed G MalleStrong(Q,G) is refuted for G=C₃≀C₂≤S₆. The cited2016 survey reports no counterexample to its weak form; this is a statement about that source, not an independently surveyed current-status claim.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `malleStrong`: MalleStrong(Q, G): ∃ c > 0, N_n(Gal = G; −X, X) ~ c X^{a(G)} (log X)^{b(Q,G)−1}.

- `malleWeak`: MalleWeak(Q, G): a lower bound ≫ X^{a(G)} and upper bounds ≪_ε X^{a(G)+ε}.

- `malleStrong_imp_malleWeak`: MalleStrong(k, G) implies MalleWeak(k, G).

- `malleStrong_iff_subfield_count`: For k = Q, MalleStrong stated with the subfield count Z(Q, G; x) is equivalent to the statement with isomorphism classes.

- `malleStrong_symmetric_two`: MalleStrong(Q, S₂) (from the count of quadratic fields).


To prove the assertion, Define Z(k, G; x) as a finite count (Hermite's theorem over k) and the two propositions by the displayed asymptotic statements. Record the known cases as tests: abelian G (Wright), S₃ ≤ S₃ (Davenport-Heilbronn), S₄, S₅ (Bhargava), and the failure for C₃ ≀ C₂.

*Needs:* [malle invariants of a permutation group](#malle-invariants-of-a-permutation-group), [number field counting function](#number-field-counting-function).

([[23]](#ref-23), Conjecture 1.3, pp. 1-2; [[21]](#ref-21), Section 10.2, p. 22.)

- The Davenport-Heilbronn theorem implies MalleStrong(Q, S₃), with c = 1/(3ζ(3)) up to the contribution of cyclic cubic fields (o(X)).

<a id="kluners-counterexample-to-malle-conjecture"></a>


**Kluners counterexample to malle conjecture.** For G = C₃ ≀ C₂ = C₃² ⋊ C₂ ≤ S₆ (order 18), a(G) = 1/2 and b(Q, G) = 1, but Z(Q, G; x) ≫ x^{1/2} log x; hence MalleStrong(Q, C₃ ≀ C₂) is false. More precisely Z̃(Q, G; x) ≥ Z(Q(ζ₃), C₃; x/27) ~ (c(Q(ζ₃), C₃)/√27) x^{1/2} log x, where Z̃ counts towers L/K/Q with Gal(L/K) = C₃, [K : Q] = 2, |d_L| ≤ x, and the C₆ and S₃(6) contributions are O(x^{1/3}) and O(x^{1/2}), respectively, which suffice for the contradiction (the source quotes a stronger S₃(6) bound).

Throughout this assertion, The failure is caused by the cyclotomic intermediate field K = Q(ζ₃): excluding it restores the predicted order x^{1/2} The lower bound uses the abelian case of Malle's conjecture (Wright) over K = Q(ζ₃), where b(K, C₃) = 2


To prove the assertion, Compute a(G) = 1/2 (the elements of order 3 with three fixed points have index 2) and b(Q, G) = 1 (the two classes of such elements are fused by the cyclotomic action over Q), but b(Q(ζ₃), C₃) = 2. Lower bound: every cyclic cubic extension L/K of K = Q(ζ₃) with Galois group of L/Q equal to G gives a sextic field with |d_L| = d_K³ N(d_{L/K}) = 27 N(d_{L/K}); by Wright's theorem Z(K, C₃; y) ~ c y^{1/2} log y; at y=x/27 the leading constant is c/√27 (b(K, C₃) = 2). The C₆ contribution is O(x^{1/3}) by the abelian case. For S₃ Galois sextic fields L, choose a conjugate cubic subfield K. The tower discriminant identity gives |Disc L|≥|Disc K|², and the Galois closure determines L from the isomorphism class of K; Davenport–Heilbronn thus gives O(x^{1/2}). Both are o(x^{1/2}logx), sufficient for the claimed counterexample. The stronger O(x^{1/3}) bound quoted without proof by Klüners is not needed here.

### 3.10 Gaussian coefficients


<a id="gaussian-binomial-coefficient"></a>


**Gaussian binomial coefficient.** For an element t of a field (or t = q a prime power) and integers 0 ≤ k ≤ n, the Gaussian binomial coefficient is [n k]_t := ∏_{i=1}^{k} (1 − t^{n−k+i})/(1 − t^{i}) when t is not a root of unity of order ≤ n, extended as the polynomial in ℤ[t] defined by the recursion [n 0]_t = [n n]_t = 1, [n+1 k]_t = [n k−1]_t + t^{k}[n k]_t, and [n k]_t := 0 for k > n. For a finite field 𝔽_q, [n k]_q equals the number of k-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽_q^n.

Throughout this assertion, 0 ≤ k for the subspace count: q = #𝔽_q a prime power

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `gaussBinom`: [n k]_t as an element of a field, via the recursion (0 for k > n).

- `gaussBinom_zero_right`: [n 0]_t = 1.

- `gaussBinom_self`: [n n]_t = 1.

- `gaussBinom_succ_succ`: [n+1 k+1]_t = [n k]_t + t^{k+1}[n k+1]_t.

- `gaussBinom_eq_prod`: When no t^i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) equals 1: [n k]_t = ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − t^{n−k+i})/(1 − t^i).

- `gaussBinom_symm`: [n k]_t = [n n−k]_t for k ≤ n.

- `gaussBinom_one`: [n k]_1 = Nat.choose n k.

- `card_submodules_finrank_eq_gaussBinom`: For a finite field K with q elements, #{W ≤ K^n : dim W = k} = [n k]_q.


To prove the assertion, Define [n k]_t by the recursion in ℤ[t] (a polynomial), and evaluate at t. Product formula: induct on n; the recursion [n+1 k]_t = [n k−1]_t + t^k[n k]_t is the identity (1 − t^{n+1})/(1 − t^{k}) · P = P' + t^k P'' between the products, checked by clearing denominators (routine algebra in the fraction field). Subspace count: the k-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽_q^n are the orbits of GL_k(𝔽_q) acting freely on linearly independent k-tuples; divide mathlib:card_linearIndependent (#independent k-tuples = ∏_{i<k}(q^n − q^i)) by mathlib:Matrix.card_GL_field (#GL_k(𝔽_q) = ∏_{i<k}(q^k − q^i)) and compare with the product formula.

*Needs:* `card_linearIndependent` (Mathlib), `Matrix.card_GL_field` (Mathlib), `Polynomial.coeff` (Mathlib).

([[28]](#ref-28), Proof of Proposition 2.6(e), p. 7; [[25]](#ref-25), §2, Case 2.12, p. 9 (arXiv v2).)


**Checks.**


- gaussBinom 2 4 2 = 35.

- gaussBinom t n 0 = 1 and gaussBinom t 0 k = 0 for k ≥ 1.

- gaussBinom 1 5 2 = 10 = Nat.choose 5 2.

- gaussBinom 2 3 1 = 7 ≠ 3 = Nat.choose 3 1: the q-analogue is not the ordinary binomial.

- [n k]_1 = binomial(n, k) (specialisation t = 1 of the polynomial).

- [4 2]_2 = 35 = number of 2-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽_2^4.

- [n k]_t = [n n−k]_t.


<a id="cauchy-q-binomial-theorem"></a>


**Cauchy q binomial theorem.** For an element t of a commutative ring and n ≥ 0, in the polynomial ring in z: ∏_{i=0}^{n−1} (1 + t^{i} z) = Σ_{k=0}^{n} t^{k(k−1)/2} [n k]_t z^{k}.

Throughout this assertion, n ≥ 0; t arbitrary


To prove the assertion, Induct on n: multiply the identity for n by (1 + t^{n} z) and compare coefficients of z^{k} using the recursion [n+1 k]_t = t^{k}[n k]_t + [n k−1]_t ([gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient), API gaussBinom_succ_succ and gaussBinom_symm). Coefficient comparison is routine algebra in ℤ[t][z] (mathlib:Polynomial.coeff).

*Needs:* [gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient), `Polynomial.coeff` (Mathlib).

([[28]](#ref-28), Proof of Proposition 2.6(e), p. 7.)


**Checks.**


- n = 1: 1 + z = 1 + z.

- n = 2: (1 + z)(1 + tz) = 1 + (1 + t)z + t z².


### 3.11 Finite abelian groups and Cohen–Lenstra mass


<a id="isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>


**Isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups.** The carrier L of isomorphism classes of finite abelian p-groups is the type of pairs (n, λ) with n ∈ ℕ and λ a partition of n (Mathlib Nat.Partition n). For a prime p the class (n, λ) is realised by the standard representative A_λ = ⊕_i ℤ/p^{λ_i} (parts in decreasing order), a group of order p^n. Attached data: the conjugate partition λ'_i = #{j : λ_j ≥ i} (so λ'_1 is the p-rank and p^{λ'_1} = |A_λ[p]|), the multiplicity m_i(λ) = #{j : λ_j = i}, the automorphism count |Aut A_λ|, and the trivial class (0, ∅). Every finite abelian p-group is isomorphic to A_λ for exactly one λ.

Throughout this assertion, p prime (for the realisation and the classification)

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `FinAbPGroupClass.toGroup`: The standard representative ⊕_i ℤ/p^{λ_i} of a class, an additive commutative group.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.card_toGroup`: For p prime, |toGroup p (n, λ)| = p^n.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.exists_addEquiv_toGroup`: Every finite abelian group G in which every element is killed by a power of p is isomorphic to toGroup p A for some class A (compatibility with Mathlib's structure theorem AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite).

- `FinAbPGroupClass.eq_of_addEquiv`: If toGroup p A ≅ toGroup p B then A = B.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.conjPart`: The conjugate partition λ'_i = #{j : λ_j ≥ i}.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.partMult`: The multiplicity m_i(λ) of the part i.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.card_torsion_eq_pow_conjPart`: |{x ∈ A_λ : p x = 0}| = p^{λ'_1} (the p-rank).

- `FinAbPGroupClass.autCard`: |Aut(A_λ)|, the number of additive automorphisms of the representative.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.autCard_pos`: |Aut A_λ| > 0.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.trivial`: The trivial class (0, ∅).

- `FinAbPGroupClass.subsingleton_toGroup_trivial`: The representative of the trivial class is the zero group.


To prove the assertion, Define the carrier as the dependent pair type Σ n, Nat.Partition n; sort the parts decreasingly and take the product of ZMod (p^{λ_i}) as representative, with its AddCommGroup structure from the Pi instance. Order: |A_λ| = ∏ p^{λ_i} = p^{Σλ_i} = p^n (ZMod.card and Fintype.card of a Pi type). Existence of a class for a finite abelian p-group G: apply AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite to get G ≅ ⊕ ℤ/q_i^{e_i}; since G is p-primary every q_i = p (or e_i = 0), so the exponents form a partition of log_p|G|. Uniqueness: the conjugate partition is recovered from the invariants |p^{i-1}G/p^iG| = p^{λ'_i}, which are isomorphism invariants, and a partition is determined by its conjugate. The p-torsion count |A_λ[p]| = p^{λ'_1}: each cyclic factor ℤ/p^{λ_j} with λ_j ≥ 1 contributes a factor p.

*Needs:* `Nat.Partition` (Mathlib), `AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite` (Mathlib), `ZMod.card` (Mathlib), `Multiset.sort` (Mathlib).

([[37]](#ref-37), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771; [[39]](#ref-39), arXiv 1407.3066v1, §2, p. 3–4.)


**Checks.**


- |Aut(ℤ/p)| = p − 1 for the class (1, (1)).

- The trivial class has exactly one automorphism.

- Nat.card of the representative of (2, (1,1)) is p².

- The representatives of (2, (2)) and (2, (1,1)) are not isomorphic although they have the same order, so a carrier indexed by the order alone is wrong.

- |A_{(1)}| = p, |Aut A_{(1)}| = p − 1; the trivial class has one automorphism.

- ℤ/p² and (ℤ/p)² both have order p² and are different classes (conjugate partitions (1,1) and (2)).


<a id="automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>


**Automorphism count of finite abelian p groups.** For p prime and a partition λ with conjugate partition λ' and part multiplicities m_i, |Aut(A_λ)| = p^{Σ_i (λ'_i)²} · ∏_i ∏_{s=1}^{m_i} (1 − p^{−s}). Equivalently (Hillar–Rhea, Theorem 4.1), for A = ⊕_{k=1}^{n} ℤ/p^{e_k} with e_1 ≤ … ≤ e_n, d_k = max{l : e_l = e_k}, c_k = min{l : e_l = e_k}: |Aut A| = ∏_k (p^{d_k} − p^{k−1}) ∏_j (p^{e_j})^{n−d_j} ∏_i (p^{e_i−1})^{n−c_i+1}.

Throughout this assertion, p prime λ a partition


To prove the assertion, Describe End(A) as the ring of n×n matrices (a_{ij}) with a_{ij} ∈ ℤ/p^{e_i} and p^{e_i−e_j} | a_{ij} when e_i > e_j (Hillar–Rhea Theorem 3.3). An endomorphism is an automorphism iff its reduction modulo p is invertible on each block of equal exponents (Hillar–Rhea Theorem 3.6): count the block-triangular matrices over F_p with invertible diagonal blocks and multiply by the number of lifts of each entry. Collect the powers of p into p^{Σ(λ'_i)²} using Σ_{i,j} min(λ_i, λ_j) = Σ_i (λ'_i)² and the diagonal-block orders |GL_{m_i}(F_p)| = p^{m_i²} ∏_{s=1}^{m_i}(1 − p^{−s}) (Mathlib Matrix.card_GL_field).

*Needs:* [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), `Matrix.card_GL_field` (Mathlib).

([[40]](#ref-40), Amer. Math. Monthly 114 (2007); arXiv math/0605185v1, Theorem 4.1, PDF/printed p. 6 (matrix description and invertibility criterion pp. 3–5); [[39]](#ref-39), arXiv 1407.3066v1, Lemma 3 and p. 4.)


**Checks.**


- |Aut(ℤ/p^k)| = p^k − p^{k−1}; |Aut((ℤ/p)^m)| = |GL_m(F_p)|.

- |Aut(ℤ/p² × ℤ/p)| = p³(p − 1)²; for p = 3: 108 = |Aut(ℤ/9 × ℤ/3)|, the value used in EVW item 125.


<a id="surjection-count"></a>


**Surjection count.** For additive abelian groups X and A, Sur(X, A) is the set of surjective group homomorphisms X → A and |Sur(X, A)| its cardinality (Nat.card; it is finite when X is finitely generated and A finite).

Throughout this assertion, X, A abelian groups

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `surjCard`: |Sur(X, A)| as a natural number.

- `surjCard_congr`: Isomorphisms X ≅ X', A ≅ A' give |Sur(X, A)| = |Sur(X', A')|.

- `surjCard_toGroup_self`: |Sur(A_λ, A_λ)| = |Aut(A_λ)|.

- `surjCard_le_card_hom`: |Sur(X, A)| ≤ |Hom(X, A)| for finite X, A.

- `surjCard_punit`: |Sur(X, 0)| = 1.

- `surjCard_eq_zero_of_card_lt`: If |X| < |A| (finite) then |Sur(X, A)| = 0.


To prove the assertion, Define |Sur(X, A)| as Nat.card of the subtype {f : X →+ A // f surjective}. Invariance: composing with isomorphisms X ≅ X', A ≅ A' is a bijection on surjections. For finite X, A: a surjection from a group of smaller order does not exist; surjective endomorphisms of a finite group are automorphisms.

*Needs:* `MonoidHom` (Mathlib), `Function.Surjective` (Mathlib), `Nat.card` (Mathlib).

([[37]](#ref-37), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771; [[38]](#ref-38), arXiv 1504.04391v1, §1, p. 3.)


**Checks.**


- |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p)| = p − 1.

- |Sur(ℤ/p × ℤ/p, ℤ/p)| = p² − 1.

- |Sur(ℤ/5, 0)| = 1.

- |Sur(ℤ/p, ℤ/p²)| = 0 although |Hom(ℤ/p, ℤ/p²)| = p: a definition counting homomorphisms fails.

- |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p)| = p − 1 and |Sur((ℤ/p)², ℤ/p)| = p² − 1.

- |Sur(X, 0)| = 1 for every X.


<a id="exact-surjection-count-formula"></a>


**Exact surjection count formula.** Let p be prime, X = A_ξ and A = A_α finite abelian p-groups with conjugate partitions x_i = ξ'_i and a_i = α'_i. If x_i < a_i for some i then |Sur(X, A)| = 0. Otherwise |Sur(X, A)| = ∏_{i ≥ 1} p^{x_i a_{i+1}} ∏_{j = a_{i+1}}^{a_i − 1} (p^{x_i} − p^j).

Throughout this assertion, p prime X, A finite abelian p-groups


To prove the assertion, Use the coordinate perfect pairings A_λ × A_λ → Q/Z, with each Z/p^e factor paired by xy/p^e mod Z. Dualizing a homomorphism gives a bijection Sur(X,A) ≃ Inj(A,X); these pairings explicitly identify each finite group with its character dual. Let V_i = p^{i−1}X[p^i] ⊆ X[p]. These form a decreasing flag of F_p-spaces of dimensions x_i. Write A as a direct sum with m_i=a_i−a_{i+1} cyclic generators of order p^i, and choose their images from the largest i downwards. An additive map A→X is injective iff it is injective on A[p]: every nonzero subgroup of a finite p-group meets A[p]. The order-p images already chosen from longer cyclic factors span a_{i+1} independent vectors in V_i. Choosing the m_i new order-p images therefore gives ∏_{j=a_{i+1}}^{a_i−1}(p^{x_i}−p^j). If x_i<a_i for some i, this cannot be done. Each chosen order-p vector in V_i lifts to X[p^i] under p^{i−1} in exactly |X[p^{i−1}]| = p^{Σ_{k<i}x_k} ways. For all m_i generators the total lift exponent is Σ_i m_i Σ_{k<i}x_k = Σ_k x_k a_{k+1}. Multiplying gives the stated formula.

*Needs:* [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), [surjection count](#surjection-count).

([[37]](#ref-37), Annals 183 (2016), proof of Lemma 8.4, p. 772.)


**Checks.**


- |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p)| = p − 1, |Sur(ℤ/p², ℤ/p²)| = p(p − 1) = |Aut(ℤ/p²)|, |Sur(ℤ/p × ℤ/p², ℤ/p²)| = p²(p − 1).

- Exhaustive check for p = 2 and all pairs with |X| ≤ 16: the formula agrees with direct enumeration of homomorphisms (carried out by direct finite enumeration).


<a id="partitions-with-large-parts-by-largest-part"></a>


**Partitions with large parts by largest part.** For u, m ≥ 0 let a_m be the number of partitions of m with every part ≥ u + 1 and b_{i,j} the number of partitions of i with largest part exactly j. Then a_m = Σ_{i + uj = m} b_{i,j}; equivalently, as formal power series, ∏_{j ≥ u+1} (1 − q^j)^{−1} = Σ_{n ≥ 0} f_n(q) q^{nu} with f_n(q) = Σ_N b_{N,n} q^N.

Throughout this assertion, u ∈ ℕ


To prove the assertion, Adding u copies of the row of length j to the Young diagram of a partition of i with largest part j gives a partition of i + uj whose largest part occurs at least u + 1 times, and this is a bijection. Conjugation exchanges 'largest part occurs at least u + 1 times' with 'every part is at least u + 1'. The generating function of partitions with all parts ≥ u + 1 is ∏_{j≥u+1}(1 − q^j)^{−1} (Mathlib Nat.Partition.hasProd_powerSeriesMk_card_restricted with the predicate u + 1 ≤ ·); regroup the right side by n.

*Needs:* `Nat.Partition.hasProd_powerSeriesMk_card_restricted` (Mathlib), `Nat.Partition.restricted` (Mathlib).

([[39]](#ref-39), arXiv 1407.3066v1, Lemmas 1–2, p. 2.)


**Checks.**


- u = 0: a_m = p(m) = Σ_j b_{m,j}.

- m = 2, u = 1: a_2 = 1 (the partition (2)) and b_{2,0} + b_{1,1} = 0 + 1 = 1.


<a id="hall-partition-identity"></a>


**Hall partition identity.** For every n ≥ 0 and a prime p, with q = p^{−1}: f_n(q) := Σ_{N≥0} b_{N,n} q^N = Σ_{λ ⊢ n} 1/|Aut A_λ|, where b_{N,n} counts partitions of N with largest part exactly n. Equivalently f_n(q) = Σ_{μ ⊢ n} q^{Σ μ_i²} ∏_i ψ_{μ_i, μ_{i−1} − μ_i}(q) with ψ_{a,b}(q) = ∏_{i=1}^{a+b}(1 − q^i)/(∏_{i=1}^{a}(1 − q^i) ∏_{i=1}^{b}(1 − q^i)), ψ_{a,∞}(q) = 1/∏_{i=1}^{a}(1 − q^i) and μ_0 = ∞.

Throughout this assertion, p prime n ∈ ℕ


To prove the assertion, Given a partition ν of N with largest part n, take the Young diagram D of ν' (height n) and cut out the Durfee-type squares μ_1 × μ_1, μ_2 × μ_2, … stacked vertically down the left edge (μ_1 largest with (μ_1, μ_1) ∈ D, μ_i largest with (μ_1+…+μ_i, μ_i) ∈ D); then |μ| = n. The cells to the right of the i-th square form a partition of height ≤ μ_i and width ≤ μ_{i−1} − μ_i, counted by ψ_{μ_i, μ_{i−1}−μ_i}(q); the construction is reversible. The rows of the i-th strip are μ₁+⋯+μ_{i−1} < x ≤ μ₁+⋯+μ_i; the source incorrectly prints a strict upper inequality. The rectangle generating function ψ is the Gaussian binomial, obtained by splitting partitions at the last row/column and applying its recursion. Substitute the automorphism count ([automorphism count of finite abelian p groups](#automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups)): 1/|Aut A_λ| = q^{Σ(λ'_i)²}∏_i 1/(q)_{λ'_i−λ'_{i+1}}, and the product ∏_i ψ_{μ_i, μ_{i−1}−μ_i}(q) telescopes to ∏_i 1/(q)_{μ_i−μ_{i+1}}; with μ = λ' the right side is Σ_{λ⊢n} 1/|Aut A_λ|.

*Needs:* [automorphism count of finite abelian p groups](#automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), `Nat.Partition` (Mathlib), [gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient).

([[39]](#ref-39), arXiv 1407.3066v1, pp. 5–6 (following Hall 1938).)


**Checks.**


- n = 1: Σ_N b_{N,1} q^N = q/(1 − q) = 1/(p − 1) = 1/|Aut ℤ/p|.

- n = 0: both sides are 1.


<a id="weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum"></a>


**Weighted inverse automorphism sum.** For a prime p and u ≥ 0: Σ_{A ∈ L} 1/(|A|^u |Aut A|) = ∏_{j ≥ u+1} (1 − p^{−j})^{−1}, the sum converging in ℝ.

Throughout this assertion, p prime u ∈ ℕ


To prove the assertion, Group the sum by n = log_p|A|: Σ_A |A|^{−u}|Aut A|^{−1} = Σ_n q^{nu} Σ_{λ⊢n} |Aut A_λ|^{−1} with q = 1/p. By Hall's identity Σ_{λ⊢n}|Aut A_λ|^{−1} = f_n(q) ([hall partition identity](#hall-partition-identity)). By [partitions with large parts by largest part](#partitions-with-large-parts-by-largest-part), Σ_n f_n(q) q^{nu} = ∏_{j≥u+1}(1 − q^j)^{−1}; the power series converge absolutely at q = 1/p < 1, so the formal identity specialises (nonnegative coefficients, monotone convergence). To justify analytic evaluation independently of the formal-series topology, expand finite products as nonnegative series and apply monotone convergence as the allowed part sizes grow. Their values are bounded by the positive convergent inverse Euler product, since Σ_j q^j < ∞. Thus the full series is finite; evaluation at q is not asserted to be continuous for the formal-series topology.

*Needs:* [hall partition identity](#hall-partition-identity), [partitions with large parts by largest part](#partitions-with-large-parts-by-largest-part), [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups).

([[39]](#ref-39), arXiv 1407.3066v1, Theorem, p. 1; [[38]](#ref-38), arXiv 1504.04391v1, proof of Lemma 3.2, p. 10.)


**Checks.**


- u = 0: Σ_A 1/|Aut A| = ∏_{j≥1}(1 − p^{−j})^{−1} (Hall's 'strange formula').

- p = 2, u = 0: the truncation to |A| ≤ 2 gives 1 + 1 = 2 ≤ ∏(1 − 2^{−j})^{−1} ≈ 3.46.


<a id="cohen-lenstra-mass-formula"></a>


**Cohen lenstra mass formula.** For a prime p and u ≥ 0, Σ_{A ∈ L} c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|) = 1, i.e. the Cohen–Lenstra weights have total mass one.

Throughout this assertion, p prime u ∈ ℕ


To prove the assertion, Multiply [weighted inverse automorphism sum](#weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum) by c_{p,u} = ∏_{j≥u+1}(1 − p^{−j}); the product is multipliable and nonzero, so c_{p,u}·c_{p,u}^{−1} = 1. Transport the real series to ℝ≥0∞ (ENNReal.ofReal of nonnegative terms) to get the HasSum statement used by the PMF.

*Needs:* [weighted inverse automorphism sum](#weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum), [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups).

([[38]](#ref-38), arXiv 1504.04391v1, Lemma 3.2, p. 9; [[37]](#ref-37), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771.)


**Checks.**


- For u = 0, p = 3: the masses of 0, ℤ/3, ℤ/9, (ℤ/3)² are ≈ 0.5601, 0.2801, 0.0934, 0.0117.

- The statement fails for the weights 1/|A|^u alone (they do not sum to a finite value for u = 0).


<a id="cohen-lenstra-measure"></a>


**Cohen lenstra measure.** For a prime p and an integer u ≥ 0 put c_{p,u} = ∏_{i ≥ u+1} (1 − p^{−i}). The Cohen–Lenstra measure μ_{p,u} is the probability measure on the isomorphism classes L of finite abelian p-groups with μ_{p,u}(A) = c_{p,u} / (|A|^u · |Aut A|). The case u = 0 is the Cohen–Lenstra distribution of EVW §8.1 (imaginary quadratic fields); u = 1 is the real-quadratic distribution. Total mass one is the mass formula ([cohen lenstra mass formula](#cohen-lenstra-mass-formula)), which the construction takes as input.

Throughout this assertion, p prime u ∈ ℕ

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `cohenLenstraConstant`: c_{p,u} = ∏_{i≥u+1} (1 − p^{−i}).

- `cohenLenstraWeight`: The weight c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|) ∈ [0, ∞].

- `cohenLenstraMeasure`: μ_{p,u} as a probability mass function on the carrier (built from the mass formula).

- `cohenLenstraMeasure_apply`: μ_{p,u}(A) = c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|).

- `cohenLenstraConstant_pos`: 0 < c_{p,u}.

- `cohenLenstraConstant_lt_one`: c_{p,u} < 1.

- `cohenLenstraConstant_eq_mul_succ`: c_{p,u} = (1 − p^{−(u+1)}) c_{p,u+1}.

- `cohenLenstraWeight_trivial`: μ_{p,u}(0) = c_{p,u}.

- `cohenLenstraWeight_mul_card_autCard`: μ_{p,u}(A) · |A|^u |Aut A| = c_{p,u}: the measure is proportional to 1/(|A|^u |Aut A|).

- `cohenLenstraMeasure_rank_eq`: The p-rank law: μ_{p,u}(p-rank = k) = p^{−k(k+u)} ∏_{i=1}^{k}(1 − p^{−i})^{−1} ∏_{i=1}^{k+u}(1 − p^{−i})^{−1} ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{−i}) (Wood, Corollary 3.5).


To prove the assertion, Define c_{p,u} as the convergent infinite product ∏_{i≥0} (1 − p^{−(i+u+1)}) (tprod), positive and < 1 because Σ p^{−i} < ∞. Define the weight w(A) = c_{p,u}/(|A|^u |Aut A|) in [0, ∞] using the carrier's order p^{A.1} and autCard. By the mass formula the weights sum to 1, so they define a probability mass function (Mathlib PMF).

*Needs:* [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), [automorphism count of finite abelian p groups](#automorphism-count-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), [cohen lenstra mass formula](#cohen-lenstra-mass-formula).

([[37]](#ref-37), Annals 183 (2016), §8.1, p. 771; [[38]](#ref-38), arXiv 1504.04391v1, Theorem 1.3, p. 3; [[45]](#ref-45), arXiv 1511.02212v1, §5.7.1, p. 35.)


**Checks.**


- μ_{p,0}(0) = c_{p,0}.

- μ_{p,0}(ℤ/p) = c_{p,0}/(p − 1).

- μ_{p,1}(ℤ/p) = c_{p,1}/(p(p − 1)) (the real-quadratic weight carries the extra 1/|A|).

- μ_{p,0}(ℤ/p²) = (p² − 1) μ_{p,0}((ℤ/p)²): a measure depending only on |A| is wrong.

- 0.56 < c_{3,0} < 0.561.

- μ_{p,0}(0) = c_{p,0}; c_{3,0} ≈ 0.5601 is the predicted proportion of imaginary quadratic fields with 3 ∤ h.

- μ_{p,0}(ℤ/p²) = (p² − 1) μ_{p,0}((ℤ/p)²).


### 3.12 Surjection moments and extension groupoids


<a id="surjection-moment"></a>


**Surjection moment.** For a nonnegative measure ν on L (a function L → [0, ∞]) and a class A, the A-moment of ν is ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν = Σ_{X ∈ L} ν(X) |Sur(X, A)| ∈ [0, ∞]. The trivial-target moment is the total mass; all rearrangements are of nonnegative series.

Throughout this assertion, p prime (to realise classes as groups)

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `surjectionMoment`: ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν = Σ_X ν(X)|Sur(X, A)|.

- `surjectionMoment_trivial`: The moment at the trivial class is the total mass Σ_X ν(X).

- `surjectionMoment_add`: The moment is additive in ν.

- `surjectionMoment_const_mul`: The moment is homogeneous in ν.

- `surjectionMoment_mono`: ν ≤ ν' pointwise implies ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν ≤ ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν'.

- `surjectionMoment_single`: The moment of the Dirac mass at X is |Sur(X, A)|.


To prove the assertion, Define the moment as the ℝ≥0∞-valued tsum of ν(X)·|Sur(X_p, A_p)| over the carrier. Linearity and monotonicity in ν follow from ENNReal.tsum_add and monotonicity of tsum. For A trivial, |Sur(X, 0)| = 1, so the moment is Σ ν(X).

*Needs:* [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), [surjection count](#surjection-count), `ENNReal.tsum_add` (Mathlib), `PMF.tsum_coe` (Mathlib).

([[37]](#ref-37), Annals 183 (2016), §8.2, p. 771.)


**Checks.**


- The zero measure has all moments 0.

- The Dirac mass at ℤ/p has ℤ/p-moment p − 1.

- A probability mass function has trivial-target moment 1.

- The moment counts surjections, not homomorphisms: the Dirac mass at (ℤ/p)² has ℤ/p-moment p² − 1, not |Hom((ℤ/p)², ℤ/p)| = p².

- Every probability measure has trivial-target moment 1.


<a id="extension-groupoid-of-finite-abelian-groups"></a>


**Extension groupoid of finite abelian groups.** For finite abelian groups G and K, consider exact sequences 0 → K →ι B →f G → 0 with B abelian, and isomorphisms of such sequences that are the identity on K and on G. Then Σ over isomorphism classes of sequences of 1/|Aut(sequence)| = 1. Equivalently, Σ_{[B]} #{f ∈ Sur(B, G) : ker f ≅ K}/|Aut B| = 1/|Aut K|.

Throughout this assertion, G, K finite abelian groups


To prove the assertion, Write G = ⊕_i ℤ/n_i (Mathlib AddCommGroup.equiv_directSum_zmod_of_finite, after splitting into cyclic factors). An extension is determined up to isomorphism by choosing lifts b_i ∈ B of the generators: n_i b_i lies in ι(K), and its class in K/n_iK does not depend on the lift; conversely every tuple (k_i) ∈ ∏_i K/n_iK arises (B = (K ⊕ ℤ^r)/⟨n_i e_i − k_i⟩). So the isomorphism classes are in bijection with ∏_i K/n_iK. The automorphisms of a sequence are φ = id + ι∘h∘f with h ∈ Hom(G, K) ≅ ∏_i K[n_i]. |K/n_iK| = |K[n_i]| (kernel and cokernel of multiplication by n_i on the finite group K have the same order), so the groupoid cardinality is ∏|K/n_iK| / ∏|K[n_i]| = 1. For the second form: a fixed B contributes #{(ι, f)}/|Aut B| by orbit counting, and #{(ι, f)} = #{f ∈ Sur(B, G) : ker f ≅ K}·|Aut K|.

<a id="cohen-lenstra-moments"></a>

Reindex by K: Σ_i p^{−iu} Σ_{|K| = p^i/|A|} 1/|Aut K| = |A|^{−u} Σ_K 1/(|K|^u|Aut K|) = |A|^{−u} c_{p,u}^{−1} ([weighted inverse automorphism sum](#weighted-inverse-automorphism-sum)); multiply by c_{p,u}.

### 3.13 Moment uniqueness and convergence


<a id="cohen-lenstra-contraction-constant"></a>


**Cohen lenstra contraction constant.** For an odd prime ℓ, c_ℓ = ∏_{i≥1}(1 − ℓ^{−i}) > 1/2; hence β = c_ℓ^{−1} − 1 < 1. For ℓ = 2, c_2 ≈ 0.2888 < 1/2 and β > 1.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ an odd prime


To prove the assertion, c_ℓ is increasing in ℓ (each factor increases), so c_ℓ ≥ c_3. Bound c_3 from below: ∏_{i≥1}(1 − 3^{−i}) ≥ (1 − 1/3)(1 − 1/9)(1 − Σ_{i≥3} 3^{−i}) = (2/3)(8/9)(1 − 1/18) = 0.5597… > 1/2 (using ∏(1 − x_i) ≥ 1 − Σ x_i for the tail, Mathlib geometric series). For ℓ = 2: (1 − 1/2)(1 − 1/4) = 3/8 < 1/2 already bounds c_2 above.

*Needs:* [cohen lenstra measure](#cohen-lenstra-measure), `tsum_geometric_of_lt_one` (Mathlib).

<a id="moments-determine-the-cohen-lenstra-measure"></a>


**Moments determine the cohen lenstra measure.** Let ℓ be an odd prime and ν a probability measure on L with ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν = 1 for every A ∈ L. Then ν = μ_{ℓ,0}.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ an odd prime ν a probability measure on L all surjection moments of ν equal 1


To prove the assertion, Put u_A = |Aut A|·ν(A) ≥ 0. The moment identity reads u_A + Σ_{B ≠ A} (|Sur(B, A)|/|Aut B|) u_B = 1 (EVW (8.2.1)). By [cohen lenstra moments](#cohen-lenstra-moments) with u = 0 the same identity holds for u_B = c_ℓ, so β_A := Σ_{B≠A}|Sur(B, A)|/|Aut B| = c_ℓ^{−1} − 1 =: β for every A. If L ≤ u_B ≤ U for all B then 1 − βU ≤ u_A ≤ 1 − βL; starting from 0 ≤ u ≤ 1 the bounds are alternating partial sums of Σ(−β)^k. Since β < 1 ([cohen lenstra contraction constant](#cohen-lenstra-contraction-constant)) both bounds converge to 1/(1 + β) = c_ℓ, so ν(A) = c_ℓ/|Aut A| = μ_{ℓ,0}(A).

<a id="enlargement-of-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>


**Enlargement of finite abelian p groups.** For finite abelian ℓ-groups A, A' and s ≥ 0, A' is an s-enlargement of A if some surjection A' ↠ A has kernel of order ℓ^s (a 1-enlargement is an enlargement). Equivalently |A'| = ℓ^s|A| and the Young diagram of A is contained in that of A' (a_i ≤ a'_i for the conjugate partitions). The set E_s(A) of isomorphism classes of s-enlargements is finite, with at most p(s + m) elements where ℓ^m = |A|. The surjection is data separate from the isomorphism class.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ prime

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement`: A' is an s-enlargement of A: ∃ surjection A' ↠ A with kernel of order ℓ^s.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.enlargements`: The finite set E_s(A) of classes of order ℓ^{s}|A| whose diagram contains that of A.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.isEnlargement_iff_conjPart`: IsEnlargement ℓ s A' A ↔ |A'| = ℓ^s|A| and a_i ≤ a'_i for all i.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.mem_enlargements`: B ∈ E_s(A) ↔ B is an s-enlargement of A.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.card_enlargements_le`: |E_s(A)| ≤ p(m + s), the number of partitions of m + s.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.IsEnlargement.trans`: An s-enlargement of a t-enlargement is an (s + t)-enlargement.

- `FinAbPGroupClass.isEnlargement_zero_iff`: The 0-enlargements of A are A itself.


To prove the assertion, Define IsEnlargement ℓ s A' A by the existence of a surjective homomorphism of the representatives with kernel of cardinality ℓ^s. Characterisation: by exact-surjection-count-formula, a surjection A′↠A exists precisely when every conjugate-partition coordinate of A is bounded by the corresponding coordinate of A′. The order condition then fixes the kernel cardinality and s. Hence E_s(A) is the image of the partitions of m + s containing α, a finite set of size ≤ p(m + s). Composition: an s-enlargement of a t-enlargement is an (s+t)-enlargement (compose the surjections, orders multiply).

*Needs:* [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), [surjection count](#surjection-count), [exact surjection count formula](#exact-surjection-count-formula).

<a id="aggregate-enlargement-inequality"></a>


**Aggregate enlargement inequality.** Let ℓ be prime and X, A finite abelian ℓ-groups with Sur(X, A) ≠ ∅ and |X| > |A|. Then there is a 1-enlargement A' of A with |Sur(X, A')| ≥ (ℓ − 1)|Sur(X, A)|. One may take A' with conjugate partition a'_j = a_j + 1 at the least j with x_j > a_j, and a'_i = a_i otherwise.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ prime Sur(X, A) ≠ ∅ |X| > |A|


To prove the assertion, Since X ↠ A, x_i ≥ a_i for all i ([exact surjection count formula](#exact-surjection-count-formula)), and |X| > |A| gives some i with x_i > a_i; let j be the least. For j>1, minimality of j gives a_{j−1}=x_{j−1}≥x_j≥a_j+1, so increasing a_j preserves the partition inequalities. For j=1 there is no preceding coordinate to check. In both cases a′ contains a and has total size one greater, hence defines a 1-enlargement. Compare the products of the exact formula for (X, A') and (X, A): the factor at index j − 1 changes by ℓ^{x_{j−1}}/(ℓ^{x_{j−1}} − ℓ^{a_j}) ≥ 1, and index j gains the factor ℓ^{x_j} − ℓ^{a_j} ≥ ℓ^{a_j}(ℓ − 1) ≥ ℓ − 1; all other factors agree. When j=1 omit the j−1 factor; there is no index-zero factor in the formula. EVW's argument that every f ∈ Sur(X, A) lifts through a fixed A' ↠ A is false; only the aggregate count is used.

*Needs:* [exact surjection count formula](#exact-surjection-count-formula), [enlargement of finite abelian p groups](#enlargement-of-finite-abelian-p-groups).

<a id="partition-tail-domination"></a>


**Partition tail domination.** For an integer ℓ ≥ 3 and fixed m ≥ 0, p(s + m)(ℓ − 1)^{−s} → 0 as s → ∞, where p(n) is the number of partitions of n.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ ≥ 3 m ∈ ℕ


To prove the assertion, Choose r with (ℓ − 1)^{−1} < r < 1 (possible since ℓ − 1 ≥ 2). Expand finite Euler products with nonnegative coefficients and use monotone convergence to obtain Σ_n p(n)r^n=∏_{j≥1}(1−r^j)⁻¹<∞. Positivity and nonvanishing of the product follow from Σ_j r^j<∞. The formal partition identity identifies the coefficients, but its formal topology alone does not justify evaluation at nonzero r. Hence p(n)r^n→0. p(s + m)(ℓ − 1)^{−s} = p(s + m) r^{s+m} · r^{−m} · (r(ℓ − 1))^{−s} → 0.

*Needs:* `Nat.Partition.hasProd_powerSeriesMk_card_restricted` (Mathlib), `tsum_geometric_of_lt_one` (Mathlib).

<a id="finite-enlargement-domination-of-tails"></a>


**Finite enlargement domination of tails.** Let ℓ be an odd prime, ε > 0 and A ∈ L with |A| = ℓ^m. There are c(A) and a finite nonempty M ⊂ L such that for every X ∈ L with |X| > c(A): |Sur(X, A)| ≤ ε · (Σ_{A'∈M} |Sur(X, A')|)/|M|. One may take M = E_s(A) and c(A) = ℓ^s|A| for any s with p(s + m)(ℓ − 1)^{−s} ≤ ε.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ odd prime ε > 0


To prove the assertion, Pick s by [partition tail domination](#partition-tail-domination); put M = E_s(A) (nonempty: ℤ/ℓ^s ⊕ A). If Sur(X, A) = ∅ the inequality is trivial. Otherwise iterate [aggregate enlargement inequality](#aggregate-enlargement-inequality) s times (possible while |X| > ℓ^t|A|): there is A' ∈ E_s(A) (by IsEnlargement.trans) with |Sur(X, A')| ≥ (ℓ − 1)^s|Sur(X, A)|. Hence |Sur(X, A)| ≤ (ℓ − 1)^{−s} Σ_{A'∈M}|Sur(X, A')| = (ℓ − 1)^{−s}|M| · (average) ≤ p(s + m)(ℓ − 1)^{−s} · (average) ≤ ε · (average), using |M| ≤ p(s + m) (card_enlargements_le).

*Needs:* [aggregate enlargement inequality](#aggregate-enlargement-inequality), [partition tail domination](#partition-tail-domination), [enlargement of finite abelian p groups](#enlargement-of-finite-abelian-p-groups).

<a id="finite-moment-control-of-masses"></a>


**Finite moment control of masses.** Let ℓ be an odd prime, ε_0 > 0 and L_0 ⊂ L finite. There exist δ > 0 and a finite L' ⊂ L such that every probability measure ν on L with ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν ∈ [1 − δ, 1 + δ] for all A ∈ L' satisfies |ν(A) − μ_{ℓ,0}(A)| ≤ ε_0 for all A ∈ L_0.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ odd prime ε_0 > 0 L_0 finite


To prove the assertion, Suppose not; with L'_k = {|A| ≤ k} and δ = 1/k obtain ν_k with moments within 1/k on L'_k and |ν_k(A_k) − μ(A_k)| > ε_0 for some A_k ∈ L_0; pass to a subsequence with A_k constant. The masses ν_k(B) lie in [0, 1]; by compactness of [0, 1]^L (Tychonoff, countable index, sequential compactness: Mathlib CompactSpace.tendsto_subseq) pass to a pointwise convergent subsequence ν_k → ν_∞. Fatou (ENNReal.tsum_eq_liminf_sum_nat) gives ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_{ν_∞} ≤ 1. For the reverse, split the moment at |B| ≤ c(A) (finitely many B, limits commute) and bound the tail Σ_{|B|>c}ν_k(B)|Sur(B, A)| ≤ ε · max_{A'∈M}⟨Sur(−, A')⟩_{ν_k} ≤ ε(1 + 1/k) by [finite enlargement domination of tails](#finite-enlargement-domination-of-tails); hence ⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_{ν_∞} = 1 for all A. A = 0 shows ν_∞ is a probability measure; [moments determine the cohen lenstra measure](#moments-determine-the-cohen-lenstra-measure) gives ν_∞ = μ, contradicting |ν_k(A) − μ(A)| > ε_0 in the limit.

### 3.14 Random p-adic cokernels


<a id="cokernel-law-of-haar-random-p-adic-matrices"></a>


**Cokernel law of haar random p adic matrices.** For a prime p and n, u ≥ 0, equip M_{n×(n+u)}(ℤ_p) (viewed as maps ℤ_p^{n+u} → ℤ_p^n) with its normalised Haar measure (the additive Haar measure of the compact group, total mass 1, Borel σ-algebra of ℤ_p). The cokernel law is ν_{n,u}(A) = Haar{M : coker M = ℤ_p^n/Mℤ_p^{n+u} ≅ A} for classes A ∈ L; it is a probability measure on L.

Throughout this assertion, p prime n, u ∈ ℕ

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `padicMatrixHaar`: Normalised Haar measure on M_{n×m}(ℤ_p), total mass 1.

- `padicCokernel`: coker(M) = ℤ_p^n / M ℤ_p^m.

- `cokernelLaw`: The finite-n law A ↦ P(coker M ≅ A) for Haar M ∈ M_{n×(n+u)}(ℤ_p).

- `padicMatrixHaar_univ`: The Haar measure is a probability measure.

- `cokernelLaw_le_one`: Each mass is at most 1.

- `tsum_cokernelLaw`: The finite-n law has total mass 1 (finite cokernel almost surely).

- `surjectionMoment_cokernelLaw`: E|Sur(coker M, A)| = |Sur(ℤ_p^n, A)|·|A|^{−(n+u)}.

- `cokernelLaw_trivial_eq`: For square matrices P(coker M = 0) = |GL_n(F_p)|/p^{n²} (Mathlib Matrix.card_GL_field).

- `tendsto_cokernelLaw`: The finite-n laws converge pointwise to μ_{p,u} ([friedman washington cokernel law](#friedman-washington-cokernel-law)).


To prove the assertion, Give ℤ_p the Borel σ-algebra; the Pi type of matrices is a compact abelian topological group (PadicInt.compactSpace, Tychonoff), so the additive Haar measure normalised on the whole group exists (Mathlib haarMeasure, additive version). Define coker M as the quotient of ℤ_p^n by the range of mulVecLin M and ν_{n,u}(A) as the measure of the set of M with coker M ≅ A_p. Finiteness almost surely: if n=0 the cokernel is zero. For n>0 the determinant of the first n columns is a nonzero polynomial in the entries. Its zero set has Haar measure zero by induction on the number of variables, one-variable root finiteness, and Fubini. A nonzero determinant has finite p-adic valuation; the adjugate identity shows that its image contains p^k Z_p^n for some k, so the full cokernel is a finite p-group. Full rank modulo p is sufficient but not necessary (the 1×1 matrix [p] has finite nonzero cokernel). Measurability of each class event: apply Smith normal form over the DVR Z_p to the matrix image (Mathlib Submodule.smithNormalForm). ### 3.15 Finite-field kernel laws


<a id="matrix-kernel-law-over-a-finite-field"></a>


**Matrix kernel law over a finite field.** For a finite field F and m, n, j ≥ 0, P_F(m, n, j) is the probability that a uniformly random m × n matrix over F has right kernel (in F^n) of dimension j: P_F(m, n, j) = #{M ∈ M_{m×n}(F) : dim ker M = j}/|F|^{mn}. Koymans–Pagano's P(m, n, j) is P_{F_2}(m, n, j).

Throughout this assertion, F finite field

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `matrixKernelLaw`: P_F(m, n, j) as a rational number.

- `sum_matrixKernelLaw`: Σ_{j=0}^{n} P_F(m, n, j) = 1.

- `matrixKernelLaw_eq_zero_of_lt`: P_F(m, n, j) = 0 unless n − m ≤ j ≤ n.

- `matrixKernelLaw_zero_eq_card_GL`: P_F(n, n, 0) = |GL_n(F)|/|F|^{n²} (Mathlib Matrix.card_GL_field).


To prove the assertion, Define the ratio of the cardinality of the subtype of matrices with finrank of ker (mulVecLin M) = j to |F|^{mn} (Matrix.card_matrix). The events for j = 0, …, n partition M_{m×n}(F) (rank–nullity).

<a id="rank-count-of-matrices-over-a-finite-field"></a>


**Rank count of matrices over a finite field.** For a finite field F with q elements and r ≤ min(m, n), #{M ∈ M_{m×n}(F) : rank M = r} = ∏_{i=0}^{r−1} (q^m − q^i)(q^n − q^i)/(q^r − q^i) = [m choose r]_q ∏_{i=0}^{r−1}(q^n − q^i). Hence, for n − min(m,n) ≤ j ≤ n, P_F(m, n, j) = q^{−mn} ∏_{i=0}^{n−j−1} (q^m − q^i)(q^n − q^i)/(q^{n−j} − q^i). Outside that range P_F(m,n,j)=0.

Throughout this assertion, F finite field with q elements r ≤ min(m, n)


To prove the assertion, A rank-r matrix is determined by its column space W ⊆ F^m (dim r) and a surjective linear map F^n ↠ W. The number of r-dimensional subspaces is the Gaussian binomial [m choose r]_q ([gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient), owned by part S of this stage). Surjections F^n ↠ F^r are counted by choosing r linearly independent rows: ∏_{i<r}(q^n − q^i) (as in Mathlib Matrix.card_GL_field / card_linearIndependent).

<a id="koymans-pagano-rank-identity"></a>


**Koymans pagano rank identity.** For every m ≥ 0: 1/(2^{m+1} − 1) = Σ_{n=0}^{m} (1/(2^{n+1} − 1)) · P(m, m, n)/2^m, with P(m, m, n) = P_{F_2}(m, m, n).

Throughout this assertion, m ∈ ℕ

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `koymansPaganoRankIdentity`: For m>=0, sum over n=0,...,m of P_F2(m,m,n)/(2^m (2^(n+1)-1)) equals 1/(2^(m+1)-1).


To prove the assertion, Replace the invalid independent-(T,U) conditioning in the source by a normalized kernel-weight argument. Let V=F_2^(m+1), W=F_2^m, and U range uniformly over all linear maps V -> W (equivalently pairings V x W^dual -> F_2). Rank-nullity makes K_U=ker U nonzero, including m=0. For nonzero x in V put w_x(U)=1/(#K_U-1) if x is in K_U, and zero otherwise. For each U, summing w_x(U) over all nonzero x gives exactly 1. Average this finite identity over U. If g is an automorphism of V, U -> U composed with g^(-1) permutes the set of maps and carries K_U to g(K_U), preserving its cardinality. Any nonzero x,y can be extended to bases and carried to one another by such a g. Therefore E_U[w_x(U)] is constant in nonzero x; its value is 1/(2^(m+1)-1). This is the law obtained by sampling U uniformly and then a nonzero vector of its kernel uniformly, not by sampling pairs (U,x) uniformly. For a fixed nonzero x, choose a basis beginning with x. The event U(x)=0 has probability 2^(-m). Conditional on it, U factors through V/<x> and the remaining m by m block is uniformly random. If that block has kernel dimension n, then dim K_U=n+1; hence P(x in K_U and dim K_U=n+1)=2^(-m) P(m,m,n). Partition the weighted sum defining E_U[w_x(U)] by n=0,...,m. On the corresponding event the weight is 1/(2^(n+1)-1). Substituting the preceding event counts proves the displayed identity for every m>=0. Check m=0 separately as a degenerate normalization test: there is one map F_2 -> 0 and its kernel has one nonzero vector, so both sides are 1.

### 3.16 Symmetric border-rank recurrences


<a id="symmetric-image-obstruction"></a>


**Symmetric image obstruction.** For a field F, n ≥ 0, a symmetric matrix S in M_n(F), and v in F^n, v belongs to im S if and only if v·z = 0 for every z in ker S. The pairing is the ordinary bilinear coordinate dot product, without conjugation.

Throughout this assertion, F is a field; the finiteness and cardinality assumptions are exactly those stated. No restriction on the characteristic.


To prove the assertion, If v=Sx and Sz=0, symmetry gives v·z=x·Sz=0. For the converse use the native dual-annihilator criterion for W=im S. Every functional φ vanishing on W is a dot product z·(−): take z_i=φ(e_i) and expand with the coordinate basis and its finite reconstruction theorem. Vanishing on each S e_i says Sᵀz=0, hence Sz=0 by symmetry. The assumed annihilation gives φ(v)=z·v=0. The dual-annihilator criterion implies v∈W. This argument does not identify bilinear forms with quadratic forms and uses no division by two.

**Symmetric border rank in image.** For a field F and symmetric S in M_n(F), let x∈F^n, v=Sx, a∈F, and B=[[S,v],[vᵀ,a]] on F^n⊕F. Then rank B = rank S if a=x·Sx, and rank B = rank S+1 otherwise, equivalently rank S plus the indicator of a≠x·Sx.

To prove the assertion, Put c=a−x·Sx. The invertible coordinate change (y,t)↦(y+tx,t) identifies ker B with ker S × {t∈F : ct=0}. Indeed B(y,t)=0 is equivalent to S(y+tx)=0 and ct=0, since vᵀy=xᵀSy. When c=0 the second factor is F and adds one to the kernel dimension; when c≠0 it is zero-dimensional. Use native finrank invariance, the product-dimension identity and rank-nullity in dimension n+1. **Symmetric border rank fibers.** Let F have q elements and S∈M_n(F) be symmetric of rank r. For every k≥0, the number of pairs (v,a)∈F^n×F for which [[S,v],[vᵀ,a]] has rank k is q^r if k=r; (q−1)q^r if k=r+1; q^(n+1)−q^(r+1) if k=r+2; and zero otherwise. The diagonal entry a is unrestricted.

There are q^n−q^r columns outside the image, and every one of their q corners increases rank by two. The outside-image rank lemma excludes all other ranks. The bound r≤n ensures each natural subtraction is exact. Sum the disjoint finite fibers.

<a id="symmetric-rank-count-recurrence"></a>


**Symmetric rank count recurrence.** Let F have q elements, and let N_F(n,k) count symmetric matrices in M_n(F) of rank k, using the existing native finite subtype. Define the numerical coefficient c_q(n,r,k) to be q^r when k=r, (q−1)q^r when k=r+1, q^(n+1)−q^(r+1) when k=r+2, and zero otherwise. Then for every n,k≥0, N_F(n+1,k)=Σ_{r=0}^n N_F(n,r)c_q(n,r,k). This notation introduces no new carrier or separately defined library object.

Throughout this assertion, F is a field; the finiteness and cardinality assumptions are exactly those stated. No restriction on the characteristic.


To prove the assertion, Reindex Fin(n+1) by Fin n plus a singleton. Reading the principal block, the extra column and the corner is a bijection from symmetric matrices to triples (S,v,a); writing the symmetric block matrix is its inverse. The ratios P_q(n,k)/D, P_q(n,k−1)/D and P_q(n+1,k)/D are respectively C(t−1)(t/q−1), t−1 and C(at−1)(t−1). The recurrence reduces to qa·C(t−1)(t/q−1)+(q−1)a(t−1)+a(t−1)=C(at−1)(t−1). If k is odd, k≥3; put C=a/(a−1). The same three ratios are C(t−1)(t/q−1), C(t−1) and C(at−1)(t−1). The reduced identity is qa·C(t−1)(t/q−1)+(q−1)a·C(t−1)+a(t−1)=C(at−1)(t−1). The factor with i=s makes every P_q(s,k) with k>s vanish, so these cases agree with the left side. Cast the natural coefficients to ℚ using r≤n before distributing subtraction.

### 3.17 Finite-field kernel laws


<a id="macwilliams-symmetric-rank-count"></a>


**Macwilliams symmetric rank count.** For a finite field F with q elements and 0 ≤ k ≤ s, writing k = 2h or 2h + 1, the number of symmetric s × s matrices of rank k is N(s, k) = ∏_{i=1}^{h} q^{2i}/(q^{2i} − 1) · ∏_{i=0}^{k−1} (q^{s−i} − 1).

Throughout this assertion, F finite field with q elements k ≤ s


To prove the assertion, Use the native subtype count N_F(n,k), with N_F(0,0)=1 and N_F(0,k)=0 for k>0: the empty matrix is unique and its image has dimension zero. For k>n the count is zero by the native rank-width bound. The characteristic-free symmetric-rank-count-recurrence gives every next row from the preceding row; its finite sum also covers k=0,1 and k>n+1. The rational product has the same initial row and satisfies symmetric-rank-product-recurrence. Induction on n, simultaneously for every k, equates the natural count cast to ℚ with the product. Specialize to k≤s and write k=2h or 2h+1 to obtain the stated product. Characteristic two uses precisely the same border kernels; alternating matrices are included with their unrestricted symmetric-matrix companions.

<a id="limit-of-the-symmetric-kernel-law"></a>


**Limit of the symmetric kernel law.** Over F_2, for every n ≥ 0: lim_{r→∞} P_Sym(r, n) = P_Sym(∞, n) := ∏_{j≥0}(1 − 2^{−(2j+1)}) / ∏_{i=1}^{n}(2^i − 1), and |P_Sym(r, n) − P_Sym(∞, n)| ≤ 2^{n+1−r} for all r ≥ 1. The limits sum to 1.

By [macwilliams symmetric rank count](#macwilliams-symmetric-rank-count) with k = r − n = 2h or 2h + 1: P_Sym(r, n) = 2^{−n(n+1)/2} ∏_{i=1}^{h}(1 − 2^{−2i})^{−1} ∏_{j=n+1}^{r}(1 − 2^{−j}) (the exponent kr − k(k−1)/2 − r(r+1)/2 simplifies to −n(n+1)/2). Letting r → ∞: P_Sym(∞, n) = 2^{−n(n+1)/2}∏_{i≥1}(1 − 2^{−2i})^{−1}∏_{j≥n+1}(1 − 2^{−j}) = ∏_{j odd}(1 − 2^{−j})/∏_{i=1}^{n}(2^i − 1). Rate: P_Sym(r, n) = P_Sym(∞, n)·R with R = ∏_{i>h}(1 − 2^{−2i})/∏_{j>r}(1 − 2^{−j}); since 2h + 2 ≥ r − n + 1, 1 − (2/3)2^{n−r} ≤ R ≤ 1 + 2^{1−r}, and P_Sym(∞, n) ≤ 1. Explicitly, the omitted even-factor tail is at most (4/3)2^{−2h−2}≤(2/3)2^{n−r}; the denominator tail is at least 1−2^{−r}, and (1−2^{−r})⁻¹≤1+2^{1−r} for r≥1. Σ_n P_Sym(∞, n) = ∏_{j odd}(1 − 2^{−j}) Σ_n 2^{−n(n+1)/2}/∏_{i≤n}(1 − 2^{−i}) = ∏_{j odd}(1 − 2^{−j})∏_{i≥1}(1 + 2^{−i}) = 1 (Euler).

The stabilizer is Aut_F(L), and Disc_S(L)=(χ(β)²Δ_n(v)) as fractional O_S ideals, with the idele character interpreted componentwise.
