### 3.22 Four-rank expansions and limiting laws


<a id="quadratic-four-rank-conic-formula"></a>


**Quadratic four rank conic formula.** For a fundamental quadratic discriminant D, let C_D be the narrow class group. Then 2^{rk₄ C_D} is one half the number of positive squarefree divisors b of D for which b′ is the signed squarefree part of D/b and the conic b x²−b′ y²=z² has a nonzero rational point. All signs and the prime2 conditions are retained; replacing this by residue conditions only at the odd primes is insufficient.

Throughout this assertion, D is a fundamental discriminant, D≠1; for positive D the class group is narrow.


To prove the assertion, Represent the two-torsion classes by ramified ideals and apply the quadratic genus-character test for being a square. Translate the square condition to the conic; use its local-to-global principle and quadratic reciprocity. Count the two complementary factorizations for each class.

<a id="quadratic-four-rank-jacobi-expansion"></a>


**Quadratic four rank jacobi expansion.** If D<0 is odd and fundamental, then 2^{rk₄ C_D}=2^{-1−ω(|D|)} Σ_{|D|=D₀D₁D₂D₃}(D₂/D₀)(D₁/D₃)(D₃/D₀)(D₀/D₃), over positive pairwise coprime squarefree factors. Raising this to k gives the (F₂²)^k-indexed sum with weight 2^{-kω(∏D_u)}, phase Φ_k(u,v) and prefactor 2^{-k}. For the other five sign/congruence families the same phase persists with the precise characters at −1 and2 supplied by Lemmas28,34,39,41,43. Explicitly write u=(a_j,b_j)_{j=1}^k, λ_k(u)=Σ_j a_jb_j, ξ_j(u)=(a_j+1)(b_j+1), Q_Γ(u)=Σ_{j∈Γ}a_jb_j+Σ_{j∉Γ}ξ_j(u), and V_Γ(u)=Σ_{j∉Γ}(a_j+b_j), all in F₂. In each moment sum let W(D_u)=∏_u2^{−kω(D_u)}∏_{u,v}(D_u/D_v)^{Φ_k(u,v)}, with positive odd pairwise coprime squarefree D_u. For negative odd discriminants sum 2^{−k}W with ∏D_u≤X and ∏D_u≡−1 mod4; for positive odd ones sum 2^{−k}W∏_u(−1/D_u)^{λ_k(u)}, with product≡1 mod4. For negative discriminants divisible by8 sum W∏_u(2/D_u)^{λ_k(u)}, with product≤X/8 and either odd residue mod4. For the positive8 family sum 2^{−k} over Γ of W∏_u(2/D_u)^{λ_k(u)}(−1/D_u)^{Q_Γ(u)}, in the same product domain. For the negative4 mod8 family sum 2^{−k} over Γ of W∏_u(2/D_u)^{V_Γ(u)+k−|Γ|}, with product≤X/4 and product≡1 mod4; for the positive4 mod8 family multiply each such summand by ∏_u(−1/D_u)^{λ_k(u)} and require product≡−1 mod4.

**Fk maximal unlinked support.** An unlinked subset U of (F₂²)^k has at most 2^k members. Equality holds exactly for the affine translates of k-dimensional totally singular subspaces for P_k. ### 3.23 Rigid fields and relative torsion


<a id="rigid-embedded-field-family"></a>


**Rigid embedded field family.** Fix a number field k, its algebraic closure, n≥1 and a transitive subgroup G≤S_n. A rigid G-field consists of a finite degree-n intermediate field K/k in that algebraic closure and a bijection e:Hom_k(K,kbar)→Fin n for which the transported Galois-action image is exactly G. Count these pairs by absolute discriminant. The underlying fields are embedded fields; conjugate fields and different labelings are retained. Aut_perm(G) is the normalizer N_{S_n}(G), not the abstract automorphism group of G. Group-signature restrictions use conjugacy classes of complex conjugation at the real base places.

Throughout this assertion, k is a number field; n≥1; G≤S_n is transitive; all fields use the fixed algebraic closure.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `FieldStatistics.RigidField`: The embedded degree-n field and its compatible numbering of embeddings.

- `FieldStatistics.RigidField.field`: Forget the numbering to an actual intermediate field of kbar/k.

- `FieldStatistics.RigidField.relabel`: The normalizer of G acts on labels by postcomposition; identity and composition laws hold.

- `FieldStatistics.rigidFieldCount`: Cardinality of the absolute-discriminant-bounded rigid pairs, with isomorphism-invariant local conditions supplied by a selection predicate.

- `FieldStatistics.rigidFieldCount_eq_normalizer_mul_embedded`: The rigid count is |N_{S_n}(G)| times the embedded-field count.

- `FieldStatistics.rigidFieldCount_eq_weightedIso`: It is the sum over field isomorphism classes of |N_{S_n}(G)| n/|Aut_k K|.

- `FieldStatistics.rigidFieldCount_mono`: Increasing the discriminant bound or enlarging the local condition increases the count.


To prove the assertion, Use the embedding-action predicate, keeping its numbering rather than existentially discarding it. Prove the labels over a fixed admissible embedded field form a normalizer torsor. Use Hermite finiteness for the underlying fields and finiteness of labels to obtain the height count.

*Needs:* [number field counting function](#number-field-counting-function), [number fields ordered by discriminant](#number-fields-ordered-by-discriminant), `NumberField.discr` (Mathlib), `NumberField.finite_of_discr_bdd` (Mathlib).

([[95]](#ref-95), §1 notation, p.2; Definition6.7 and Lemma6.8, pp.33–34.)

- For n=1,G=1 the only field is k; the count is1 above its absolute discriminant and0 below.

- Each quadratic field contributes two rigid pairs: it has one embedded copy and two compatible labels.

- A non-Galois S₃ cubic isomorphism class contributes18 rigid pairs: three embedded copies, each with six labels. Counting only abstract automorphisms would give a wrong multiplicity.

- A singleton field with absolute discriminant D contributes zero for X<D and its full label multiplicity at X=D.


<a id="relative-torsion-splitting"></a>


**Relative torsion splitting.** For a finite extension L/K of number fields and a prime ℓ not dividing d=[L:K], the norm and extension maps split Cl_L[ℓ] as Cl_{L/K}[ℓ]×Cl_K[ℓ]. Hence h_ℓ(L)=h_ℓ(L/K)h_ℓ(K). In a tower of quadratic extensions h₃ therefore factors over all steps. Cl_{L/K} is the kernel of the native relative class-group norm, not a second class-group carrier. The same splitting and cardinal factorization hold for Cl⁺ using ideal norm and extension on the native narrow class groups: total positivity makes both maps descend, and their composite is the dth power. Define the relative narrow group as this norm kernel.

Throughout this assertion, L/K is finite; ℓ is prime and ℓ∤[L:K].


To prove the assertion, Use norm∘extension=power d on the native class group. Invert d on its ℓ-torsion by Bézout and construct a section of norm. Split the finite abelian group by kernel and section, and take cardinalities. For the narrow version first descend norm and extension through totally positive principal ideals. At a real base place, norms of totally positive elements are positive, including the positive contributions of complex conjugate pairs. Then repeat the same finite-group splitting.

### 3.26 Wreath-type field counts and torsion means


<a id="wreath-transposition-fibre"></a>


**Wreath transposition fibre.** A transitive permutation2-group G≤S_{2d} contains a transposition exactly when G=C₂≀H, after conjugacy, for a unique transitive H≤S_d. Every such G-field K/k has a unique subfield F with [K:F]=2. Over a labeled H-field each quadratic K/F with a transposition has2^d compatible labelings. The permutation normalizers satisfy |Aut_perm(G)|=2^d|Aut_perm(H)|. For an arbitrary transitive H the same unique index-two subfield statement holds for G=C₂≀H.

### 3.27 Nonabelian quadratic moments


<a id="embedded-quadratic-wreath-type"></a>


**Embedded quadratic wreath type.** For a finite group G use the native regular wreath product W=G≀C₂=(C₂→G)⋊C₂. An embedded type is a subgroup F≤W. Write c(F) for its order-two elements outside the kernel of W→C₂. Admissibility means the canonical swap lies in F, the kernel projects onto G in one coordinate, and c(F) generates F. Goodness means c(F) is one F-conjugacy class. Types are equivalent under the diagonal action of Aut(G); abstract group isomorphism alone is insufficient. Aut_F(G) is the stabilizer of F under that diagonal action.

Throughout this assertion, All groups are finite; arithmetic fields have characteristic zero.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `FieldStatistics.OutsideInvolutions`: Elements w∈F with w²=1 and nontrivial C₂ projection.

- `FieldStatistics.IsAdmissibleType`: Swap membership, surjective coordinate projection of the kernel, and generation by outside involutions.

- `FieldStatistics.IsGoodType`: Admissibility and conjugacy of any two outside involutions inside F.

- `FieldStatistics.typeAutStabilizer`: The subgroup of MulAut G preserving F under the diagonal action.

- `FieldStatistics.transportType`: Diagonal automorphisms transport F; identity/composition and admissibility/goodness laws hold.

- `FieldStatistics.outsideClassCount`: The number of F-conjugacy classes in the outside-involution set.

- `FieldStatistics.goodType_iff_classCount_one`: For admissible F, goodness is equivalent to outsideClassCount=1.

- `FieldStatistics.typeAutStabilizer_abelian`: For an abelian G the inverse-graph type has full stabilizer MulAut G.


To prove the assertion, Use RegularWreathProduct with C₂=Multiplicative(ZMod2). Define the outside-involution set and its generated subgroup using native subgroup closure. Transport a subgroup by the diagonal automorphism and calculate its stabilizer.

*Needs:* `RegularWreathProduct` (Mathlib), `RegularWreathProduct.rightHom` (Mathlib), `RegularWreathProduct.inl` (Mathlib), `RegularWreathProduct.congr` (Mathlib).

- For G=C₃ its inverse-graph type is S₃, with one outside class of size3 and stabilizer of order2.

- For G=1 the sole admissible type is C₂, good with one outside involution.

- The base subgroup G×G is never admissible because it has trivial C₂ projection.


<a id="nonabelian-quadratic-moment-interface"></a>


**Nonabelian quadratic moment interface.** Fix a separable closure of Q and its infinite inertia. For each quadratic K let Γ_K be the Galois group of the maximal extension unramified at every finite prime and split at infinity. Imaginary rigid objects are continuous surjections Γ_K↠G whose induced normal-closure embedding in G≀C₂ has type F; real rigid objects also retain an outside involution (a twist). Divide their discriminant-bounded totals by the number of quadratic fields of the selected sign. Unrigid counts forget the isomorphism to G. For a good F they differ by |Aut_F(G)| in the imaginary case and |c(F)||Aut_F(G)| in the real case. Wood’s good-type prediction is rigid mean |H₂(F,c)[2]|; bad-type prediction is divergence, and inadmissible types have zero counts. These predictions are named propositions, not asserted arithmetic theorems. The refined good-type prediction restricts to tame quadratic fields and gives mean1 for each lifting-invariant value, evaluated at a generator of μ_L for L=Q(μ_{4|F̃_c|}), or equivalently for each Hom-valued invariant μ_L→H₂(F,c)[2]. Changing generators permutes the strata by a power automorphism. An arbitrary root of unity, in particular1, cannot index these strata.

Throughout this assertion, All groups are finite; arithmetic fields have characteristic zero.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `FieldStatistics.rigidQuadraticMoment`: Discriminant-bounded average of continuous surjections, with real twists retained.

- `FieldStatistics.unrigidQuadraticMoment`: The corresponding average of extension subfields with embedded type modulo diagonal Aut(G).

- `FieldStatistics.rigidMoment_imaginary_eq`: For admissible F the imaginary rigid count is |Aut_F(G)| times the unrigid count.

- `FieldStatistics.rigidMoment_real_good_eq`: For good F the real factor is |c(F)||Aut_F(G)|.

- `FieldStatistics.GoodTypeMomentPrediction`: The two rigid averages tend to |H₂(F,c)[2]|.

- `FieldStatistics.BadTypeMomentPrediction`: Both averages tend to positive infinity.

- `FieldStatistics.rigidMoment_inadmissible`: Inadmissible types have no arithmetic objects.

- `FieldStatistics.RefinedGoodTypeMomentPrediction`: Each tame signed rigid invariant stratum has mean1, with generator evaluation or Hom-valued invariant.

- `FieldStatistics.liftingInvariant_generator_change`: Replacing u by u^a with gcd(a,|μ_L|)=1 permutes the invariant values by h↦h^a.

State conjectural limits as predicates and retain the reduced-multiplier correction. ### 3.28 Small generators and mixed-trace field bounds


<a id="small-trace-zero-element"></a>


**Small trace zero element.** Every degree-n number field K/Q,n≥2, has an integral nonzero nonrational element α of trace zero with archimedean L² norm O_n(D_K^{1/(2n−2)}). If K has no proper intermediate field, α generates K; its monic minimal polynomial then has a₁=0 and |a_i|≪_nD_K^{i/(2n−2)}. Without primitivity it may lie in a proper subfield, so the coefficient box alone does not count every field.

Throughout this assertion, n≥2; fields are counted up to Q-isomorphism.


To prove the assertion, Use the trace-zero integral lattice and its covolume, then Minkowski’s first theorem. The only rational algebraic integer of trace zero is0. Under the no-intermediate-field hypothesis the nonrational element generates K; bound elementary symmetric polynomials of its conjugates.

*Needs:* [number field counting function](#number-field-counting-function), `Completed/EffectiveBounds Layer 1` (Tau Ceti).

<a id="schmidt-field-count-bound"></a>


**Schmidt field count bound.** For n≥2 the number of degree-n Q-isomorphism classes with absolute discriminant≤X is O_n(X^{(n+2)/4}). For a fixed number-field base k the same exponent holds for relative degree n and relative discriminant norm≤X, with constant depending on k,n.

Throughout this assertion, All fields have characteristic zero; all asymptotics are for the fixed family as X tends to infinity.


To prove the assertion, For primitive fields count the trace-zero coefficient boxes. For imprimitive fields choose a maximal chain of intermediate fields and apply the relative primitive estimate at each step. Use the discriminant tower identity and sum dyadic base-discriminant intervals; retain the base-discriminant saving that makes the sum converge.

**Mixed trace finite fibres.** For n≥6 and3≤r≤n, if binomial(d+r−1,r−1)>rn, there is a set of rn degree-d multi-indices whose mixed-trace map on r ordered n-tuples has nonzero Jacobian and, outside a fixed hypersurface, at most the product of its coordinate degrees many points per fibre. ### 3.32 Polynomial-order reduction and coefficient sieves


<a id="polynomial-order-lattice-reduction"></a>


**Polynomial order lattice reduction.** For monic real g of degree n with nonzero discriminant, form A_g=R[X]/(g), its basis1,θ,…,θ^{n−1}, and the Z-span of that basis. For a real binary n-ic f with a₀≠0 and nonzero discriminant, put θ=X in R[X]/(f(X,1)) and ζ_k=Σ_{j=0}^{k−1}a_jθ^{k−j}; use1,ζ₁,…,ζ_{n−1}. The norm is the sum of the squares at real embeddings and |z|² for one embedding from each complex pair. A basis is Minkowski-reduced when at each step it minimizes norm among vectors extending the preceding vectors to a Z-basis. Monic quasi-reduction permits upper unitriangular integral basis changes; binary quasi-reduction permits an SL₂(Z) representative. Strong quasi-reduction means uniqueness of the reduced basis modulo independent signs. It is a separate condition. This Euclidean metric must not be replaced by the all-embeddings weighted metric.

Throughout this assertion, n≥2; real coefficients; nonzero discriminant; binary leading coefficient nonzero.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:

<a id="refinement-wood-subgroup-bound"></a>


**Wood subgroup bound.** There is an absolute F>0 such that for every prime p and finite abelian p-group G of partition type λ, Σ_{G₁≤G}|∧²G₁|≤F^(λ₁) p^(Σ_i λ′_i(λ′_i−1)/2), where λ′ is the conjugate partition and λ₁ is the exponent length. The trivial group contributes1. For finitely many primes the bound factors over primary parts.


To prove the assertion, Use the exact subgroup count by conjugate partition, retaining the Gaussian-binomial denominators. Absorb their reciprocal Euler-product bounds into one absolute F per exponent layer. Complete the quadratic exponents and sum the resulting geometric Gaussian tails.

*Needs:* [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), [gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient), [exact surjection count formula](#exact-surjection-count-formula).

**Checks.**


- Retain every stated hypothesis and the exact normalization and convergence mode.

- For G=Z/p the subgroup sum is 2 and the p-exponent in the bound is zero; the uniform constant must absorb that factor.


<a id="refinement-wood-grid-uniqueness"></a>


**Wood grid uniqueness.** Let p₁,…,p_s be distinct primes, m_j≥1, and M the product of antitone nonnegative integer profiles of lengths m_j. Let x_µ,y_µ≥0 have finite equal exponential moments C_λ=Σ_µ x_µ∏_j p_j^(Σ_i λ_ji µ_ji)=Σ_µ y_µ∏_j p_j^(Σ_i λ_ji µ_ji). Assume C_λ≤∏_j F^(m_j)p_j^(Σ_i λ_ji(λ_ji−1)/2) for some F>0. Then x_µ=y_µ for every µ. The finite-moment and summability hypotheses are part of the statement.


To prove the assertion, For each profile ν expand the product of grid separators in its Taylor coefficients. The absolute coefficient bound and moment growth make the interchange of the coefficient and mass sums absolutely convergent. Use well-founded lexicographic induction on the finite concatenation of the nonnegative integer profiles. Lexicographic order on a fixed finite power of N is a well-order, and restricting to antitone profiles preserves well-foundedness. The triangular separator vanishes above the chosen profile; the absolutely convergent sum over lower profiles is already determined by induction.

*Needs:* [wood grid separator](#refinement-wood-grid-separator), [wood coefficient bound](#refinement-wood-coefficient-bound).

([[121]](#ref-121), Theorem 8.2 and proof, pp. 29–31.)


**Checks.**


- Retain every stated hypothesis and the exact normalization and convergence mode.

- With no selected primes the profile carrier is a singleton and equality of the zero moment determines its mass.


<a id="refinement-wood-bounded-moment-limit"></a>


**Wood bounded moment limit.** Let a≥1 and A_a be finite abelian group classes of exponent dividing a. Let X_n be random finitely generated abelian groups and suppose E#Sur(X_n,G)→M_G for every G∈A_a, with 0≤M_G≤|∧²G|. For every H∈A_a, Pr(X_n/aX_n≅H) has a limit; these limiting masses sum to1 and have the moments M_G. A second sequence with the same moments has the same limiting quotient law. The theorem concerns X_n/aX_n, not an unproved full-group limit.


To prove the assertion, Convert surjection moments to homomorphism moments by the finite sum over image subgroups; use the exterior-square subgroup bound. For each test type λ choose the dominating type with conjugate entries2λ′_i+1; the sum of homomorphism-count ratios is finite and controls tails. Extract subsequential masses on the countable exponent-bounded carrier, preserve moments by domination and apply grid uniqueness. The trivial-group moment fixes total mass1; uniqueness upgrades subsequences to the whole sequence. The all-p,u target consumes this theorem together with exponent-tail control.

*Needs:* [wood subgroup bound](#refinement-wood-subgroup-bound), [wood grid uniqueness](#refinement-wood-grid-uniqueness), [surjection count](#surjection-count), [surjection moment](#surjection-moment).

([[122]](#ref-122), Theorem 3.1, pp. 9–10; proof inputs Wood Lemma 7.4, Theorems 8.2–8.3, pp. 27–32.)

### Supporting arithmetic and moment arguments

<a id="support-character-sums"></a>

For quadratic four-ranks prove the Jacobi expansion in each of the six fundamental-discriminant sign/congruence families, including the characters at minus one and two, and the linked-variable estimates with constants depending on the fixed moment k. The small/intermediate/large-variable decomposition gives `O_(k,ε)(X(log X)^(-2^(-k)+ε))`; maximal unlinked affine supports give the stated main coefficient. The rank-marginal uniqueness argument uses exponential moments of `p^r`, Gaussian subspace coefficients and a tightness/uniform-tail estimate. It is not an application of a full finite-group law to a sequence for which only rank moments are known. Sources: Fouvry–Klüners, Theorems 1–3 and the Jacobi expansions and linked-variable lemmas cited above; Delaunay–Jouhet, Theorem 5 and proof, pp. 6–8. The limiting rank weights are `p^(-r(r+u))η∞/(η_rη_(r+u))`, including p=2 and u=0,1.

For mixed traces prove that the chosen rn monomials have a nonzero Jacobian on r ordered n-tuples and that outside its discriminant hypersurface the fibre has degree at most the product of coordinate degrees. Quantitative exclusion and lattice counting then use the small trace-zero generator bound and successive minima. The nonzero Jacobian is a polynomial identity and must be witnessed, not assumed from the number of coordinates. Sources: Lemke Oliver–Thorne, mixed-trace lemmas and the proof of their field-count theorem; the exact numerical ranges are those in the targets above.

For the spin/governing-field application the short real-character-sum conjecture is an explicit hypothesis `C_n` for every n≥3, with KM §2.5's ranges and constants. For the full-two-torsion twist law, prove the Kane/Swinnerton-Dyer character-sum and combinatorial inputs for the stated signed-integer twist denominator, with the no-rational-cyclic-four-isogeny condition. This does not supply a general p-infinity twist distribution. Sources: Koymans–Milovic, §§2–4, and Kane, Theorem 2 with its character-sum and Markov/combinatorial estimates.

<a id="support-embedded-types"></a>

The embedded type calculation is relative to the fixed permutation representation and distinguished quotient to C2. Prove the outside-involution generation criterion, the diagonal Aut(G) orbit relation and its stabilizer multiplicities, and identify the signature character representation used by Cohen–Martinet. Generic Goursat and reduced-multiplier constructions are imported; only this marked wreath and signature specialization is built here. For a good admissible type, its abelianization is C2; for an odd abelian kernel the reduced multiplier has no two-torsion, but its `(q-1)`-torsion need not be trivial. Wood's table includes `C3²` with reduced multiplier C3. Sources: Wood, §§2–3 and Tables 1–2, arXiv:1702.04644v2, pp. 4–16 and 33–34; Liu–Wood–Zureick-Brown, §§10–12 for the arithmetic lifting comparison.

<a id="support-type-certificates"></a>

A finite type computation must provide a multiplication table or certified permutation group, the normal subgroup and quotient map, the induced automorphism, all outside involutions, their generated subgroup, the diagonal automorphism orbits and stabilizers. A reduced-multiplier certificate additionally specifies a central-cover presentation and the quotient by commuting-lift relations. Check the order96 A4 closure type through its actual S3-module action and distinguish kernel counts, pairs of conjugate kernels, and 24 or 48 rigid surjections. Source: Wood's appendix and Tables 1–2, pp. 30–34. Exhaustive cubic lists and certified class-group/action computations prove an exact finite-discriminant count; a sample does not prove an asymptotic average.

For the classical and low-degree arithmetic counts prove the remaining original counting inputs in their stated scope: primitive indefinite quadratic classes weighted by the positive norm-one regulator; cyclic prime-degree class-field characters divided by p-1; fixed-resolvent cubic series with the exceptional `Q(√-3)` logarithm; and Baily's weighted quartic multiplicity bound for an arbitrary *specified* resolvent subfamily. These are the respective Siegel, Wright, Cohen–Morra/Datskovsky–Wright and Baily assertions cited at their targets, not uniform statements as the base field or resolvent varies. Deduce each partial-summation application before absorbing logarithms into ε. Certify the D4 numerical comparison by interval bounds for the convergent Euler products and weighted sums; decimal values alone are illustrations, not error-bounded inequalities.

For polynomial-to-field lower bounds, formulate the transfer as follows. Suppose a positive-volume regular family in the trace band `0≤a1<n` or a specified binary slice has the stated uniform sieve and at most C representatives for each field, uniformly on its dilations. Then dividing its polynomial count by C proves the displayed field lower exponent. Proving that multiplicity assumption is a separate supporting target; eventual weak quasi-reduction does not prove strong uniqueness. At n=2 the trace-zero squarefree density is zero because `disc(X²+a2)=-4a2`. The monogenic asymptotic remains a named conjectural proposition requiring finite volume, cusp control and asymptotic uniqueness modulo translation and sign. Sources: BSW I, §5, especially Lemma 5.3 and Remark 5.6, and BSW II, the field-count applications and binary-order comparison. Likewise the unramified alternating-extension lower bound needs its original class-field correspondence and rigidity calculation, beyond a count of S_n fields.

### Examples

For a real quadratic field, ordinary and narrow four-ranks need not agree individually; the comparison above is averaged. The fundamental discriminant one is excluded from quadratic fields. At the prime three the order-conductor rank bound includes one possible wild extra dimension, so `3∤f` is essential to the sharper factor.

For `G=C3≀C2≤S6`, an element rotating one block has index two. The quadratic intermediate field `Q(ζ3)` admits two rational cyclotomic conjugacy classes of nontrivial C3 elements, producing the extra logarithm. Removing the cyclic C6 and regular S3 subfamilies preserves the lower bound and refutes the original strong logarithmic prediction, while a factor log X is compatible with every `X^ε` upper allowance.

The group-profile moment warning has a concrete witness: put mass `p^-n` on `(Z/p)^n` and the remaining mass on a fixed limiting law. The measures converge in total variation, but the extra `#Sur(-,Z/p)=p^n-1` contribution tends to one. Thus limiting probability masses cannot be substituted into unbounded surjection averages without a tail argument.

### Dependencies

Layers 0–2 and the finite statistical tools constructed earlier in this layer; ClassFieldTheory, GlobalNumberFields, NumberFieldArithmetic and PolynomialGaloisGroups; GN.0–GN.4; IG.2–IG.5; the companion analytic Dirichlet-series and character-sum interfaces; and the marked embedded-type certificates above. Scalar moment determinacy remains an imported boundary; the discrete group/rank moment estimates are local work.


## Layer 4: Selmer averages and arithmetic applications

The two-Selmer calculation is a quotient of two asymptotics with positive matching local masses. The local Kummer index contributes two at p=2 and one half at infinity; their product is one, and the PGL2 Tamagawa factor is two. Higher Selmer means use their own integral representations. Rank and analytic-rank applications specify separately which parity, residual, ordinary and local-restriction hypotheses they need.


### 4.1 Height averages and rational orbit weights


<a id="rational-orbit-weight"></a>


**Rational orbit weight.** Let a group G act on a set V, let Γ ≤ G be a subgroup and Y ⊆ V a Γ-stable subset. For v ∈ V put G_{v,Y} := {g ∈ G : g·v ∈ Y}; it is a union of right cosets Γg. The orbit weight of v is w_{Γ,Y}(v) := #(Γ\G_{v,Y}), the number of right cosets Γg contained in G_{v,Y} (a natural number when the coset set is finite; the value 0 marks an infinite set, following Nat.card), and the orbit count is n_{Γ,Y}(v) := #(Γ\(G·v ∩ Y)). For binary quartic forms, with PGL_2 acting through the twisted action γ·f(x,y) = (det γ)^{-2} f((x,y)·γ) of Layer 0: the global weight of f ∈ V_Z is m(f) := w_{PGL_2(Z),V_Z}(f) for G = PGL_2(Q) acting on V_Q, and the local weight of f ∈ V_{Z_p} is m_p(f) := w_{PGL_2(Z_p),V_{Z_p}}(f) for G = PGL_2(Q_p) acting on V_{Q_p}; PGL_2(Z) and PGL_2(Z_p) are the images of GL_2(Z) and GL_2(Z_p). Equivalently m(f) = #[PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(Q)_f] and m_p(f) = #[PGL_2(Z_p)\PGL_2(Q_p)_f] with PGL_2(Q)_f := {γ : γ·f ∈ V_Z}, the description used in the proof of Proposition 3.6.

Throughout this assertion, Y is Γ-stable, so that membership g·v ∈ Y depends only on the right coset Γg. The action is the twisted action (21)/(32): the centre acts trivially and I, J are invariant. With the untwisted action every scalar would stabilise the invariants only up to a power, and G_{v,Y} would not descend to PGL_2. The source defines m(f) as the stabilizer sum Σ_{f'∈B(f)} #Aut_Q(f')/#Aut_Z(f'); the coset count is equal to it whenever Aut_Q(f) is finite (lemma orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum), in particular whenever Δ(f) ≠ 0.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `orbitWeight`: w_{Γ,Y}(v) = #(Γ\{g ∈ G : g·v ∈ Y}), counted with Nat.card.

- `orbitCount`: n_{Γ,Y}(v) = #(Γ\(G·v ∩ Y)), counted with Nat.card.

- `one_le_orbitWeight`: If v ∈ Y and the coset set Γ\G_{v,Y} is finite then 1 ≤ w_{Γ,Y}(v).

- `orbitWeight_smul`: w_{Γ,Y}(g·v) = w_{Γ,Y}(v) for every g ∈ G.

- `orbitWeight_eq_one_iff`: For v ∈ Y: w_{Γ,Y}(v) = 1 if and only if G_{v,Y} = Γ.

- `orbitWeight_of_eq_top`: If Γ = G and v ∈ Y then w_{Γ,Y}(v) = 1.

- `orbitCount_le_orbitWeight`: If Stab_G(v) is finite and both counts are finite then n_{Γ,Y}(v) ≤ w_{Γ,Y}(v), with equality exactly when Stab_Γ(v') = Stab_G(v') for every v' ∈ G·v ∩ Y (from orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum).

- `binaryQuarticWeight`: m(f) for f ∈ V_Z: the orbit weight for PGL_2(Z) ≤ PGL_2(Q) acting on V_Q with Y = V_Z.

- `localBinaryQuarticWeight`: m_p(f) for f ∈ V_{Z_p}: the orbit weight for PGL_2(Z_p) ≤ PGL_2(Q_p) acting on V_{Q_p} with Y = V_{Z_p}.

- `binaryQuarticWeight_smul`: m(γ·f) = m(f) for γ ∈ PGL_2(Q) with f, γ·f ∈ V_Z; likewise m_p over Q_p.


To prove the assertion, Form G_{v,Y} ⊆ G and its image in the right-coset space Γ\G; w_{Γ,Y}(v) is the cardinality of that image. Γ-stability of Y gives (γg)·v ∈ Y ⟺ g·v ∈ Y, so G_{v,Y} is a union of right Γ-cosets. Specialise to (G, Γ, Y) = (PGL_2(Q), PGL_2(Z), V_Z) and (PGL_2(Q_p), PGL_2(Z_p), V_{Z_p}), using the twisted action of [binary quartic form](#binary-quartic-form) descended to PGL_2 (the scalar matrices act trivially).

*Needs:* [binary quartic form](#binary-quartic-form), `Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup` (Mathlib), `QuotientGroup.rightRel` (Mathlib), `Nat.card` (Mathlib), `PadicInt` (Mathlib).

([[1]](#ref-1), §3.2, p. 24, definition of m(f); [[1]](#ref-1), Proof of Proposition 3.6, pp. 24–25.)


**Checks.**


- For S_3 acting on Fin 3 by permutation, Γ = ⊥ and Y = {0}: w_{Γ,Y}(0) = 2.

- For Γ = ⊤ and Y = Set.univ, w_{Γ,Y}(v) = 1 for every v.

- In the S_3 example, n_{Γ,Y}(0) = 1 ≠ 2 = w_{Γ,Y}(0): the weight is not the number of Γ-orbits in the G-orbit.

- ZMod 6 acting on itself by addition, Γ = {0, 3}, Y = {0, 1, 3, 4}: w_{Γ,Y}(0) = 2 = n_{Γ,Y}(0).

- w is G-invariant: w(g·v) = w(v), through the bijection Γh ↦ Γhg^{-1} of coset sets.

- For S_3 acting on {0,1,2}, Γ = 1 and Y = {0}: w(0) = 2 while n(0) = 1, so the weight is not the orbit count.


<a id="locally-soluble-forms-attached-to-a-family"></a>


**Locally soluble forms attached to a family.** Let F be a family of elliptic curves over Q defined by congruence conditions (Layer 0), with invariant set Inv(F) = {(I(E), J(E)) : E ∈ F} ⊆ Z², local sets Inv_p(F) ⊆ Z_p² and sign set Inv_∞(F) ⊆ R². Define S(F) := {f ∈ V_Z : f is locally soluble and (I(f), J(f)) = (2⁴I, 2⁶J) for some (I, J) ∈ Inv(F)}, each PGL_2(Z)-orbit weighted by 1/m(f); for every prime p, S_p(F) := {f ∈ V_{Z_p} : f is Q_p-soluble, 2⁴ | I(f) and 2⁶ | J(f) in Z_p, and (2^{-4}I(f), 2^{-6}J(f)) ∈ Inv_p(F)}, weighted by 1/m_p(f); and S_∞(F) := {f ∈ V_R : f is R-soluble and (I(f), J(f)) ∈ Inv_∞(F)}. Here a form over a field K is K-soluble when z² = f(x, y) has a solution with x, y, z ∈ K and (x, y) ≠ (0, 0), and locally soluble means R-soluble and Q_p-soluble for every p (Layer 1). The set S_p(F) is the local condition set; the source calls S_p(F) the p-adic closure of S(F) and then uses exactly this description.

Throughout this assertion, F is presented as F_Σ by closed local sets Σ_p with null boundary (Layer 0), so that Inv_p(F) ⊆ Σ_p is relatively closed in the nonsingular locus. This does not by itself imply null boundary for Inv_p(F); that additional assertion is justified in the positive-mass case at count-of-curves-in-a-large-family. The scaling (2⁴, 2⁶) is forced by Theorem 3.5 (Layer 1): Selmer elements of E^{I,J} are classes of integral forms with invariants (2⁴I, 2⁶J), not (I, J). Because Inv_∞(F) is a union of sign conditions, it is invariant under (I, J) ↦ (λ²I, λ³J) for λ > 0; in particular (2⁴I, 2⁶J) ∈ Inv_∞(F) iff (I, J) ∈ Inv_∞(F).

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `locallySolubleSet`: S(F) ⊆ V_Z.

- `localSolubleSet`: S_p(F) ⊆ V_{Z_p}.

- `realSolubleSet`: S_∞(F) ⊆ V_R.

- `invariants_of_mem_locallySolubleSet`: If f ∈ S(F) then 2⁴ | I(f), 2⁶ | J(f) and (I(f)/2⁴, J(f)/2⁶) ∈ Inv(F).

- `locallySolubleSet_smul`: S(F) is stable under PGL_2(Z), S_p(F) under PGL_2(Z_p) and S_∞(F) under PGL_2(R); moreover for γ ∈ PGL_2(Q_p) with f, γ·f ∈ V_{Z_p}, f ∈ S_p(F) iff γ·f ∈ S_p(F).

- `disc_ne_zero_of_mem_localSolubleSet`: Every f ∈ S_p(F) has Δ(f) ≠ 0, because Inv_p(F) excludes Δ = 0.

- `mem_locallySolubleSet_iff`: For f ∈ V_Z: f ∈ S(F) iff f ∈ S_∞(F) and f ∈ S_p(F) for every prime p (promoted to the lemma locally-soluble-set-is-cut-out-by-local-conditions).


To prove the assertion, Define the three sets as subsets of V_Z, V_{Z_p} and V_R through the invariants I, J of [binary quartic invariants](#binary-quartic-invariants) and the solubility predicates of Layer 1. Attach the weights 1/m and 1/m_p of rational-orbit-weight. Record PGL_2(Z)- (resp. PGL_2(Z_p)-, PGL_2(R)-) stability: solubility and the invariants are preserved by the twisted action.

<a id="average-over-a-height-ordered-family"></a>


**Average over a height ordered family.** Let F be an arithmetic family in the sense of Layer 0 (a set with a height h having finite sublevel sets) and φ a real function on F. For X ∈ R let N(F; X) := #{E ∈ F : h(E) < X} and Avg_F(φ; X) := (Σ_{E ∈ F, h(E) < X} φ(E)) / N(F; X) (with value 0 when N(F; X) = 0). φ has average c over F if Avg_F(φ; X) → c as X → ∞; its upper average is limsup_{X→∞} Avg_F(φ; X). For elliptic curves over Q the height is H(E) = max{4|A|³, 27B²} or H'(E) = max{|I(E)|³, J(E)²/4}; since 27H = 4H' (Layer 0) the two orderings give the same averages and upper averages. The average size of the 2-Selmer group over F is the average of E ↦ #S_2(E).

Throughout this assertion, The average is a limit of ratios of finite sums; its existence is part of any theorem asserting it. Upper averages (limsup) are used for statements, such as the rank bound, that assert no limit. Rescaling the height by a positive constant changes N(F; X) into N(F; cX) and does not change limits or limsups as X → ∞.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `familyAverage`: Avg_F(φ; X) = (Σ_{h(E)<X} φ(E))/N(F; X).

- `HasFamilyAverage`: The proposition Avg_F(φ; X) → c as X → ∞.

- `upperFamilyAverage`: limsup_{X→∞} Avg_F(φ; X).

- `hasFamilyAverage_const`: If F is infinite, the constant function c has average c.

- `HasFamilyAverage.add`: Averages add: if φ has average c and ψ has average d then φ + ψ has average c + d.

- `HasFamilyAverage.const_mul`: If φ has average c then aφ has average ac.

- `upperFamilyAverage_mono`: If φ ≤ ψ pointwise, Avg_F(ψ; X) is eventually bounded above and Avg_F(φ; X) is cobounded below along atTop, then the real-valued upper average of φ is at most that of ψ (matching the suggested Filter.limsup signature). Nonnegative φ supplies the lower condition. Real limsup has junk values for functions tending to −∞, so the lower condition cannot be dropped.

- `HasFamilyAverage.upperFamilyAverage_eq`: If φ has average c then its upper average is c.

- `hasFamilyAverage_rescale_iff`: For c > 0, φ has average d for the height h iff it has average d for the height c·h.


To prove the assertion, Define N(F; X) and the partial sums with the counting API of [arithmetic family](#arithmetic-family) (strict inequality h < X, as in the source). Define the average as a filter limit at X → ∞ and the upper average as the limsup.

*Needs:* [arithmetic family](#arithmetic-family), [elliptic curves over q ordered by height](#elliptic-curves-over-q-ordered-by-height), [quartic to curve height normalisation](#quartic-to-curve-height-normalisation), `Filter.limsup` (Mathlib).

([[1]](#ref-1), Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, pp. 1–2; [[1]](#ref-1), §3, p. 22.)


**Checks.**


- For an infinite family, the constant function 1 has average 1.

- For X below every height, Avg_F(φ; X) = 0.

- For the family of elliptic curves, an average with respect to H equals the average with respect to H' = (27/4)H.

- Avg_F(φ; X) is a ratio, not the partial sum: for φ = 1 the partial sum N(F; X) tends to ∞ while the average is 1.

- The constant function c has average c over any infinite family.

- Over all elliptic curves the indicator of {B = 0} has average 0 (#{A : 4|A|³ < X} ≍ X^{1/3} while N ≍ X^{5/6}).

- Changing H to H' leaves every average unchanged.


<a id="orbit-weight-as-a-stabilizer-sum"></a>


**Orbit weight as a stabilizer sum.** In the setting of rational-orbit-weight let v ∈ Y with Stab_G(v) finite and Γ\(G·v ∩ Y) finite. Then w_{Γ,Y}(v) = Σ_{Γv' ∈ Γ\(G·v ∩ Y)} #Stab_G(v') / #Stab_Γ(v'), and #Stab_G(v') = #Stab_G(v) for every v' ∈ G·v. Consequently n_{Γ,Y}(v) ≤ w_{Γ,Y}(v) ≤ #Stab_G(v)·n_{Γ,Y}(v), and w_{Γ,Y}(v) = n_{Γ,Y}(v) iff Stab_Γ(v') = Stab_G(v') for every v' ∈ G·v ∩ Y; in particular w = n when Stab_G(v) = 1. For binary quartic forms: m(f) = Σ_{f' ∈ B(f)} #Aut_Q(f)/#Aut_Z(f') and m_p(f) = Σ_{f' ∈ B_p(f)} #Aut_{Q_p}(f)/#Aut_{Z_p}(f'), and for the PGL_2(Z_p)-orbits f_1, …, f_k inside one PGL_2(Q_p)-class, Σ_i 1/#Aut_{Z_p}(f_i) = m_p(f)/#Aut_{Q_p}(f).

Throughout this assertion, Stab_G(v) finite; for binary quartic forms with Δ(f) ≠ 0 the stabilizer in PGL_2(K) is isomorphic to E^{I,J}(K)[2] (Layer 1, Theorem 3.2), of order at most 4. Stab_Γ(v') = Γ ∩ Stab_G(v') is a subgroup of Stab_G(v'), so each ratio is a positive integer.


To prove the assertion, The orbit map G_{v,Y} → G·v ∩ Y, g ↦ g·v, is surjective and Γ-equivariant, so it induces a surjection Γ\G_{v,Y} → Γ\(G·v ∩ Y). The fibre over Γv' with v' = g'·v is {Γg : g·v ∈ Γ·v'} = Γ\(Γg'Stab_G(v)), in bijection with (g'^{-1}Γg' ∩ Stab_G(v))\Stab_G(v) ≅ Stab_Γ(v')\Stab_G(v'), of size #Stab_G(v')/#Stab_Γ(v') by Lagrange (mathlib:Subgroup.card_mul_index). Stabilizers along one G-orbit are conjugate, so #Stab_G(v') = #Stab_G(v); sum over the fibres. The ratio is ≥ 1 with equality iff Stab_Γ(v') = Stab_G(v'), which gives the comparison with n and the equality criterion. For the last formula apply the first one inside the class of f and use m_p(f_i) = m_p(f).

### 4.2 Local translates and the global weight product


<a id="cartan-decomposition-of-pgl2-over-qp"></a>


**Cartan decomposition of pgl2 over qp.** For every prime p and every γ ∈ GL_2(Q_p) there are k_1, k_2 ∈ GL_2(Z_p) and integers a ≤ b with γ = k_1·diag(p^a, p^b)·k_2, and (a, b) is uniquely determined by γ (a = min of the valuations of the entries, a + b = v_p(det γ)). Consequently every element of PGL_2(Q_p) outside PGL_2(Z_p) lies in PGL_2(Z_p)·diag(1, p^k)·PGL_2(Z_p) for a unique integer k ≥ 1, and each such double coset is a finite union of p^{k−1}(p + 1) right cosets PGL_2(Z_p)·g.

Throughout this assertion, Z_p is a principal ideal domain (a discrete valuation ring). The statement is about GL_2 and its image PGL_2 = GL_2/Q_p^×; scaling by p^m shifts (a, b) to (a + m, b + m), so the PGL_2 invariant is k = b − a.


To prove the assertion, Multiply γ by a power of p so that it has entries in Z_p; then the Z_p-lattice Z_p²·γ is a submodule of Z_p². Apply the Smith normal form over the PID Z_p (mathlib:Submodule.smithNormalForm): there is a basis of Z_p² in which the submodule is spanned by d_1e_1, d_2e_2 with d_1 | d_2; write d_i = u_i p^{a_i} with units u_i. The change-of-basis matrices lie in GL_2(Z_p); absorb the units into k_1 to obtain γ = k_1 diag(p^a, p^b) k_2. Uniqueness: the minimum valuation of the entries and v_p(det) are invariant under multiplication by GL_2(Z_p) on either side. The coset count: the right cosets in PGL_2(Z_p) diag(1, p^k) PGL_2(Z_p) correspond to the sublattices of Z_p² of index p^k with cyclic quotient, of which there are p^{k−1}(p + 1).

*Needs:* `Submodule.smithNormalForm` (Mathlib), `PadicInt` (Mathlib), `Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup` (Mathlib).

([[1]](#ref-1), Proof of Proposition 3.18, p. 32.)


**Checks.**


- diag(p, p) is scalar, hence trivial in PGL_2(Q_p): k = 0.

- diag(1, p) has (a, b) = (0, 1) and k = 1; there are p + 1 right cosets in its double coset.


<a id="nonintegral-local-translates-force-square-discriminant"></a>


**Nonintegral local translates force square discriminant.** Let p be any prime and f ∈ V_{Z_p} with Δ(f) ≠ 0. If γ·f ∈ V_{Z_p} for some γ ∈ PGL_2(Q_p) \ PGL_2(Z_p) (twisted action), then p² | Δ(f). Equivalently: if p² ∤ Δ(f) then PGL_2(Q_p)_f = PGL_2(Z_p) and m_p(f) = 1; in particular m_p(f) = 1 whenever p ∤ Δ(f). More precisely, if γ·f ∈ V_{Z_p} with γ ∈ PGL_2(Z_p) diag(1, p^k) PGL_2(Z_p) then p^{2k} | Δ(f); hence PGL_2(Q_p)_f is a finite union of right PGL_2(Z_p)-cosets and m_p(f) is finite.

Throughout this assertion, Valid for every prime p, including p = 2 and p = 3 (only the solubility half of Proposition 3.18 needs p odd). The twisted action preserves I, J and Δ, and elements of PGL_2(Z_p) preserve integrality.


To prove the assertion, By cartan-decomposition-of-pgl2-over-qp write γ = k_1 δ k_2 with δ = diag(1, p^k) or diag(p^k, 1), k ≥ 1; since k_1 preserves V_{Z_p}, δ·(k_2·f) ∈ V_{Z_p}, and Δ(k_2·f) = Δ(f) ([relative invariance of i and j](#relative-invariance-of-i-and-j)). Replace f by k_2·f. For δ = diag(1, p^k) the twisted action sends the coefficients (a, b, c, d, e) to (p^{-2k}a, p^{-k}b, c, p^{k}d, p^{2k}e); integrality forces p^{2k} | a and p^{k} | b. For diag(p^k, 1) the roles of (a, b) and (e, d) are exchanged. Δ lies in the ideal (a, b²) of Z[a, b, c, d, e]: Δ(0, b, c, d, e) = −b²(27b²e² − 18bcde + 4bd³ + 4c³e − c²d²) = b²·disc(bx³ + cx² + dx + e); and Δ(a, b, c, d, e) = Δ(e, d, c, b, a). Every monomial of Δ is therefore divisible by a or by b², hence p^{2k} | Δ(f). Since v_p(Δ(f)) is finite, k ≤ v_p(Δ(f))/2, and each double coset contains finitely many right cosets; so PGL_2(Z_p)\PGL_2(Q_p)_f is finite.

<a id="class-number-one-for-pgl2-over-q"></a>


**Class number one for pgl2 over q.** The diagonal map τ: PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(Q) → ∏'_p PGL_2(Z_p)\PGL_2(Q_p), into the families (σ_p)_p with σ_p the identity coset for all but finitely many p, is a bijection. Equivalently: PGL_2(Q) ∩ ∏_p PGL_2(Z_p) = PGL_2(Z) inside ∏_p PGL_2(Q_p), and for every such family (σ_p) there is γ ∈ PGL_2(Q) with PGL_2(Z_p)γ = σ_p for all p.

Throughout this assertion, The restricted product condition (σ_p trivial for almost all p) is necessary: the image of any γ ∈ PGL_2(Q) is integral at all p not dividing the entries' denominators and det. Right cosets PGL_2(Z)γ correspond to homothety classes of lattices Z²γ ⊆ Q².


To prove the assertion, Right cosets GL_2(Z)γ ↔ lattices L = Z²γ ⊆ Q² (free of rank 2, as submodules of Q² over the PID Z: mathlib:Submodule.smithNormalForm); likewise GL_2(Z_p)γ_p ↔ Z_p-lattices in Q_p². Local–global principle for lattices: L ↦ (Z_p L)_p is a bijection from lattices in Q² onto families (L_p) of Z_p-lattices with L_p = Z_p² for almost all p, with inverse (L_p) ↦ Q² ∩ ⋂_p L_p (clear denominators and use the Chinese remainder theorem). Pass to PGL_2: homothety classes. The map Q^× → ⊕_p Z, t ↦ (v_p(t))_p (mathlib:padicValRat), is surjective with kernel {±1}, so homothety classes of global lattices correspond bijectively to families of local homothety classes. Injectivity in group form: if γ ∈ PGL_2(Q) lies in PGL_2(Z_p) for every p, take a primitive integral representative g; then det g is a p-adic unit for all p, so det g = ±1 and γ ∈ PGL_2(Z).

<a id="global-weight-is-product-of-local-weights"></a>


**Global weight is product of local weights.** For every f ∈ V_Z with Δ(f) ≠ 0: m_p(f) = 1 for every p ∤ Δ(f), each m_p(f) is finite, and m(f) = ∏_p m_p(f).

To prove the assertion, By rational-orbit-weight, m(f) = #PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(Q)_f and m_p(f) = #PGL_2(Z_p)\PGL_2(Q_p)_f. The diagonal map τ: PGL_2(Z)\PGL_2(Q)_f → ∏_p PGL_2(Z_p)\PGL_2(Q_p)_f is well defined; the product is finite by nonintegral-local-translates-force-square-discriminant (PGL_2(Q_p)_f = PGL_2(Z_p) for p ∤ Δ(f)), and each factor is finite by the same lemma. τ is injective by class-number-one-for-pgl2-over-q (PGL_2(Q) ∩ ∏_p PGL_2(Z_p) = PGL_2(Z)). τ is surjective: class-number-one-for-pgl2-over-q gives γ ∈ PGL_2(Q) with prescribed local cosets; then γ·f ∈ V_{Z_p} for all p, so γ·f ∈ V_Z and γ ∈ PGL_2(Q)_f.

### 4.3 Finite-field quartics and local solubility


<a id="count-of-nonsingular-binary-quartic-forms-over-a-finite-field"></a>


**Count of nonsingular binary quartic forms over a finite field.** For every finite field F_q, #{f ∈ V_{F_q} : Δ(f) ≠ 0} = q²(q + 1)(q − 1)², where Δ is the integral discriminant polynomial of Layer 0 reduced to F_q.

Throughout this assertion, Holds for every finite field, including characteristic 2 and 3 (verified by exhaustive count for q = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11). Δ(f) is the discriminant of the dehomogenisation f(x, 1) when a ≠ 0 ([quartic discriminant is the polynomial discriminant](#quartic-discriminant-is-the-polynomial-discriminant)), and Δ(0, b, c, d, e) = b²·disc(bx³ + cx² + dx + e).


To prove the assertion, Case a ≠ 0: Δ(f) = disc(f(x, 1)) ≠ 0 iff f(x, 1) is separable (mathlib:Polynomial.resultant_deriv with mathlib:Polynomial.resultant_eq_zero_iff) iff it is squarefree (mathlib:PerfectField.separable_iff_squarefree, finite fields being perfect); scaling out a gives (q − 1)(q⁴ − q³) forms by count-of-squarefree-monic-polynomials-over-a-finite-field. Case a = 0: Δ(f) = b²·disc(bx³ + cx² + dx + e) ≠ 0 iff b ≠ 0 and the cubic is squarefree: (q − 1)(q³ − q²) forms. Sum: (q − 1)(q⁴ − q²) = q²(q + 1)(q − 1)².

*Needs:* [count of squarefree monic polynomials over a finite field](#count-of-squarefree-monic-polynomials-over-a-finite-field), [quartic discriminant is the polynomial discriminant](#quartic-discriminant-is-the-polynomial-discriminant), [binary quartic invariants](#binary-quartic-invariants), `Polynomial.discr` (Mathlib), `Polynomial.resultant_deriv` (Mathlib), `Polynomial.resultant_eq_zero_iff` (Mathlib), `PerfectField.separable_iff_squarefree` (Mathlib).

<a id="nonsingular-binary-quartic-forms-over-finite-fields-are-soluble"></a>


**Nonsingular binary quartic forms over finite fields are soluble.** Let p be an odd prime and f ∈ V_{F_p} with Δ(f) ≠ 0. Then f is F_p-soluble: there are x, y, z ∈ F_p with (x, y) ≠ (0, 0) and z² = f(x, y). Consequently, for p ≥ 5 and (I, J) ∈ F_p² with Δ(I, J) ≠ 0, Σ_{f ∈ PGL_2(F_p)\V_{F_p}(I, J)} 1/#Aut_{F_p}(f) = 1 (the second assertion of Lemma 3.15).

Throughout this assertion, p odd. For p ≥ 5 the proof is uniform; p = 3 is a finite verification; p = 2 is excluded (squares are not a proper subgroup of F_2^×). The PGL_2(F_p)-action is the twisted action, which preserves (I, J).


To prove the assertion, (p ≥ 5) For (I, J) with Δ(I, J) ≠ 0 let E = E^{I,J}. By Layer 1 (Theorem 3.2 over K = F_p, characteristic ≠ 2, 3) the F_p-soluble PGL_2(F_p)-orbits in V(I, J) := {f : (I(f), J(f)) = (I, J)} correspond to E(F_p)/2E(F_p), and every stabilizer is isomorphic to E(F_p)[2]. E(F_p) is finite (tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.finite_point), and for a finite abelian group #(G/2G) = #G[2] (mathlib:Subgroup.index_ker with mathlib:Subgroup.card_mul_index applied to multiplication by 2). Orbit–stabilizer (mathlib:MulAction.card_orbit_mul_card_stabilizer_eq_card_group): the number of soluble f ∈ V(I, J) is #PGL_2(F_p)·#(E/2E)/#E[2] = #PGL_2(F_p) = p(p² − 1). There are p² − p pairs (I, J) with Δ(I, J) ≠ 0 (the curve J² = 4I³ has the p points (t², 2t³)), so the number of soluble nonsingular forms is (p² − p)p(p² − 1) = p²(p + 1)(p − 1)², which is the number of all nonsingular forms by count-of-nonsingular-binary-quartic-forms-over-a-finite-field. Hence every nonsingular form is soluble, and the mass formula follows. (p = 3) Exhaustive check of the 3⁵ = 243 forms over F_3: each of the 144 forms with Δ ≠ 0 vanishes at a point of P¹(F_3) or takes the nonzero square value 1 there.

If z̄ = 0, (x̄ : ȳ) is a simple root of f̄ and lifts to a root of f in P¹(Q_p), giving a solution with z = 0. If f ≡ 0 (mod p) then p⁶ | Δ(f). If p | Δ(f) and f̄ ≠ 0, f̄ has a repeated factor; its splitting type is (1²11), (1²2), (1³1), (1²1²), (2²) or (1⁴). Types (1²11) and (1³1) have a simple F_p-rational root, which lifts as above. Type (1²2): work modulo p: move the double root to [0:1], then complete the square in the irreducible quadratic factor using a change preserving that root. This gives f̄ = ā x²(x² − n̄ y²), with n̄ a nonsquare. If ā is a square, f̄(1,0) is a nonzero square. Otherwise take the first square (c+1)n̄ in n̄,2n̄,…,(p−1)n̄, choose x̄₀²=(c+1)n̄, and note x̄₀²−n̄=cn̄ is a nonsquare. Thus f̄(x̄₀,1) is a nonzero square. Lift its square root by Hensel; no simultaneous exact p-adic diagonalization is needed. Types (1²1²), (2²), (1⁴) mean f̄ = c·ḡ² for a binary quadratic form ḡ. Δ and its gradient vanish identically on forms c·g² (polynomial identity), so Δ(c g² + p h) ≡ 0 (mod p²) for all lifts.

### 4.4 Local constancy and real solubility


<a id="local-weights-and-solubility-are-locally-constant"></a>


**Local weights and solubility are locally constant.** Let p be a prime. On the open set {f ∈ V_{Z_p} : Δ(f) ≠ 0} the functions f ↦ m_p(f) and f ↦ 1[f is Q_p-soluble] are locally constant; precisely, m_p is constant on f + p^{δ+1}V_{Z_p} where δ = v_p(Δ(f)). The set {f ∈ V_{Z_p} : Δ(f) = 0} is closed and has Haar measure zero. Consequently, for a family F defined by congruence conditions whose actual invariant closure Inv_p(F) has null boundary, φ_p := 1_{S_p(F)}/m_p is a function V_{Z_p} → [0, 1] that is locally constant outside the closed null set {Δ = 0} ∪ {f : (2^{-4}I(f), 2^{-6}J(f)) ∈ ∂Inv_p(F)}.

Throughout this assertion, For the final consequence, assume μ_p(∂Inv_p(F)) = 0 explicitly. Closedness and null boundary of Σ_p alone do not justify it for a closed subset Inv_p(F). For large families with positive local specification masses, count-of-curves-in-a-large-family supplies this assertion by CRT and the discriminant tail estimate. The zero-mass case of the weighted count uses an upper bound at one prime instead. The invariant map is a submersion on the nonsingular locus, so the p-adic inverse-function/change-of-variables input pulls Haar-null subsets of Q_p² back to null subsets of Q_p⁵. Use the nonsingular submersion change-of-variables assertion stated below, independently of the full orbit-integral formula. The divisibility conditions at 2 cut out clopen subsets.


To prove the assertion, m_p: by nonintegral-local-translates-force-square-discriminant only double cosets PGL_2(Z_p) diag(1, p^k) PGL_2(Z_p) with 2k ≤ δ can meet PGL_2(Q_p)_f; whether δ_k·(κ·f) is integral (κ ∈ PGL_2(Z_p)) depends only on f modulo p^{2k}; f' ≡ f (mod p^{δ+1}) has v_p(Δ(f')) = δ, so the same cosets occur for f and f'. Solubility is open: a solution (x, y, z) with z ≠ 0 persists because Q_p^{×2} is open (Hensel's lemma, mathlib:hensels_lemma); a solution with z = 0 is a simple root of f (Δ(f) ≠ 0) and persists under perturbation by Hensel's lemma. Insolubility is open: if f is insoluble, f(x, y) lies in the open set Q_p^× \ Q_p^{×2} for all primitive (x, y) ∈ Z_p², a compact set; by continuity of (f, x, y) ↦ f(x, y) and compactness (tube lemma) the same holds on a neighbourhood of f. {Δ = 0} is null: for fixed (a, b, c, d) with (a, b) ≠ (0, 0), Δ is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most 3 in e, so it has at most 3 roots; Fubini on Z_p⁴ × Z_p with the Haar measure (mathlib:MeasureTheory.Measure.haarMeasure) gives measure zero. φ_p takes values in [0, 1] because m_p ≥ 1 (rational-orbit-weight) and is locally constant off the displayed closed null set.

A form with a real root takes the value 0; a positive definite form takes positive values; a negative definite form takes only negative values on R² \ {0}. <a id="jacobian-of-the-orbit-map"></a>


**Jacobian of the orbit map.** Let s_{I,J} := x³y − (I/3)xy³ − (J/27)y⁴, so that I(s_{I,J}) = I and J(s_{I,J}) = J, and let ψ: PGL_2 × A² → V, ψ(g, I, J) := g·s_{I,J} (twisted action). Let ω be the left-invariant top-degree form on PGL_2 whose value at the identity on the images of E_{11}, E_{12}, E_{21} in pgl_2 = gl_2/(scalars) is 1 (these images form a Z-basis of gl_2(Z)/Z·1, so ω generates the invariant top-degree forms of PGL_2 over Z, as in the source's Proposition 2.8), and let dv = da ∧ db ∧ dc ∧ dd ∧ de. Then ψ*(dv) = −(1/27)·ω ∧ dI ∧ dJ identically on PGL_2 × A², over every commutative ring in which 3 is invertible. At g = 1 the Jacobian matrix (rows a, …, e; columns E_{11}, E_{12}, E_{21}, ∂_I, ∂_J) is [[0,1,0,0,0],[1,0,0,0,0],[0,−I,3,0,0],[I/3,−4J/27,0,−1/3,0],[2J/27,0,−I/3,0,−1/27]], of determinant −1/27.

To prove the assertion, The twisted action of g on V has determinant 1 (polynomial identity), and ω is left-invariant, so the Jacobian of ψ at (g, I, J) equals its value at (1, I, J). At g = 1 the derivative of t ↦ (1 + tE)·s_{I,J} for E ∈ {E_{11}, E_{12}, E_{21}} and the partial derivatives ∂_I s, ∂_J s give the displayed matrix; its determinant (mathlib:Matrix.det) is −1/27, independent of (I, J). ### 4.15 Hyperelliptic degree-one torsors and orbit weights


<a id="refinement-admissibility"></a>


**Admissibility.** For n=2g+2 with g≥1 and a congruence family F of integral binary forms, let L_p be its actual p-adic coefficient closure. The added admissibility predicate says that there is P such that, for every prime p>P, L_p contains every coefficient tuple a for which z²=Σ_i a_i x^(n−i)y^i has a Q_p-point with (x,y)≠(0,0). Smooth nonzero-discriminant models suffice: for closed L_p, point-bearing singular equations lie in their closure by point-preserving smooth perturbation. This predicate supplements the imported congruence-family definition; it does not assert positive density, local Div¹-solubility at small places or admissibility of an arbitrary collection of local sets.

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_threshold`: Admissibility is equivalent to a single integer threshold beyond which all local point-bearing tuples are allowed.

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_mono`: If L_p⊆M_p for every prime and L is admissible, M is admissible.

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_finite_change`: If L is admissible and L_p=M_p beyond a fixed threshold, M is admissible.

- `ArithmeticSelmerRefinement.admissible_of_local_points`: Containing the local point locus at every prime implies admissibility.


To prove the assertion, Use Layer 0 coefficient models and the actual local closures from Layer 2. At each sufficiently large prime impose inclusion of the point-bearing locus. Closedness permits smooth perturbation; changing finitely many local conditions preserves the predicate.

<a id="refinement-degree-one-arithmetic-comparison"></a>


**Degree one arithmetic comparison.** For a smooth hyperelliptic C/Q of genus g≥1 with a Q-rational degree-two hyperelliptic divisor class d represented by a divisor, and actual degree-one divisors over every completion, every rational Picard-scheme point descends to an actual line bundle/divisor. Thus J¹(Q)≠∅ iff C has a point over some finite odd-degree extension iff index(C)=1; otherwise index(C)=2. Here index is the positive generator of the degree subgroup of rational divisors, not the minimum degree of a closed point.


To prove the assertion, Apply the Picard/Brauer obstruction sequence and global-to-local injectivity of Br(Q); local actual Div¹ kills the obstruction. Trace an odd-degree point, then subtract ((k−1)/2)d. Conversely an odd-degree rational divisor must involve an odd-degree closed point. The rational degree-two divisor forces the index to divide two.

### Examples

For the two-descent local ratio, an additive Z_2 open subgroup has index two under multiplication by two, while an additive Z_p open subgroup has index one for odd p. Over R the ratio of the two-division quotient to two-torsion is one half in both component types. Hence the extra factors `2·(1/2)` cancel. The remaining product is `2ζ(2)∏_p(1-p^-2)=2`, giving mean nonidentity two-Selmer size two and total mean three.

The average of `#Sel2-#im(Sel4→Sel2)` at least `3/5` is an aggregate element count. Dividing by the mean Sel2 size three gives at least one fifth of elements, not one fifth of curves. For the rank-one family, twisting by -39 multiplies height by `39^6`, so the count scale `X^(5/6)` loses `39^5`; this explains the density lower bound `c_F/(2c_E39^5)`.

An empty degree-one Selmer torsor has cardinal zero; it is not the trivial group of cardinal one. If the nonzero generic Weierstrass class belongs to Sel2(J) and J(Q)[2]=0, a nonempty rational degree-one torsor forces positive rank. This is the empty-or-infinite dichotomy, without finiteness of all Sha.

## Layer 5: Probability models and function-field distributions

The finite and locally compact random-intersection models supply exact probability laws. Arithmetic conjectures identify a specified empirical family with such a law and separately assert its unbounded moments. Function-field theorems instead use the class-field/Hurwitz dictionary, arithmetic component action, trace estimates and their specified order of limits. The full component profile includes the unstable boundary, so a stable-range lower bound does not imply an ordinary limit.


### 5.1 Cohen–Lenstra arithmetic conjectures


<a id="cohen-lenstra-heuristic-for-quadratic-fields"></a>


**Cohen lenstra heuristic for quadratic fields.** Conjecture (a proposition, not a theorem). Let p be an odd prime and K_d = ℚ(√d) for squarefree d ≠ 1. (Imaginary, u = 0) For every finite abelian p-group B, #{d < 0 : |disc K_d| ≤ X, Cl(K_d)_p ≅ B} / #{d < 0 : |disc K_d| ≤ X} → μ_{p,0}(B). (Real, u = 1) The same with d > 0 and limit μ_{p,1}(B) = ∏_{k≥1}(1 − p^{−k−1})/(|B||Aut B|). Here Cl(K)_p is the p-primary part of the class group and the fields are ordered by absolute discriminant. Proved instances in the moment form: the ℤ/3-moment (Davenport–Heilbronn, Layer 3) and its Datskovsky–Wright extension; the full distribution is presented as a conjecture in the cited sources, and is retained as a conjecture.

Throughout this assertion, p odd prime u ∈ {0, 1} K_d ≅ ℚ(√d) for squarefree d ≠ 1

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `CohenLenstraHeuristic`: The conjecture as a proposition in p, u and the family K.

- `IsQuadraticFamily`: K d ≅ ℚ(√d) for all squarefree d ≠ 1.

- `quadraticFamilyUpTo`: The squarefree d of the given sign with |disc K_d| ≤ X.

- `classGroupPrimary`: The p-primary part of the class group, as an additive group.

- `quadraticFamilyUpTo_finite`: The counting sets are finite.

- `cohenLenstraHeuristic_iff_primary_independent`: The conjecture does not depend on the chosen family K (isomorphic fields have isomorphic class groups).

- `cohenLenstraHeuristic_tsum_limits`: The predicted limits sum to 1 (no escape of mass in the prediction).


To prove the assertion, Encode the family by a function d ↦ K_d with [K_d : ℚ] = 2 and a square root of d in K_d (IsQuadraticFamily); the class-group isomorphism type of K_d does not depend on the choice. Define the counting sets S^±_X of squarefree d of the given sign with |NumberField.discr K_d| ≤ X (finite: at most 2X + 1 values of d since |disc| ≥ |d|). ### 5.2 Cohen–Martinet predictions and wreath-type comparisons


<a id="cohen-martinet-predicted-surjection-moment"></a>


**Cohen martinet predicted surjection moment.** For a finite group G, a prime p, a finite F_p[G]-module Z (representation ρ) and elements σ_v ∈ G (one for each infinite place v of the base field k, σ_v in the conjugacy class of complex conjugation over v), the predicted moment is M(Z, σ) = ∏_v |Z^{σ_v}|^{−1}, where Z^{σ} = {z : ρ(σ)z = z}.

Throughout this assertion, G finite group p prime Z a finite F_p[G]-module

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:

- `cohenMartinetPredictedMoment_cons`: M(Z, σ :: σ') = |Z^{σ}|^{−1} M(Z, σ').

- `cohenMartinetPredictedMoment_eq_pow`: M(Z, σ) = p^{−Σ_v dim Z^{σ_v}}.

- `equivariantSurjCard`: |Sur_G(M, Z)|, the number of G-equivariant surjections.


To prove the assertion, Define the product over the list σ of |ker(ρ(σ_v) − 1)|, then invert. Since Z^{σ} is an F_p-subspace, M(Z, σ) = p^{−Σ_v dim Z^{σ_v}}.

Then (x−t_i x)/(2c_i)=e_i lies in the G-stable span of x. Transitivity of H gives all e_j. A single signed permutation need not take x to e_i; the group-algebra linear combination is necessary. ### 5.3 Joint Frobenius cokernels


<a id="enhanced-cohen-lenstra-finite-level-law"></a>


**Enhanced cohen lenstra finite level law.** For a prime ℓ, g ≥ 0 and a tuple n = (n_1, …, n_k) of positive integers, the finite-level law on k-tuples of classes is CL^{(g)}_{n,ℓ}(H_1, …, H_k) = Haar_g(F ∈ End_g(ℤ_ℓ) : coker(1 − F^{n_j}) ≅ H_j for all j). The enhanced law CL_{n,ℓ} (Lipnowski–Tsimerman Definition 5.16, distinct n_j) is its limit as g → ∞, defined only where the limit exists (EnhancedCohenLenstraLimitExists); CL_{n,S} is the product over ℓ ∈ S.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ prime n_j ≥ 1

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `enhancedCokernelLaw`: The finite-g joint law of (coker(1 − F^{n_j}))_j.

- `EnhancedCohenLenstraLimitExists`: The proposition that every finite-g mass converges as g → ∞.

- `enhancedCohenLenstra`: CL_{n,ℓ}(H) as the limit of the finite-g masses.

- `enhancedCokernelLaw_one`: For n = (1) the finite-g law is the law of coker(1 − F).

- `enhancedCohenLenstra_one`: CL_{(1),ℓ} = μ_{ℓ,0} (by Friedman–Washington).

- `tsum_enhancedCokernelLaw`: Each finite-g law has total mass 1.

- `enhancedCokernelLaw_zero_zero`: CL^{(g)}_{(1,2),ℓ}(0, 0) = P(1 − F² invertible mod ℓ) for F uniform in M_g(F_ℓ).


To prove the assertion, Define the finite-g law as the Haar measure of the set of F with the prescribed cokernels (padicMatrixHaar on M_g(ℤ_ℓ)). Each det(1−F^{n_j}) is a nonzero polynomial (its value at F=0 is 1). Its Haar-zero vanishing set follows by one-variable root finiteness and Fubini, as in the Haar-cokernel law. Outside the finite union of these null sets all cokernels are finite. Smith normal form makes each prescribed finite-cokernel event measurable via a sufficiently deep finite congruence quotient. The joint class events therefore partition a full-measure set. Define the existence proposition for the limits and the limit (limUnder) as separate declarations; no limiting measure is asserted.

*Needs:* [friedman washington cokernel law](#friedman-washington-cokernel-law), [friedman washington translation form](#friedman-washington-translation-form), [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), `MeasureTheory.Measure.haarMeasure` (Mathlib).

([[45]](#ref-45), arXiv 1511.02212v1, Definition 5.16, p. 35.)


**Checks.**


- For g = 0 all cokernels are trivial: the mass of (0, 0) is 1.

- The mass of (ℤ/ℓ, 0) for n = (1, 2) is 0: the components are not independent, so a product of Cohen–Lenstra measures is the wrong definition.

- For n = (1) the finite-g laws converge to μ_{ℓ,0}.

- n = (1) recovers the Friedman–Washington law of coker(1 − F) ([friedman washington translation form](#friedman-washington-translation-form)).

- The components are dependent: coker(1 − F) is a quotient-compatible piece of coker(1 − F²) since 1 − F² = (1 − F)(1 + F).


<a id="zero-cokernel-probability-at-two"></a>


**Zero cokernel probability at two.** For F uniform in M_g(F_2), P(1 − F² ∈ GL_g(F_2)) = |GL_g(F_2)|/2^{g²} = ∏_{j=1}^{g}(1 − 2^{−j}); it decreases to ∏_{j≥1}(1 − 2^{−j}) = c_{2,0} ≈ 0.2888 > 0. Hence CL^{(g)}_{(1,2),2}(0, 0) = ∏_{j=1}^{g}(1 − 2^{−j}).

Throughout this assertion, g ∈ ℕ


To prove the assertion, In characteristic 2, 1 − F² = (1 − F)², which is invertible iff 1 − F is. F ↦ 1 − F is a bijection of M_g(F_2), so the count equals |GL_g(F_2)| (Matrix.card_GL_field) out of 2^{g²} matrices. For the ℓ-adic law: coker(1 − F) = coker(1 − F²) = 0 iff 1 − F² is invertible over ℤ_2 iff it is invertible mod 2 (enhancedCokernelLaw_zero_zero), and Haar measure pushes forward to the uniform measure mod 2.

**Enhanced cohen lenstra conjecture.** Conjecture (a proposition about one family). Let p be a prime, S a finite set of primes not containing p, n = (n_1, …, n_k) distinct positive integers, and (F_g)_g a family of g-dimensional abelian varieties over F_p with sampling laws P_g. Lipnowski–Tsimerman state it for 'geometric' families, which the source does not define; the proposition here is attached to a given family.

Throughout this assertion, p prime S finite set of primes with p ∉ S n_j distinct and positive EnhancedCohenLenstraLimitExists for ℓ ∈ S

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:

- `EnhancedCohenLenstraConjecture.apply`: Given the CL_S hypothesis, the joint convergence to ∏_ℓ CL_{n,ℓ}.

- `enhancedCohenLenstraConjecture_single`: For n = (1) the conjecture holds for every family.


To prove the assertion, Represent the family by probability mass functions P_g on finite sets Ω_g and the ℓ-primary point groups pt(g, ω, m, ℓ) of A_ω(F_{p^m}) as classes. State the implication between the two convergence statements, with CL_S from [cohen lenstra measure over a finite set of primes](#cohen-lenstra-measure-over-a-finite-set-of-primes) and CL_{n,ℓ} from [enhanced cohen lenstra finite level law](#enhanced-cohen-lenstra-finite-level-law).

### 5.4 Finite quadratic intersection laws


<a id="maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space"></a>


**Maximal isotropic subspaces of a quadratic space.** Let K be a field, V a finite-dimensional K-vector space and Q : V → K a quadratic form (Mathlib QuadraticForm, any characteristic), with polar form b_Q(x, y) = Q(x + y) − Q(x) − Q(y). For a subspace W let W^⊥ be its b_Q-orthogonal. W is maximal isotropic if Q|_W = 0 and W^⊥ = W; I_V denotes the set of maximal isotropic subspaces. (V, Q) is nondegenerate if b_Q is nondegenerate, and weakly metabolic if moreover I_V ≠ ∅. For K = 𝔽_p this is Poonen–Rains' definition for a quadratic form with values in (1/p)ℤ/ℤ ≅ 𝔽_p. The condition Q|_W = 0 is part of the definition: in characteristic 2, W^⊥ = W does not imply it.

Throughout this assertion, V finite-dimensional over K Q a quadratic form on V

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `IsMaxIsotropic`: IsMaxIsotropic Q W ↔ (∀ w ∈ W, Q w = 0) ∧ W^⊥ = W, with W^⊥ for the polar form.

- `maxIsotropicSubspaces`: I_V := {W : Submodule K V | IsMaxIsotropic Q W}.

- `IsWeaklyMetabolic`: Polar form nondegenerate and I_V nonempty.

- `IsMaxIsotropic.finrank_eq`: If the polar form is nondegenerate and finrank V = 2n then finrank W = n for W ∈ I_V.

- `isMaxIsotropic_iff_finrank`: For nondegenerate polar form and finrank V = 2n: W ∈ I_V ↔ Q|_W = 0 ∧ finrank W = n.

- `IsMaxIsotropic.map_isometryEquiv`: An isometry V ≃ V' of quadratic spaces maps I_V bijectively to I_{V'}.

- `maxIsotropicSubspaces_hyperbolicPlane`: For Q(x, y) = xy on K², I_V = {K × 0, 0 × K}.


To prove the assertion, Define W^⊥ as LinearMap.BilinForm.orthogonal of QuadraticMap.polarBilin Q. Define IsMaxIsotropic Q W := (∀ w ∈ W, Q w = 0) ∧ W^⊥ = W, and I_V as the set of such W. Nondegenerate: LinearMap.BilinForm.Nondegenerate of the polar form; weakly metabolic: nondegenerate and I_V nonempty.

*Needs:* `QuadraticForm` (Mathlib), `QuadraticMap.polarBilin` (Mathlib), `LinearMap.BilinForm.orthogonal` (Mathlib), `LinearMap.BilinForm.Nondegenerate` (Mathlib), `LinearMap.BilinForm.finrank_add_finrank_orthogonal` (Mathlib).

([[28]](#ref-28), §2.1, p. 5; [[28]](#ref-28), §2.1, Remark 2.3, p. 5.)


**Checks.**


- For K = 𝔽_p and Q(x, y) = x y on K², the set maxIsotropicSubspaces Q has exactly 2 elements.

- Over 𝔽_2 with Q(x, y) = x y, W = span{(1, 1)} has W^⊥ = W for the polar form but is not maximal isotropic.

- Q(x, y) = x² + x y + y² on 𝔽_2² is nondegenerate but has no maximal isotropic subspace, so it is not weakly metabolic.

- On V = 0 the unique maximal isotropic subspace is ⊥ (the zero subspace).

- (K², xy) is weakly metabolic with exactly two maximal isotropic subspaces K × 0 and 0 × K.

- If (V, Q) is weakly metabolic of dimension 2n then every W ∈ I_V has dimension n.

- Over 𝔽_2 the form Q(x, y) = xy and the line W = 𝔽_2(1, 1) satisfy W^⊥ = W but Q(1, 1) = 1, so W ∉ I_V.


<a id="isotropic-reduction-map"></a>


**Isotropic reduction map.** Let (V, Q) be a nondegenerate quadratic space over a field K and X ⊆ V an isotropic subspace (Q|_X = 0). Then X ⊆ X^⊥, the quotient X^⊥/X carries the induced quadratic form Q_X(v + X) := Q(v), which is well defined and has nondegenerate polar form, and dim X^⊥/X = dim V − 2 dim X. For W ∈ I_V, the subspace (W ∩ X^⊥) + X lies in I_V and its image π_X(W) := ((W ∩ X^⊥) + X)/X lies in I_{X^⊥/X}. The map π_X : I_V → I_{X^⊥/X} is the isotropic reduction map; if X ⊆ W then π_X(W) = W/X, and for X ⊆ Y isotropic, π_{Y/X} ∘ π_X = π_Y.

Throughout this assertion, (V, Q) nondegenerate, finite-dimensional X isotropic: Q|_X = 0

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `isotropicQuotientForm`: Q_X on X^⊥/X, Q_X(v + X) = Q(v).

- `isotropicQuotientForm_nondegenerate`: The polar form of Q_X is nondegenerate.

- `finrank_isotropicQuotient`: dim X^⊥/X = dim V − 2 dim X.

- `isotropicReduction`: π_X : I_V → I_{X^⊥/X}, W ↦ ((W ⊓ X^⊥) ⊔ X)/X.

- `isotropicReduction_of_le`: X ≤ W ∈ I_V ⇒ π_X(W) = W/X: its preimage in X^⊥ is W (note W = W^⊥ ⊆ X^⊥).

- `isotropicReduction_bot`: π_0 = id: the preimage of π_0(W) is W.

- `isotropicReduction_comp`: For X ≤ Y isotropic and W ∈ I_V, π_Y factors through π_X under (Y^⊥/X)/(Y/X) ≅ Y^⊥/Y; in particular dim π_Y(W) = dim π_X(W) − (dim Y − dim X).


To prove the assertion, Well-definedness of Q_X: for x ∈ X and v ∈ X^⊥, Q(v + x) = Q(v) + Q(x) + b_Q(v, x) = Q(v). Nondegeneracy of Q_X: if v ∈ X^⊥ pairs to zero with X^⊥ then v ∈ (X^⊥)^⊥ = X (double orthogonal for a nondegenerate form, from mathlib:LinearMap.BilinForm.finrank_add_finrank_orthogonal and inclusion). Dimension: dim X^⊥ = dim V − dim X by nondegeneracy, so dim X^⊥/X = dim V − 2 dim X (mathlib:Submodule.finrank_quotient_add_finrank). W' := (W ∩ X^⊥) + X is isotropic: Q vanishes on W ∩ X^⊥ ⊆ W and on X, and b_Q(W ∩ X^⊥, X) = 0. dim W' = n when dim V = 2n: dim(W ∩ X^⊥) = 2n − dim(W + X) = n − dim X + dim(W ∩ X) (orthogonal of a sum, W^⊥ = W), so dim W' = dim(W ∩ X^⊥) + dim X − dim(W ∩ X) = n; an isotropic subspace of dimension n in a nondegenerate 2n-space equals its orthogonal, so W' ∈ I_V. Its image in X^⊥/X is maximal isotropic by the lattice correspondence between subspaces of X^⊥ containing X and subspaces of X^⊥/X. Compatibility π_{Y/X} ∘ π_X = π_Y: unwind the definitions using the third isomorphism theorem.

*Needs:* [maximal isotropic subspaces of a quadratic space](#maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space), `LinearMap.BilinForm.finrank_add_finrank_orthogonal` (Mathlib), `Submodule.finrank_quotient_add_finrank` (Mathlib).

<a id="fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map"></a>


**Fibres of the isotropic reduction map.** Let (V, Q) be a weakly metabolic quadratic space of dimension 2n over 𝔽_p and X ⊆ V an isotropic subspace. Then every fibre of π_X : I_V → I_{X^⊥/X} has exactly ∏_{i=1}^{dim X} (p^{n−i} + 1) elements.

Throughout this assertion, (V, Q) weakly metabolic over 𝔽_p, dim V = 2n X isotropic


To prove the assertion, Reduce to dim X = 1 by choosing a full flag 0 = X_0 ⊂ X_1 ⊂ … ⊂ X_k = X and factoring π_X as the composite of the reductions π_{X_{i}/X_{i−1}} ([isotropic reduction map](#isotropic-reduction-map), API isotropicReduction_comp); the space at stage i has dimension 2(n − i + 1). Case X = 𝔽_p v: fix W̄ ∈ I_{X^⊥/X} and its preimage W ⊇ X in I_V. The map Z ↦ Z ∩ W from the fibre over W̄ to {hyperplanes of W not containing v} ∪ {W} is a bijection: if v ∈ Z then Z = W; if v ∉ Z then Z ∩ W is a hyperplane W_1 of W. Conversely, for a hyperplane W_1 ⊂ W not containing v, the Z ∈ I_V containing W_1 correspond to maximal isotropic lines of the 2-dimensional weakly metabolic space W_1^⊥/W_1 ≅ (𝔽_p², xy), of which there are exactly two ([maximal isotropic subspaces of a quadratic space](#maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space), API maxIsotropicSubspaces_hyperbolicPlane): one is W, the other Z has Z ∩ W = W_1 and reduces to W̄. Since v∉W₁, the other Z cannot contain v (otherwise it contains W₁+F_pv=W and equals W). The printed source omits this necessary hyperplane restriction. Count: the hyperplanes of the n-dimensional W not containing v number (p^n − 1)/(p − 1) − (p^{n−1} − 1)/(p − 1) = p^{n−1}; adding Z = W gives p^{n−1} + 1 elements in each fibre when dim X = 1; the product over the flag gives ∏_{i=1}^{dim X}(p^{n−i} + 1).

*Needs:* [isotropic reduction map](#isotropic-reduction-map), [maximal isotropic subspaces of a quadratic space](#maximal-isotropic-subspaces-of-a-quadratic-space), [gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient).

**Checks.**

- n = 1, X a line: the fibre over the single point of I_0 is all of I_V, of size p^0 + 1 = 2.


<a id="number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces"></a>


**Number of maximal isotropic subspaces.** If (V, Q) is a weakly metabolic quadratic space of dimension 2n over 𝔽_p, then #I_V = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1} (p^{j} + 1).

Throughout this assertion, (V, Q) weakly metabolic over 𝔽_p, dim V = 2n

<a id="intersection-dimension-generating-function"></a>


**Intersection dimension generating function.** Let (V, Q) be weakly metabolic of dimension 2n over 𝔽_p and fix W ∈ I_V. For Z uniform on I_V let X_n := dim(Z ∩ W) and a_{d,n} := Prob(X_n = d). Then X_n is distributed as a sum of independent Bernoulli variables B_1, …, B_n with Prob(B_i = 1) = 1/(p^{i−1} + 1); equivalently Σ_{d≥0} a_{d,n} z^{d} = ∏_{i=0}^{n−1} (z + p^{i})/(1 + p^{i}), i.e. Σ_{Z ∈ I_V} z^{dim(Z ∩ W)} = ∏_{i=0}^{n−1} (z + p^{i}) as polynomials in z.

Throughout this assertion, (V, Q) weakly metabolic over 𝔽_p, dim V = 2n W ∈ I_V fixed Z uniformly distributed on the finite set I_V


To prove the assertion, Induction on n; n = 0 is trivial. For n > 0 fix 0 ≠ v ∈ W and X = 𝔽_p v, and write Z̄ := π_X(Z) ([isotropic reduction map](#isotropic-reduction-map)). dim(Z ∩ W) = dim(Z̄ ∩ W̄) + [v ∈ Z], where W̄ = W/X ∈ I_{X^⊥/X} (dim 2n − 2). Z̄ is uniform on I_{X^⊥/X} because every fibre of π_X has the same size p^{n−1} + 1 ([fibres of the isotropic reduction map](#fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map)); so dim(Z̄ ∩ W̄) has the law of X_{n−1}. Conditionally on Z̄, exactly one of the p^{n−1} + 1 elements of the fibre contains v (the preimage of Z̄ in X^⊥), so [v ∈ Z] is Bernoulli with parameter 1/(p^{n−1} + 1), independent of Z̄. Multiply generating functions: (z + p^{n−1})/(1 + p^{n−1}) times the generating function of X_{n−1}; the count form follows from [number of maximal isotropic subspaces](#number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces).

*Needs:* [isotropic reduction map](#isotropic-reduction-map), [fibres of the isotropic reduction map](#fibres-of-the-isotropic-reduction-map), [number of maximal isotropic subspaces](#number-of-maximal-isotropic-subspaces).

**Intersection dimension law closed form.** In the setting of [intersection dimension generating function](#intersection-dimension-generating-function), for 0 ≤ d ≤ n: a_{d,n} = ∏_{j=0}^{n−1} (1 + p^{−j})^{−1} · ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^{j} − 1) · ∏_{j=0}^{d−1} (1 − p^{j−n}).

Simplify p^{−d(d−1)/2}[n d]_{1/p} = ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^j − 1) · ∏_{j=0}^{d−1}(1 − p^{j−n}) using the product formula gaussBinom_eq_prod ([gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient)); routine algebra.
