### 5.5 The Poonen–Rains law and parity


<a id="poonen-rains-distribution"></a>


**Poonen rains distribution.** For a prime p, the Poonen–Rains distribution is the probability measure on ℤ_{≥0} with Prob(X_{Sel_p} = d) = a_d := c_p ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^{j} − 1), where c_p := ∏_{j≥0} (1 + p^{−j})^{−1} = (1/2) ∏_{i≥0} (1 − p^{−(2i+1)}). (The j = 0 factor is 1/2.) That the a_d sum to 1 is the theorem [intersection law converges to poonen rains](#intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains), which is used to package the weights as a probability mass function.

Throughout this assertion, p prime

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `poonenRainsConstant`: c_p := ∏'_{j≥0} (1 + p^{−j})^{−1}.

- `poonenRainsWeight`: a_d := c_p ∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^{j} − 1).

- `poonenRainsDistribution`: The probability mass function on ℕ with weights a_d.

- `poonenRainsConstant_eq_half_prod`: c_p = (1/2) ∏'_{i≥0} (1 − p^{−(2i+1)}).

- `poonenRainsWeight_succ`: a_{d+1} = a_d · p/(p^{d+1} − 1).

- `poonenRainsWeight_pos`: a_d > 0 for every d.

- `poonenRainsDistribution_apply`: poonenRainsDistribution p d = a_d.

- `poonenRainsDistribution_even`: The total mass on even d is 1/2 (parity equidistribution).

- `poonenRainsDistribution_eq_alternatingKernelLimit`: a_d equals the parity-averaged limit law of dim ker of a random alternating n×n matrix over 𝔽_p ([alternating kernel law limit is poonen rains](#alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains)).


To prove the assertion, Define c_p as the convergent infinite product ∏_{j≥0}(1 + p^{−j})^{−1} (convergent since Σ p^{−j} < ∞; mathlib:tprod, mathlib:Multipliable). Define the weights a_d by the finite products and the measure from the summation theorem. The second expression for c_p: substitute 1 + p^{−j} = (1 − p^{−2j})/(1 − p^{−j}) for j ≥ 1 and cancel (telescoping of even exponents).

*Needs:* [intersection dimension law closed form](#intersection-dimension-law-closed-form), `tprod` (Mathlib), `Multipliable` (Mathlib).

([[28]](#ref-28), Proposition 2.6(f), p. 6; [[28]](#ref-28), Definition 2.9, p. 7.)


**Checks.**


- poonenRainsWeight p 0 = poonenRainsConstant p.

- poonenRainsWeight 2 1 = 2 · poonenRainsWeight 2 0.

- poonenRainsWeight 2 0 ≠ ∏'_{i≥1}(1 − 2^{−i}) (the Cohen–Lenstra probability that the 2-rank is 0), since c_2 < 1/4 < 0.28.

- poonenRainsWeight p d > 0 for all d, so no dimension is excluded.

- p = 2: c_2 = (1/2)∏_{i≥0}(1 − 2^{−(2i+1)}) ≈ 0.2097, a_0 ≈ 0.2097, a_1 ≈ 0.4194, a_2 ≈ 0.2796.

- a_{d+1}/a_d = p/(p^{d+1} − 1).


<a id="intersection-law-converges-to-poonen-rains"></a>


**Intersection law converges to poonen rains.** For every d ≥ 0, a_{d,n} → a_d as n → ∞; Σ_{d≥0} a_d = 1; Σ_d a_d z^d = ∏_{i≥0}(1 + p^{−i}z)/(1 + p^{−i}) for every complex z (both sides converge absolutely); and the laws of X_n converge in total variation to the Poonen–Rains distribution.

Throughout this assertion, p prime


To prove the assertion, Termwise limit: in the closed formula ([intersection dimension law closed form](#intersection-dimension-law-closed-form)) the factor ∏_{j=0}^{d−1}(1 − p^{j−n}) → 1 and ∏_{j=0}^{n−1}(1 + p^{−j})^{−1} → c_p (mathlib:tprod of a multipliable family). Total mass: a_{d,n} ≤ C·∏_{j=1}^{d} p/(p^j − 1) with C independent of n, and Σ_d ∏_{j=1}^d p/(p^j−1) < ∞ (ratio test: consecutive ratio p/(p^{d+1} − 1) → 0); dominated convergence for sums (mathlib:ENNReal.tsum_mul_left for the rearrangement) gives Σ_d a_d = lim_n Σ_d a_{d,n} = 1. For each fixed complex z the same majorant with an extra |z|^d is summable by the ratio test. Dominated convergence therefore passes the finite generating polynomial to Σ_d a_d z^d. The finite products converge absolutely because Σ_i |z−1|p^{−i}/(1+p^{−i})<∞. This also proves both convergence assertions in the complex generating-function statement. Total variation: pointwise convergence of probability mass functions with limit of total mass 1 (Scheffé's lemma for counting measure) implies convergence in total variation.

*Needs:* [intersection dimension law closed form](#intersection-dimension-law-closed-form), [poonen rains distribution](#poonen-rains-distribution), `tprod` (Mathlib), `ENNReal.tsum_mul_left` (Mathlib).

([[28]](#ref-28), Proposition 2.6(d),(f), p. 6; proof of (f), p. 7.)

### 5.6 Alternating matrices and symplectic cokernels


<a id="count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices"></a>


**Count of nondegenerate alternating matrices.** Let M_m(𝔽_p)^alt be the set of alternating m × m matrices over 𝔽_p (zero diagonal, Aᵗ = −A), of cardinality p^{m(m−1)/2}, and GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt its subset of invertible ones. If m is odd, GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt = ∅. If m is even, #GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt / #M_m(𝔽_p)^alt = ∏_{i=1}^{m/2} (1 − p^{1−2i}).

Throughout this assertion, p prime m ≥ 0


To prove the assertion, #M_m(𝔽_p)^alt = p^{m(m−1)/2}: an alternating matrix is determined freely by its strictly upper triangular entries. Odd m: det A = det Aᵗ = det(−A) = −det A in odd dimension, and for p = 2 an alternating (zero-diagonal symmetric) form of odd rank does not exist; in all characteristics the rank of an alternating form is even (symplectic basis), so A is singular. The m=0 case is the unique empty matrix and gives the empty product 1. For even m≥2, Even m, induction on m: the first column of an invertible alternating A is any of the p^{m−1} − 1 nonzero vectors with zero first entry; the number of completions does not depend on it (a change of basis in GL_m(𝔽_p) fixing e_1 moves any admissible column to any other), and splitting off the hyperbolic plane spanned by e_1 and a partner leaves p^{m−2} free coupling entries times an invertible alternating (m − 2)-matrix: #GL_m^alt = (p^{m−1} − 1) p^{m−2} #GL_{m−2}^alt. Divide by p^{m(m−1)/2} = p^{2m−3} p^{(m−2)(m−3)/2}: the factor is (p^{m−1} − 1)/p^{m−1} = 1 − p^{1−m}; with m = 2i this is 1 − p^{1−2i}.

*Needs:* `Matrix.card_GL_field` (Mathlib).

<a id="alternating-matrix-kernel-law"></a>


**Alternating matrix kernel law.** For a prime p and integers n ≥ j ≥ 0, P_p(j | n) is the probability that a uniformly random alternating n × n matrix over 𝔽_p has kernel of dimension exactly j: P_p(j | n) := #{A ∈ M_n(𝔽_p)^alt : dim ker A = j} / p^{n(n−1)/2}. It vanishes unless j ≡ n (mod 2). The parity-averaged limit law is P_p(j | ∞) := lim_{n→∞} (1/2)(P_p(j | 2n) + P_p(j | 2n+1)). For p = 2 these are Smith's P^Alt(j | n) and P^Alt(j | ∞) (Smith I, Definition 1.4); (P_2(j' | j))_{j,j'} are the transition probabilities of the Markov chain r_2 ≥ r_4 ≥ … of 2^k-Selmer ranks in Smith's theorem.

Throughout this assertion, p prime 0 ≤ j ≤ n

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `alternatingKernelLaw`: P_p(j | n) as a rational number (finite count divided by p^{n(n−1)/2}).

- `alternatingKernelLaw_eq_zero_of_parity`: j ≢ n (mod 2) ⇒ P_p(j | n) = 0.

- `alternatingKernelLaw_self`: P_p(n | n) = p^{−n(n−1)/2}.

- `sum_alternatingKernelLaw`: Σ_{j=0}^{n} P_p(j | n) = 1.

- `alternatingKernelLaw_eq_formula`: Closed formula ([alternating kernel law formula](#alternating-kernel-law-formula)).

- `alternatingKernelLimit`: P_p(j | ∞) := lim (1/2)(P_p(j | 2n) + P_p(j | 2n+1)).

- `alternatingKernelLimit_eq_poonenRains`: P_p(j | ∞) = poonenRainsWeight p j.


To prove the assertion, Define the finite count over the finite set of alternating matrices (Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) (ZMod p) with zero diagonal and transpose equal to the negative) and the kernel dimension via Module.finrank of LinearMap.ker of mulVecLin. Define the parity-averaged limit as a limit of real sequences; its existence and value are [alternating kernel law limit is poonen rains](#alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains).

For p = 2 this corrects the display in Smith II, Case 2.13, whose factor 1 − 2^{−n−j+k} must read 1 − 2^{−n+j−k}.

There are [n j]_p subspaces K ([gaussian binomial coefficient](#gaussian-binomial-coefficient)) and, for each, #GL_{n−j}(𝔽_p)^alt = p^{(n−j)(n−j−1)/2}∏_{i=1}^{(n−j)/2}(1 − p^{1−2i}) forms ([count of nondegenerate alternating matrices](#count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices)). For fixed j only one of P_p(j | 2n), P_p(j | 2n+1) is nonzero, giving P_p(j | ∞) = a_j. <a id="symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups"></a>


**Symplectic finite abelian p groups.** A symplectic p-group is a finite abelian p-group G with a nondegenerate alternating bilinear pairing [ , ] : G × G → ℚ_p/ℤ_p; Sp(G) is the group of automorphisms preserving [ , ]. G admits such a pairing if and only if G ≅ H × H for a finite abelian p-group H, and any two symplectic structures on the same group are isomorphic; hence isomorphism classes of symplectic p-groups are the classes of groups H × H, indexed by partitions all of whose parts occur with even multiplicity ([isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups)), and #Sp(G) depends only on the class of G.

Throughout this assertion, p prime G finite abelian p-group

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `IsSymplecticClass`: A class ⟨n, λ⟩ is symplectic iff every part of λ has even multiplicity (G ≅ H × H).

- `symplecticAutCard`: #Sp(G) for the standard symplectic structure on the representative of a symplectic class.

- `isSymplecticClass_iff_exists_pairing`: A finite abelian p-group admits a nondegenerate alternating ℚ_p/ℤ_p-valued pairing iff its class is symplectic.

- `symplectic_pairing_unique`: Two nondegenerate alternating pairings on the same group are isomorphic.

- `symplecticAutCard_pos`: #Sp(G) ≥ 1.

- `symplecticAutCard_elementary`: #Sp((ℤ/p)^{2k}) = p^{k²}∏_{i=1}^{k}(p^{2i} − 1).


To prove the assertion, Define the pairing condition (bilinear into ℚ_p/ℤ_p, alternating [x, x] = 0, nondegenerate: the adjoint G → Hom(G, ℚ_p/ℤ_p) is bijective). Normal form: a nondegenerate alternating pairing on a finite abelian p-group has a symplectic basis {e_i, f_i} with ⟨e_i⟩ ≅ ⟨f_i⟩ ≅ ℤ/p^{a_i} and [e_i, f_i] = p^{−a_i}; induct on the exponent by splitting off a hyperbolic pair generated by an element of maximal order and a partner of equal order (routine). Existence on H × H: the standard pairing [(h, χ), (h', χ')] := χ'(h) − χ(h') on H × H^∨ with H^∨ ≅ H; uniqueness follows from the normal form.

*Needs:* [isomorphism classes of finite abelian p groups](#isomorphism-classes-of-finite-abelian-p-groups), `LinearMap.IsAlt` (Mathlib).

<a id="alternating-cokernel-law"></a>


**Alternating cokernel law.** For n even and a finite abelian p-group class G, π_n(G) is the probability that coker(A) ≅ G for A Haar-random in M_n(ℤ_p)^alt. It is computed at finite level: for any e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0, π_n(G) = #{Ā ∈ M_n(ℤ/p^e)^alt : coker(Ā) ≅ G} / p^{e·n(n−1)/2}, and this is independent of such e. (A cokernel coker(A) ≅ ℤ_p^s ⊕ F is isomorphic to G iff s = 0 and F ≅ G, which is detected mod p^e.)

Throughout this assertion, p prime n even e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `alternatingCokernelLaw`: π_n(G) via the finite-level count modulo p^e with e one greater than the largest exponent a among the cyclic factors Z/p^a of G (take e=1 for G=0).

- `alternatingCokernelLaw_eq_of_le`: The finite-level count is the same for every e ≥ 1 with p^{e−1}G = 0.

- `alternatingCokernelLaw_trivial`: π_n(0) = ∏_{i=1}^{n/2}(1 − p^{1−2i}).

- `alternatingCokernelLaw_eq_zero_of_not_symplectic`: π_n(G) = 0 if G is not symplectic.

To prove the assertion, Define the finite count over alternating matrices with entries in ZMod (p^e) and the cokernel as the quotient of (ℤ/p^e)^n by the image of Ā, compared with the standard representative of G. Independence of e: reduction M_n(ℤ/p^{e+1})^alt → M_n(ℤ/p^e)^alt is surjective with fibres of size p^{n(n−1)/2}, and for p^{e−1}G = 0 the condition coker ≅ G is detected mod p^e (a cyclic summand ℤ/p^f, f ≥ e, or a free summand would give an element of order p^e in the reduction).

<a id="bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit"></a>


**Bklpr alternating cokernel limit.** (a) For each symplectic p-group G, lim_{n→∞, n even} π_n(G) = A_0(G) := #G/#Sp(G) · ∏_{i≥1}(1 − p^{1−2i}), and Σ_G A_0(G) = 1. (b) For r ≥ 0, define A_r(G) := (#G)^{1−r}/#Sp(G) · ∏_{i≥r+1}(1 − p^{1−2i}) for symplectic G; then Σ_G A_r(G) = 1, and A_r is the limit as n → ∞ (n − r even) of the laws of (coker A)_tors for A drawn from the natural probability measure on alternating n × n matrices over ℤ_p of rank n − r (BKLPR Theorem 3.11).

Throughout this assertion, p prime G a symplectic p-group


To prove the assertion, (a) Fix G and m = n − dim_{𝔽_p} G[p]. Surjections ℤ_p^n → G pull back the pairing of G to alternating pairings on ℤ_p^n inducing G; Sp(G) acts freely on Sur(ℤ_p^n, G) with these pairings as orbits, so there are #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/#Sp(G) of them ([symplectic finite abelian p groups](#symplectic-finite-abelian-p-groups), [surjection count](#surjection-count)). The probability that the pairing of A equals a fixed one is #GL_m(𝔽_p)^alt/#M_m(𝔽_p)^alt · (#G)^{1−n} (BKLPR Corollaries 3.4–3.5: A ∈ D + D M_n(ℤ_p) D with rank condition), so π_n(G) = #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/#Sp(G) · #GL_m^alt/#M_m^alt · (#G)^{1−n}; as n → ∞, #Sur(ℤ_p^n, G)/(#G)^n → 1 and [count of nondegenerate alternating matrices](#count-of-nondegenerate-alternating-matrices) gives the limit. Total mass: Σ_G π_n(G)=1 because the determinant polynomial is not identically zero on even alternating matrices, so its zero set has Haar measure zero. Let c=∏_{i≥1}(1−p^{1−2i})>0. Fatou and the established pointwise limit c·#G/#Sp(G) give Σ_G #G/#Sp(G)≤1/c<∞. The bound π_n(G)≤#G/#Sp(G) is now a summable domination, so dominated convergence yields Σ_G A_0(G)=1. (b) For r ≥ 1 the measure on rank-(n − r) alternating matrices is the normalised canonical measure on the ℤ_p-points of that scheme (BKLPR Proposition 2.1, Lemma 3.13); its existence and the pushforward identity are the Oesterlé–Serre measure contract stated below. Given it, the proof integrates |det|^r (BKLPR Lemma 3.12) and repeats (a).

### 5.7 p-adic isotropic intersections


<a id="bklpr-model"></a>


**Bklpr model.** For a prime p, the BKLPR distribution Q is the probability measure on pairs (r, T), r ∈ ℤ_{≥0} and T a symplectic p-group class, given by Q(r, T) := (1/2) A_r(T) for r ∈ {0, 1} and Q(r, T) := 0 for r ≥ 2 (A_r from [bklpr alternating cokernel limit](#bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit)). A pair (r, T) stands for the split short exact sequence 0 → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r → (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r ⊕ T → T → 0 of co-finite type ℤ_p-modules, which models 0 → E(k) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p → Sel_{p^∞}(E) → Ш(E)[p^∞] → 0; every isomorphism class of such split sequences with finite cokernel arises from exactly one pair. BKLPR define Q as the limit of the laws Q_{2n} of intersections of random maximal isotropic ℤ_p-submodules; their proof of Theorem 1.2 identifies Q_{2n} with this mixture ([bklpr random isotropic intersection law](#bklpr-random-isotropic-intersection-law)).

Throughout this assertion, p prime

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:

- `bklprModel_rank_marginal`: The marginal law of r is uniform on {0, 1}.

- `bklprModel_sha_conditional`: Conditionally on r ∈ {0, 1}, T has law A_r.

- `bklprModel_selmer_p_rank`: The law of r + dim T[p] under bklprModel is poonenRainsDistribution p.

<a id="bklpr-random-isotropic-intersection-law"></a>


**Bklpr random isotropic intersection law.** Let n≥1 and V = ℤ_p^{2n} with the hyperbolic form Q(x, y) = Σ x_i y_i, OGr_n(ℤ_p) its maximal isotropic direct summands with the canonical probability measure, and Z, W ∈ OGr_n(ℤ_p) independent random. Put R := (Z ∩ W) ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p, S := (Z ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p) ∩ (W ⊗ ℚ_p/ℤ_p) and T := S/R. Then: (i) R ≅ (ℚ_p/ℤ_p)^r with r = rk(Z ∩ W) ∈ {0, 1}, each with probability 1/2 (Proposition 5.6); (ii) T is finite and the sequence splits (Corollaries 5.2–5.3); (iii) the law Q_{2n} of (r, T) converges as n → ∞ to the BKLPR model Q, and the law T_{2n,r} of T given r converges to A_r (Theorems 1.2, 1.6(a)–(b), 1.10(b)); (iv) S[q] ≅ Z/qZ ∩ W/qW for q a power of p (Proposition 5.4).

Throughout this assertion, p prime Z, W independent and distributed by the canonical measure on OGr_n(ℤ_p) n ≥ 1; when n=0 the only pair is Z=W=0 and the rank law is concentrated at 0.


To prove the assertion, Canonical measure: OGr_n is a smooth projective ℤ-scheme of relative dimension n(n − 1)/2 with two isomorphic components distinguished by parity (BKLPR Propositions 4.4–4.5); the measure on OGr_n(ℤ_p) is the normalised limit of counts mod p^e (Proposition 2.1). This input is the integral orthogonal geometry and canonical-measure target below. (i): the Schubert loci S_{n,r} with r ≥ 2 have smaller dimension (Proposition 4.9) hence measure zero; the parity of rk(Z ∩ W) is equidistributed by the isomorphism of the two components. (ii),(iv): divisibility and co-finite type arguments (BKLPR Proposition 5.1, Corollaries 5.2–5.3, Proposition 5.4); routine module theory over ℤ_p. (iii): represent Z = W_1ᵀ ⊕ graph(A) for a random decomposition and a random alternating A of corank r, so T ≅ (coker A)_tors; the size n − m of A tends to ∞ in probability ([alternating matrix kernel law](#alternating-matrix-kernel-law) and BKLPR Lemma 3.7), so T_{2n,r} → A_r by [bklpr alternating cokernel limit](#bklpr-alternating-cokernel-limit); combine with (i).

For fixed m, both finite products tend to 1 as n→∞. The finite-field isotropic-reduction node supplies motivation; over Z/p^e use the direct-summand orthogonal quotient and a hyperbolic basis, as in the lifting charts of maximal-isotropic-direct-summands-modulo-prime-powers.

**Poonen rains selmer conjecture.** For a prime p, the Poonen–Rains conjecture over ℚ is the proposition PR(p): over the family of elliptic curves E_{A,B} : y² = x³ + Ax + B (A, B ∈ ℤ, 4A³ + 27B² ≠ 0, no prime ℓ with ℓ⁴ | A and ℓ⁶ | B) ordered by the naive height H(E_{A,B}) = max(4|A|³, 27B²) (the family and height of Layer 0), (a) for every d ≥ 0 the set {E : dim_{𝔽_p} Sel_p(E) = d} has density a_d (the Poonen–Rains weight), and (c) for every m ≥ 1 the m-th moment of #Sel_p(E) exists and equals ∏_{i=1}^{m}(p^{i} + 1) (moments as in [height moments in an arithmetic family](#height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family)); (b) is (c) with m = 1, average p + 1. Sel_p(E) is the p-Selmer group of Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 7. Poonen–Rains state it over any global field with an unspecified height on the coefficients; the definition is pinned over ℚ with the height above.

### 5.9 Twist laws and corank consequences


<a id="two-selmer-distribution-in-full-two-torsion-twist-families"></a>


**Two selmer distribution in full two torsion twist families.** Let E : y² = (x − c_1)(x − c_2)(x − c_3) with c_i ∈ ℚ distinct and none of (c_i − c_j)(c_i − c_k) a rational square (equivalently E(ℚ)[2] = E[2] and E has no ℚ-rational cyclic subgroup of order 4), and for b ∈ ℤ \ {0} let E_b : y² = (x − bc_1)(x − bc_2)(x − bc_3) be the quadratic twist by ℚ(√b). Then for every d ≥ 0, lim_{N→∞} #{b ∈ ℤ : 0 < |b| ≤ N, dim_{𝔽_2} Sel_2(E_b) = d + 2}/(2N) = a_d, the Poonen–Rains weight at p = 2 ([poonen rains distribution](#poonen-rains-distribution)); the same holds among positive b, and among squarefree b prime to any fixed D divisible by 8 and the bad primes (relative density). For E : y² = x³ − x this is Heath-Brown's theorem.

Throughout this assertion, c_1, c_2, c_3 ∈ ℚ distinct (c_i − c_j)(c_i − c_k) ∉ ℚ^{×2} for {i, j, k} = {1, 2, 3}


To prove the assertion, Swinnerton-Dyer's algebraic step: for b = p_1 ⋯ p_n squarefree prime to D, Sel_2(E_b) is the intersection of two Lagrangian subspaces of a symplectic 𝔽_2-space determined by the classes of p_i in (ℤ/D)^×/(ℤ/D)^{×2} and the Legendre symbols (p_i/p_j); the proportion π_d(n) of such data with dim Sel_2 = d tends to α_d = a_{d−2} as n → ∞ (a Markov chain whose stationary law is the Poonen–Rains law; [alternating kernel law limit is poonen rains](#alternating-kernel-law-limit-is-poonen-rains) identifies that law). Kane's analytic step: the moments of #Sel_2(E_b)/4 over squarefree b ≤ N prime to D converge to the Poonen–Rains moments ([poonen rains moments](#poonen-rains-moments)), using |U ∩ W| = |V|^{−1/2}Σ_{u,w}(−1)^{u·w} and bounds for character sums in Legendre symbols of the prime factors (large sieve, [coefficient sieves](#support-sieves) and [quadratic character-sum bounds](#support-character-sums)). Thus the unnormalised m-th moments of #Sel₂ are 4^m∏_{i=1}^m(2^i+1), accounting for the fixed rational 2-torsion.

<a id="function-field-3-selmer-average-bound"></a>


**Function field 3 selmer average bound.** For all sufficiently large prime powers q of characteristic different from three, let E run over F_q(t)-isomorphism classes of elliptic curves of exact geometric height d. This height is the least d admitting a long Weierstrass equation whose coefficient A_i is a homogeneous section of O(id) on P¹. Put C(q)=3/((1−q^(−3))(1−q^(−2))²(1−q^(−1))²) and L(q)=(1−q^(−9))(1−q^(−10))/(1−q^(−1)). Then limsup_(d→∞) average_E #Sel3(E) ≤ 1+C(q)/L(q)=4+O(q^(−1)). This is an exact-height limsup, not existence of an ordinary height limit. The weighted version uses weight 1/#Aut(E,0).

Throughout this assertion, The carrier consists of isomorphism classes over the fixed base F_q(t); the automorphisms fix the origin and the base. Height d is exact, with d tending to infinity before q. For the unweighted comparison take q larger than the absolute constant arising from the constant-j Selmer bound; no assertion uniform over small q is made.


To prove the assertion, de Jong Theorem 1.2 bounds q^(−10d−1) Σ_(h(E)=d)(#Sel3(E)−1)/#Aut(E,0) by C(q) in limsup. Its inputs are the genus-one torsor/surface comparison (Proposition 5.14), projective ternary-cubic orbit bound (Proposition 7.5) and evaluated geometric sum (Proposition 7.9). Proposition 4.12 gives q^(−10d−1) Σ_(h(E)=d)1/#Aut(E,0)→L(q)>0. Divide only after this positive limit to get weighted mean at most 1+C(q)/L(q). Outside constant j, #Aut(E,0)=2. Propositions 4.14 and Lemma 10.2 bound the number of constant-j curves by O(dq^(9d)) and their three-Selmer dimension by C₁d with an absolute C₁. For fixed q>3^(C₁), their unweighted Selmer contribution is O(d(3^(C₁)q⁹)^d)=o(q^(10d)). Remove these curves from numerator and denominator, cancel the factor two, and obtain the unweighted comparison. The rational functions C(q) and L(q) tend to three and one with error O(q^(−1)). Any other coefficient family or cumulative-height convention requires its own denominator and boundary comparison.

*Needs:* [height moments in an arithmetic family](#height-moments-in-an-arithmetic-family), [poonen rains selmer conjecture](#poonen-rains-selmer-conjecture).

For a squareclass s ∈ F^×/F^{×2} let E^s be the quadratic twist of E by F(√s)/F (E^s ≅ E when s is a square; Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 5). (iii) For a probability vector π = (π_r)_{r≥0}, E has twist-corank law π at p (in ordering (i) or (ii)) if every proportion converges to π_r; lower bounds are stated with liminf. For F = ℚ the squareclass height of the class of a squarefree d is |d|.

<a id="smith-twist-family-hypothesis"></a>


**Smith twist family hypothesis.** An elliptic curve A/ℚ satisfies Smith's Assumption 1.1 if one of the following holds: (1) A(ℚ)[2] = 0; (2) A(ℚ)[2] ≅ ℤ/2 and, for the unique ℚ-isogeny φ : A → A_0 of degree 2, ℚ(A_0[2]) ≠ ℚ and ℚ(A_0[2]) ≠ ℚ(A[2]); (3) A(ℚ)[2] ≅ (ℤ/2)² and A has no cyclic ℚ-isogeny of degree 4. For a model y² = f(x) with f ∈ ℚ[x] monic separable cubic this is equivalent to: (1) f has no rational root; or (2) f has exactly one rational root e and, writing f(x + e) = x(x² + ax + b), neither b nor b(a² − 4b) is a rational square; or (3) f = (x − e_1)(x − e_2)(x − e_3) with e_i ∈ ℚ and none of (e_i − e_j)(e_i − e_k) ({i, j, k} = {1, 2, 3}) is a rational square. The cubic form is the one used in Lean.

Throughout this assertion, A/ℚ given by y² = f(x), f monic separable cubic

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `SmithTwistHypothesis`: The disjunction of the three cubic-root conditions for a monic separable cubic f ∈ ℚ[x].

- `SmithTwistHypothesis.caseThree`: Case (3): three rational roots with no (e_i − e_j)(e_i − e_k) a square.

- `smithTwistHypothesis_of_irreducible`: If f is irreducible over ℚ (no rational root) then case (1) holds.

- `smithTwistHypothesis_caseThree_iff`: For f = (x − e_1)(x − e_2)(x − e_3): case (3) ↔ ¬IsSquare((e_1 − e_2)(e_1 − e_3)) ∧ ¬IsSquare((e_2 − e_1)(e_2 − e_3)) ∧ ¬IsSquare((e_3 − e_1)(e_3 − e_2)).

- `smithTwistHypothesis_twist`: The hypothesis holds for f(x) iff it holds for d³f(x/d) (the twist by d ≠ 0).


To prove the assertion, A(ℚ)[2] \ {O} = {(e, 0) : f(e) = 0, e ∈ ℚ} (2-torsion of a Weierstrass curve; Mathlib WeierstrassCurve points). Case (2): for A : y² = x(x² + ax + b) the 2-isogenous curve is A_0 : y² = x(x² − 2ax + a² − 4b) (Vélu; Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 1), so ℚ(A[2]) = ℚ(√(a² − 4b)) and ℚ(A_0[2]) = ℚ(√b); two quadratic fields coincide iff the product of the radicands is a square. Case (3): a cyclic subgroup of order 4 is ⟨P⟩ with 2P = (e_i, 0) and x(P) = e_i ± √((e_i − e_j)(e_i − e_k)); ⟨P⟩ is Galois-stable iff x(P) ∈ ℚ; so no cyclic ℚ-isogeny of degree 4 iff no (e_i − e_j)(e_i − e_k) is a square (equivalence stated by Kane, §1).

*Needs:* `WeierstrassCurve` (Mathlib), `Polynomial.coeff` (Mathlib).

<a id="smith-selmer-rank-limit-equals-corank"></a>


**Smith selmer rank limit equals corank.** Let E be an elliptic curve over a number field F and ℓ a prime. For k ≥ 1 let r_{ℓ^k}(E/F) be the largest r such that (ℤ/ℓ^k)^r injects into Sel_{ℓ^k}(E/F)/im(E(F)_tors). Then r_ℓ ≥ r_{ℓ²} ≥ …, the sequence is eventually constant, and its limit r_{ℓ^∞}(E/F) equals corank_{ℤ_ℓ} Sel_{ℓ^∞}(E/F).

To prove the assertion, Kummer: the sequence 0 → E(F)[ℓ^∞]/ℓ^k → Sel_{ℓ^k}(E/F) → Sel_{ℓ^∞}(E/F)[ℓ^k] → 0 is exact (surjectivity of H¹(F, E[ℓ^k]) → H¹(F, E[ℓ^∞])[ℓ^k] with kernel E(F)[ℓ^∞]/ℓ^k, compatible with local conditions; requests Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 7 and SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L2). The image of E(F)_tors in Sel_{ℓ^k} is the image of E(F)[ℓ^∞]/ℓ^k (the prime-to-ℓ torsion is ℓ^k-divisible), so Sel_{ℓ^k}/im(E(F)_tors) ≅ Sel_{ℓ^∞}[ℓ^k]. Sel_{ℓ^∞} ≅ (ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ)^c ⊕ G with G finite (co-finite type; L2), c the corank; so Sel_{ℓ^∞}[ℓ^k] ≅ (ℤ/ℓ^k)^c ⊕ G[ℓ^k] and the largest free ℤ/ℓ^k-rank is c + #{cyclic factors of G of order ≥ ℓ^k}, which equals c once ℓ^k exceeds the exponent of G.

### 5.10 Three-isogeny ratios and twist averages


<a id="selmer-ratio-of-an-isogeny"></a>


**Selmer ratio of an isogeny.** Let φ : E → E' be an isogeny of elliptic curves over a number field F. For a place v of F put c_v(φ) := #coker(φ : E(F_v) → E'(F_v)) / #ker(φ : E(F_v) → E'(F_v)) ∈ ℚ_{>0} (finite: the kernel is finite and the cokernel is finite since E'(F_v)/φE(F_v) injects into H¹(F_v, E[φ])). The global Selmer ratio is c(φ) := ∏_v c_v(φ), a finite product because c_v(φ) = 1 for all finite v ∤ deg φ at which E has good reduction; c_v is multiplicative under composition of isogenies (index multiplicativity). For s ∈ F^×/F^{×2} let φ_s : E^s → E'^s be the quadratic twist of φ (twisting by the same cocycle, Tau Ceti EllipticCurves Layer 5). For deg φ = 3, c(φ_s) ∈ 3^ℤ and t(φ_s) := ord_3 c(φ_s); for m ∈ ℤ, T_m(φ) := {s ∈ F^×/F^{×2} : c(φ_s) = 3^m} (signed; BKLOS §9 notation), and |T|_m := T_m ∪ T_{−m} is BKLOS §2's T_m.

Throughout this assertion, E, E' elliptic over a number field F φ : E → E' an F-isogeny

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `localSelmerRatio`: c_v(φ) = #coker/#ker of φ on F_v-points, as a positive rational.

- `globalSelmerRatio`: c(φ) = ∏_v c_v(φ) (finite support).

- `logSelmerRatio`: t(φ) = ord_3 c(φ) for a 3-isogeny.

- `selmerRatioClass`: T_m(φ) = {s : c(φ_s) = 3^m}.

- `localSelmerRatio_of_good`: If the finite kernel and cokernel have the same cardinality, their ratio is 1. The local Tamagawa formula proves this at good finite places away from deg φ; it does not assert that the map on local points is bijective.

- `localSelmerRatio_complex`: If φ is surjective on points with kernel of order 3 (a 3-isogeny at a complex place) then c(φ) = 1/3.

### 5.11 CM three-isogeny twists


<a id="cm-curves-have-a-twist-with-good-reduction"></a>


**Cm curves have a twist with good reduction.** Let E/F be an elliptic curve over a number field with End_F(E)=O_K for an imaginary quadratic field K⊆F. At each finite place v there is a twist of E by an O_K^×-valued character having good reduction; for j(E)∉{0,1728} the twist is quadratic. This is the maximal-order setting of Rubin Corollary 5.22, fixed at the start of §5.1; it is the case needed by cm-three-isogeny-has-selmer-ratio-one.

Throughout this assertion, E/F has End_F(E)=O_K, with all CM endomorphisms defined over F and K⊆F.


To prove the assertion, Use the Hecke character ψ_E of Rubin Theorem 5.15, supplied by the main theorem of CM (CM.1). On local units U_v, part (i) places ψ_E(U_v) in O_K^×; part (ii) identifies it with the inertia action on prime-to-v Tate modules. This conclusion requires the Hecke-character theorem: finite order in (K⊗Q_ℓ)^× alone does not imply membership in K. For the local assertion, extend ψ_E|U_v to F_v^× by assigning 1 to a uniformizer. Local class field theory gives an O_K^×-valued Galois character χ with that inertia restriction. Twist by χ⁻¹: inertia acts trivially, so Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich gives good reduction. Rubin Corollary 5.22 constructs even a global twist using the corresponding character-extension statement. If j is neither 0 nor 1728, Aut(E)=O_K^×={±1}, so this twist is quadratic. The non-maximal-order case of the final corank theorem uses the separate isogeny to maximal order, not this lemma.

### 5.12 Hypersurface local-density moments


<a id="polynomial-congruence-under-perturbation"></a>


**Polynomial congruence under perturbation.** Let R be a commutative ring, σ a set of variables, f ∈ R[X_i : i ∈ σ] and x, h ∈ R^σ. Then f(x + h) − f(x) lies in the ideal (h_i : i ∈ σ). In particular, for R = ℤ and h ≡ 0 mod p^c coordinatewise, f(x + h) ≡ f(x) mod p^c; applied to the partial derivatives, ∇f(x + h) ≡ ∇f(x) mod p^c.

Throughout this assertion, R commutative f a polynomial x, h vectors in R^σ


To prove the assertion, Let I = (h_i : i ∈ σ) and π: R → R/I the quotient map. Evaluation commutes with ring homomorphisms (Mathlib MvPolynomial.eval_map): π(f(x + h)) = (π f)(π(x + h)) = (π f)(π(x)) = π(f(x)), since π(h_i) = 0. Hence π(f(x + h) − f(x)) = 0, i.e. f(x + h) − f(x) ∈ I (Mathlib Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem).

*Needs:* `MvPolynomial.eval_map` (Mathlib), `Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem` (Mathlib).

<a id="gradient-valuation-strata"></a>


**Gradient valuation strata.** Let p be prime and r ≥ 1. For a vector v ∈ (ℤ/p^rℤ)^I, its capped valuation v_p(v) is the largest e ∈ {0, …, r} with v ≡ 0 mod p^e. For a form f let ∇f = (∂f/∂X_i)_{i=0..n}. For 0 ≤ e ≤ r and N = N_{d,n}, the gradient stratum is R^{(e)}_N(p^r) = {a ∈ R_N(p^r) : ∃ x ∈ R_{n+1}(p^r) with f_a(x) ≡ 0 mod p^r and v_p(∇f_a(x)) = e}. The strata for e = 0, …, r cover F^loc(p^r) = {a ∈ R_N(p^r) : f_a has a primitive zero modulo p^r} (5.18); they are defined existentially and overlap in general, so their cardinalities do not add up to #F^loc(p^r).

Throughout this assertion, p prime r ≥ 1 0 ≤ e ≤ r

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `FormDensity.vecValuation`: The capped valuation v_p(v) ∈ {0, …, r} of v ∈ (ℤ/p^r)^I.

- `FormDensity.vecValuation_le`: v_p(v) ≤ r.

- `FormDensity.vecValuation_eq_iff`: For e < r: v_p(v) = e iff p^e divides every coordinate and p^{e+1} does not divide some coordinate.

- `FormDensity.grad`: ∇f(x) = (∂f/∂X_i(x))_i.

- `FormDensity.gradientStratum`: R^{(e)}_N(p^r) as a finite set of coefficient vectors.

- `FormDensity.gradientStratum_subset`: R^{(e)}_N(p^r) ⊆ R_N(p^r).

- `FormDensity.mem_biUnion_gradientStratum_iff`: (5.18): the union over e = 0, …, r is F^loc(p^r).

- `FormDensity.gradientStratum_eq_empty_of_lt`: R^{(e)} = ∅ for e > r.

- `FormDensity.gradientStratum_smul_unit`: Membership is invariant under scaling a by a unit.


To prove the assertion, Define v_p(v) = max{e ≤ r : p^e divides every coordinate}, via Mathlib Nat.findGreatest on the residues' representatives. Define ∇f_a through the partial derivatives (Mathlib MvPolynomial.pderiv) and R^{(e)} by the existential condition. (5.18): a zero x of f_a has some valuation e ∈ {0, …, r} of ∇f_a(x), and conversely a ∈ R^{(e)} has the zero x.

<a id="fixed-gradient-valuation-hensel-lifting"></a>


**Fixed gradient valuation hensel lifting.** Let p be prime, s ≥ 1, F ∈ ℤ[t_1, …, t_s], A ∈ ℤ, a ∈ ℤ^s and integers m, ℓ, δ ≥ 0 with m ≥ 2δ + 1 and δ ≤ m − ℓ. Put R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ) = {t ∈ (ℤ/p^mℤ)^s : F(t) ≡ A mod p^m, v_p(∇F(t)) = δ, t ≡ a mod p^ℓ}. Then for every k ∈ ℤ, #R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ)/p^{m(s−1)} = #R_δ(p^{m+1}, A + kp^m; p^ℓ)/p^{(m+1)(s−1)}. In the form used by Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin (s = n + 1, A = k = 0, δ = e, ℓ = e + 1, a = x with v_p(∇F(x)) = e): for every s′ ≥ 2e + 2, #{b mod p^{s′} : b ≡ x mod p^{e+1}, F(b) ≡ 0 mod p^{s′}}/p^{s′n} equals the same quantity at level s′ − 1.

Throughout this assertion, p prime m ≥ 2δ + 1 δ ≤ m − ℓ


To prove the assertion, For t ∈ R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ) and t′ ∈ ℤ^s: F(t + p^{m−δ}t′) ≡ F(t) + p^{m−δ}⟨t′, ∇F(t)⟩ ≡ A mod p^m by first-order-taylor-congruence (2(m − δ) ≥ m and p^δ | ∇F(t)); ∇F(t + p^{m−δ}t′) ≡ ∇F(t) mod p^{m−δ} by polynomial-congruence-under-perturbation, and m − δ ≥ δ + 1, so the valuation δ is kept; t + p^{m−δ}t′ ≡ a mod p^ℓ since ℓ ≤ m − δ. So R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ) is a union of cosets modulo p^{m−δ}. For t mod p^{m+1} reducing into R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ), the vectors t + p^{m−δ}t′ (t′ mod p) run through p^s cosets modulo p^{m+1−δ}, and t + p^{m−δ}t′ ∈ R_δ(p^{m+1}, A + kp^m; p^ℓ) iff p^{−m}(F(t) − A) + p^{−δ}⟨t′, ∇F(t)⟩ ≡ k mod p, which has exactly p^{s−1} solutions t′ mod p because p^{−δ}∇F(t) is nonzero modulo p. Counting cosets: #R_δ(p^{m+1}, A + kp^m; p^ℓ) = p^{s−1}·#R_δ(p^m, A; p^ℓ). For the BLS form: every b ≡ x mod p^{e+1} has v_p(∇F(b)) = e (perturbation congruence), so the displayed set is R_e(p^{s′}, 0; p^{e+1}); apply the lemma with m = s′ − 1 ≥ 2e + 1.

*Needs:* [first order taylor congruence](#first-order-taylor-congruence), [polynomial congruence under perturbation](#polynomial-congruence-under-perturbation), [gradient valuation strata](#gradient-valuation-strata), `MvPolynomial.pderiv` (Mathlib).

### 5.13 Concentration of polarized isogeny types


<a id="convex-concentration-inequality"></a>


**Convex concentration inequality.** Let g ∈ ℝ, 1/2 < ε < 1 and x_1, …, x_k ∈ ℝ with 0 ≤ x_i ≤ εg and Σ_i x_i = g. Then Σ_i x_i² ≤ (ε² + (1 − ε)²)g² = (1 − 2ε(1 − ε))g².

Throughout this assertion, 1/2 < ε < 1 0 ≤ x_i ≤ εg Σ x_i = g


To prove the assertion, If g ≤ 0 the hypotheses force every x_i = 0 and g = 0. Let g > 0 and let x_1 be a largest coordinate. If x_1 < g/2: Σ x_i² ≤ x_1 Σ x_i < g²/2 ≤ (ε² + (1 − ε)²)g², since ε² + (1 − ε)² ≥ 1/2. If x_1 ≥ g/2: Σ_{i≥2} x_i² ≤ (Σ_{i≥2} x_i)² = (g − x_1)², so Σ x_i² ≤ x_1² + (g − x_1)², which is increasing in x_1 on [g/2, εg] and equals (ε² + (1 − ε)²)g² at x_1 = εg. (The source argues by convexity: the maximum over the polytope {x ∈ [0, εg]^k : Σx = g} is at a vertex, and the vertices are the k(k − 1) permutations of (εg, (1 − ε)g, 0, …, 0).)

*Needs:* `Real.rpow` (Mathlib), `Finset.sum` (Mathlib).

The left side is at most 0.25005 g² log g + Cg². In both cases the left side is below 0.495 g² log g once 0.0049 log g > C, i.e. for g ≥ g_0 = ⌈exp(C/0.0049)⌉ + 1 (log n_j ≥ 0 by Mathlib Real.log_nonneg).

### 5.14 Spacing measures and Frobenius model obstructions


<a id="kolmogorov-distance"></a>


**Kolmogorov distance.** For Borel probability measures μ, ν on ℝ with distribution functions F_μ(x) = μ((−∞, x]) and F_ν, the Kolmogorov distance is d_K(μ, ν) = sup_{x ∈ ℝ} |F_μ(x) − F_ν(x)|. It takes values in [0, 1], is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, vanishes exactly when μ = ν, and dominates |μ((−∞, x]) − ν((−∞, x])| for every x.

Throughout this assertion, μ, ν Borel probability measures on ℝ

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.kolmogorovDist`: d_K(μ, ν) = sup_x |F_μ(x) − F_ν(x)|.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.kolmogorovDist_nonneg`: d_K ≥ 0.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.kolmogorovDist_comm`: d_K(μ, ν) = d_K(ν, μ).

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.kolmogorovDist_le_one`: d_K ≤ 1.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.abs_cdf_sub_le_kolmogorovDist`: |F_μ(x) − F_ν(x)| ≤ d_K(μ, ν) for every x.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.kolmogorovDist_triangle`: d_K(μ, ρ) ≤ d_K(μ, ν) + d_K(ν, ρ).

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.kolmogorovDist_eq_zero_iff`: For probability measures, d_K(μ, ν) = 0 iff μ = ν.


To prove the assertion, Define d_K as the supremum over x of |cdf μ x − cdf ν x| (Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.cdf); the family is bounded by 1 (Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.cdf_le_one), so the supremum is a real number and dominates each term (Mathlib le_ciSup). For probability measures cdf μ x = μ((−∞, x]) (Mathlib ProbabilityTheory.cdf_eq_real); equal distribution functions give equal measures.

*Needs:* `ProbabilityTheory.cdf` (Mathlib), `ProbabilityTheory.cdf_eq_real` (Mathlib), `ProbabilityTheory.cdf_le_one` (Mathlib), `le_ciSup` (Mathlib).

([[45]](#ref-45), arXiv v1, Corollary 5.14, p.34.)


**Checks.**


- d_K(μ, μ) = 0.

- d_K(δ_0, δ_1) = 1.

- d_K((δ_0 + δ_1)/2, δ_0) = 1/2: the distance is not the indicator of inequality.

- d_K((δ_0 + δ_1)/2, δ_0) = 1/2.


<a id="normalized-eigenangle-spacing-measure"></a>


**Normalized eigenangle spacing measure.** Let θ be a finite multiset of N ≥ 1 angles in [0, 2π) (repetitions kept). Sort it as θ_1 ≤ ⋯ ≤ θ_N; its cyclic gaps are θ_{i+1} − θ_i (1 ≤ i < N) and the wrap-around gap θ_1 + 2π − θ_N. The normalized spacing measure is μ(θ) = (1/N) Σ_gaps δ_{(N/2π)·gap}, a probability measure on [0, ∞) of mean 1. For an integral polynomial P, its eigenangles are the arguments in [0, 2π) of its complex roots with multiplicity; for a g-dimensional abelian variety A/𝔽_p the spacing measure of A is μ(θ(P_A)) for its Frobenius polynomial P_A (degree 2g, roots of absolute value √p), and μ_g is the average of these over the uniform measure on the isomorphism classes of g-dimensional ppavs over 𝔽_p.

Throughout this assertion, θ a finite multiset of angles in [0, 2π)

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.cyclicGaps`: The N cyclic gaps of a multiset of N angles, including the wrap-around gap.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.spacingMeasure`: μ(θ) = (1/N)Σ δ_{(N/2π)·gap}.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.eigenangles`: The eigenangles in [0, 2π) of an integral polynomial, with multiplicity.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.length_cyclicGaps`: There are exactly N gaps.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.cyclicGaps_nonneg`: For angles in [0, 2π) every gap is ≥ 0.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.sum_cyclicGaps`: The gaps of a nonempty multiset sum to 2π.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.spacingMeasure_univ`: μ(θ) is a probability measure for θ ≠ ∅.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.spacingMeasure_Iio_zero`: μ(θ) gives no mass to (−∞, 0).

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.card_eigenangles`: A nonzero P has natDegree P eigenangles with multiplicity.

- `AbelianVarietyStatistics.sub_one_div_le_spacingMeasure_zero`: An angle of multiplicity ≥ h forces μ(θ){0} ≥ (h − 1)/N.


To prove the assertion, Sort θ (Mathlib Multiset.sort), form the list of consecutive differences with the wrap-around gap, rescale by N/2π and average the point masses (Mathlib MeasureTheory.Measure.dirac). Eigenangles: map the roots of P in ℂ (Mathlib Polynomial.roots) to Complex.arg reduced into [0, 2π) (Mathlib toIcoMod). The gaps are nonnegative and sum to 2π (telescoping), so μ(θ) is a probability measure on [0, ∞) with mean 1. The average μ_g over ppav classes uses Layer 0's ppav count and the Frobenius-polynomial interface specified in the supplier contracts.

*Needs:* `Multiset.sort` (Mathlib), `MeasureTheory.Measure.dirac` (Mathlib), `Polynomial.roots` (Mathlib), `Complex.arg` (Mathlib), `toIcoMod` (Mathlib).

<a id="zero-gap-mass-from-repeated-angles"></a>


**Zero gap mass from repeated angles.** Let θ be a multiset of N angles in [0, 2π) containing two distinct values s ≠ t each with multiplicity at least h. Then the normalized spacing measure satisfies μ(θ)({0}) ≥ 2(h − 1)/N.

Throughout this assertion, θ ⊂ [0, 2π) finite with N elements s ≠ t each of multiplicity ≥ h


To prove the assertion, In the sorted list the ≥ h copies of s are consecutive and give ≥ h − 1 zero gaps; likewise for t; these gap positions are distinct. The wrap-around gap θ_1 + 2π − θ_N is positive for angles in [0, 2π), so it is not counted among them. Each zero gap contributes mass 1/N at 0.

<a id="kolmogorov-distance-lower-bound-from-an-atom"></a>


**Kolmogorov distance lower bound from an atom.** For Borel probability measures μ, ν on ℝ and x ∈ ℝ: μ((−∞, x]) − ν((−∞, x]) ≤ d_K(μ, ν). In particular, if μ is supported on [0, ∞) and ν((−∞, 0]) = 0 (for instance ν atomless and supported on [0, ∞)), then d_K(μ, ν) ≥ μ({0}).

### 5.15 Class-group moments as Hurwitz counts


<a id="generalized-dihedral-cover-datum"></a>


**Generalized dihedral cover datum.** Let A be a finite abelian group of odd order. Put G_A := A ⋊ Z/2, where the generator τ of Z/2 acts on A by inversion, and let c_A ⊂ G_A be the set of elements with nontrivial image in Z/2, i.e. c_A = {aτ : a ∈ A}. Then (i) c_A is exactly the set of involutions of G_A; (ii) c_A is a single conjugacy class, stable under invertible powers (hence a rational class); (iii) c_A generates G_A; (iv) if A ≠ 0 the centre of G_A is trivial; (v) (G_A, c_A) is nonsplitting: for every subgroup H ≤ G_A, c_A ∩ H is empty or a single H-conjugacy class. For A of order a power of an odd prime ℓ and q prime to 2ℓ, the Hurwitz scheme X_n := Hn^{c_A}_{G_A,n} ⊗ F_q of tame G_A-covers of A¹ branched at n points with all finite inertia in c_A is the scheme of EVW §8.6.

Throughout this assertion, |A| odd (for (i), (ii), (v)) A ≠ 0 for (iv); for A = 0, G_A = Z/2 has full centre and is treated separately as the trivial moment

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `inversionAction`: The homomorphism Z/2 → Aut(A) sending the generator to a ↦ −a.

- `generalizedDihedral`: G_A := A ⋊ Z/2 with the inversion action.

- `outsideInvolutions`: c_A := {x ∈ G_A : image of x in Z/2 is nontrivial}.

- `mem_outsideInvolutions_iff`: For |A| odd: x ∈ c_A ⇔ orderOf x = 2.

- `outsideInvolutions_isConj`: For |A| odd, any two elements of c_A are conjugate in G_A.

- `closure_outsideInvolutions`: The subgroup generated by c_A is all of G_A.

- `center_generalizedDihedral`: For |A| odd and A ≠ 0 the centre of G_A is trivial.

- `outsideInvolutions_nonsplitting`: For |A| odd and H ≤ G_A, c_A ∩ H is empty or a single H-conjugacy class.


To prove the assertion, Construct the inversion action Z/2 → Aut(A) and the semidirect product (Mathlib SemidirectProduct); c_A is the preimage of the nontrivial element under rightHom. (i) (aτ)² = a·τaτ^{−1} = a − a = 0, while an element a ≠ 0 of A has odd order; so involutions are exactly c_A. (ii) b(aτ)b^{−1} = (a + 2b)τ and 2 is invertible on A, so A acts transitively on c_A; invertible powers of an involution are itself. (iii) (aτ)(0τ) = a, so ⟨c_A⟩ contains A and τ. (iv) a central element commutes with τ, forcing 2a = 0 hence a = 0 on the A-part, and aτ is not central when A ≠ 0. (v) For H ≤ G_A meeting c_A, H = (H ∩ A) ⋊ ⟨a₀τ⟩ and c_A ∩ H = {(h + a₀)τ : h ∈ H ∩ A} = one (H ∩ A)-orbit by (ii) applied to the odd group H ∩ A. This is the instance of EVW Lemma 3.2 used in §8.6; the general odd-index lemma belongs to the Hurwitz homological-stability roadmap.

*Needs:* `SemidirectProduct` (Mathlib), `SemidirectProduct.inl` (Mathlib), `SemidirectProduct.inr` (Mathlib), `SemidirectProduct.rightHom` (Mathlib), `MulEquiv.inv` (Mathlib), `Subgroup.center` (Mathlib).

<a id="class-group-surjection-pair"></a>


**Class group surjection pair.** Let q be odd, n odd, L ∈ S_n with ring O_L (integral closure of F_q[t] in L), and A a finite abelian group. A pair (L, α) consists of L and a surjective homomorphism α : Cl(O_L) → A. Two pairs (L, α), (L', α') are isomorphic if there is a K-isomorphism φ : L → L' with α' ∘ φ_* = α. The nontrivial automorphism σ of L/K acts on Cl(O_L) by −1, so (L, α) ≅ (L, β) iff β = ±α. The moment m_A(L) := |Sur(Cl(O_L), A)| counts pairs with fixed L before identification.

- `quadraticClassGroup`: Cl(O_L), a finite abelian group.

- `ClassGroupSurjectionPair`: Surjective homomorphisms Cl(O_L) → A, as a subtype.

- `ClassGroupSurjectionPair.neg`: The involution α ↦ −α, induced by σ.

- `ClassGroupSurjectionPair.neg_ne_self`: For A ≠ 0 of odd order, −α ≠ α.

- `classGroupMoment`: m_A(L) = |Sur(Cl(O_L), A)| (zero if y² − f is reducible, which does not occur for odd n).

- `classGroupMoment_trivial`: m_0(L) = 1.

For |A| odd and A ≠ 0, −α ≠ α for every surjection α (else 2α = 0, forcing α = 0), so the sign action on Sur(Cl(O_L), A) is free.

<a id="involution-quotient-of-the-unramified-pro-l-group"></a>


**Involution quotient of the unramified pro l group.** Let q be odd, ℓ an odd prime not dividing q, n odd and L ∈ S_n with nontrivial automorphism σ over K = F_q(t). Here Cl(O_L)_ℓ is the ℓ-primary part, and Cl(O_L) ≅ Pic⁰(C_L)(F_q) because C_L has a unique point over ∞.

Throughout this assertion, q odd; ℓ odd prime, ℓ ∤ q A nontrivial finite abelian ℓ-group n odd G_A centre-free, so F_q-points of the Hurwitz scheme are covers defined over F_q (not only Galois-stable geometric classes)

Indeed the constant-field quotient of G_A is cyclic, hence factors through G_A^ab=C₂. The quadratic subfield L is geometric because it ramifies at infinity, so this quotient is trivial. **Lower and upper degree densities.** For a real sequence u : ℕ → ℝ, its upper (lower) odd-degree density is limsup (liminf) of u(n) as n → ∞ through odd n. - `lowerClassGroupDensity`: δ^−(q, A) := lower odd density of n ↦ ν_{q,ℓ,n}(A).


To prove the assertion, Define δ^± via Mathlib Filter.limsup (and its order dual liminf) of u(2m + 1) along m → ∞. For bounded u, δ^− ≤ δ^+, with equality iff u converges along odd n, in which case both equal the limit.

### 5.16 Uniform trace bounds and large-q distributions


<a id="top-cohomology-counts-rational-components"></a>


**Top cohomology counts rational components.** Let X be a smooth separated scheme of finite type and pure dimension n over F_q, and λ a prime not dividing q. Then H^{2n}_c(X_{F̄_q}, Q_λ) ≅ Q_λ(−n)^{π₀(X_{F̄_q})}, the permutation representation on geometric connected components twisted by Q_λ(−n); hence Tr(Frob_q | H^{2n}_c(X_{F̄_q}, Q_λ)) = q^n · #{geometric components fixed by Frobenius}. In particular the trace is q^n exactly when one geometric component is defined over F_q.

Throughout this assertion, X smooth, separated, finite type, pure dimension n over F_q λ ∤ q


To prove the assertion, Decompose X_{F̄_q} into its connected components, which are smooth irreducible of dimension n and permuted by Frobenius. For each geometrically connected smooth component C, Poincaré duality (EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.2) gives H^{2n}_c(C, Q_λ) ≅ H^0(C, Q_λ)^∨(−n) = Q_λ(−n). Frobenius permutes the summands; only fixed components contribute to the trace, each contributing q^n (geometric Frobenius acts on Q_λ(−n) by q^n).

*Needs:* EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.2, SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2.

([[37]](#ref-37), Proof of Theorem 8.8, p.778–779 (Annals 183); [[51]](#ref-51), Proof of Theorem 1.4, p.40 (arXiv v2).)


**Checks.**


- X = A^n: trace q^n.

- X = two conjugate copies of A^n over F_{q²} viewed over F_q (non-split): no fixed component, trace 0.


<a id="uniform-trace-error-estimate"></a>


**Uniform trace error estimate.** Let X be a smooth separated finite-type F_q-scheme of pure dimension n, λ ∤ q a prime, and C ≥ 1 a real number with dim H^i(X_{F̄_q}, Q_λ) ≤ C^{i+1} for all i ≥ 1. If exactly one geometric connected component of X is fixed by Frobenius and √q > C, then |q^{−n}|X(F_q)| − 1| ≤ Σ_{i ≥ 1} C^{i+1} q^{−i/2} = C²/(√q − C). The numerical core: for reals t_j (0 ≤ j < 2n) with |t_j| ≤ q^{j/2} C^{2n−j+1}, |q^{−n} Σ_{j<2n} (−1)^j t_j| ≤ C²/(√q − C).

Throughout this assertion, X is smooth, separated and of finite type over F_q, of pure dimension n. Betti bound dim H^i ≤ C^{i+1} for i ≥ 1 exactly one Frobenius-fixed geometric component √q > C ≥ 1


To prove the assertion, Grothendieck–Lefschetz: |X(F_q)| = Σ_j (−1)^j Tr(Frob | H^j_c(X_{F̄_q}, Q_λ)) (SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2). The j = 2n term is q^n ([top cohomology counts rational components](#top-cohomology-counts-rational-components)). Deligne's weight bound (DeligneWeightsAndPurity:DWP.7): every Frobenius eigenvalue on H^j_c has absolute value ≤ q^{j/2}; with Poincaré duality dim H^j_c = dim H^{2n−j} (EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.2), |Tr(Frob | H^j_c)| ≤ q^{j/2} C^{2n−j+1}. Sum the finite range j < 2n first, then bound by the geometric series Σ_{i≥1} (C/√q)^i · C = C²/(√q − C) (put i = 2n − j).

*Needs:* [top cohomology counts rational components](#top-cohomology-counts-rational-components), SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2, EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.2, DeligneWeightsAndPurity:DWP.7.

### 5.17 Hyperelliptic monodromy


<a id="hyperelliptic-torsion-local-system"></a>


**Hyperelliptic torsion local system.** Let k be a field with 2ℓ invertible (ℓ an odd prime), n = 2g + 1 odd, and over Conf_n ⊗ k (monic squarefree degree-n polynomials f) let C_f be the smooth projective curve birational to y² = f(x), of genus g, with its unique point at ∞. For each m ≥ 1 the ℓ^m-torsion V_m := Jac(C_f)[ℓ^m] forms a locally constant étale sheaf of free Z/ℓ^m-modules of rank 2g on Conf_n ⊗ k, the Tate module T = lim V_m is a lisse Z_ℓ-sheaf of rank 2g, and the Weil pairing (from the canonical principal polarization) is a perfect alternating pairing V_m × V_m → μ_{ℓ^m}. Consequently geometric monodromy lies in Sp(V_m) and, over k = F_q, a Frobenius element acts in GSp_q(V_m) (similitude multiplier q).

Throughout this assertion, ℓ odd prime, 2ℓ invertible on the base n = 2g + 1 ≥ 3 odd; g = (n − 1)/2 k arbitrary (F_q or the function field of Conf_n) Frobenius on torsion points and Tate modules means arithmetic Frobenius, with cyclotomic multiplier q. The trace formula on compactly supported cohomology uses geometric Frobenius; these representations and conventions are not interchanged.


To prove the assertion, The Jacobian of the relative smooth proper curve y² = f(x) over Conf_n ⊗ k (completed at the unique point over ∞) is an abelian scheme of relative dimension g (tauceti JacobianChallenge Layer D: Pic⁰ and the Jacobian). [ℓ^m] is finite étale of degree ℓ^{2mg} when ℓ is invertible, so V_m is a locally constant sheaf, free over Z/ℓ^m of rank 2g (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli:A3). The canonical principal polarization induces the Weil pairing V_m × V_m → μ_{ℓ^m}, perfect and alternating (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli:A3); monodromy preserves it up to the cyclotomic character, which is trivial on the geometric fundamental group and equals q on Frobenius over F_q.

*Needs:* [odd degree quadratic function field family](#odd-degree-quadratic-function-field-family), AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli:A3.

<a id="hyperelliptic-boundary-degeneration"></a>


**Hyperelliptic boundary degeneration.** Let k be algebraically closed with 2ℓ invertible, g ≥ 3. The moduli space H̃_g of labelled hyperelliptic (Z/2-)curves of genus g degenerates to the boundary stratum Δ_{1,1}: there are clutching maps κ_L : H̃_{g−1} × H̃_1 → H̃_g^ct, κ_R : H̃_1 × H̃_{g−1} → H̃_g^ct and κ : H̃_1 × H̃_{g−2} × H̃_1 → H̃_g^ct factoring through both, whose images meet the closure of H̃_g. Here H̃_g^ct is the compact-type locus of the compactification; the clutching images lie on its boundary, in the closure of the smooth locus H̃_g. They do not map into the smooth locus itself.

To prove the assertion, Achter–Pries Lemma 2.5: the class vector of H̃_g splits into γ1 = γ3 = (1,1,1,1) and γ2 of length 2g − 2, giving the Δ_{1,1} degeneration. The dual graph is a tree, so the nodal curve is of compact type and Pic⁰ is an abelian scheme; the displayed product is not a statement about a smooth glued curve. Achter–Pries Lemma 3.1(b): the Galois cover trivialising the product local system has group H1 × H2, so the monodromy of the image of κ is the product.

<a id="overlapping-symplectic-subgroups-generate"></a>


**Overlapping symplectic subgroups generate.** Let F be a finite field of odd characteristic and V = V1 ⊕ V2 ⊕ V3 a nondegenerate symplectic F-space with the V_i pairwise orthogonal and all nonzero. If a subgroup H ≤ Sp(V) contains Sp(V1 ⊕ V2) × Sp(V3) and Sp(V1) × Sp(V2 ⊕ V3), then H = Sp(V).

To prove the assertion, Sp(V) over a field is generated by the symplectic transvections t_{v,a}(x) = x + a⟨x, v⟩v (v ∈ V, a ∈ F): the transvection-generation assertion under the monodromy inputs below. Transvections along vectors of V1 ⊕ V2 or of V2 ⊕ V3 lie in H by hypothesis (they are the transvections of those nondegenerate summands, extended by the identity). For v = v1 + v2 + v3 with v1 + v2 ≠ 0: Sp(V1 ⊕ V2) acts transitively on nonzero vectors of V1 ⊕ V2 and V2 ≠ 0, so some h ∈ Sp(V1 ⊕ V2) ⊂ H sends v1 + v2 into V2; then h(v) ∈ V2 ⊕ V3, t_{h(v),a} ∈ H and t_{v,a} = h^{−1} t_{h(v),a} h ∈ H. If v1 + v2 = 0 then v ∈ V3. Hence H contains all transvections and H = Sp(V). This elementary argument replaces Achter–Pries's appeal to the maximality of Sp(V1 ⊕ V2) × Sp(V3) in Sp(V) (Kleidman–Liebeck), which needs V1 ⊕ V2 and V3 of different dimensions.

**Mod l hyperelliptic monodromy is symplectic.** Let ℓ be an odd prime and k an algebraically closed field in which 2ℓ is invertible. For every g ≥ 1 the mod-ℓ monodromy groups of the labelled hyperelliptic moduli space H̃_g ⊗ k and of the hyperelliptic moduli space H_g ⊗ k (tautological curves, ℓ-torsion of Pic⁰) are both Sp_{2g}(F_ℓ).

In the exceptional base case (g,ℓ)=(1,3), SL₂(F₃) has abelianization C₃ and its nontrivial proper quotients have a C₃ quotient, whereas S₄ has no C₃ quotient; this excludes a common nontrivial quotient as well. ### 5.18 Similitude orbits and rational components


<a id="symplectic-similitude-group"></a>


**Symplectic similitude group.** Let R be a commutative ring and V a free R-module of rank 2g with a perfect alternating pairing ω (in matrix form, V = R^{2g} with ω(x, y) = xᵀJy, J the standard alternating matrix). The similitude group GSp(V) consists of the R-linear automorphisms h with ω(hx, hy) = m(h)·ω(x, y) for a unit m(h) ∈ R^×, the multiplier; m : GSp(V) → R^× is a homomorphism with kernel Sp(V). For a unit m, GSp_m(V) := m^{−1}(m) is a coset of Sp(V). In matrices: h ∈ GSp_m ⇔ h J hᵀ = m J. The multiplier homomorphism and the assertion that its fibres are labelled cosets require g≥1. The displayed matrix subsets and their union remain defined at g=0, when every multiplier gives the same singleton subset.

Throughout this assertion, R commutative (in the application Z_ℓ or Z/ℓ^k, ℓ odd) ω perfect and alternating

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `similitudeCoset`: GSp_m = {h : h J hᵀ = m J} for a unit m.

- `similitudeGroup`: GSp = ⋃_m GSp_m, a submonoid of matrices (a group on units).

- `mem_similitudeCoset_iff`: h ∈ GSp_m ⇔ h J hᵀ = m J.

- `similitudeCoset_one`: GSp_1 is the carrier of Mathlib's symplecticGroup.

- `similitudeCoset_mul_mem`: GSp_m · GSp_{m'} ⊆ GSp_{m m'}.

- `similitudeCoset_map`: A ring homomorphism R → R' maps GSp_m(R) into GSp_{φ(m)}(R').


To prove the assertion, Define the multiplier coset {h : h J hᵀ = m J} and GSp as their union over units m; closure under products and inverses is a computation (multipliers multiply). For g≥1 a standard entry of J is 1, so mJ=m′J implies m=m′; invertibility of an empty matrix alone would not prove uniqueness. The equations hJhᵀ=mJ and hᵀJh=mJ are equivalent because J⁻¹=−J and h is invertible. The multiplier-one subset recovers Mathlib symplecticGroup.

*Needs:* `Matrix.symplecticGroup` (Mathlib), `SymplecticGroup.mem_iff` (Mathlib), `Matrix.J` (Mathlib).

([[37]](#ref-37), Proof of Theorem 8.8, p.779–780 (Annals 183).)

- −1 lies in GSp_1 = Sp.

- Over Z_ℓ with g = 1, diag(1, ℓ) satisfies h J hᵀ = ℓ J but is not in similitudeGroup, since ℓ is not a unit.

- diag(I_g, q I_g) ∈ GSp_q.

- −I ∈ Sp.

- A matrix with multiplier ℓ over Z_ℓ is not a similitude: the multiplier must be a unit.


<a id="monodromy-orbits-and-rational-components"></a>


**Monodromy orbits and rational components.** In the range of [monodromy of the odd degree polynomial family](#monodromy-of-the-odd-degree-polynomial-family) (A a nontrivial finite abelian ℓ-group, ℓ odd, q odd with ℓ ∤ q, ℓ^m A = 0): the geometric connected components of X_n ⊗ F̄_q correspond bijectively to Sp(V_m)-orbits on Sur(V_m, A), and an orbit O gives a component defined over F_q iff the stabilizer in GSp(V_m) of some (equivalently every) x ∈ O meets GSp_q(V_m). Via T → V_m these are the Sp(T)-orbits on Sur(T, A) whose stabilizer meets GSp_q(T).

Throughout this assertion, as in [monodromy of the odd degree polynomial family](#monodromy-of-the-odd-degree-polynomial-family) and [geometric generic fibre of the unmarked hurwitz cover](#geometric-generic-fibre-of-the-unmarked-hurwitz-cover) Frobenius on torsion points and Tate modules means arithmetic Frobenius, with cyclotomic multiplier q. The trace formula on compactly supported cohomology uses geometric Frobenius; these representations and conventions are not interchanged.


To prove the assertion, Connected components of a finite étale cover of a geometrically connected base are orbits of the geometric fundamental group on the geometric generic fibre; a component is defined over F_q iff Frobenius preserves the orbit (InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.0, IG.1). The fibre is Sur(V_m, A)/{±1} ([geometric generic fibre of the unmarked hurwitz cover](#geometric-generic-fibre-of-the-unmarked-hurwitz-cover)); since −I ∈ Sp, the orbit sets agree with those on Sur(V_m, A). The geometric image is Sp(V_m) ([finite level monodromy of the polynomial family](#finite-level-monodromy-of-the-polynomial-family)) and a Frobenius element lies in GSp_q(V_m); Frobenius fixes the orbit of x iff some element of Sp·F = GSp_q ∩ (image) fixes x, i.e. the stabilizer of x meets GSp_q. Lift to T using surjectivity GSp_q(T) → GSp_q(V_m) and Sur(V_m, A) = Sur(T, A).

*Needs:* [geometric generic fibre of the unmarked hurwitz cover](#geometric-generic-fibre-of-the-unmarked-hurwitz-cover), [finite level monodromy of the polynomial family](#finite-level-monodromy-of-the-polynomial-family), [symplectic similitude group](#symplectic-similitude-group), InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.0, InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.1.

<a id="primary-decomposition-for-a-multiplier-q-similitude"></a>


**Primary decomposition for a multiplier q similitude.** Let ℓ be odd, V free of rank 2g over Z_ℓ with a perfect alternating pairing, q ∈ Z_ℓ^× with q − 1 ∈ Z_ℓ^×, and h ∈ GSp_q(V). Let V_1 (resp. V_q) be the set of v ∈ V with (h − 1)^N v → 0 (resp. (h − q)^N v → 0) ℓ-adically, and W := ⋂_N (h − 1)^N (h − q)^N V. Then V = V_1 ⊕ V_q ⊕ W as Z_ℓ-modules, each summand is h-stable, h − 1 is invertible on V_q ⊕ W and h − q is invertible on V_1 ⊕ W.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ odd prime q and q − 1 units of Z_ℓ h ∈ GSp_q(V)


To prove the assertion, Factor the characteristic polynomial of h mod ℓ into its (x − 1)-primary part, (x − q)-primary part and a coprime remainder (1 ≠ q in F_ℓ); lift the coprime factorisation by Hensel's lemma to Z_ℓ[x]. The corresponding idempotents in Z_ℓ[h] give an h-stable decomposition V = V_1 ⊕ V_q ⊕ W with the stated invertibility (a polynomial coprime mod ℓ to the char. poly. of h on a summand acts invertibly on it). Identify the idempotent summands with the limit descriptions (EVW's definitions): on V_1, h − 1 is topologically nilpotent; on the complement it is invertible.

*Needs:* [symplectic similitude group](#symplectic-similitude-group), `PadicInt` (Mathlib), `Module.End.maxGenEigenspace` (Mathlib).

<a id="symplectic-normal-forms-over-z-l"></a>


**Symplectic normal forms over z l.** Let M be a finite free Z_ℓ-module with a perfect alternating pairing. (i) M has a symplectic basis; any basis x_1, …, x_g of a Lagrangian direct summand extends to one; hence Sp(M) acts transitively on Lagrangian direct summands. (ii) Each factor in an orthogonal direct-sum decomposition of M inherits a perfect pairing. (iii) M = M_+ ⊕ M_− with M_± Lagrangian. (iv) If M = P ⊕ Q with P, Q isotropic, both are Lagrangian (of rank half of M). (v) Every automorphism of a Lagrangian M_+ extends, by inverse transpose on a complementary Lagrangian M_−, to an element of Sp(M).

Throughout this assertion, ℓ prime (odd in the application) M finite free over Z_ℓ, pairing perfect and alternating


To prove the assertion, (i) Given a basis x_i of a Lagrangian summand, choose y_j with ω(x_i, y_j) = δ_ij by perfectness, then correct y_j by combinations of the x_i to make ⟨y_i, y_j⟩ = 0 (EVW's argument); transitivity follows by mapping one symplectic basis to another. (ii) Choose bases of the two orthogonal direct summands. The Gram matrix is block diagonal, and its determinant is a unit by perfectness. Each block determinant is therefore a unit in Z_ℓ, proving perfectness of both restricted pairings; absence of a radical alone would not suffice over Z_ℓ. (iii) Take the spans of the two halves of a symplectic basis. (iv) Reduce mod ℓ and use the field statement (isotropic subspaces have dimension at most half). (v) With respect to a symplectic basis adapted to M_+ ⊕ M_−, the block matrix diag(a, (aᵀ)^{−1}) is symplectic.

*Needs:* [symplectic similitude group](#symplectic-similitude-group), `PadicInt` (Mathlib), `Matrix.symplecticGroup` (Mathlib).

<a id="orthogonality-and-a-killed-lagrangian"></a>


**Orthogonality and a killed lagrangian.** In [primary decomposition for a multiplier q similitude](#primary-decomposition-for-a-multiplier-q-similitude): V_1 and V_q are isotropic, V_1 ⊕ V_q is orthogonal to W, and W is nondegenerate; W = W_+ ⊕ W_− with W_± isotropic, and then W_+ ⊕ V_1 and W_− ⊕ V_q are complementary maximal isotropic (Lagrangian) direct summands of V. If f : V → A satisfies f ∘ h = f, then the Lagrangian W_− ⊕ V_q lies in the image of h − 1, hence in ker f.

Throughout this assertion, as in [primary decomposition for a multiplier q similitude](#primary-decomposition-for-a-multiplier-q-similitude) f : V → A a homomorphism with f ∘ h = f


To prove the assertion, For x ∈ V_1 and y ∈ V_1 ⊕ W write y = (h − q)^N z_N; using ω(hx, hy) = q ω(x, y), ω(x, y) ∈ ω((h − 1)^N x, V) for all N, hence 0 (EVW's iteration). Symmetrically for V_q. More explicitly the adjoint of h−q is −q h⁻¹(h−1). Its N-th power puts the pairing in the ideal generated by the coordinates of (h−1)^N x; the integral factors q^N h⁻N preserve divisibility. Those coordinates tend to zero ℓ-adically, forcing the pairing to vanish. W is nondegenerate as an orthogonal summand of a perfect pairing (EVW fact (ii)); decompose W into two isotropic summands (EVW fact (iii), a symplectic basis: [symplectic normal forms over z l](#symplectic-normal-forms-over-z-l)). (V_1 ⊕ W_+) ⊕ (V_q ⊕ W_−) = V with both summands isotropic, so both are maximal isotropic (fact (iv)). h − 1 is invertible on V_q ⊕ W, so V_q ⊕ W_− ⊆ im(h − 1); f ∘ (h − 1) = 0 gives V_q ⊕ W_− ⊆ ker f.

*Needs:* [primary decomposition for a multiplier q similitude](#primary-decomposition-for-a-multiplier-q-similitude), [symplectic normal forms over z l](#symplectic-normal-forms-over-z-l).

### 5.19 Uniform trace bounds and large-q distributions


<a id="uniform-function-field-surjection-moment-estimate"></a>


**Uniform function field surjection moment estimate.** Let ℓ be an odd prime and A a finite abelian ℓ-group. There is a constant B(A) such that for every odd prime power q with ℓ ∤ q(q − 1) and √q > B(A), and every odd n > B(A), | (Σ_{L ∈ S_n} m_A(L))/|S_n| − 1 | ≤ B(A)/√q, where m_A(L) = |Sur(Cl(O_L), A)|. <a id="large-q-cohen-lenstra-theorem"></a>


**Large q cohen lenstra theorem.** Let ℓ be an odd prime and A a finite abelian ℓ-group. As q → ∞ through odd prime powers with ℓ ∤ q(q − 1), both the upper density δ^+(q, A) and the lower density δ^−(q, A) — taken over odd n → ∞ of the proportion of L ∈ S_n (imaginary quadratic extensions of F_q(t), ramified at ∞) with Cl(O_L)_ℓ ≅ A — converge to the Cohen–Lenstra mass μ(A) = ∏_{i≥1}(1 − ℓ^{−i})/|Aut A|. Precisely: for every ε > 0 there is Q such that |δ^±(q, A) − μ(A)| ≤ ε for all such q > Q.

Throughout this assertion, ℓ odd prime A finite abelian ℓ-group q odd, ℓ ∤ q, ℓ ∤ q − 1


To prove the assertion, Fix A₀ and ε > 0. Apply finite moment control ([finite moment control of masses](#finite-moment-control-of-masses), EVW Proposition 8.3) with the finite set {A₀}: it yields δ > 0 and a finite set L' of finite abelian ℓ-groups such that any probability measure ν with |⟨Sur(−, A)⟩_ν − 1| ≤ δ for all A ∈ L' satisfies |ν(A₀) − μ(A₀)| ≤ ε. The measures ν_n ([empirical l primary class group law](#empirical-l-primary-class-group-law)) are probability measures whose A-moments are the averages of m_A over S_n. By [uniform function field surjection moment estimate](#uniform-function-field-surjection-moment-estimate), choose Q > max_{A ∈ L'} max(1, B(A), B(A)²) with B(A)/√Q < δ for all A ∈ L'; then for q > Q allowed and odd n > Q, |ν_n(A₀) − μ(A₀)| ≤ ε. Hence every limit point of ν_n(A₀) along odd n lies in [μ(A₀) − ε, μ(A₀) + ε], i.e. δ^±(q, A₀) are within ε of μ(A₀) ([lower and upper degree densities](#lower-and-upper-degree-densities)). The quantifiers are in this order: finitely many moments first, then uniform thresholds in q and n.

*Needs:* [uniform function field surjection moment estimate](#uniform-function-field-surjection-moment-estimate), [empirical l primary class group law](#empirical-l-primary-class-group-law), [lower and upper degree densities](#lower-and-upper-degree-densities), [finite moment control of masses](#finite-moment-control-of-masses), [cohen lenstra measure](#cohen-lenstra-measure).

### 5.20 Good nonabelian function-field moments


<a id="eventual-degree-large-q-limit"></a>


**Eventual degree large q limit.** For m ≥ 1 let A_m be the filter on N of prime powers q coprime to m, tending to infinity. For a function E(q, n) of a prime power q and a degree n, and a target c(n), say E has eventual-degree large-q limit c if there is n₀ such that for every fixed n ≥ n₀, E(q, n) → c(n) as q → ∞ along A_m. Wood (2019) uses this mode. EVW’s final distribution theorem instead takes upper/lower degree densities first and then q→∞; these are distinct convergence modes; it is not the fixed-q, large-degree limit of the direct function-field analogue of the number-field conjectures, and the two limits may not be interchanged without a new uniform estimate.

Throughout this assertion, m ≥ 1 (the moduli excluded from q) E : prime powers × N → R, c : N → R

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `allowedPrimePowers`: The filter A_m of prime powers coprime to m tending to infinity.

- `allowedPrimePowers_neBot`: A_m is a proper filter when m≠0; its Lean instance requires [NeZero m]. At m=0 it is bottom.

- `EventualDegreeLargeQLimit`: The predicate ∃ n₀, ∀ n ≥ n₀, E(·, n) → c(n) along A_m.

- `EventualDegreeLargeQLimit.unique`: For m≠0, two targets of the same E agree for all sufficiently large n.

- `EventualDegreeLargeQLimit.mono`: If m divides m′, the allowed filter for m′ refines that for m, preserving the limit. Numerical m≤m′ alone is insufficient.


To prove the assertion, Define A_m := atTop ⊓ principal{q : q a prime power, gcd(q, m) = 1}; it is a proper filter (infinitely many primes are coprime to m). Define the predicate ∃ n₀, ∀ n ≥ n₀, Tendsto (q ↦ E(q, n)) A_m (nhds c(n)). Limits are unique along the proper filter A_m, so c(n) is determined for n ≥ n₀.

*Needs:* `Filter.Tendsto` (Mathlib), `Filter.atTop` (Mathlib), `tendsto_nhds_unique` (Mathlib).

([[50]](#ref-50), §1 after Theorem 1.2, p.3 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.380).)

- A_0=⊥ because no prime power is coprime to zero. Consequently every function converges to every target along A_0; uniqueness and liminf consequences must require m≠0.

- For E(q, n) = n^{N−1} and M ≡ 1, PBL holds with w = 1.

- For E ≡ 0 and N = 1, PBL fails (w > 0).

- For E(q, n) = n^{N−1}·c(q) with c(q) = 3 if q ≡ 1 (mod 4) and c(q) = 1 otherwise, and M ≡ 1, the liminf bound holds with w = 1 but PBL fails (both residues occur for infinitely many allowed prime powers, so there is no limit in q).

- The liminf lower bound does not entail existence of an ordinary limit.

- A stable-range component formula alone does not control the complete profile: include all boundary components in the eventual-constancy test.


<a id="whole-fixed-degree-component-profile"></a>


**Whole fixed degree component profile.** Fix a centre-free admissible F = G′ with outside involution classes c_1, …, c_N, a sign ± and n ≥ 2; put d = 2n − 1 and g = (1, 1, σ) in the imaginary case, d = 2n and g = 1 in the real case. For q coprime to |F| let C_n^±(q) be the total number of Frobenius-fixed geometric components of ⊔_m CHur^{c,g}_{F,m} over all multidegrees m ∈ Z_{≥0}^N with Σ m_i = d, and M(q) := |H₂(F, c)[q − 1]| ≥ 1. The profile is P_n^±(q) := C_n^±(q)/M(q) ∈ Q_{≥0}. It includes every multidegree, not only the stable range m_i ≥ N₀. In the component-count interface the geometric counts are carried as data: a function m ↦ C_m(q) and the normaliser M.

Throughout this assertion, F centre-free admissible; q coprime to |F| n ≥ 2 all multidegrees of total degree d are included

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `FixedDegreeComponentData`: Data (N, d, counts C_m(q) for m of total degree d, normaliser M(q) ≥ 1) abstracting the Hurwitz component counts.

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile`: P(q) := (Σ_{Σ m_i = d} C_m(q))/M(q) ∈ Q.

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile_nonneg`: P(q) ≥ 0.

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile_mem_finite`: If Σ_m C_m(q) ≤ B and M(q) ≤ K for all q, then P takes values in the finite set {a/b : 0 ≤ a ≤ B, 1 ≤ b ≤ K}.


To prove the assertion, The set of multidegrees of total degree d is finite (the antidiagonal tuples). Geometric components are open and closed (the schemes are smooth, finite étale over Conf_d: IG.5), and Frobenius permutes them; C_m(q) counts the fixed ones. P_n^±(q) := (Σ_m C_m(q))/M(q).

*Needs:* InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5, `Nat.choose` (Mathlib).

([[50]](#ref-50), Theorem 4.5(3), p.21 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.404).)


**Checks.**


- If every count C_m(q) is 0 then the profile is 0.

- For N = 1, d = 3, C_{(3)}(q) = 2 and M(q) = 1, the profile is 2.

- For N = 2, d = 2, N₀ = 1 and counts C_{(2,0)} = 1, C_{(1,1)} = 0, C_{(0,2)} = 0, M = 1, the profile is 1 although the stable-range sum (all m_i ≥ 1) is 0.

- If every C_m(q) = 0 the profile is 0.

- N = 1: a single multidegree (d).


<a id="boundary-component-remainder"></a>


**Boundary component remainder.** In [whole fixed degree component profile](#whole-fixed-degree-component-profile) fix the stable threshold N₀ of Wood Theorem 4.5(3). Split the multidegrees of total degree d into the stable ones (every m_i ≥ N₀) and the boundary ones (some m_i < N₀), and C_n(q) = C_{stable,n}(q) + C_{boundary,n}(q) accordingly. The boundary remainder is R_{boundary,n}(q) := C_{boundary,n}(q)/M(q) ≥ 0. No formula for it is assumed: the stable lifting-invariant classification does not describe braid components in the boundary.

Throughout this assertion, as in [whole fixed degree component profile](#whole-fixed-degree-component-profile) N₀ a stable threshold for F

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `stableMultidegrees`: The multidegrees m with Σ m_i = d and every m_i ≥ N₀.

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.stableCount`: C_stable(q) = Σ over stable multidegrees.

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.boundaryRemainder`: R_boundary(q) = (Σ over non-stable multidegrees)/M(q).

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.profile_eq_stable_add_boundary`: P(q) = C_stable(q)/M(q) + R_boundary(q).

- `FixedDegreeComponentData.boundaryRemainder_nonneg`: R_boundary(q) ≥ 0.


To prove the assertion, The stable and boundary sets partition the finite set of multidegrees of total degree d. Sum the counts over each part; divide by M(q).

*Needs:* [whole fixed degree component profile](#whole-fixed-degree-component-profile).

([[50]](#ref-50), Proof of Theorem 4.8, bad case, p.24 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.409).)


**Checks.**


- With N₀ = 0 the boundary remainder is 0 for every q.

- For N = 2, d = 4, N₀ = 1 the stable multidegrees are (1,3), (2,2), (3,1): three of them.

- (0, 4) is a multidegree of total degree 4 but not a stable one for N₀ = 1.

- N₀ = 0: every multidegree is stable and the remainder is 0.

- The remainder is nonnegative, which is all the bad-type argument uses.


<a id="complete-stable-range-component-sum"></a>


**Complete stable range component sum.** Let F = G′, c = ⊔_{i ≤ N} c_i its outside involution classes, A = H₂(F, c), g ∈ c ∪ {1}, q odd coprime to |F| and N₀ a stable threshold. For a set S ⊆ {0,1}^N of surviving parity vectors (those compatible with [g] in F^ab and with v₂(q − 1) ≥ t_A(b(g, ε)) + 1, Wood Proposition 4.1/Remark 4.2 as refined in the marked-cover comparison), define Σ_stable(d) := Σ_{ε ∈ S} #{m : m_i ≥ N₀, m_i ≡ ε_i (mod 2), Σ m_i = d}. Then C_{stable,d}^g(q)/|A[q − 1]| = Σ_stable(d): each surviving parity class of stable multidegrees contributes exactly |A[q − 1]| Frobenius-fixed components per multidegree, the others none. The boundary remainder is not included.

Throughout this assertion, F centre-free admissible, q odd coprime to |F| N₀ a stable threshold S the surviving parity vectors determined by the reduced-Schur-multiplier criterion

The interface exposes the following operations and identities:


- `parityMultidegreeCount`: #{m ∈ N^N : m_i ≥ N₀, m_i ≡ ε_i mod 2, Σ m_i = d}.

- `stableRangeComponentSum`: Σ_stable(d) = Σ_{ε ∈ S} parityMultidegreeCount N N₀ d ε.

- `stableRangeComponentSum_empty`: Σ_stable = 0 for S = ∅.

- `stableRangeComponentSum_union`: Additivity over disjoint unions of parity sets.

- `parityMultidegreeCount_eq`: The stars-and-bars formula of [stable parity multidegree count](#stable-parity-multidegree-count).


To prove the assertion, Define the parity-class count ([stable parity multidegree count](#stable-parity-multidegree-count)) and sum it over S. For each stable m, the Frobenius-fixed components are the q^{−1}-fixed lifting invariants over (g, m) (Theorem 4.5(3), IG.5); their number is |A[q − 1]| if the parity vector of m survives and 0 otherwise (the marked-cover comparisonuse the reduced-cover and marked-lifting contracts of IG.3–IG.5). The survival criterion depends only on m mod 2, so the stable count is |A[q − 1]| times Σ_stable(d).

*Needs:* [stable parity multidegree count](#stable-parity-multidegree-count), [boundary component remainder](#boundary-component-remainder), InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups:IG.5, [embedded types and signature representations](#support-embedded-types).

([[50]](#ref-50), Remark 4.2, p.19 (arXiv v2; Duke 168, p.401).)


**Checks.**
